en: The Exposition of Technical Terms from the Śārṅgadharasaṃhitā;
the First Chapter in the First Section.
May that Enemy of Tripura grant you prosperity—
he, upon whose outpouring of bodily splendor Bhavānī shines resplendent, like a great medicinal herb blazing on the Himalayas amidst the stainless moonlight.

For the sake of pleasing virtuous people, Śārṅgadharasūri has compiled here a well-arranged collection of those medicinal formulations which, along with their root sources and purposes, are renowned for their efficacy, have been employed by sages, and have been repeatedly experienced by physicians.
Having first determined the disease, the physician— well-versed in application— should examine all the ailments of the patient according to their causes, forms, constitutions, suitability, and types,
and then perform the treatment known as depletion and nourishment in accordance with the prescribed rules.

Knowing that the powers of medicinal herbs— the many diverse manifestations of divine plants— shine forth like those of the gods, the wise should cast aside doubt and recognize these various potencies as worthy of reliance. 4.
The purpose of this treatise is as follows:

it is said that natural and adventitious physical ailments may arise from the defects of past karma; therefore, for the sake of severing those [defects], one should apply oneself to the excellent yogas consisting of supreme bliss, which remove all misfortune. 5.

I shall describe, for the benefit of all the world, the greatness of this treatise— established through practice, scripture, direct perception, and inference— in a manner that is not overly prolix. 6.
The sequence of chapters for the first section (Pūrvakhaṇḍa) is as follows:

first comes the Paribhāṣā (General Explanations), then the Bhaiṣajyākhyānaka (Description of Medicines), followed by Nāḍīparīkṣā (Examination of the Pulse), Ādividhi (Initial Procedures), and then Dīpanapācana (Digestive and Carminative Treatments). 7.
Then follows the description of the Kalās and so forth, as well as the movement of food and other matters, and the enumeration of diseases; this is declared to be the first section (pūrvakhaṇḍa).
Now, the sequence of chapters for the middle section (madhyamakhaṇḍa): [8]

Fresh juice, decoction, phāṇṭa, hima, paste, powder, as well as pills, electuaries, medicated fats, fermented preparations, purification of the metals, and mercury— these are known as the middle [category]. 9.
The sequence of chapters for the Uttarakhanda:

the drinking of medicated fats (sneha-pāna), the procedure for sudation (sveda-vidhi), emesis (vamana), purgation (virecana), followed by oil enema (sneha-basti), and then the non-unctuous enema (nirūhaṇa). 10
Following that, the urethral enema (uttara-basti) is prescribed, then the procedure for nasal medication (nasya),
the procedure for smoking (dhūmapāna), as well as the procedure for gargling (gaṇḍūṣa) and so forth;
the procedure for external applications (lepa) and the like is well-known, as is the method for bloodletting (śoṇitavisruti).
And this subsequent section shall consist of the types of ophthalmic procedures;
this compendium is recorded as containing thirty-two chapters and a total of twelve thousand verses.
One hundred and twenty-six verses have been counted here. (13) There is a necessity for measurement; without measurement, the determination of substances is never possible.

Therefore, for the purpose of practical application, I shall here state the measurement; first, the definition of the Māgadha measure: a *trasareṇu* is said by the wise to consist of thirty atoms (*paramāṇu*).
A *trasareṇu* is called by the synonymous name *vaṃśī*. As for the definition of the atom (*paramāṇu*) and the *vaṃśī*:
The thirtieth part of that is called an atom (paramāṇu). When the sunbeams pass through a lattice, a tiny mote is perceived;
these are designated as "marīci" and so forth.
Six *vaṃśīs* make one *marīci*; six of those make one *rājikā*, and three *rājikās* are said by the wise to be one *sarṣapa*.
Eight *sarṣapas* are called a *yava*, and four of those make a *guñjā*.
Six *raktikās* shall constitute a *māṣaka*, which is known as both gold and grain;
four *māṣakas* are called a *śāṇa* or a *kola*, and that is declared to be a *dharaṇa*.
That very [unit] is called a *ṭaṅka*; two of those are said to be a *kola*, as well as a *kṣudrako* and a *vaṭaka*; that is declared to be a *draṅkṣaṇa*.
A *karṣa* is the synonym for that.
Two *kola*s shall be one *karṣa*, which is declared to be a *pāṇimānikā*.
An *akṣa*, a *picu*, a *pāṇitala*, a *kiñcitpāṇi*, a *tinduka*, a *viḍālapadaka*, and likewise a *ṣoḍaśikā* are considered to be [synonyms for] that same measure. 21–22.
*Karamadhya*, *haṃsapada*, *suvarṇa*, *kavalagraha*, and *udumbara* are synonyms for a *karṣa*; it is also designated as half a *pala* and a *pala*. (23)
Two *karṣas* shall be half a *pala*, as shall a *śukti* and an *aṣṭamikā*;
two *śuktis* are to be known as one *pala*, as are a *muṣṭi*, an *āmra*, and a *caturthikā*.
A *prakuñca*, a *ṣoḍaśī*, and a *bilva* are likewise declared here to be equal to one *pala*. (24)
The designations *prasṛti*, *kuḍava*, and so forth, as well as *śarāva*, are known [as follows]:
two *pala*s are to be understood as one *prasṛti*, and it is also called a *prasṛta*.
Two *prasṛti*s constitute an *añjali*; a *kuḍava* is half a *śarāva*. (25)
That should be known as eight mānas; two kuḍavas make a mānikā, and likewise a śarāva is to be known by the wise here as eight palas.
[The measures] named prastha and āḍhaka are as follows: 26.
Two śarāvas make one prastha; likewise, four prasthas make one āḍhaka.
That vessel known as a kaṃsapātra consists of sixty-four palas. A droṇa and a droṇī are designated by these same measures.
Four *āḍhakas* make one *droṇa*. *Kalaśa*, *nalvaṇa*, *armaṇa*, *unmāna*, *ghaṭa*, *rāśi*, and *droṇa* are synonyms.
Two *droṇas* make a *śūrpa* and a *kumbha*, as well as sixty-four *śarāvakas*.
Two *śūrpa*s make a *droṇa*, which is also known as a *vāhī* or a *goṇī*.
Four *droṇas* are said by those of subtle intellect to be the measure called a *khārī*.
That [weight] consisting of four thousand and ninety-six palas is designated as a *bhāra-tulā*;
and two thousand palas are proclaimed to be one *bhāra*.
A *tulā* should be known as one hundred *palas*; this is the certain rule everywhere.
As for the subsequent units, each is four times the preceding: *māṣa*, *ṭaṅka*, *akṣa*, *bilva*, *kuḍava*, *prastha*, and *āḍhaka*.

A *rāśi*, a *goṇī*, and a *khārī* are each four times the size of the preceding one (32). This is the conventional rule for the measurement of liquid, fresh, and dry substances where no specific measure has been stated, beginning from the *guñjā* up to the point of the *kuḍava*.
For liquid, moist, and dry substances, an equal measure is considered appropriate (33).
This is a technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) for the purpose of taking double the quantity of liquids and moist substances;
starting from measures such as a *prastha*, that [measure] is doubled for liquids and moist things.
Likewise, a double measure for a balance (tulā) is nowhere prescribed in the traditional texts.
[34] Regarding the method of constructing vessels for measuring liquids, dry goods, and *kuḍava* measures:
a vessel made of clay, wood, bamboo, iron, or other materials should be four finger-breadths [in height].
That measure which is both broad and likewise high, one should call it a *kuḍava*.
Regarding the technical terminology of formulations (*yoga-paribhāṣā*), when a medicinal substance is mentioned first in a particular formulation, [it serves as the standard].

Indeed, that yoga is called by that very name here in this definitive treatise (viniścaya). There is no fixed rule regarding the measure (mātrā); one must consider the time, the digestive fire, age, and strength.

Having observed the constitution, the [nature of the] doshas, and the location, one should determine the dosage. 37. The reasons for determining the Kalinga measure are that in the Kali age, men have weak digestion, short stature, and diminished strength.
Therefore, the measure appropriate for that [weight] is declared by the wise and approved by the learned as being one *mātrā*.
A *yava* is said by the wise to be the measure of twelve white mustard seeds (*gaurasarṣapa*). 38–39.
Two *yava*s make one *guñjā*; three *guñjā*s are called a *valla*.
A *māṣa* may consist of eight or sometimes seven *guñjā*s. Four *māṣakas* make a *śāṇa*, which is also known as a *niṣka* or a *ṭaṅka*.
Six *māṣakas* make one *gadyāṇa*, and ten *māṣakas* constitute a *karṣa*.
A *pala* is said by the wise to consist of four *karṣas* and to be measured at ten *śāṇas*.
Four *palas* make a *kuḍava*; the *prastha* and subsequent measures are considered to follow the same progression as before.
There are two kinds of measurement:
Kāliṅga and Māgadha; these two types of measurement are declared.
Those who know measurement understand that the Māgadha measurement is superior to the Kāliṅga. 43

Regarding the definitions of medicinal substances, there is an investigation here into what is appropriate and inappropriate for them: indeed, in all therapeutic procedures, only fresh substances should be employed, with the exception of *viḍaṅga*, *kṛṣṇā* (long pepper), jaggery, grains, clarified butter, and honey. 44
O Sadāprarudrārṇya! The substances are twofold: guḍūcī, kuṭaja, vāsā, kūṣmāṇḍa, śatāvarī, aśvagandhā, sahacarī, śatapuṣpā, and prasāriṇī. 45.
One should always employ fresh substances; one should never cause double [the amount] to be used.
Freshness is the primary quality of a substance;
whatever substance is new and dry should be employed in all rituals.
One should apply double the amount of *ārdra-raṃ*; this is the rule for all cases.

(47) When no specific state is mentioned, the rule of general convention applies; when no time is mentioned, it shall be at dawn; when no part of the body is mentioned, it refers to the matted locks (*jaṭā*).
If no specific portion is mentioned, it shall be equal; if no vessel is mentioned, it shall be made of clay;

if no liquid is mentioned, water is to be taken; and if no oil is mentioned, that produced from sesame seeds is to be used. (48) Furthermore, this is the rule for the quantity of substances when they are repeated.

Whichever single medicinal substance is mentioned again in a particular formulation, that substance is declared by the seers of reality to be double the measure of the others. (49) This is the rule for substances such as red and white sandalwood.

Powders, unctuous substances, fermented liquors, and electuaries are generally combined with *candana*; likewise, red sandalwood (*raktacandana*) is mostly employed for decoctions and external applications. (50) Well-known medicinal substances lose their potency through the lapse of time.
After one year, that medicinal form becomes devoid of its potency;
likewise, a powder loses its strength after two months. Pills and electuaries attain a state of diminished efficacy after one year.

Ghee, oil, and the like become inferior after four months; likewise, medicinal herbs undergo light digestion and lose their potency after a year. However, aged *āsava* liquors, metallic preparations, and juices remain endowed with their full qualities.
An investigation into substances appropriate or inappropriate for a disease:

A wise person should discard any substance that is unsuitable for a disease even if it is mentioned in the group [of drugs], and should employ any substance that is suitable even if it is not mentioned therein. (54)
In substances, there is a difference in qualities according to the difference in location:
the Vindhya mountains and others are considered fiery (āgneya), while the snowy mountain (Himalaya) is considered lunar (saumya);
therefore, by these reasons, their medicinal herbs are of corresponding natures.

They also grow in other forests and groves; one should collect them with a joyful mind and in a state of purity on an auspicious morning. 55–56. Regarding the method of collecting substances: one should gather them with a well-disposed mind and being pure, early in the morning on a favorable day. 56.
Facing the sun, observing silence, and having bowed to Śiva in his heart,
he should take common ground and substances situated to the north;
there should be a rejection of substances produced from despicable places.

Herbs grown on anthills, in desolate places, marshy lands, cremation grounds, or saline soil, as well as those pervaded by insects, fire, or frost, do not grant success in one's undertakings. Regarding the selection of substances according to the specific task at hand, there are particular seasonal requirements.
In autumn, one should collect potent medicinal herbs for the purpose of all [therapeutic] actions;
and at the end of spring, one should gather them for the purpose of purgation and emesis.
Regarding the collection of substances whose specific parts have not been mentioned, the consideration of the [appropriate] part is as follows: 59.
The wise should take the bark from those roots whose matted fibers are excessively thick;

a person of intelligence should also take all the fine rootlets. The bark of the *nyagrodha* and other such trees should be taken, while the heartwood (*sāra*) is obtained from the *bījaka* and similar species.
One should procure the leaves of *tālīśa* and others, the fruit from *triphalā* and others,
the flowers of *dhātakī* and others, and the latex of *snuhī* and others.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Exposition of Technical Terms," in the first section of the *Śrī Śārṅgadharasaṃhitā*.
The Story of Medicine;
now the second chapter:
A general exposition on the appropriate time for consuming medicinal drugs.
A wise person should generally take medicine at dawn, especially decoctions; the specific distinctions regarding this are now shown.
[This concludes] the instruction on the five-fold timing for the administration of medicinal substances.
The time for the administration of medicine to human beings should be known as fivefold:
when the sun has slightly risen, at the time of the midday meal,
at the evening meal, frequently during the day, and likewise at night.
Among these, the first period is generally for when there is an excess of pitta and kapha; one should administer medicine for the purpose of purgation, emesis, or scraping at dawn.
Thus, this should be the first time for men to take medicine;
the second time is when the downward wind (apāna) is disordered, in which case it is recommended to take medicine at the beginning of a meal.

In cases of lack of appetite, one should provide delicious food mixed with various appetizing dishes. When the Samāna Vāyu is deranged and the digestive fire is weak, a skilled physician should administer medicine that kindles the fire in the midst of the meal.
In cases of vitiation of the Vyāna wind, one should administer medicine at the end of a meal;
in cases of hiccups, convulsions, and tremors, it should be taken both before and after eating. Thus, the second occasion for the administration of medicine has been described.
The third period:
when the *udāna* wind is provoked and causes hoarseness of voice and other ailments,
the medicine should be administered between mouthfuls of food during the evening meal.

When the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is severely impaired, medicine is generally administered by the wise at the end of the evening meal; this is the third time (*kāla*). The fourth time is as follows: [10]
And in cases of thirst, vomiting, hiccups, dyspnea, and poisoning, one should administer medicine along with food; this is the fourth time. The fifth time [is as follows].
In disorders above the clavicle, as well as in cases requiring emaciation or nourishment, a digestive or pacifying medicine should be administered at night when no food is taken;
this is declared to be the fifth period for the administration of medicinal therapy. 12.

In a substance, there are five states: taste and the rest; in a substance, these five states—taste, quality (guṇa), potency (vīrya), post-digestive transformation (vipāka), and power (śakti)—are proclaimed in sequence according to their respective relationships. 13.
Among those, the tastes— sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent— are known as these six tastes (rasa), which reside in various substances. 14

The production of the sweet and other tastes arises from earth, water, earth, fire, water, fire, space, and air; the origin of the tastes occurs in sequence through these pairs of elements: air-fire, earth-air, and so forth. 15.
Heaviness, oiliness, sharpness, dryness, and lightness are generally recorded as the qualities of earth, water, fire, air, and ether, respectively. 16.
Other accumulations of qualities are included within these very qualities; virility, heat, and likewise coldness generally reside in substances.
All that is seen in the three worlds belongs to Agni and Soma; whatever other heroic deeds there may be, they shall all be contained within this very ripening. 18.
Vipākaḥ.

The post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*) of a substance is of three kinds, consisting of sweet, sour, and pungent. A sweet taste generally transforms into sweet, while a sour taste transforms into sour. (19) The post-digestive transformation of astringent, pungent, and bitter tastes is generally pungent.
From the sweet [taste] phlegm (śleṣman) is produced; from the sour [taste] bile (pitta) is produced;
from the pungent [taste] wind (vāyu) is produced—these are the actions according to their post-digestive transformation (vipāka). This is their specific potency (prabhāva).

As for specific potency (*prabhāva*), it is as follows: although the *dhātrī* fruit is similar to the *lakuca* in its taste and other qualities, it effects the destruction of the three humors (*doṣatraya*).
In some cases, however, a substance performs an action through its specific potency alone.
Just as the root of *sahadevī*, when bound upon the head, destroys fever; so too,
the influence of taste, potency, and the rest is distinct in each case— whether it be the taste, the quality, the potency, the post-digestive effect, or even the specific power.
Those who remain dependent on material substances perform their respective actions (karma).

Indeed, it is through the differentiation of the seasons that the accumulation, provocation, and pacification of the humors (doṣas), such as wind (vāta) and the others, occur. 24. It is in this [context] that the accumulation, provocation, and pacification of the humors take place.
That is declared to be the six seasons resulting from the Sun's transit through the zodiac signs.
The designation of the six seasons according to the sequence of the signs is as follows:
Aries and Taurus are said to be the summer; the rainy season is in Gemini and Cancer.
The rainy season is said to correspond to Leo, while autumn belongs to Libra and Scorpio;
Dhanus and Sagittarius are Hemanta (early winter), and spring corresponds to Aquarius and Pisces.
These are the periods for the accumulation, aggravation, and pacification of the three humors, beginning with Vata.
In summer, vāyu is accumulated; in the rainy season, it becomes aggravated.
In the rains, pitta is accumulated; in the autumn, it becomes aggravated.
In the early winter, kapha is accumulated; and in spring, it becomes aggravated. (27)

Generally, the wind subsides by itself during the autumn season and the spring; bile [subsides] in the rainy season, and phlegm in the winter. This is the instruction regarding the timing of the fangs of Yama.
The eight days of Kārttika and the eight days of Āgrayaṇa are known as Yamadaṃṣṭrā; indeed, one who eats very little during these survives.
Even at improper times, the accumulation, provocation, and subsidence of the *doṣas* occur through eating and other such acts.
The humors (doṣas), through the accumulation and pacification [of their respective qualities], undergo change even out of season due to identical or contrary modes of conduct, diet, and lifestyle.
These are the causes for the provocation and pacification of the wind (vāyu).
From food that is light, dry, or insufficient; from excessive cold, physical exertion, and likewise from the evening twilight; from lust, grief, fear, anxiety, and staying awake at night (32);
from injury, immersion in water, and the depletion of the bodily constituents when food has been digested.
Vāyu becomes aggravated by these factors and is pacified by their opposites.
(33) The causes for the aggravation and pacification of pitta are as follows: through foods that are burning, pungent, sour, and hot, and by the excessive consumption of very hot things.

At midday, due to the obstruction of hunger and thirst, when food is being digested, bile (pitta) undergoes provocation; at midnight, it is provoked by these same factors and is pacified by their opposites. These are the causes for the provocation and pacification of phlegm (kapha).

When the digestive fire is weak due to the consumption of sweet, unctuous, cold, and similar foods, as well as from daytime sleep, eating at dawn, immediately after a meal, or from physical exhaustion, phlegm (śleṣman) undergoes provocation; it is pacified by these aforementioned antagonistic factors. 36
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Exposition of Medicines," in the first section of the *Śrī Śārṅgadharasaṃhitā*.
Now begins the third chapter: "The Procedure for Pulse Examination and Other Methods."
The method for examining the pulse:
the vessel at the base of the thumb of the hand is the witness of life;
by its movement, pleasure and pain of the body are to be known by the wise. (1)
The characteristic of the pulse arising from aggravated vāta:
when vāta is provoked, the pulse exhibits the movement of a leech or a snake.
The characteristic of the pulse arising from aggravated pitta:
Due to the provocation of bile (pitta), one adopts the gait of a kuliṅga bird, a crow, or a frog;
due to the provocation of phlegm (śleṣman), one assumes the gait of a swan or a pigeon, which are the characteristics of a channel produced by the aggravated phlegm.
The characteristics of the pulse produced by the combination of all three humors (sannipāta) are as follows:
the movement [of the pulse] resembles that of a quail, a partridge, or a vartī bird due to sannipāta. This is the characteristic of the pulse produced by two humors.

Sometimes moving slowly and sometimes flowing with great speed, it should be known as a vein afflicted by the provocation of two humors (doṣas); moreover, when displaced from its location, it is a sign of an incurable disease and kills.
That pulse which, having remained still for a while, moves again, is known as "life-destroying";
being extremely weak and cold, it undoubtedly kills the patient.
(7) [The characteristics of the pulse in fever.]
In the aggravation of fever, however, the pulse becomes hot and forceful.
(8) The characteristics of the pulse for those possessed by lust, anger, anxiety, and fear are as follows:
it flows with lust, anger, and agitation; it is diminished when overwhelmed by anxiety and fear. (9)
Regarding the characteristics of the pulse during the stages of weak digestion, depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātu), provocation of blood, and the presence of undigested matter (sāma):
the pulse of one with weak digestion and depleted constituents becomes very slow; it is filled with blood, slightly warm, heavy, and extremely sluggish due to the presence of sāma. (10)
Regarding the characteristics of the pulse for those with a blazing digestive fire, those who are comfortable, and those who are hungry or satiated:
it is considered that for one with a blazing fire, the pulse flows lightly;
for one who is comfortable, it is known to be steady; and likewise, it is recorded as being strong.
To one who is hungry, she may seem fickle, but to one who is satisfied, she remains steadfast.
Examination of the Messengers:
Messengers should be of their own kind, free from physical defects, skillful, and wearing clean garments.

Happy people, mounted on horses and bulls, endowed with white flowers and fruits, of noble birth and auspicious conduct, situated in the direction of the living (the east), reach the physician at the proper time for the sake of the patient's well-being. 12.
That channel through which the vital breath blows is endowed with life; such are the omens of the messenger as he goes to summon the physician for the sake of the patient.
An auspicious and gentle omen is not one that brings happiness when it is ablaze; however, for a physician—a doctor going to perform medical treatment for a patient—such omens are auspicious. 13.
That which has been described as an auspicious omen for a journey is not favorable if it is "blazing" (dīpta).
The characteristics of one who is curable are: being endowed with one's own natural constitution and complexion, and possessed of mental fortitude (sattva).
A patient who is devoted to his physician and has conquered his senses is curable by a physician. Now follows the examination of auspicious and inauspicious dreams;
therein are the characteristics of bad dreams.
In his dreams, he saw men who were naked and shaven-headed, clothed in red and black garments,
deformed, mutilated, dark-complexioned, and equipped with nooses and weapons;
they were binding and striking others while stationed toward the southern direction.
He who sees men and women mounted upon buffaloes, camels, or donkeys—if healthy, he incurs disease; if ill, he surely meets his death. 16.
There are other characteristics of bad dreams as well.
He who falls from on high, or dissolves in water or fire, or even he who is slain by beasts of prey or swallowed by fish and the like;
he whose eyes dissolve, or whose lamp goes out— 17.
He may drink oil or liquor, or he obtains iron or sesame seeds;
he receives cooked food and eats it, or he enters a well or the netherworld (rasātala).
The healthy man acquires disease, and the sick man surely meets his death.
The ritual procedure to be performed upon seeing a bad dream:
having seen such bad dreams as these, one should not speak of them to anyone; one should bathe at dawn and give gold, sesame seeds, and iron. 20.
A mortal who recites hymns to the gods and dwells in a temple at night, having performed this for three days, is liberated from bad dreams. (21) [Now follow] the characteristics of auspicious dreams.
He who, in dreams, sees gods, kings, living friends, brahmins, cows, kindled fires, and sacred fords, shall obtain happiness.
22 Furthermore:
Having crossed over waters that are turbid and having conquered even hosts of enemies,
one may become happy by mounting palaces, mountain peaks, and elephant-vehicles. (23) Moreover:
Having obtained white flowers, garments, meat, fish, and fruits, may the afflicted become happy, and the healthy obtain wealth.
(24) Furthermore:
Sexual intercourse with a forbidden woman, being smeared with excrement, weeping, and death,
as well as eating raw meat in a dream, the wise know to be omens for the attainment of wealth and health.
(25) Furthermore:
Whether it be a leech, a bee, a snake, or even a fly that bites him,
may that patient become free from disease, restored to health, and obtain wealth.
(26) Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Procedure for Pulse Examination and Other Methods," in the first section of the *Śrī Śārṅgadharasaṃhitā*.
The Fourth Chapter: An Exposition on Stimulating Digestion, Ripening [the Doshas], and Other Matters;
therein, the exposition on stimulating digestion, ripening, and so forth.
Among those, the definition of a digestive stimulant (*dīpana*) substance is that which promotes digestion and stimulates the digestive fire; for example, *miśi* (Nigella sativa).
Regarding the definitions of both a digestive (*pācana*) and a digestive-stimulant (*dīpana*) substance: [the former] promotes digestion, while [the latter] stimulates the digestive fire.
One should know that which digests raw matter without burning the fire as *pācana* (digestive);
likewise, one should understand *citraka* to be both a digestive stimulant (*dīpana*) and a digestive agent (*pācana*), like *nāgakeśara*.
This is the definition of a *saṃśamana* (pacifying) substance.

It does not purify nor does it provoke aversion; it equalizes equally aggravated humors and balances those that are uneven. That pacification is like nectar; such is the characteristic of a substance that acts in accordance with nature (anulomana).
That which, having ripened the impurities, breaks their bond and leads them downward,
should be known as *anulomana* (facilitating downward movement), such as the aforementioned *harītakī*. This is the definition of a laxative substance (*sraṃsana-dravya*).

That which causes the downward movement of undigested waste and other impurities that have become adhered within the digestive tract, even before they have been digested, is *sraṃsana* (laxative); for example, *kṛtamālaka*.
This is the definition of a liquefying (*bhedana*) substance.
That which causes the expulsion of impurities— whether they are unbound, or bound and aggregated by other humors—
and breaks them down before falling away, like the *kaṭukī* plant, is the characteristic of a purgative liquid (*recanadravya*). 6.

That which brings to a liquid state what is either matured or immature, such as impurities and the like, and also causes it to be discharged, should be known as a purgative, such as *trivṛtā*; this is the characteristic of a purgative substance. 7.
The characteristic of an emetic substance.
That which forcibly carries upwards the undigested pitta and kapha should be known as emesis, just like the fruit of the *madana* tree;
this is the characteristic of purificatory substances.
One should expel the accumulation of impurities from its location, either upward or downward;
that constitutes the purification of the body, just like the fruit of the *devadālī*. This is the characteristic of the liquid for excision (*chedanadravya*).
That which forcibly uproots the adherent humors such as phlegm (kapha) and others is called excision (chedana);
for example, alkalis, black pepper, and bitumen (śilājatu). This is the definition of an excising liquid.
That which dries up and scrapes away the bodily elements (dhātus) or impurities (malas) is called *lekhana* (scraping); for example, honey, water, warm [water], *vacā*, and barley.
This is the characteristic of astringent (grāhin) liquids.
That which is digestive, promotes digestion, and dries up fluids due to its heat is astringent;
such as ginger, cumin, and long pepper. This is the definition of a fluid-stabilizing (stambhana) substance.
That which is produced from dryness, coldness, astringency, and light digestion is a Vata-aggravating astringent (stambhana), such as *vatsaka* and *ṭuṇṭuka*.
This is the characteristic of substances used for rejuvenation (*rasāyana*).
That which destroys old age and disease should be known as *rasāyana*,
such as *amṛtā*, *rudantī*, *guggulu*, and *harītakī*.
[14] This is the definition of aphrodisiac substances (*vājīkaraṇa*).
That substance from which sexual excitement arises in women is an aphrodisiac (*vājīkaraṇa*);
for example, *nāgabalā* and others, as well as the seeds of *kapikacchu*. This is the definition of substances that increase virility.
Because it causes the increase of semen, it is indeed called *śukrala* (semen-prolific);
for example, *aśvagandhā*, *musalī*, sugar, and *śatāvarī*.
These are substances that generate semen and act as purgatives.

Milk, black gram, the marrow of the marking-nut (bhallātaka), and myrobalans are said to be both galactagogues and stimulants of semen; this is the specific distinction among aphrodisiac substances. 17.
The specific distinction among aphrodisiac substances.

The *pravartanī* (promoter) is the female [organ], the *recanī* (purgative) is the fruit of the *bṛhatī*, the *stambhanī* (astringent/arresting) is the nutmeg (*jātīphala*), and the *śoṣaṇī* (drying) is the *harītakī*. 18.
This is the definition of subtle fluidity (*sūkṣmadravatva*).
That which enters the subtle pores of the body is called "subtle" (sūkṣma); for example, rock salt, honey, neem oil, and castor oil possess the characteristics of being pervasive and liquid. 19.
These are the characteristics of substances that are penetrative and fluid.
First it pervades the entire body and then undergoes digestion; that which is pervasive (vyavāyi) is characterized by expansion and fluidity, such as hemp and the foam arising from the ocean. 20.
This is the definition of the expansive (vikāśi).
It loosens the joints and causes them to expand; it separates the *ojas* from the tissues (*dhātus*), just as the *kramuka* and *kodrava* grains [separate their own essence].
This is the characteristic of the intoxicating fluid of the *mada-kārin*.
That substance which impairs the intellect and causes intoxication is called *mada-kāri*; it is dominated by the quality of *tamas*, such as wine, liquor, and the like.
This is the definition of a substance that takes away life.

Poison is known to be pervasive, expansive, subtle, cutting, intoxicating, fiery, life-taking, and capable of being modified by combination; its characteristic is that it causes agitation and flows freely. (23)
That substance which, by its own potency, expels the accumulation of the *doṣas* from the channels is called *pramāthin*; for example, black pepper (*marica*) and *vacā*.
This is the characteristic of a substance that causes secretions (*abhiṣyandi*).
Because of its sliminess and heaviness, it obstructs the vessels that carry the rasa;
the heaviness it thereby produces is that which makes a substance *abhiṣyandi*, such as curd.
(25) Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Stimulants, Digestives, and Related Substances," in the first section of the *Śrī Śārṅgadharasaṃhitā*.
Now begins the fifth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Kalās and Other Principles.
Therein, the exposition of the Kalās and other principles constitutes the body [of this chapter].
The exposition of the *kalās* and so forth:

the *kalās* are seven, the *āśayas* are seven, the *dhātus* are seven, their impurities (*malas*) are seven, the secondary constituents (*upadhātus*) are seven, and the skins (*tvacas*) are proclaimed to be seven. (1)
There are three humors, nine hundred ligaments,
and likewise two hundred and ten joints; there are three hundred bones,
one hundred and seven vital points (marmas), and seven hundred vessels (sirās).
Twenty-four vessels are declared to be carriers of rasa;
the wise have stated that there are five hundred muscles in men,
while in women there are twenty more, as well as sixteen tendons.
In the body of a man there are ten apertures, and in the body of a woman there are thirteen; this has been stated in brief, and it is now described in detail. Now, the seven *kalās*.
The three [kalās] consist of flesh, blood, and fat; the fourth is that of the liver and spleen; likewise, the fifth is of the intestines; the sixth is considered to be the *agnidharā*;
and the seventh would be the *retodharā*. Thus, the seven *kalās* are traditionally taught. (6)
Now, there are seven receptacles:
the receptacle of phlegm (śleṣmāśaya) is in the chest; below that is the receptacle of undigested food (āmāśaya);
and above the navel, on the left side, is situated the receptacle of fire (agnyāśaya).

Above that, the receptacle for sesame seeds (the stomach) is to be known; below that is the receptacle for wind (the large intestine). Below that is the receptacle for impurities (the small intestine), and below that is the bladder, the receptacle for urine.
The chest is to be known as the receptacle for vital essence and blood; these are the seven receptacles. 8–9.
The specific internal organs of women are greater than those of men; furthermore, there are three other organs unique to women:
the uterus is called *dharā*, and the two breasts are considered the *stanyāśayas* (milk-seats). 10.

Now, the names of the seven constituents (dhātus) and their order of production: chyle, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen are the constituents; all of them arise from one another, being cooked by the heat of the bile (pitta). 11.

From the essence (rasa) comes blood; from that, flesh; from flesh, fat is produced; from fat, bone; from that, marrow; and from marrow, the production of semen occurs. Now, [follow] the impurities of the seven constituents (dhātus) and the sequence of their production.
The fluids of the tongue, eyes, and cheeks, as well as bile and the coloring agent (rañjaka), the impurities produced from the ears, feces, tongue, teeth, armpits, penis, and so forth,
the filth of the nails and eyes, oiliness in the mouth, and likewise pustules— these are [the humors]. 13.
These impurities of the seven tissues (dhātus) arise in this sequence. According to another opinion,
the impurities of the tissues are phlegm (kapha), bile (pitta), excretions from the orifices, sweat, nails, and body hair.
The impurities of the bodily constituents (dhātus) are, in their respective order: tears from the eyes, and unctuousness (sneha) from the skin.
Next, the secondary impurities (upadhātus) are breast milk and the menstrual flow (rajas) of women, which appear at the proper time and then pass away.
The oily substance derived from pure flesh is proclaimed as *vasā*.
Sweat, teeth, hair, and likewise *ojas* as the seventh—these seven are to be known as the secondary constituents (*upadhātu*) arising from the primary elements (*dhātu*). 16–17.
Now, the characteristics of *ojas*: *Ojas* is situated throughout the entire body; it is considered to be cold, unctuous, and stable.
Being of the nature of Soma, it is regarded as that which produces strength and nourishment for the body. (18)
Now, seven layers of skin (tvac) are to be known; the first is considered the seat of *sidhma* and is called *avabhāsinī*.
The second is to be known as *lohitā*, the birthplace of *tilaka*, *alaka*, and *janya*. 19.
The third is reckoned as Śvetā, which is the location of Carmadalakuṣṭha; the fourth should be known as Tāmrā, the stage of Kilāsa and Śvitra;
the fifth is called Vedanī, from which all types of kuṣṭha arise. 20.
The well-known *rohiṇī* is the sixth, located in the condition of *granthi*, *gaṇḍa*, and *apacī*.
The seventh is known as the thick (*sthūlā*) skin, and it is the site for abscesses (*vidradhi*) and the like.
Thus, the seven layers of skin have been described; the thick one measures two units of a *vrīhi* grain.
Now, as for the humors (doṣas), their names are Vāyu, Pitta, and Kapha; they are the humors, the bodily constituents (dhātus), and likewise the wastes (malas).
Furthermore, each of these is said to be fivefold because of their respective roles in sustaining the body. (23)
An explanation of the alternative names for the *doṣas* based on their functions:
they are known as *doṣas* because they corrupt the body, as *dhātus* because they sustain the body, and as *malas* because they cause impurity. (24)
In that regard, the predominance of vāyu and a description of its effects are as follows:
"Pitta is lame, kapha is lame, and the waste products and tissues are lame;
wherever they are led by vāyu, there they go, like clouds. (25)
Among these, wind (pavana) is considered powerful due to its capacity for division;
it consists of the quality of rajas, and is subtle, cold, dry, light, and mobile. (26) Thus, wind is fivefold according to its different functions.

The wind moves in five ways: in the receptacle of impurities (the colon), in the abdominal cavity, in the seat of fire (the stomach), in the heart, in the throat, and throughout all parts of the body.
These are the five names of the wind.
Apāna, samāna, prāṇa, udāna, and likewise vyāna— these are declared to be the names of the vital wind (samīra) in their proper sequence. (28) [Now follows] the description of pitta.

Pitta is hot, liquid, yellowish-blue, and characterized by a predominance of the *sattva* quality; it should be known as having pungent and bitter tastes, and when improperly digested (*vidagdha*), it turns sour.
Its locations, functions, and names [are as follows]. 29. Its locations, functions, and names.
Pitta, which is of the nature of fire, exists in the seat of the digestive fire (the stomach) in a quantity equal to a sesame seed;
it should be known as that which produces luster in the skin and acts as a digestant through applications such as ointments and massages.
That pitta which is visible in the liver should be understood to transform rasa into blood.
That pitta which, in the pair of eyes, effects the perception of forms; that pitta which resides in the heart and produces intelligence and wisdom;
as well as the digestive (pācaka), the illuminating (bhrājaka), the coloring (rañjaka), and the ocular (ālocaka) pittas.
And "sādhaka" (the accomplisher)—these are the five names of pitta in sequence. Now follows the description of kapha and its functions: kapha is unctuous, heavy, white, slimy, and cold.
That which is predominant in the quality of *tamas* (tamoguṇa) is sweet, pungent, and salty.
(33) The statement of the locations and names of *kapha*:
*Kapha* resides in the stomach (*āmāśaya*), the head, the throat, the heart, and the joints.
Remaining [in the body], it provides stability to the body and dexterity to all its limbs.
Kledana (moistening), snehana (lubricating), rasana (tasting), avalambana (supporting), and śleṣmaka (adhesive)—these are the names of kapha stated in their respective order. (34-35)
The description of the sinews: The sinews are said to be the binding of the flesh, bones, and fat within the body. (36) The description of the joints.
The joints (sandhi) are said to be located in the body due to the joining of its parts and are associated with phlegm (kapha). 37.
The wise know that bones in the body consist of cavities, supports, and essential marrow (sāra). 38.
The opening of the vital points (*marmans*): the sages have generally declared that the *marmans* are the supports of life. (39) The opening of the vessels (*śirās*).
The vessels (śirās) that form the joints and ligaments carry the humors (doṣas) and tissues (dhātus).
[40] Description of the channels (dhamanīs):
the channels that carry the nutrient essence (rasa) pulsate with the vital air (pavana) throughout the body. [41]
The Description of the Muscle-fibers:
The muscle-fibers serve for strength and as supports for embodied beings. (42) The Description of the Tendons.
The tendons (kaṇḍarā) are considered to be responsible for the extension and contraction of the limbs.
(43) Regarding the openings of the cavities: two apertures each are proclaimed for the nose, the eyes, and the ears.
The apertures of the two eyes, the two nostrils, and the mouth are each called a single opening;
the tenth is said to be at the crown of the head—these are known as the "openings" (randhra) of men. In women, there are three additional openings: the two breasts and the path of the womb.

Furthermore, other subtle pores are considered to exist in the skin of living beings. (44) Regarding the description of the lungs, spleen, and liver: the lungs are held to be on the left side, while the spleen and liver are on the right.
The lungs are declared by the wise to be the support of the udāna breath;
the spleen is known by the great sages as the root of the blood-carrying vessels; and the liver is the seat of the rakta-pitta and the reservoir of the blood. 45
Description of the kidneys (tilakloṃma): The kidney is the root of the water-carrying channels and the coverer of thirst. 46.
Description of the kidneys.
The two kidneys are said to provide satisfaction for the fat residing in the abdomen.
(47) Description of the testicles and the penis:
The testicles are the supports for the channels that carry semen and bring about virility.
The *liṅga* (genital organ) is that which effects conception and is the passage for semen and urine.
[Verse 48] The description of the heart:
the heart is considered the seat of consciousness (*cetanā*) and the locus of vitality (*ojas*). [Verse 49]
The description of the function of nourishing the body:
the vessels and arteries situated at the navel pervade the entire body and, through their connection with the wind, incessantly nourish it by means of all the bodily constituents (dhātus). 50
An explanation of the functions of the vital breath (prāṇavāyu):
The vital air situated at the navel, having touched the interior of the heart-lotus,
emerges from the throat to drink the nectar of Viṣṇu’s feet.

Having drunk the nectar of the sky, it returns with speed, nourishing the entire body and enlivening the digestive fire; such is the true nature of both life and death. 51. The nature of life and death.

Thus, from the union of the body and the vital breath, it is called "life" (āyuḥ); and by their separation through time, it is termed "death" (pañcatva) by the wise. (52) In this regard, the instruction on the duties to be performed for physicians is as follows:
No living being whatsoever is born immortal anywhere on this earth; therefore, death is unavoidable, but one may ward off disease.
(53) This is the instruction regarding the classification of diseases as curable and so forth, for the purpose of warding off disease.
That which is curable becomes manageable, and that which is manageable proceeds toward incurability;
however, the incurable destroys the life of a man who fails to provide a remedy. (54) This is the instruction on the protection of the body, which is the means for achieving dharma and other goals.
Since the body is the instrument for achieving dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa,
a person who understands the ripening of karma should protect the body from diseases;
for it is the fruit of the equilibrium or imbalance of the bodily humors.

The elements and their impurities are the defects; when they are unbalanced, they destroy the body, but when balanced, they should be known to lead to happiness, strength, and nourishment. (56) This is the sequence of creation.
For the Person (Puruṣa), the source of the world, who is devoid of desire and whose sole nature is consciousness and bliss, there exists an eternal Prakṛti, like a reflection of the sun.
(57) This is the description of the origin of creation through the conjunction of Prakṛti and Puruṣa.
Though insentient, through union with the consciousness of the Supreme Self,

she fashioned the entire impermanent universe like a dramatic performance. (58) This is the description of the origin of the intellect (*buddhi*), the faculty of goodness (*sattva*), and the ego (*ahaṅkāra*).

Primordial Nature (Prakṛti), the mother of the universe, first gave birth to Intellect (Buddhi), which consists of desire and possesses a vast form; from that, the Ego (Ahaṅkāra) arose, and it too became threefold through the qualities of Rajas, Sattva, and Tamas. 59

From that *ahaṃkāra* consisting of the three *guṇas*, which is endowed with *sattva* and *rajas*, the ten sense organs and the mind were born; they are called the ear, the skin, the eye, and likewise— 60.
The tongue, nose, speech, hands, feet, generative organ, and anus—
these five are called the organs of perception (buddhīndriya), while the other five are described by those of subtle intellect as the organs of action (karmendriya). (61)

The exposition on the arising of the five subtle elements (tanmātras): Then, from the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) in which the quality of darkness (tamas) predominates over the quality of goodness (sattva), the five subtle elements arose; their names have been declared by the wise.
The subtle element of sound, the subtle element of touch, the subtle element of form,
the subtle element of taste, and the subtle element of smell— these they know as such.
(62) This is the description of the names and the origin of the five gross elements.

From those five subtle elements (tanmātras), the five gross elements (bhūtas) are produced; they are considered to consist of ether, air, fire, water, and earth. These are the specific manifestations (viśeṣas) of the subtle elements.

Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, in their respective order, are the specific manifestations of the subtle elements (tanmātras) once they have attained a gross state; these are the objects of the sense organs. 64.
The objects of the sense organs.
The five objects of the sense organs of cognition are considered to be sound and the rest; the objects of the organs of action are speech, grasping, movement,
as well as pleasure and excretion, as declared by the seers of reality.
Description of the twenty-four principles (*tattva*). Among them, the designation of the names of the first principle, *prakṛti*:
it is *pradhāna*, *prakṛti*, *śakti*, eternal (*nityā*), and likewise unevolved (*avikṛti*).
These are her names, she who exists by resorting to Śiva.
This is the enumeration of the seven principles known as the primary and the modified:
the Great One (Mahat), the Ego (Ahaṅkāra), and the five subtle elements (Tanmātras) individually.
The wise have declared these seven to be both primordial nature (prakṛti) and its transformations (vikṛti).
The ten sense organs, the mind (citta), and the five great elements (mahābhūtas)—these sixteen are to be known as the transformations; they remain pervading the entire world.
The description of the nature of the soul:

Thus, when the house of the body has been established by means of the twenty-four principles, the individual soul (jīvātman)—which is determined and eternal—dwells therein, accompanied by its own internal messenger. 70

That embodied being is said to be pervaded and bound by the mind through artificial bonds of karma— namely, sin, merit, suffering, pleasure, and so forth. (71) These are the bonds of the embodied being.
Desire and anger, greed and delusion, and egoism as the fifth,
along with the ten sense organs and the intellect— these lead to the bondage of the embodied soul.
This is the exposition of the bondage and liberation, and of the suffering and happiness, of the individual soul.
One incurs bondage through ignorance and is liberated through self-knowledge;
that which produces the conjunction with suffering is disease, and that which brings about happiness is health.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Narration of Kalādikā," in the first section of the *Śrī-Śārṅgadharasaṃhitā*.
Now begins the sixth chapter, the Exposition of the Destinies of Food and Other Matters;
therein is the exposition of the destinies of food and other matters.
The explanation of the sequence of digestion of food:
First, impelled by the prāṇa-wind, the food goes to the stomach;
though it possesses six tastes, it attains sweetness and a frothy state. 1.
The description of the sourness of food, its transport to the *grahaṇī*, and the pungent qualities [of the digestive fire]:
then, being scorched by the *pācaka-pitta* (digestive bile), it attains acidity;
thereafter, it is brought to the *grahaṇī* by the *samāna-vāyu* (equalizing wind).
In the *grahaṇī*, digestion occurs by means of the digestive fire (*vahni*) within the abdominal cavity; from this, a pungent state arises.
This is the description of the stages of the food's essence (*rasa*):
from that which is fully digested comes the *rasa*, while from that which is undigested arises *āma*.

Through the power of the digestive fire, the essence of the fully digested food attains sweetness and unctuousness; that well-matured essence, like nectar, properly nourishes all the bodily constituents (dhātus). 4.
The functions of *āmarasa* (undigested taste) are characterized by weak digestion and a burning sensation; its taste becomes pungent or sour,
it may turn into poison, or it may produce a combination of diseases.
Regarding the description of the essence and the waste products of food:
the essence of food is its *rasa* (nutritive fluid); that which is devoid of essence is the liquid waste (*mala*).
Carried by the vessels (*sirās*) to the bladder (*vasti*), that water attains the state of urine (*mūtra*). (6)

That waste and impurity should be known to reside in the receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya). Impelled by the downward wind (apāna), it passes through the three folds [of the anus]—the three folds being the *pravāhiṇī*, the *sarjanī*, and the *grāhikā*. 7.
Regarding the designation of rasa as "red":
impelled by the samāna vāyu, rasa reaches the heart; there, colored and cooked by pitta, it attains the state of blood (rakta). 8.
The description of blood in terms of its predominance and essential nature:
Blood, which resides throughout the entire body, is the supreme support of the living being; it is unctuous, heavy, mobile, and sweet, and when vitiated, it becomes like bile (pitta). 9.
The sequence of maturation of the constituents such as rasa:
the constituents beginning with rasa, being cooked by the heat of pitta, gradually attain the state of semen over the course of a month; likewise, the menstrual flow (rajas) occurs in women. 10.
The explanation of the origin of the embryo:
through the union of the couple out of desire, an embryo arises in a woman from pure blood and semen; once born, he is called a child. 11.
Regarding the explanation of the causes for the birth of female, male, or neuter offspring:

when *rajas* (the female constituent) predominates, a daughter is born; when *śukra* (the male constituent) predominates, a son is born; and through their equality, a neuter is born—or it may be according to the supreme Lord’s will. 12.
The prescription for the dosage of medicine for an infant:
in the first month of life, one *raktikā* of medicine should be given to the child,
prepared as a single electuary with milk, honey, sugar, and ghee.
One should increase it by one [māṣa] each until it becomes one year;
beyond that, the increase shall be by māṣas until sixteen years;
thereafter, it should remain stable until seventy years.

Then, like a child, she should be gradually weaned from the mother; this [mother] provides four times the amount of medicinal pastes, powders, and decoctions required for life-long wholesome practices.
16. From birth, these are the actions that constitute wholesome habits (*sātmya*).

Collyrium, as well as ointments, bathing, oil massage, emesis, and nasal drops (pratimarśa) are recommended from birth onwards. The application of gargles and other such treatments should be prescribed according to the patient's age.
Gargling [is prescribed] from the fifth year; the administration of food [and medicine] from the eighth;
purgation from the sixteenth year; and sexual intercourse from the twentieth.
This is the instruction regarding the duration of the decline of childhood and the other stages.
Childhood, growth, complexion, intellect, skin, vision, semen, prowess, understanding, the organs of action, the mind, and life— these ten diminish with each decade.
(19) This is the characteristic of the wind-temperament (*vāta-prakṛti*).
A man of windy temperament (vātaprakṛti) has sparse hair, is emaciated and rough, talkative, fickle-minded, and wanders through the sky in his dreams. 20.
Characteristics of the bilious temperament (pittaprakṛti).
A man of bilious temperament (pittaprakṛti) is characterized by premature graying of hair, is intelligent, perspires easily, is prone to anger, and sees celestial lights in his dreams. 21.
Characteristics of the phlegmatic temperament (śleṣmaprakṛti).
A man of deep intellect, with stout limbs, glossy hair, and great strength,
who observes reservoirs of water in his dreams, is of a phlegmatic (ślaiṣmika) constitution. [22] Regarding the characteristics of the dual- and triple-humoral constitutions:
Men in whom two or three doshas are aggravated should be recognized by their mixed signs (verse 23).
Sleep, fainting, confusion, and drowsiness are the characteristics of tamas; sleep arises from tamas and kapha, while fainting arises from pitta and tamas.
Confusion arises from *rajas*, *pitta*, and *anila*; drowsiness (*tandrā*) from *śleṣman*, *tamas*, and *anila*.
(24) Regarding the symptoms of exhaustion (*glāni*) and laziness (*ālasya*): exhaustion results from the depletion of *ojas*, from suffering, from indigestion (*ajīrṇa*), and from fatigue.
That lack of enthusiasm despite possessing capability is declared to be indolence (ālasya).
As for the characteristic of yawning (jṛmbhā):
it is that which, due to a slackening of consciousness, exhales after inhaling a single breath.

When the mouth is wide open and there is labored breathing, that is called yawning by the wise; the characteristic of sneezing arises from the upward union of the udāna and prāṇa breaths, resulting in the flow of mucus from the head.
Sound arises from the nose; that is called sneezing by the wise.
Furthermore, that which occurs due to the agitation of the *udāna* breath and the stabilization of food is characterized as eructation (*udgāra*).
The upward movement of the wind is called *udgāra* (eructation).
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Movement of Food and Other Substances," in the first section of the *Śrī Śārṅgadharasaṃhitā*. [Now follows] the enumeration of diseases.
Now begins the seventh chapter:
The Chapter on the Enumeration of Diseases;
the Declaration of the Enumeration of Diseases.
The enumeration of diseases previously proclaimed by the sages is now being declared by me here; its divisions are considered to be many. First, the varieties of fever (jvara).

Twenty-five fevers have been enumerated; their specific divisions are now described: they are traditionally held to be of three types—arising from the individual doshas, from the combinations of two doshas, and one from the combination of all three (sannipāta); their further subdivisions are said to be numerous.

The distinctions between irregular fevers (*viṣama-jvara*) and those caused by exogenous factors (*āgantu-jvara*) are as follows: for the most part, five types of irregular fevers arise from the derangement of the *sannipāta* (the combination of all three humors):
the continuous (*santata*), the frequent (*satata*), the quotidian (*anyedyuṣka*), and the tertian (*tṛtīyaka*). (3)
The quartan fever is also mentioned; thus, the irregular fevers (viṣamajvara) are proclaimed to be [these four].
Furthermore, the exogenous fever (āgantujvara) is considered to be of thirteen types:
it is threefold—due to malevolent magic (abhicāra), possession by spirits (grahāveśa), and curses (śāpa).

Fever born of the four types of injury arises from exhaustion, wounds, burning sensations, and [suppressed] urges. There are six fevers caused by external possession (abhiṣaṅga), arising from desire, fear, grief, anger, poison, and the smell of medicine. Such is the determination of fever.
The varieties of diarrhea (atisāra), malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), and dysentery (pravāhikā) are distinct;
they arise from each of the three doṣas individually, from all three combined, and also from grief, undigested matter (āma), and fear.
Thus, diarrhea is of seven types, while grahaṇī is considered to be of five types.
There are five types of diarrhea (*pravāhikā*): four arising from the individual *doṣas*, one from their combination (*sannipāta*), and one from undigested food (*āma*).
Furthermore, there are four types caused by the individual *doṣas* and one from blood (*āsṛt*).
These are the distinctions between indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) and lassitude (*ālasya*).
Indigestion (ajīrṇa) is said to be of three types: that caused by vāyu is considered viṣṭabdha;
that caused by pitta is known as vidagdha; and that caused by kapha is called āma.
Poisonous indigestion arises from the rasa [dhatu], while alasaka is of three kinds according to the doshas.
The varieties of *viṣūcī*, *daṇḍakālasaka*, and *vilambikā* are as follows:
*viṣūcī* is said to be of three types, arising separately from each of the *doṣas*; *daṇḍakālasaka* is likewise [of three types]; and *vilambikā* is only one. (11)

The varieties of hemorrhoids (arśas) and anal warts (carmakīla): They say that hemorrhoids are of six types—due to vāta, pitta, kapha, blood, and the combination of all three (sannipāta), as well as from their mutual association (saṃsarga). Their classification is traditionally recorded as twofold. 12
The types of *carmakīla* (skin-nail) are threefold, arising from wind, bile, and phlegm; likewise, they are distinguished by being congenital or acquired, and by being dry or moist.
There are also various types caused by worms.
There are twenty-one types of worms, and they are of two kinds:

external and internal. Among them, lice (*yūkā*) are those that move externally; nits (*likṣā*) and others are those that move internally, arising from phlegm (*kapha*) and originating in the heart region.
The Antrādās, Udarāveṣṭas, Curavas, Mahāgudas,
Sugandhas, Darbhakusumas, Raktas, Mātṛs, Saurasas, Lomavidhvaṃsas, Romadvīpas, and Udumbaras. (15–16)
Likewise, there are others such as the Keśādā, the Śakṛjjātā, the Makerukā,
the Lelihā, the Saśūla, the Sausurādā, and the Kakerukā (17). Furthermore, another known as the Snāyuka is said to be produced from phlegm and blood.
Other external sources of poison are the worms within a wound (18).
There are various types of anemia and jaundice; furthermore, there are five kinds of anemia, which are threefold according to vāta, pitta, and kapha.

There is one type of jaundice known as *kāmalā* caused by the three *doṣas* and by earth; there is another called *kumbhakāmalā*, and likewise one called *halīmaka*. These are the varieties of *raktapitta*.

Raktapitta (hemorrhagic disease) is said to be of three types: that which moves upward is born from kapha; that which moves downward should be known as arising from vāta; and that which follows both paths arises from both. (20) The varieties of cough:

Five types of cough have been enumerated; three of them arise from the three humors (doṣas), the fourth arises from injury to the chest, and the fifth arises from wasting (kṣaya) of the bodily constituents (dhātu). These are the varieties of wasting.

The varieties of consumption (śoṣa) should be known as five: three are caused by the three doṣas, the fourth is by their combination (sannipāta), and the fifth arises from chest injury (uraḥkṣata). 22. These are the classifications of consumption.

There are six types of wasting diseases (śoṣa): they arise from excessive sexual indulgence, grief, wounds, the fatigue of travel, physical exertion, and even old age. (23) [The following are] the varieties of dyspnea (śvāsa).
Five types of dyspnea (śvāsa) are to be recognized: kṣudra, tamaka, ūrdhvaśvāsa, mahāśvāsa, and chinnaśvāsa as the fifth. These are the varieties of hiccup (hikkā).
The five types of hiccup have been described; they are the minor (kṣudrā), the food-born (annajā),
the deep-seated (gambhīrā), the twin (yamalā), and the great (mahatī) as the fifth—
these being varieties of the disorder of fire (agnivikāra).

There are four modifications of fire: that which arises from vāta is irregular (viṣama), from pitta it is sharp (tīkṣṇa), from kapha it is dull (manda), and bhasmaka arises from both vāta and pitta. These are the varieties of anorexia (arocaka).

There are five types of anorexia to be known: three caused by vāta, pitta, and kapha respectively, one from the combination of all three (sannipāta), and one from mental distress; these are the varieties of vomiting.

Vomiting is considered to be of seven types: three arising from the individual doshas, one from worms, one from the combination of all doshas (sannipāta), one from disgust, and likewise one that arises in women from conception. 27–28.

There are six types of hoarseness (svarabheda). Three arise from vāta, pitta, and kapha respectively; the fourth is caused by medas (fat), the fifth by sannipāta (the combination of all three humors), and the sixth is proclaimed to result from wasting (kṣaya). 29

The varieties of thirst and thirst itself are said to be sixfold: from wind (vāta), from bile (pitta), and from phlegm (kapha); also from the provocation of the three humors (tridoṣa), and the sixth is from the depletion of the bodily elements (dhātu). 30
Fainting (mūrchā), giddiness (bhrama), sleep (nidrā), drowsiness (tandrā), syncope (saṃnyāsa), and exhaustion (glāni) are the varieties [of these states].

Fainting is to be known as fourfold, arising separately from vāta, pitta, and kapha; the fourth is caused by the combination of all three (sannipāta). Likewise, giddiness is recorded as being of one type.

Sleepiness, lethargy, fainting, and exhaustion are each recorded as distinct varieties of the disease of intoxication (*mada*). Seven types of intoxication have been fully described: three caused by *vāta*, *pitta*, and *kapha*.
Due to the three *doṣas*, blood, alcohol, and even poison—this is the seventh [type].
These are the varieties of *madātyaya* (alcoholism), along with their sub-varieties;
*madātyaya* is also fourfold, arising from *vāta*, *pitta*, *kapha*, and [blood].
One [type] is to be known as arising from all three doṣas, and likewise one is paramada;
similarly, there is one for indigestion from drinking, and one for pānavibhrama,
and likewise one for pānātyaya.
Regarding burning sensations and piercing pains, seven types of *dāha* (burning) are recognized:
those arising from *raktapitta*, from blood, from thirst, and from *pitta*. (35)
Due to the depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātu), injury to the vital spots (marman), and even from the abdomen being filled with blood, [these arise]. 36.
Regarding the types of insanity: six types of insanity have been described; three of them are caused by the three doṣas.
The sixth type, arising from the combination [of humors] or from poison, should be known by the suffering of the mind.
(37) These are the classifications of insanity caused by spirits (*bhūta*); there are twenty such types of insanity caused by spirits, originating from gods as well as from *dānavas*.
From a Gandharva, a Kinnara, and other Yakṣas; from the Pitṛs, and from the curse of a Guru; from a Preta, a Guhyaka, an elder, a Siddha, a Bhūta, and a Piśāca;
from the deity of the waters, a Nāga, and a Brahmarākṣasa.
[One is protected] even from Rākṣasas, Kūṣmāṇḍas, Kṛtyās, and Vetālas.
(39) The varieties of Apasmāra:
Apasmāra is fourfold, arising from Vāta, Pitta, [Kapha, and Sannipāta].
The third [type] arises from phlegm (śleṣman), and the fourth from the combination of all three humors (sannipāta).
These are the four varieties of āmavāta; furthermore, there are three types of āmavāta caused by vāta, pitta, and kapha respectively.
The fourth is caused by the combination [of all three humors];
the wise have declared that there are eight types of colic (śūla). 41.
The [first] three types arise from individual doshas; the next three are due to the combination of two doshas (dvandva);
the seventh is declared to be caused by ama; and the eighth is caused by sannipāta.
These are the varieties of *pariṇāma-śūla*.

The colic arising from transformation (pariṇāmaja) is proclaimed to be of eight types; the number of colics caused by the impurities (mala) is the same as those born of transformation. In colic caused by bile (pitta) due to the digestion of food, [the symptoms are as follows: 43.
The wise have enumerated each of these as distinct types of Udāvarta: that arising from food and drink, and likewise that arising from chronic Pitta.
There are thirteen types of Udāvarta:
the first is said to arise from the suppression of hunger, the second from the suppression of thirst,
the third would be from the destruction of sleep, and the fourth from the suppression of breath.
The fifth [vow] arises from the suppression of vomiting; the sixth from the suppression of sneezing (46).
The seventh would arise from the suppression of yawning; the eighth from the suppression of belching.
The ninth would be from the suppression of tears; the tenth from the retention of semen (47).

Due to the obstruction of urine, the obstruction of feces, and the suppression of flatus, these three types of Udāvarta arise, which cause terrible complications, including distension and its various forms. 48.
Ānāha-bheda.

Ānāha is known to be of two types: one arising from the pakvāśaya (large intestine) and another arising from the āmāśaya (stomach); the latter is called pratyānāha. There are also the varieties of urograha and hṛdagra.
Urograha is likewise one; thus five types of heart-disease (hṛdroga) are proclaimed.
Three are said to arise from vāta and the other [doshas], the fourth from the combination of all three (sannipāta), and the fifth is produced by worms (krimi).
The varieties of abdominal diseases (udararoga) are likewise eight types of abdominal enlargements (udara),
three arising from vāta, pitta, and kapha, one from the three doṣas combined, and one from water.
The eighth [type] is proclaimed as arising from injury to the spleen (plīhna) or from intestinal obstruction (baddhaguda).
There are eight varieties of abdominal tumors (gulma); specifically, three are declared to be caused by vāta, pitta, and kapha. 51–52.
Three types of dual combinations (dvandva) have been described, the seventh arising from the combination of all three humors (sannipāta),
and the eighth is known as that caused by blood; these are the varieties of urinary obstruction (mūtrāghāta).
There are thirteen types of urinary obstruction (mūtrāghāta):
first is vātakuṇḍalikā, followed by vātāṣṭhīlā; the third is vātabasti, and the fourth is mūtrātīta. 53–54.
The fifth is urinary abdominal enlargement (mūtrajaṭhara), the sixth is known as urinary depletion (mūtrakṣaya),
the seventh is the obstruction of urination (mūtrotsarga), and the eighth is the urinary tumor (mūtragranthi).
Urinary semen (mūtraśukra) is the ninth, while fecal obstruction (viḍghāta) is known as the tenth.
Mūtrasāda, uṣṇavāta, and likewise vastikuṇḍalikā—these three severe types of urinary obstruction (mūtraghāta) are proclaimed separately; they are varieties of dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra). 56.
Varieties of dysuria.

There are eight types of dysuria (*mūtrakṛcchra*): three caused by vāta, pitta, and kapha; the fourth arises from the combination of all three (*sannipāta*); the fifth is seminal dysuria (*śukrakṛcchra*);
the sixth is declared to be fecal dysuria (*viṭkṛcchra*); and the seventh is obstructive dysuria (*ghātakṛcchra*).
And the eighth is the difficult treatment for urinary calculi;
there are four types of urinary calculi recognized. 58.
From wind (vāta), bile (pitta), phlegm (kapha), and semen (śukra), there are likewise twenty types of urinary disorders (meha).
The varieties of kaphaja-meha are:
ikṣumeha, surāmeha, piṣṭameha, and sāndrameha.
Śukramēha, udarkamēha, lālāmēha, śītakamēha, and sikatāmēha, along with śanairmēha— these ten are born from kapha. [60] These are the varieties of mēha arising from pitta.
Mañjiṣṭhāmeha, Haridrāmeha, Nīlameha, Raktameha,
Kṛṣṇameha, and Kṣārameha— these six arise from Pitta. [The following are] the varieties of Vātika meha.
Hastimeha, vasāmeha, majjāmeha, and madhuprabha—these four are the disorders arising from vāta; thus, there are twenty types of meha. (62) [Note:
This is the distinction between somaroga and prameha-piṭikā.]
Likewise, there is one type of somaroga (glandular swelling), and ten types of prameha-piṭikās (pustules associated with urinary disorders):
śarāvikā, kacchapikā, putriṇī, vinatā, alajī, masūrikā, sarṣapikā, jālinī, and vidārikā.

Vidradhi— these ten are the types of abscesses (piṭikā) arising from urinary disorders (meha). Medodoṣa, swelling (śotha), and diseases (rogas)— medodoṣa is one, while nine diseases of swelling are recorded.

Due to the humors individually, in pairs, or all together, as well as from injury and poison— these are the seven types of swellings (vṛddhi) described according to their diseases, arising from vāta, pitta, and kapha.
Due to blood and fat, there is enlargement of the bladder and intestines as the seventh [type].
There are the diseases of *aṇḍavṛddhi* (scrotal enlargement), *gaṇḍamālikā*, and *gaṇḍālajī*;
likewise, there is one type of *aṇḍavṛddhi* and one type of *gaṇḍamālikā*.
There is also one called Gaṇḍālajī; the Granthibheda swellings are considered to be of nine types. 67
There are three types [of *arbuda*] arising from the three doshas, three from the blood, one from the vessels, one from the fat, one from the wound, one from the bone, and one from the flesh;
these are the varieties of *arbuda*.

Likewise, there are six types of elephantiasis (ślīpada): those arising from wind (vāta), bile (pitta), phlegm (kapha), blood (rakta), muscle (māṃsa), and fat (medas). 68–69. These are the varieties of elephantiasis.

Elephantiasis (ślīpada) is said to be of three types: from vāta, from pitta, and also from kapha. Regarding abscesses (vidradhi), they are known to be of six kinds; three are caused by vāta, pitta, and kapha.
From blood, from injury, and from the three doṣas— these fifteen types of wounds have been described. 71

These [wounds] have four types of divisions: exogenous (āgantuka), endogenous (dehaja), pure (śuddha), and malignant (duṣṭa); their respective numbers are stated separately as follows: wind-wound (vātavraṇa), bile-born (pittaja), phlegm-born (kaphaja), and blood-born wound (raktaja). 72.

Another arises from wind and bile, likewise one from wind and phlegm, as well as one from bile and phlegm, and the eighth from the combination of all three (sannipāta). The ninth is caused by vātarakta, and the tenth by raktapitta.
Another arises from phlegm and blood; another from wind, bile, and blood;

one produced from wind and phlegm and blood; one originating from bile, phlegm, and blood; and one arisen from the combination of all three (sannipāta) and blood—thus there are fifteen types of ulcers.
The classifications of fresh wounds (sadyovraṇa) are eightfold: aviklipta, vilambita, chinna, bhinna, pracalita, ghr̥ṣṭa, viddha, and nipātita. (76)
The classifications of abdominal trauma:
abdominal trauma is said to be of two types—ruptured intestine and protruded intestine. The classifications of bone fractures: [77]

The fracture of bones is said to be of eight types: those involving the breaking of the back, those that are split, those that are dislocated, those that are separated, those that are displaced sideways, those that have gone downward, those that have gone upward,
and those that are fractures of the joints.
The varieties of cauterization by fire are fourfold:
it is proclaimed as *pluṣṭa* (scorched), *vidagdha* (burned), *durdagdha* (badly burned), and *samyagdagdha* (properly burned). 78–79.
The types of sinus ulcers (nāḍī-vraṇa) are declared to be fivefold: those caused by Vāta, Pitta, and Kapha— thus three types—
and those caused by the three doṣas combined, as well as those caused by a foreign body (śalya).
There are eight types of fistula-in-ano; thus, there are eight fistulas:
the *śataponaka* arises from wind (*vāta*), and the *uṣṭragrīva* arises from bile (*pitta*).
Parisrāva is known to arise from kapha; Ṛju is born from vāta and kapha (81).
Parikṣepī arises from marut and pitta; Arśoja is born from kapha and pitta;
Unmārgī is caused by external factors; and Śaṅkhāvarta is born from all three doṣas (82).
The varieties of upadaṃśa (venereal sores):
there are five types of upadaṃśa in the penis— three caused by vāta, pitta, and kapha, one by the combination of all three (sannipāta), and one from blood (rakta).
The varieties of *śūka* (hair-like growths) are as follows:
those on the penis (*meḍhra*) are likewise twenty-four, and there is also *liṅgārśas* (anal polypus) and *grathita* (nodular growth). 83.
Nivṛtta, avamantha, mṛdita, śataponaka, aṣṭhīlikā, sarṣapikā, tvakpāka, avapāṭikā, māṃsapāka, sparśahāni, and niruddhamaṇi are the [twenty] uttamā [fever types]. 84.
Māṃsārbuda, Puṣkarikā, Saṃmūḍhapiḍikā,
Alajī (85), Raktārbuda, Vidradhi, Kumbhikā, Tilakālaka, Niruddhaprakaśa, and likewise Parivarttikā are described. (86)

Regarding the varieties of leprosy, eighteen types of *kuṣṭha* have been described: from *vāta* arises *kāpālika*, from *pitta* *udumbara* is said to arise, and from *kapha* arise *maṇḍala* and *carcikā*. (87)
From *marut* (vāta) and *pitta*, *ṛṣyajihva* arises; likewise, from *śleṣman* (kapha) and *vāta*, *vipādikā*.
Furthermore, *sidhma*, *ekakuṣṭha*, *kiṭibha*, and *alasa* [arise from the same].
Again, from *kapha* and *pitta*, *dadru*, *pāmā*, and *visphoṭaka* arise.

Mahākuṣṭha, carmadala, puṇḍarīka, and śatāruka—these are known to arise from the three doṣas; likewise, there is another called śivatrā. Furthermore, it occurs in three ways: through vāta, pitta, and śleṣman.
The minor diseases (kṣudraroga) are sixty in number; among them, first are śarkarārbuda, indravṛddhā, panasikā, vivṛtā, and likewise andhālajī. 91.
Varāhadaṃṣṭra, valmīka, kacchapī, tilakālaka, gardabhī, rakasā, yavaprakhyā, vidārikā,
kadara, maṣaka, nīlikā, and jālagardabha.
Irivelli, jatumaṇi, gudabhraṃśa, agnirohiṇī (93),
sanniruddhaguda, koṭha, kunakha, anuśayī, as well as padminīkaṇṭaka, cippa, alasa, and mukhadūṣikā (94).
Kakṣā, vṛṣaṇa, kacchū, gandha, pāṣāṇagardabha, and likewise rājikā—thus vyaṅga is proclaimed to be fourfold.
It has been stated that [these arise] from vāta, pitta, kapha, and rakta; such is the definition of vyaṅga.
Regarding the minor diseases (kṣudraroga), carbuncles (visphoṭa) are described as being of eight types:

three caused by the individual doṣas, three by their combinations (dvaṃdva), the seventh from blood (asṛj), and the eighth by the combination of all doṣas (sannipāta). Among the minor diseases, the masūrikā is [one such type]. 96–97.
It is said to be of fourteen types; it is threefold due to the three [humors], and of various kinds arising from two [humors]; the seventh is produced by the combination of all three (sannipāta).
The eighth is known as being located in the skin, and the ninth is remembered as being born from the blood.

The tenth [type] arises from the flesh; the other four, located in the fat, bone, marrow, and semen, are difficult to overcome and are called minor diseases (kṣudraroga). These are the varieties of visarpa.
The disease of visarpa (erysipelas) is of nine types: three caused by vāta, pitta, and kapha;
three by the combination of two doṣas (dvandva); the seventh by the combination of all three (sannipāta); the eighth by fire-burn; and the ninth is that born of trauma. 100–101.
Udarda and śītapitta constitute one [type of] disease; likewise, udarda is proclaimed to arise from both kapha and pitta.
Furthermore, one type of śītapitta disease is recorded as arising from vāta and pitta. 102
The varieties of *amlapitta*:
*Amlapitta* is said to be of three types— by *vāta*, by *śleṣman*,
and the third by both *śleṣman* and *vāta*.
The varieties of vātarakta are likewise eightfold:
[caused] by an excess of vāta, by pitta, by kapha, and by all three doṣas combined. (103)

Due to the predominance of blood, or through the combination of two humors (doṣas), it is known to be threefold. (104) The eighty varieties of wind diseases (vātaroga) spoken by the sages are now described.
Facial paralysis, lockjaw, thigh stiffness, rigidity of the head (105), external extension, internal extension, pain in the flanks, stiffness of the waist,
tetanus, lameness, tongue-stiffness, and likewise hiccups (106).
Hemiplegia, torticollis, stiffness of the neck, lameness, a knee-joint deformity like a *kalāya* seed, *tūnī*, *pratitūnī*, and general lameness;
