107. *pādaharṣa*, sciatica (*gṛdhrasī*), *viśvācī*, and *apabāhuka*.
Apatāna, vraṇāyāma, vātakaṇṭha, and apatantraka; 108.
aṅgabhedo (paining of the limbs), aṅgaśoṣa (wasting of the limbs), minminatva (nasal speech), gadgada (stammering), pratyaṣṭhīlā, aṣṭhīlikā, vāmanatva (dwarfism), and kubjatā (hunchback); 109.

Pain in the limbs, aching of the limbs, contraction, stiffness, and dryness; breaking of the limbs, displacement of the limbs, constipation, and hard stools; muteness, excessive yawning, frequent belching, and rumbling in the intestines—[these are the symptoms]. 110.
The movement of wind (vāta) causes throbbing, the distension of the vessels,
trembling, emaciation, a dusky complexion, delirium, frequent urination, loss of sleep, loss of perspiration, weakness, and a decline in strength.

Excessive discharge of semen, emaciation, loss of virility, instability of mind, hardness [of the body], a bad taste in the mouth, astringent taste in the mouth, flatulence, recurrent flatulence, and coldness [are the symptoms]. 113.

Horripilation, timidity, pricking pain, itching, loss of the sense of taste, loss of the sense of sound, numbness, loss of the sense of smell, and loss of vision— these are the various types of pitta diseases. (114)
Now, forty diseases arising from bile (pitta) are described here: 115.
There is smoky eructation, a burning sensation, heat in the limbs, confusion of mind, loss of luster, dryness of the throat, dryness of the mouth, and diminished semen. 116.
A bitter taste in the mouth, acidity of the face, discharge of sweat, inflammation of the limbs, exhaustion, a greenish complexion, lack of satiety, yellowness of the body,
discharge of blood, tearing of the limbs, and likewise a metallic odor in the mouth. 117.
Foul odor, yellow urine, restlessness, yellow feces,
yellow vision, yellow eyes, yellow teeth,
a desire for cold, yellow nails, aversion to light, and little sleep— 118–119.
Anger, exhaustion of the limbs, loose stools, blindness, hot breathing, and heat of the urine and excrement;
seeing darkness and seeing yellow circles [before the eyes]. 120.

The inability of the bile (pitta) to withstand [its own heat] is also mentioned; thus, forty diseases of pitta are recorded. Twenty varieties of phlegm (kapha) diseases have been declared, including lassitude (tandrā) and excessive sleepiness (atinidratā).
Dignity, sweetness of the mouth, coating of the mouth, salivation (122), looking at white things, having white excrement, having white urine,
whiteness of the complexion of the limbs, coldness, a desire for warmth, and a longing for bitter things (123).

Excess of impurity, abundance of semen, excessive urination, laziness, dullness of intellect, satiety, a gurgling voice, and lack of consciousness— these twenty diseases born of phlegm (kapha) have been described. 124
The varieties of blood diseases: ten diseases of the blood have been described; among them are heaviness, red circular patches, redness of the eyes, and redness of the urine. 125.
Spitting of blood, the appearance of blood-filled pustules, heat, a foul odor, pain, and suppuration arise; these are the varieties of mouth diseases (mukharoga). 126.
Thus, seventy-four types of diseases of the mouth have been described;
among those, eleven varieties of diseases of the lips have been enumerated by the wise.
Due to vāta, pitta, and kapha— thus by the three doṣas— as well as by blood, injury, and flesh, there are fleshy tumors (māṃsārbuda), cleft lip (khaṇḍoṣṭha), and watery tumors (jalārbuda);
along with fat-tumors (medo'rbuda) and simple tumors (arbuda), these are the eleven diseases arising in the lips.
The varieties of dental diseases: ten dental diseases are declared, namely dālana, kṛmidantaka, dantaharṣa,
karāla, dantacāla, and śarkarā.
Adhidanta, śyāvadanta, dantabheda, and kapālikā (130)—
these are the varieties of diseases of the roots of the teeth; likewise, thirteen such dental root ailments are recorded (131).
Śītāda, upakuśa, dantavidradhi, puppuṭa, adhimāṃsa, vidarbha, mahāsauṣira, and sauṣira—these are the [diseases];
in these very [locations], there are five types of courses arising from vāta, pitta, and kapha as well. 132.
From the combination [of humors], there is another type; the blood-vessel is the fifth.
(133) Thus, there are six varieties of tongue diseases, and these tongue ailments are threefold, arising from vāta, pitta, and kapha.
Alāsa is the fourth, and adhijihva is the fifth;
the sixth is ujjapajihva—these are the varieties of diseases of the palate. 134.
Likewise, there are eight diseases arising in the palate:
arbuda, tālupiṭikā, kacchapī, tālusaṃhati, galaśuṇḍī, tāluśoṣa, tālupāka, and puppuṭa. (135–136)
The varieties of throat diseases (galaroga) are thus known by the wise to be eighteen in number:
first, Vāta-rohiṇikā, and second, Pitta-rohiṇī.
Kapha-rohiṇikā is described, and by the three doṣas it is also called rohiṇī (137).
Medo-rohiṇikā, vṛnda, galaugha, galavidradhi, svarahā, tuṇḍikerī, śataghnī, śāluka, and abuda (138).
The galāyu (goiter), valaya (ring-like swelling), and likewise the gaṇḍa (tumor) from vāta, as well as the medogaṇḍa (fatty tumor)—these are the eighteen diseases arising in the throat. 139.
These are the specific types of diseases within the mouth.
Eight diseases originating within the mouth have been described by the great sages:

stomatitis (mukhapāka) may arise from vāta, likewise from pitta and from kapha; it may also arise from blood, from the combination of all three (sannipāta), and as putrid breath (pūtyāsya) or upward-moving hemorrhoids (ūrdhvaguda). 140
Including arbuda, there are seventy-four diseases originating in the mouth;
the varieties of ear diseases are declared by the wise to be eighteen in number.
Abscesses (vidradhi) arise from vāta, pitta, kapha, blood, and their combination (sannipāta). [The diseases of the ear are:

swelling (śotha), tumor (arbuda), putrid ear (pūtikarṇa), ear polyp (karṇārśas), ear-wax (karṇahallikā), deafness (bādhirya), eardrum perforation (tantrikā), itching (kaṇḍū), concha inflammation (śaṣkulī), and earworms (kṛmikarṇaka). 142–143.

Karna-nada (tinnitus) and Pratinaaha (obstruction of the ear canal)— these eighteen are the diseases arising from the ear (143). Seven types of diseases originating in the Karna-pali (the lobe of the ear) have been described here as varieties of ear-lobe disorders (144).
Utpāta, pāliśoṣa, vidārī, duḥkhavardhana,
paripoṭa, leha, and pippalī are recorded as the varieties of diseases affecting the root of the ear. 145.
There are five types of diseases at the root of the ear arising from vāta, pitta, kapha, sannipāta, and blood; likewise, there are various classifications of nasal diseases.
Likewise, diseases arising from the nose are numbered as eighteen;
among these, catarrh (pratiśyāya) is further classified into five types: those caused by vāta, pitta, kapha, rakta, and the fifth by the combination of all three (sannipāta).

Apīnasa (chronic rhinitis), pūtināsa (foul-smelling nose), nāsāśoṣa (nasal dryness), bhraṃśathu (nasal discharge), kṣava (sneezing), nāsānāha (nasal obstruction), pūti (foul odor), rakta (nasal hemorrhage), arbuda (nasal polyp), duṣṭapīnasa (morbid rhinitis), nāsāśoṣa (nasal atrophy), ghrāṇapāka (inflammation of the nose), pūyasrāva (purulent discharge), and dīptaka (nasal burning sensation). 148
The varieties of diseases of the head are likewise ten: hemiplegia, headache, and fever caused by *vāta*; affliction by *pitta*, and tertian fever. (149)

The fourth [type] is pain born of phlegm (kaphaja); those born of blood (raktaja), of the derangement of the humors (sannipātaja), from sūryāvarta, from head-tremor, from worms, and from śaṅkhaka—these are the varieties of diseases of the skull (kapālaroga). 150.
Likewise, there are nine diseases of the skull: upaśīrṣaka, aruṃṣikā, vidradhi, the terrible piṭikā, abuda, indralupta, khalita, and palita; these are the nine. 152.

Regarding the classifications of eye diseases, first are the classifications of diseases of the eyelids; thus, ninety-four diseases known to arise in the eyes are described, among which twenty-four are designated as diseases of the eyelids. 153
Kṛcchronmīla, Pakṣmapāta, Kaphotkliṣṭa, Lohita, Arun-nimeṣa, Raktotkliṣṭa, Kukūṇaka, Pakṣmārśas,
Pakṣmarodha, Pittotkliṣṭa, and Pothakī [are the diseases of the eyelids]. 154.
Kliṣṭavartman, Bahala, Pakṣmotsaṅga, Abuda, Kumbhikā, Sikatāvartman, Lagaṇa, Añjananāmikā,
Kardama, Śyāvavartman, Bisavartman, and likewise Alajī.

The diseases arising from the eyelids (vartman) are declared to be [the group] beginning with *utkliṣṭavartma* (156). Nine diseases originating in the eye-junction (*netrasaṃdhi*) have been proclaimed as the specific types of eye-junction disorders.
Jalasrāva, kaphasrāva, raktasrāva, parvaṇī, pūyasrāva, krimigranthi, upanāha, alajī,
and pūyālasa— these are declared to be the diseases arising from the joints of the eye. 157–158.
The specific types of diseases located in the white of the eye (śukla):
thus, thirteen diseases located in the white have been described by the wise:
śirotpāta, śirāharṣa, śirājāla, and śuktikā.
Śuklārma, adhimāṃsārma, prastāryarma, piṣṭaka,
sirājapiṭikā, kaphagrathitaka, ajuna, snāyvarma, and śoṇitārma— these are the diseases located in the white part of the eye (śukla). 160–161.
The specific types of diseases occurring in the black part of the eye (kṛṣṇa) are as follows: five diseases arising from the kṛṣṇa region are proclaimed,
namely śuddhaśukra, śirāśukra, kṣataśukra, and likewise ajakā.

All diseases of the head have been described, as well as those diseases pertaining to Kṛṣṇa (the pupil). Regarding the varieties of cataract (kāca), it should be known that cataract is of six types: from Vāta, Pitta, and Kapha [as well as blood, combined humors, and trauma].

The sixth type arises from the combination [of all three humors] and from blood; thus, there are six varieties of *timira* disease. These *timira*s are of three kinds, caused by *vāta*, *pitta*, and *kapha*.

Through association with blood, there is a sixth type arising from the combination of all three humors (sannipāta). (164) These are the varieties of the disease liṅganāśa; liṅganāśa is of seven types: [caused] by vāta, by pitta, and by kapha.
The various types of diseases of the visual field (dṛṣṭimaṇḍala) arise from the three doṣas, exogenous contagion,
and blood; thus, there are eight kinds of eye diseases, among which is pitta-vidagdha.
Amlapittavidagdha, as well as Uṣṇavidagdha;
Nakulāndhya, Dhūsarāndhya, Rātryandhya, Hrasvadṛṣṭika, and Gambhīradṛṣṭi—these are considered diseases located in the visual axis (dṛṣṭi). 166–167.
The varieties of *abhiṣyanda* disease:
there are four types of *abhiṣyanda*, namely those arising from blood and those from the three *doṣas*.
The varieties of *adhimantha* disease.
There are four types of *adhimantha* arising from vāta, pitta, kapha, and blood (169).
These are all the classifications of eye diseases; among them, there are eight [types], including the disorder caused by the reversal of vāta (*vātaviparyaya*).
Alpaśopha, anyatovāta, pākātyaya, śuṣkākṣipāka, adhyuṣita-śopha, and hatādhimantha— these diseases are known to arise from all parts of the eye. (170)

The specific diseases of virility, known as the defects of manhood, are said to be fivefold: namely, the envious (īrṣyaka), the ejaculatory (āsekya), the pot-like (kumbhīka), the fragrant (sugandhi), and the one designated as impotent (ṣaṇḍha). 171
The classifications of seminal defects (śukradoṣa) are likewise eightfold: arising from vāta, pitta, and kapha;
that which is like a corpse (kuṇapa) from kapha and vāta, and that which resembles pus (pūyābha) from kapha and pitta. 172

Defects of semen (śukradoṣa) are said to be: that which is diminished by vāta and pitta; that which is knotty (granthila) due to kapha and vāta; that which has the appearance of impurities (malābha) from the combination of all three humors (sannipāta); and others as previously described. (173) Now, the names of women's diseases:
Therein, the classifications of the defects of the menstrual flow (*ārtava*) are as follows;
now, the names of women's diseases are proclaimed according to the ancient scriptures:
there are eight defects of the menstrual flow, categorized triply by *vāta*, *pitta*, and *kapha*. (174)
Resembling pus, a corpse, a tumor, or like decayed filth—these are the varieties of *raktapradara*;
thus, *raktapradara* is declared to be fourfold. (175)
Gynecological diseases are of three types— caused by vāta, pitta, and kapha— and a fourth type arises from the combination of all three (sannipāta). Thus,
there are twenty varieties of gynecological disorders resulting from vāta, pitta, and kapha.
From the combination [of humors], from blood, and likewise from the depletion of blood;
also the withered, the vomiter, the fragmented, the inward-facing, the needle-mouthed, the overflowing, the child-killer, and the excessively overflowing. 177–178.

Upaplutā, Prākcaraṇā, Mahāyoni, Karṇinī, and Nandā with excessively long labia—these are declared to be the diseases of the female reproductive tract (yoniroga), which are variations of the yonikanda. 179. [End of] the classification of yonikanda.
The fourfold origin of the womb is threefold— due to wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (kapha)— and the fourth is due to the combination of all three (sannipāta);
these are the classifications of diseases of the fetus.
Likewise, there are eight types of diseases arising from the womb (180):
upaviṣṭaka-garbha, nāgodara, makkalla, mūḍha-garbha, viṣkambha, and gūḍha-garbhaka.
The defects of the placenta and the miscarriage of the fetus at the eighth month are recorded [as causes of death].
There are exactly five types of breast diseases; these breast diseases may arise from vāta, pitta, or kapha.
From the combination [of humors] and from injury,
there arise various disorders of breast milk, as well as diseases originating in the milk. 182
Regarding diseases of children, the various types of female defects have been described; three female defects are traditionally recognized. 183
One born from an unskilled man, one caused by a rival wife, and likewise one born by chance— these are the three types of diseases arising from childbirth.
Likewise, those diseases such as fever (jvara) and others arising from the puerperal state (sūtikā), which are to be treated according to the specific humor (doṣa) and the patient's strength,
are the various types of childhood diseases.
There are twenty-two diseases of childhood; among them, three arise from breast milk—those caused by vāta, pitta, and kapha—and the fourth is dantodbheda (eruption of teeth).
Then there are dantaghāta, dantaśabda, akāladanta, and ahipūtana. 186

Mukhapāka (inflammation of the mouth), mukhasrāva (salivation), gudapāka (inflammation of the anus), upaśīrṣaka (head-ache/fever), padmāruṇa (lotus-red [rash]), tālukaṇṭha (inflammation of the palate and throat), vicchinna (intermittent fever), pārīgarbhika (congenital disorders), daurbalya (weakness), gātraśoṣa (wasting of the limbs), śayyāmūtra (bed-wetting), and kukūṇaka (conjunctivitis). 187.
Weeping and ajagallī— thus twenty-two varieties are recorded (188). Likewise, twelve types of child-seizing spirits (bālagraha) are proclaimed by the lords of sages.
Skandagraha, Viśākha, Śvagraha, Pitṛgraha (189), Naigameyagraha, likewise Śakuni, Śītapūtanā, Mukhamaṇḍanikā, likewise Pūtanā, and Andhapūtanā.
Revatī is indeed enumerated, as well as Śuṣkarevatī (190).
There are various types of foot ailments and various diseases,
such as those affecting the feet, including gout (vātarakta) and others.

These forty-two types have been described by the lords of sages specifically regarding diseases; when including the various distinctions of the humors such as wind (vāta) and others, as well as those arising from the combination of all three humors (sannipāta) and so forth, there would be sixty-two varieties of the humors.
These too are reckoned among diseases; they are not mentioned separately anywhere.
The fifteen varieties of the five types of karma-diseases are proclaimed through the divisions of deficient, faulty, and excessive application.
The diseases arising from the five types of improper administration of therapeutic procedures are proclaimed among the very diseases themselves.
(193) The specific varieties of diseases resulting from deficient, excessive, or improper application of oleation and the other measures include:
oleation, sudation, fumigation, gargling, collyrium, and ocular saturation.
These eighteen [types of] secondary conditions arising from those [six primary causes] are observed in diseases;

one is considered to have cold as its secondary condition, and one is considered to have heat as its origin. (194) Cold, heat, foreign bodies, and caustics are the [primary] conditions, while cold and heat are each recognized as having their own specific secondary conditions.
One [type of treatment] is prescribed for complications from a splinter (śalya), and likewise one for those from caustic alkali (kṣāra).
Poison has various classifications; poison is threefold: stationary (sthāvara), mobile (jaṅgama), and artificial (kṛtrima). 195–196.
Among them, stationary poison (*sthāvaram viṣam*) is said to be ninefold, beginning with *kālakūṭa* and others;
mobile poison (*jaṅgamam*) is declared to be manifold. In that regard, spiders, serpents, scorpions, rats, and insects are each of four kinds. (197)
The poison of the fangs, the poison of the claws, as well as that from the hair, horns, and bones;
likewise from urine, feces, and semen; from the gaze, from the breath, and similarly from saliva and touch—these are considered the poisons of fear. (198–199)
Artificial poison is said to be of two kinds, distinguished as that which is administered by poisoning and that which is defiled;

it should be known as sevenfold, arising from the seven metals, and likewise sevenfold, born from the seven secondary minerals (upadhātu), and similarly considered sevenfold, originating from the secondary poisons (upaviṣa). 200.
There is one type of poison from contaminated water, and likewise one type of poison from poisoned arrows (201).
There is itching caused by *kapikacchū*, as well as itching caused by contaminated water;
furthermore, there is itching from *sūraṇa* and swelling caused by *bhallātaka* (202).
There are various types of intoxicants (*mada*); intoxication is of four kinds, and another is from *pūga*, *bhaṅgā*, *akṣa*, and *kodrava*.
Another fourfold type arises from substances derived from fruits, bark, roots, and leaves. (203)
This is the summary:
those afflictions well-known on earth that have been enumerated,
as well as the countless others arising from the bodily constituents, the root-elements, living beings, and so forth.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Enumeration of Diseases," in the first section of the *Śārṅgadharasaṃhitā*. With this, the first section is completed. [Now begins] the preparation of fresh juices and other formulations.
Now begins the first chapter on the preparation of fresh juices and other forms;
now the five types of decoctions (kaṣāyas);
and hereafter: fresh juice (svarasa), paste (kalka), decoction (kvātha), cold infusion (hima), and hot infusion (phāṇṭa).
These five decoctions (kaṣāya) should be known to become progressively lighter [in their potency] as they follow one after another.
Regarding the definition of *svarasa* (fresh juice):
one should extract it from a substance that has been crushed and immediately drawn out [of its juice] while still fresh.
The juice obtained by squeezing a cloth is called *svarasa* (fresh juice).
A second definition of *svarasa* is as follows:
one *kuḍava* of powdered substance is thrown into twice that amount of water.
Therefore, it should remain for a day and night, or else the juice shall be of the highest quality;
having taken a third part of the fresh juice, or a dried substance in the absence of fresh juices.

The substance should be boiled in eight times its quantity of water until one-fourth remains; it should be taken as a decoction (svarasa). Due to the heaviness of the decoction, one should employ half a *pala* as the dose.
One should drink one *pala* of the juice that has been dried and processed with fire. Regarding the substances to be added to the fresh juice and their respective quantities:
honey, white sugar, jaggery, salt, and likewise cumin.
One should add ghee, oil, and powders in quantities the size of a *kola* fruit into the juice.
Now, regarding the applications of fresh juices according to the disease:
in that regard, for urinary disorders (*prameha*), there is the fresh juice of *amṛtā* and the fresh juice of *dhātrī*.
The juice of *amṛtā* combined with honey conquers all types of *prameha*;
alternatively, the juice of *dhātrī* mixed with honey and powdered *haridrā* [is effective].
Furthermore, the fresh juice of *vāsaka* is used for conditions such as *raktapitta*.
The fresh juice of *vāsaka* should be drunk with honey; it conquers *raktapitta*, removes fever, cough, and consumption, and destroys jaundice, *kapha*, and *pitta*.
(8) In cases of jaundice, the fourfold fresh juices beginning with *triphalā* [should be used].
The juice of triphalā mixed with honey, or the juice of dārvī, or that of nimba, or of guḍūcī, when drunk, conquers jaundice (kāmalā).
In the case of irregular fever (viṣamajvara), the fresh juices of tulasī and droṇapuṣpī leaves [are used].

The juice derived from *tulasī* leaves or the juice of *droṇapuṣpī*, taken with powdered black pepper, destroys irregular fevers (*viṣamajvara*). In cases of bloody diarrhea (*raktātīsāra*), the fresh juice of *jambu* and other such fruits [is used].
The juice arising from the tender leaves of the *jambu*, mango, and *āmalakī*— when combined with honey, ghee, and milk— conquers even severe bloody diarrhea (11).
In all types of diarrhea, the fresh juices of the thornless *babbūla* leaves and the bark of *kuṭaja* and other such plants [are used].
The juice of the leaves of *sthūlababbūlikā*, when drunk, cures all types of diarrhea; alternatively, the juice of the bark of *śyonāka* and *kuṭaja* may be used.
In cases of scrotal swelling, Vāta disorders, catarrh, and similar conditions, the fresh juice of *ārdra* is beneficial.
The fresh juice of *ārdra* (Ardraka) mixed with honey cures impotence and wind disorders;
it destroys dyspnea, cough, and anorexia, and dispels catarrh.
In cases of pain in the flanks and similar conditions, the fresh juice of *bījapūra* (citron) is used.
The juice of *bījapūra* (citron), drunk with honey and alkali, conquers pain in the flanks, heart, and bladder, as well as severe abdominal wind (*koṣṭhavāta*).
In cases of *pitta*-type colic, the fresh juice of *śatāvarī* is used; for splenic disorders and *apacī* (scrofula), the fresh juice of *kanyā* (mañjiṣṭhā) is employed.
The juice of *śatāvarī* with honey is a remedy for pitta-type colic;
the juice of *kanyā* mixed with the powder of *niśā* removes splenic enlargement and scrofula.
In cases of scrofula and similar ailments, the fresh juice of *alambuṣā* [is used].
The fresh juice of Alambuṣā, drunk in a dose of two palas,
destroys scrofula, cervical lymphadenitis, and jaundice.
[Likewise,] the fresh juice of Sūryāvarta and Ardhamedaka, or of Muṇḍī...
The lukewarm juice of *śaśamuṇḍī*, sprinkled with black pepper,
conquers *sūryāvarta* and *ardhabheda* after seven days of practice.
In all cases of insanity (*unmāda*), [one should use] the four fresh juices of *brāhmī* and the others.
The fresh juices of *brāhmī*, *kūṣmāṇḍa*, *ṣaḍgranthā*, and *śaṅkhinī*,
taken separately and mixed with honey and *kuṣṭha*, when drunk, remove all forms of insanity.
In cases of intoxication caused by *kodrava* grain, the fresh juice of *kūṣmāṇḍaka* [is the remedy].
The fresh juice of *kūṣmāṇḍaka* combined with jaggery removes the intoxication produced by the consumption of spoiled kodrava grain when drunk.
The fresh juice of *gaṅgerukī* [is used] for wounds from injuries such as sword cuts.
The wound of one whose body has been cut by a sword or other weapon is instantly filled and becomes free from pain when treated with the juices of the roots of *Gāṅgerūkī*. 20.
Now begins the section on *puṭapāka* (herbal steaming).
In this regard, the reason for describing the procedure for *puṭapāka* is that the fresh juice (*svarasa*) of the paste (*kalka*) is obtained through it;
therefore, the method for *puṭapākas* is stated here by me. (21)
The procedure for *puṭapāka*: this is the measure for *puṭapāka*; the coating should be charcoal-colored, and one should make the coating two fingers thick or the size of a thumb. 22.
Wrapping [the fruit] with leaves of *kāśmarī*, *vaṭa*, *jambu*, and so forth is excellent; one *pala* of juice should be taken, and one *karṣa* of honey should be added.
As for pastes, powders, liquids, and the like, they should be administered by the wise in the same manner as the fresh juice. 23.
For all types of diarrhea, there is this *kuṭaja* leaf-packet preparation (*puṭapāka*):
the bark of *kuṭaja* freshly extracted at that time, ground with rice-water in a measure of four *palas*, and wrapped in *jambū* leaves. (24)
Bound with thread, wrapped in wheat flour,
and smeared with thick mud, one should burn it with cow-dung fire;
and seeing that the clay has become the color of charcoal, one should remove it from the fire.

Then, having extracted the juice, one should drink it cold combined with honey; this conquers all types of diarrhea, even those difficult to overcome and long-standing. (27) This is the procedure for rice-water.

One *pala* of husked rice should be placed in water eight times its quantity; having infused it, the water should be taken and used in all ritual applications. (28) In all cases of diarrhea, the *puṭapāka* preparation of *aralu* is used.
Pulpa-cooking (puṭapāka) prepared with the bark of *aralu* stimulates the digestive fire;
when combined with honey and *mocarasa*, it cures all types of diarrhea.
In the case of all forms of diarrhea, this is the *nyagrodhādi-tittiri-puṭapāka*.
One should fill the entrails-free belly of a white partridge with a paste of *nyagrodha* and other such drugs, and cook it properly by the *puṭapāka* method;
the juice of that paste, when combined with honey, cures all types of diarrhea. (30)
In all types of diarrhea, one should cook pomegranate juice by the *puṭapāka* method until it is well-cooked; that juice, when combined with honey, destroys all forms of diarrhea. (31)
For vomiting, there is a *puṭapāka* preparation using *bījapūra* and other fruits:
one should cook separately the tender leaves and roots of *bījapūra*, mango, and *jambu*; that juice, when combined with honey, [is the remedy]. (32)
It wards off severe vomiting arising from all the doṣas.
In cases such as raktapitta,
the cold decoction obtained from the puṭapāka of ground vāsā leaves is beneficial.

Combined with honey, it conquers raktapitta, cough, fever, and consumption. (34) For cough, dyspnea, and similar ailments, one should cook kṣudrā along with its five parts using the puṭapāka method; that juice [is used].
Combined with powdered pippalī, it removes cough, dyspnea, and phlegm. (35) Regarding the *bibhītaka* fruit poultice (*puṭapāka*) for cough and other ailments:
one should slightly anoint a *bibhītaka* fruit with ghee and apply [the paste].
One should cook it with wheat flour over charcoal in the manner of *puṭapāka*.
Then, having removed it once cooked, one should apply its skin to the mouth;
from this, one will conquer cough, dyspnea, catarrh, and hoarseness of voice.
In cases of diarrhea caused by undigested matter (āmātīsāra), a *puṭapāka* preparation of ginger is used:
a small amount of powdered ginger, smeared with ghee, should be wrapped in castor leaves and cooked by the *puṭapāka* method over a low fire. 38.

Then, having extracted that powder, one should take it in the morning in an amount equal to sugar; by this, the pains arising from *āmātīsāra* (diarrhea caused by undigested matter) are pacified. (39) Another method for *āmavāta* is *śuṇṭhī-puṭapāka*.

Having added a paste of ginger, one should cook it with the juices extracted from castor roots using the *puṭapāka* method; that juice, when combined with honey, overcomes even difficult-to-cure pain arising from *āmavāta*. 40
In the case of hemorrhoids, a *puṭapāka* preparation of *sūraṇa* (wild ginger) is used:
having taken a *sūraṇa* tuber, one should cook it by the *puṭapāka* method; its juice, combined with oil and salt, cures the disorder of hemorrhoids. 41.

In cases of heart pain, one should drink the ash of deer horn produced by *puṭapāka* cooking, having burnt the horn of a deer inside a pair of earthen saucers; when combined with cow’s ghee, it will certainly destroy heart pain. 42
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Formulations of Fresh Juices and Other Preparations," in the Middle Section of the *Śrīśārṅgadharasaṃhitā*.
Now begins the second chapter, titled "The Formulations of Decoctions" (*kvāthakalpanā*).
Regarding the preparation of a decoction:
one should take one pala of the crushed drug and add sixteen times as much water;
it should be boiled in an earthen vessel until one-eighth remains, and this residue should be collected.
The wise physician should cause that water to be drunk lukewarm, having been prepared over a mild fire.
"Śṛta," "kvātha," "kaṣāya," and "niryūha" are synonyms for a decoction.

The time for drinking the decoction is when the digestion of the food's essence has occurred; then, following the instruction of experienced physicians, one should drink two *pala*s of the well-prepared decoction. (3)
Regarding the quantity for adding sugar and honey to a decoction:
one should add sugar to the decoction in portions of one-fourth, one-eighth, or one-sixteenth [of the decoction's weight];
however, in cases of disorders caused by Vāta, Pitta, and Kapha, honey is prescribed in the reverse order. 4.
Regarding the quantity for adding powdered substances:
one should add one *śāṇa* each of cumin, guggulu, alkali, salt, *śilājatu*, asafoetida, and the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*) to the decoction. 5.

Regarding the quantity of liquids to be added— milk, ghee, jaggery, oil, urine, or other such liquids— as well as pastes, powders, and so forth, one should throw in a measure of one karṣa into the decoction. 6.
Regarding the prohibition against covering the vessel while boiling:
water in a vessel whose mouth is covered becomes difficult to digest;
therefore, one should determine the preparation of decoctions and the like only after removing the cover. (7)

In all fevers and in conditions such as burning sensations, a decoction of *guḍūcī* and other ingredients is used; a decoction of the *guḍūcyādi* group consisting of *guḍūcī*, *dhānyaka*, *ariṣṭa*, red sandalwood (*raktacandana*), and *padmaka* is traditionally held to alleviate all fevers.
It is digestive and overcomes burning sensations, heartburn, nausea, thirst, vomiting, and loss of appetite.
(8) This is the digestive decoction of ginger and other ingredients for all fevers:
ginger (*nāgara*), *devadāru*, coriander (*dhānyaka*), and the two types of *bṛhatī*.
One should first administer the digestive decoction (pācanaka) for those suffering from fever, as it removes fever;
in all fevers, a decoction of kṣudrā and others is used—
namely, kṣudrā, kirātatikta, śuṇṭhī, chinnā, and pauṣkara.
This decoction, when drunk, pacifies their eightfold fever.
(10) [In fever caused by Vata,
the decoction of the Guḍūcyādi group.]
A digestive decoction made from *guḍūcī*, *pippalīmūla*,
and *nāgara* is prescribed on the seventh day for a case of vāta-fever exhibiting full symptoms; or one may administer a decoction of the *śālaparṇy-ādi* group.
One should drink the lukewarm decoction of śālaparṇī, balā, drākṣā, guḍūcī, and sārivā; this destroys even severe vāta-fever. (12) This is the decoction of kāśmaryādi.
A decoction of *kāśmarī*, *sārivā*, *drākṣā*, *trāyamāṇā*, and *amṛtā* (guḍūcī), when drunk with jaggery, destroys vāta-fever. 13.
Decoctions for pitta-fever.
A decoction for digestion (pācana) made from kaṭphala and other ingredients—
water boiled with kaṭphala, indrayava, pāṭhā, tiktā, and musta—
should be administered on the tenth day for men suffering from severe pitta-type fever. 14
A decoction of parpaṭa and other herbs—
namely parpaṭa, vāsaka, tiktā, kairāta, dhanvayāsaka,
and priyaṅgu— prepared with these and combined with sugar [is used].
A decoction of raisins and other ingredients overcomes pitta-fever accompanied by thirst, burning sensations, and an excess of bile (pittāśaya).
16. The *drākṣādi-kvātha* consists of raisins (*drākṣā*), chebulic myrobalan (*harītakī*), nut-grass (*musta*), bitter melon (*kaṭukī*), and *kṛtamālaka*.
A decoction made from these, including *parpaṭa*, removes pitta-fever; it is known to alleviate thirst, fainting, burning sensations, pitta-blood disorders, and acts as a purgative.
(17) Regarding the praise of the *parpaṭa* decoction, there is a specific detail therein:
A single *parpaṭaka* is excellent for destroying fever caused by *pitta*;
how much more so if it is combined with *candana*, *uśīra*, and *bālaka*!
(18) Now, the decoctions for fever caused by *kapha*.

In that regard, the decoction for ripening [the fever] consists of citron and other such ingredients; a decoction prepared with the root of citron, chebulic myrobalan, ginger, and patchouli, along with alkali, is a digestive agent for phlegm-fever on the twelfth day. (19)
A decoction of bhūnimba,
nimba, pippalī, śaṭī, śuṇṭhī, śatāvarī, guḍūcī, and bṛhatī destroys fever caused by kapha. (20)
A decoction of paṭola and other herbs— consisting of paṭola, triphalā, tiktā, śaṭī, vāsā, and amṛtā—
when drunk mixed with honey, destroys fever caused by kapha. (21)
Now, regarding decoctions for fevers born of dual combinations (*dvandvaja-jvara*):
therein, for a fever arising from *vāta* and *pitta*, there is the *pañcabhadra* decoction, water prepared with *parpaṭa*, *abda*, *amṛtā*, *viśva*, and *kirāta*.
This "Five-Excellent" (Pañcabhadra) formulation should be known as a remedy for fever caused by vāta and pitta.
For fevers arising from kapha and vāta and similar conditions, a decoction of small quantities of *kṣudrā* and so forth is used;
likewise, a decoction of *kṣudrā*, ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), *guḍūcī*, and *pauṣkara*.

In fever characterized by a predominance of *kapha* and *vāta*, or even in fever arising from all three *doṣas*, this decoction should be drunk when it causes cough, dyspnea, anorexia, and pain in the flanks;
[this refers to] the *āragvadhādi* decoction for fever caused by *vāta* and *kapha*.

A decoction prepared from āragvadha, kaṇā, mūla, mustā, tiktā, and abhayā quickly pacifies fever arising from vāta and kapha; it alleviates āma-type colic, acts as a purgative, stimulates digestion, and promotes the digestion of undigested matter (pācana). 25.
In fever caused by pitta and kapha, a decoction of the eight ingredients beginning with amṛtā—
consisting of amṛtā, ariṣṭa, kaṭukā, mustā, indrayava, nāgara, paṭola, and candana— is boiled and mixed with the powder of pippalī. (26)
This Amṛtāṣṭaka (the group of eight nectars) cures fever caused by pitta and kapha; it destroys vomiting, anorexia, nausea, burning sensations, and thirst.
For fevers arising from pitta and kapha and similar conditions, there is the decoction of paṭola and other herbs.

The group consisting of paṭola, candana, mūrvā, tiktā, pāṭhā, and amṛtā removes pitta-śleṣma fever, vomiting, burning sensations, itching, and poison. (28) In all fevers, a decoction of kaṇṭakārī and others [is used].
The two types of *kaṇṭakārī*, *śuṇṭhī*, *dhānyaka*, and *suradāru*: a decoction prepared with these acts as a digestive (pācana) and destroys all fevers.
Now, the decoctions for *sannipāta* fever:
In that case, there is a decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla) combined with śāliparṇī, pṛśniparṇī, the two types of bṛhatī, gokṣura, bilva, agnimantha, śyonāka, kāśmarī, and pāṭalā.

One should drink that water boiled with what is known as *daśamūla*, mixed with powdered *pippalī*; it removes fever caused by *vāta* and *kapha*, cures *sannipāta* fever, and destroys the disorders of childbirth (*sūtikā-doṣa*). 31–32.
A decoction of Abhayā and other ingredients— namely Abhayā, Mustā, Dhānyaka, Raktacandana, and Padmaka— removes pain in the heart, throat, and sides, as well as drowsiness and headache. (33)
One should drink water boiled with vāsaka, kendra, yava, uśīra, guḍūcī, kṛtamālaka,
pāṭhā, nāgara, and tiktā, combined with the powder of pippalī;
this conquers fever born of the three doṣas and alleviates thirst, cough, and burning sensations.

The decoction of Pippalyādi is a supreme digestive stimulant and carminative; it destroys excessive talking, labored breathing, and drowsiness, and it cures constipation of feces, urine, and flatus, as well as vomiting, dryness, and anorexia. (36) Pippalyādi-kvātha.
Pippalī, pippalīmūla, cavya, citraka, nāgara, vacā, sātiviṣā, ajājī, pāṭhā, vatsaka, reṇukā,
kirātatiktaka, mūrvā, sarṣapa, and marica. (37)
Kaṭuka, puṣkara, bhārṅgī, viḍaṅga, karkaṭāhvaya (38), arka-root, bṛhatsiṃhī, śreyasī, along with durālabhā,
dīpyaka, ajamodā, śukanāsā, and the various types of hiṅgu (39).
These ingredients taken in equal parts constitute the group known as the "twenty-eight-fold" (aṣṭāviṃśaka-gaṇa); one should consume this decoction to alleviate fever caused by vāta and kapha.
It destroys vāta, coldness, and powerful kapha born of perspiration.
It cures incoherent speech, excessive sleep, horripilation, and loss of appetite (41).
It also cures great wind disorders, prolapse of the rectum, and a sense of emptiness in all limbs; this [formula] destroys all fevers and the thirteen types of *sannipāta* (42).
The decoction of eighteen ingredients consists of *kirātatikta*, *kaṭukī*, *mustā*, *dhānyaka*, *indrayava*, and *nāgara*, combined with *daśamūla*, *mahādāru*, and *gajapippalī*. (43)
The decoction of *kaṭphala* and other ingredients, when prepared, overcomes pain in the sides, fever caused by the derangement of the humors (*sannipāta*),
cough, dyspnea, vomiting, hiccup, drowsiness, and the oppression of the heart. (44) The *kaṭphalādi-kvātha*.

A decoction made from kaṭphala, ambuda, bhārṅgī, dhānya, rohiṣa, parpaṭa, vacā, harītakī, śṛṅgī, devadāru, and mahauṣadha cures hiccup, cough, fever, dyspnea, phlegm disorders, and throat obstructions. 45
A decoction of *guḍūcī* for chronic fever (*jīrṇajvara*), and a decoction of *parpaṭa* for bile-fever (*pittajvara*):
a decoction of *guḍūcī* combined with *pippalī* destroys chronic fever (46),
and likewise, a decoction derived from *parpaṭa* is supreme for removing bile-fever.
How much more so, then, if it were appropriate to use sandalwood, uśīra, and nāgara?
In chronic fever, the physician should administer a decoction of nidigdhikā and other such herbs; specifically, he should have the patient drink a decoction of nidigdhikā, amṛtā, and śuṇṭhī.
Combined with the powder of *pippalī*, it removes afflictions caused by asthma and cough; it destroys chronic rhinitis (*pīnasa*), anorexia, hoarseness, colic, indigestion, and fever.
(48) In cases of complications following childbirth, a decoction of *devadāru* and other ingredients [is prescribed].
Devadāru, vacā, kuṣṭha, pippalī, and viśvabheṣaja (49);
kaṭphala, musta, bhūnimba, tiktā, dhānyaka, harītakī, gajakṛṣṇā, duḥsparśā, gokṣura, and dhanvayāsaka (50).
A woman who has recently given birth should be made to drink a decoction of *bṛhatī*, *ativiṣā*, *chinnā*, *karkaṭa*, and black cumin (*kṛṣṇajīraka*), boiled down to one-eighth its original volume;
this conquers colic, cough, fever, dyspnea, fainting, tremors, and headache. (51)
Now, regarding decoctions for irregular fevers (viṣamajvara):

therein, for an irregular fever preceded by cold, there is the decoction of *bṛhat-kṣudrā* and others; [the decoction] of *kṣudrā*, coriander (*dhānyaka*), dry ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), *guḍūcī*, nut-grass (*musta*), and lotus stalks (*padmaka*).

One should consume in the morning an equal-weighted decoction of red sandalwood (*raktacandana*), *bhūnimba*, *paṭola*, *vṛṣa*, *pauṣkara*, *kaṭuka*, *indrāyava*, *ariṣṭa*, *bhārṅgī*, and *parpaṭaka*; this destroys all types of chronic fever (*śītajvara*).
A decoction of mustā and other herbs [is effective] for irregular fever (viṣamajvara).
A decoction of mustā, kṣudrā, amṛtā, śuṇṭhī, and dhātrī, combined with honey and mixed with powdered pippalī, destroys irregular fever. 54
In cases of continuous fever (santata) and other types, one should drink a decoction of paṭola, indrayava, dāru, triphalā, musta, and go-stana;
or one should drink a decoction of madhuka, amṛtā, and vāsā mixed with honey. (55)

In cases of continuous fever (*santata*), quotidian (*dvitīyaka*) or tertian (*tṛtīyaka*) fever, or in acute fever (*navajvara*) characterized by irregular intervals or preceded by a burning sensation (verse 56),
a decoction of *paṭola* and other ingredients is used for the quotidian fever.
A decoction of *paṭola*, *triphalā*, *nimba*, *drākṣā*, *śamyāka*, and *vāsaka*,
combined with sugar and honey, overcomes quotidian fever (*aikāhika-jvara*).
(57) For tertian fever (*tṛtīyaka-jvara*), there is the decoction of *guḍūcī* and others.
A patient suffering from fever should drink a decoction prepared with *guḍūcī*, coriander, *mustā*, sandalwood, *uśīra*, and ginger, combined with honey and sugar;
this destroys tertian fever and relieves thirst and burning sensations. (58–59)
A decoction of *devadāru* and other herbs for quartan fever:
in cases of quartan fever, dyspnea, cough, and weak digestive fire, [one should use] *devadāru*, *śivā*, *vāsā*, *śāliparṇī*, and *mahauṣadha*.
One should administer this decoction, boiled with *dhātrī*, cooled, and combined with honey and sugar (60).
This is the *guḍūcyādi* decoction for fever and diarrhea,
prepared from *guḍūcī*, *dhānyaka*, *uśīra*, *śuṇṭhī*, *bālaka*, and *parpaṭa*.
One should drink a cooled decoction of bilva, prativiṣā, pāṭhā, red sandalwood, vatsaka, kirātatikta, musta,
and indrayava, mixed with honey; it destroys raktapitta and cures fever and diarrhea.
One should drink a decoction prepared from these: ginger, *kuṭaja*, *musta*, *bhūnimba*, *ativiṣā*, and *amṛtā*; it destroys fever and diarrhea. (63)
In cases of colic due to undigested matter (āma-śūla), a decoction of the five grains (dhānyapañcaka) is used;
water prepared with coriander, balaka, bilva, usira, and ginger removes āma-śūla, is constipating, stimulates digestion, and is an excellent digestive aid. 64
In the case of *āmavāta*, a decoction of coriander and ginger is digestive and appetizing; when combined with castor root, it overcomes the pain of *āmavāta* caused by wind. (65)
A decoction of vatsaka and others—
prepared from vatsaka, ativiṣā, bilva, musta, and bālaka— when boiled,
conquers chronic diarrhea accompanied by undigested matter (āmātisāra), as well as blood-stained diarrhea and pain. (66)
In all types of diarrhea, a decoction of the eight *kuṭaja* drugs is used;
a decoction prepared from *kuṭaja*, *ativiṣā*, *pāṭhā*, *dhātakī*, *lodhra*, *mustaka*, *hrībera*, and pomegranate, combined with honey, [is likewise effective]. (67)
This drink, known as *kuṭajāṣṭaka*, prepared with *mocarasa* alone,
conquers diarrhea that is difficult to overcome, characterized by burning sensations, blood, and colic. (68) For chronic diarrhea, a decoction of *hrībera* and other ingredients [is recommended].
A decoction prepared from *hrībera*, *dhātakī*, *lodhra*, *pāṭhā*, *lajjālu*, *vatsaka*,
*dhānyaka*, *ativiṣā*, *mustā*, *guḍūcī*, *bilva*,
and *nāgara* will pacify chronic diarrhea.
It is known to destroy anorexia, colic, hemorrhaging, and fever, and acts as a digestive (pācana). 70.
In cases of diarrhea in children, a decoction of dhātakī and other ingredients is used:
dhātakī, bilva, rodhra, bālaka, and gajapippalī.

One should administer these prepared as a paste (kṛta), a decoction (śṛta), or a cold infusion (śīta), combined with honey, either as a linctus (avaleha) for children to alleviate all types of diarrhea.
In cases of vātika grahaṇī, a decoction of the śāliparṇyādi group [should be used].

A decoction prepared from śāliparṇī, balā, bilva, dhānyaka, and śuṇṭhī conquers vāta-type grahaṇī accompanied by flatulence and colic (72). Furthermore, in the case of grahaṇī with undigested matter (āma), a decoction of cāturbhadra is used.
A decoction prepared from *guḍūcī*, *ativiṣā*, *śuṇṭhī*, and *mustā* overcomes *grahaṇī* associated with undigested matter (*āma*); it is astringent, digestive, and carminative.
In all types of diarrhea, the decoction of *indrayava* and other ingredients [is recommended].

A decoction of *yava*, *dhānya*, and *paṭola*, combined with honey and sugar, should be administered in all types of diarrhea; likewise, a decoction derived from *bilva* and the stones of the mango is used.
Furthermore, a decoction of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) is used in cases of parasitic disease (*kṛmiroga*).
A decoction prepared from Triphalā, Devadāru, Musta, Mūṣakaparṇikā, and Śigru, combined with the powder of Pippalī and Viḍaṅga powder,
destroys worms and cures worm-related diseases. (75–76)

A decoction of the three fruits (triphalā) and so forth [is used] for jaundice and other ailments; likewise, a decoction of the three fruits, amṛtā, tiktā, nimba, kairāta, and vāsaka, taken with honey, overcomes jaundice as well as anemia (pāṇḍutā). (77)
In cases such as pale edema (pāṇḍu-śotha), a decoction of punarnavā and others is used:
a decoction made from punarnavā, abhayā, nimba, dārvī,
tiktā, paṭola, guḍūcī, and nāgara, combined with cow’s urine.

The decoction of vāsā and other herbs cures anemia, cough, dyspnea, colic, and swelling of the entire body. A decoction of vāsā, drākṣā, and abhayā, when drunk with honey and sugar, [is effective] against raktapitta and similar conditions.

It destroys severe afflictions of internal hemorrhage (raktapitta), dyspnea, and cough. (80) Regarding decoctions for internal hemorrhage and similar conditions: [this] Vāsaka decoction likewise cures internal hemorrhage, consumption, cough, and fever caused by phlegm and bile.
Vāsaka decoction alone, when drunk with honey,
destroys cough; a double decoction of vāsaka, kṣudrā, and amṛtā, taken with honey, cures fever and cough.
Kṣudrā boiled with pippalī powder cures cough; likewise,
a decoction of kṣudrā and other herbs, prepared with kṣudrā, kulattha, vāsā, and nāgara, cures both asthma and cough.
A decoction enriched with *puṣkara* powder will ward off asthma and cough. (83) A decoction of *reṇukā* and *pippalī*, combined with a paste of *hiṅgu*, [achieves the same].
Indeed, by drinking it alone, even all five types of hiccup are destroyed in an instant.
(84) In cases of vomiting, one should take a decoction of the three [substances], or a decoction of *bilva* bark and *guḍūcī* combined with honey.
Parpaṭa conquers vomiting born of the three doṣas as well as that born of pitta;
a double decoction enriched with the powders of hiṅgu and puṣkara, boiled with daśamūla, conquers gṛdhrasī.
A decoction made solely from *śephālī* leaves likewise cures *gṛdhrasī*.
For vāta affecting all seven tissues (*dhātu*), a decoction of the "five [drugs] with *rāsnā*"—
prepared with *rāsnā*, *amṛtā*, *mahādāru*, *nāgara*, and *eraṇḍa*— should be administered.

When wind (vāta) has entered the seven bodily constituents (dhātu) and is accompanied by undigested matter (sāma), causing pain throughout all limbs, one should drink the decoction of the "Seven-Ingredient Rāsnā" (rāsnāsaptaka):
namely, rāsnā, gokṣuraka, eraṇḍa, devadāru, and punarnavā. This is for conditions such as jaṅghāvāta and others.
One should boil a decoction of *guḍūcī* and *āragvadha*,
and drink it combined with powdered *śuṇṭhī* in cases of stiffness in the calves and waist,
pain in the sides, back, and thighs, and in extremely difficult *āmavāta*. (88–89)
In all diseases of Vāta, there is this Mahārāsnādi decoction:
Rāsnā should be in double parts, while each of the others—Dhanvayāsa, Balā, Eraṇḍa, Devadāru, Śaṭī, and Vacā—should be in one part. (90)
Vāsaka, ginger, harītakī, cavya, mustā, punarnavā, guḍūcī, vṛddhadāru, śatapuṣpā, gokṣura, aśvagandhā, prativiṣā, kṛtamāla, and śatāvarī. 91.
One should drink a decoction prepared from Pippalī, Sahacara, Dhānyaka, and the two types of Bṛhatī (92), combined with powdered Śuṇṭhī,
or with powdered Pippalī, or with Yogarāja-guggulu (93).
Or else, with oil made from *ajamodā* and other herbs, or with castor oil (*airaṇḍaja*),
[one should treat] trembling of all limbs, hunchbackedness, hemiplegia, avabāhuka, sciatica,
*āmavāta*, elephantiasis, and tetanus.
In cases of intestinal hernia, flatulence, and pain extending from the calves to the knees;
in disorders of semen, diseases of the penis, sterility, and vaginal ailments— the Mahārāsnādi formulation was proclaimed by Brahmā as the cause for conception.
For wind located in the breasts and other areas, a decoction of the seven *eraṇḍa* roots is used;
[the roots] of *eraṇḍa*, *bījapūra*, *gokṣura*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, *aśmabheda*, and *bilva*—a decoction prepared from these roots [is the remedy]. 97.
Castor oil enriched with asafoetida (hiṅgu), along with barley-alkali (yavakṣāra) and rock salt (saindhava),
conquers pain arising in the breasts, shoulders, waist, penis, and heart.
In cases of Vāta-type colic (vātaśūla), one should administer the decoctions of the Nāgarādi group and the two types of Yava.

A decoction of *nāgara* (ginger) and *eraṇḍa* (castor), or a decoction of *indrāyava* combined with *hiṅgu* (asafoetida) and *sauvarcala* salt, alleviates Vata-type colic (99). In Pitta-type colic, a decoction of *triphalā* and other [pitta-alleviating] drugs is used.
A decoction of triphalā and āragvadha, combined with sugar and honey,
cures raktapitta (hemorrhagic disorders) and alleviates burning sensations, pitta-related ailments, and colic.
(100) For colic caused by kapha, a decoction of eraṇḍa is used.
Two palas of castor root should be boiled in eight times its quantity of water;
that decoction, enriched with *yavaśūka*, cures pain in the sides, the heart, and disorders of *kapha*.
(101) In cases of heart disease (*hṛdroga*) and similar ailments, a decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūla*) is used.
A decoction made from the ten roots (daśamūla), combined with barley-alkali (yavakṣāra) and rock salt (saindhava),
destroys heart disease, abdominal tumors (gulma), colic, cough, and dyspnea.
(102) Regarding dysuria and similar conditions, there is the decoction of harītakī and others.
A decoction made from *harītakī*, *durālambhā*, *kṛtamāla*, *gokṣura*,
and *pāṣāṇabheda*, combined with honey,
is beneficial for constipation, dysuria, burning sensations, and pain. (103)
In diseases such as urinary calculi (*aśmarī*), a decoction of the *vīratarvādi* group is used:
*vīrataru*, *vṛkṣavandā*, *kāśa*, the three *sahacara*s, the two types of *kuśa*, *nala*, *gundrā*, *bakapuṣpa*, and *agnimantha*. (104)
Mūrvā, pāṣāṇabheda, syonāka, gokṣura, apāmārga, kamala, and brāhmī constitute the excellent group known as vīratarvādi; it cures gravel, urinary stones, and dysuria. 105.

This decoction of cardamom and other herbs destroys all urinary obstructions (mūtrāghāta) as well as all diseases caused by Vāyu, such as gravel (śarkarā) and urinary stones (aśmarī). [106–107] Cardamom (elā), licorice (madhuka), gokaṇṭa, reṇuka, castor plant (eraṇḍa), and vāsaka—[these are the ingredients]. [107]
A well-prepared decoction of these [drugs] together with *kṛṣṇā* and *aśmabheda*, combined with *śilājatu*, should be drunk; it cures urinary gravel, stones, and dysuria.
(108) Regarding dysuria and similar conditions, a decoction of *gokṣura* [is recommended].
A decoction of gokṣura with its roots, combined with sugar and honey, destroys dysuria as well as the heat of the bodily winds. 109.
Now, the decoctions for prameha (diabetes/mellitus).
The decoction of *varā* and others, the decoction of *vatsaka* and others, and the decoction of *varā*, *dārvī*, *abhda*, and *dāru* taken with honey destroy urinary disorders (*meha*).
Likewise, *vatsaka*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *dārvī*, *mustaka*, and *bījaka* [are effective]. (110)
One should drink a decoction of triphalā, musta, dārvī, and viśālā, combined with a paste of niśā, for the alleviation of all types of prameha. (111)
In cases of menorrhagia,
one should drink the cooled decoction of dārvī, rasāñjana, musta, bhallāta, śrīphala, vṛṣa, and kairāta, mixed with honey.

One shall conquer dysentery accompanied by pain, as well as vaginal discharges that are yellow, white, black, or reddish, and diseases such as vaginal ulcers, by means of a decoction of the Nyagrodhādi group.
This group consists of Nyagrodha, Plakṣa, Kośāmra, Vetasa, Badarī, and Tuṇi. (112)
Licorice, priyāla, the two types of lodhra, udumbara, pippala, madhūka, as well as pāriṣa-pippala,
śallakī, tindukī, the two types of jambū, the mango tree, and śivā. 113–114.
One should also prepare a decoction of kadamba, kakubha, and bhallātaka fruits, as well as the nyagrodhādi group of drugs, according to their availability.
This decoction is a great absorbent (hemostatic), promotes wound healing, and cures fractures.
It removes disorders of the female reproductive tract and cures burning sensations, obesity, urinary disorders, and poison. (116) Now, three formulations for disorders of fat:
bilva, agnimantha, syonāka, kāśmarī, and likewise pāṭalā.
The decoction of these [drugs], combined with honey, overcomes disorders of the fat (medas). A decoction of Triphalā drunk with honey is known to remove fat.
Likewise, cold water or warm water mixed with honey removes fat.
For abdominal diseases,
a decoction of *cavya*, *citraka*, and *viśva* prepared with *devadāru*, combined with the powder of *trivṛt* and administered with cow’s urine, shall conquer abdominal enlargements. (119)
Regarding dropsy (śothodara), a decoction of Punarnavā and others— prepared with punarnavā, amṛtā, dāru, pathyā, and nāgara,
combined with cow’s urine and guggulu— is a decoction that removes dropsy. (120)
In cases of liver disease, spleen enlargement, abdominal tumors, and abdominal dropsy, one should drink a decoction of *pathyā* and other herbs;

or, for the alleviation of liver disease, spleen enlargement, abdominal tumors, and abdominal dropsy, one should drink in the morning a decoction of *pathyā* and *rohitaka* combined with barley alkali and *kaṇā*. 121.
For swelling (śotha), a decoction of the *punarnavā* group is used:
*punarnavā*, *dāruniśā*, *niśā*, *śuṇṭhī*, *harītakī*, *guḍūcī*, *citraka*, *bhārṅgī*, and *devadāru*; [the decoction] is boiled with these.
One should ward off swelling that has reached the hands, feet, abdomen, or face.
In the case of swelling of the testicles, one should administer a decoction of the three fruits (triphalā) along with cow’s urine.
It destroys swelling of the testicles caused by vāta and kapha.
(124) For intestinal hernia (antravṛddhi), there is a decoction of the Rāsnādi group:
rāsnā, amṛtā, balā, yaṣṭī, gokaṇṭa, and eraṇḍa, boiled together.
Combined with castor oil, it overcomes [the disease] arising from the *vṛddhi* mantra.
In the case of *gaṇḍamālā*, a decoction of *kāñcanāra* bark,
or a decoction of *kāñcanāra* bark with the powder of *śuṇṭhī*, will destroy it.
Likewise, for *gaṇḍamālā*, one should take a decoction of *varuṇa* bark with honey (126).
For elephantiasis (*ślīpada*) and diseases of fat (*medas*), one should drink a decoction of *śākhoṭaka* bark combined with cow urine.
One should drink a decoction of *śākhoṭa* bark together with cow urine.

For the destruction of elephantiasis (ślīpada) and the removal of disorders of the fat (medas), two decoctions [are used]; the decoction of *punarnavā* and *varuṇa* conquers internal abscesses (*antarvidradhi*). 127.
Likewise, a decoction of *śigru* combined with *hiṅgu* and rock salt [is used];
for an internal abscess that is not yet suppurated,
a decoction of the *varuṇādi-gaṇa* [is used] for an abscess in the middle stage that is not yet suppurated.
One should drink [this] mixed with the powder of ūṣaka and other [herbs] for the purpose of pacification (129).
The group beginning with Varuṇa consists of Varuṇa, Bakapuṣpa, Bilva, Apāmārga, and Citraka.
Two types of agnimantha, two types of śigru, two types of bṛhatī,
three types of saireyaka, mūrvā, meṣaśṛṅgī, kirātaka, ajaśṛṅgī, bimbī, karañja, and śatāvarī. (130–131)

A decoction of the group of drugs beginning with *varuṇa* is known to remove phlegm and fat; it destroys abdominal tumors (*gulma*), headache, as well as internal abscesses (*vidradhi*). For fistula-in-ano (*bhagaṃdara*), a decoction of the group beginning with *khadira* is used.

A decoction of *khadira* and the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), combined with buffalo ghee and powdered *viḍaṅga*, destroys fistula-in-ano (*bhagaṃdara*). In cases of venereal sores (*upadaṃśa*), a decoction of *paṭola* and other herbs [is used].
A decoction of *paṭola*, *triphalā*, *nimba*, *kirāta*, *khadira*, and *āsana*, when drunk together with *guggulu*, conquers all types of *upadaṃśa*. In *vātarakta*, there is the *amṛtādi* decoction.
A decoction of *amṛtā*, *eraṇḍa*, and *vāsā*, taken with castor oil,
will certainly conquer *vātarakta* that has spread throughout the entire body.
(135) This is the *paṭolādi* decoction for *vātarakta*.
A decoction of paṭola, triphalā, tiktā, guḍūcī, and śatāvarī, when drunk, conquers vātāsra (hemorrhagic disorders) accompanied by burning sensations.
In cases of white leprosy (śvetakuṣṭha), a decoction of dhātrī and other ingredients combined with the powder of avalguja [is used].
A decoction enriched with the powder of *avalguja*, along with the heartwood of *dhātrī* and *khadira*,

when consumed daily while eating wholesome food, conquers vitiligo (*śvitra*) in men. (137) [In cases of] *vātarakta*, leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), and other such conditions, there is the light *mañjiṣṭhā* decoction.
A decoction prepared from mañjiṣṭhā, triphalā, tiktā, vacā, dāruniśā, amṛtā, and nimba destroys vātarakta (gout), as well as pāmā, kapālikā, kuṣṭha, raktamaṇḍala, and jinmata. 138
For all types of kuṣṭha, there is the great decoction of mañjiṣṭhā and others:
with mañjiṣṭhā, musta, kuṭaja, guḍūcī, kuṣṭha, nāgara, bhārṅgī, kṣudrā, vacā, nimba, the two types of niśā, and phalatrika. (139)
With *paṭola*, *kaṭukī*, *mūrvā*, *viḍaṅga*, *āsana*, and *citraka*;
with *śatāvarī*, *trāyamāṇā*, *kṛṣṇā*, *indrayava*, and *vāsaka*;
and with *bhṛṅgarāja*, *mahādāru*, *pāṭhā*, *khadira*, and *candana*.
Equal parts of *trivṛt*, *varuṇa*, *kairāta*, *vākucī*, *kṛtamālaka*,
*śākhoṭaka*, *mahānimba*, *karañja*, *ativiṣā*,
*indravāruṇikā*, *anantā*, *sārivā*, and *parpaṭa* [should be used]. 141–142.

One should drink a decoction prepared from these [drugs] combined with *kaṇā* and *guggulu* in cases of the eighteen types of skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), as well as in gout (*vātarakta*), facial paralysis (*ardita*), syphilis (*upadaṃśa*), elephantiasis (*ślīpada*), numbness, and hemiplegia (*pakṣaghāta*). 143.
In cases of jaundice, eye diseases, and similar ailments, the Mañjiṣṭhādi group is recommended (144).
For diseases of the head, eye diseases, and so forth, a decoction of the Pathyādi-ṣaḍaṅga is beneficial, prepared from Pathyā, Akṣa, Dhātrī, Bhūnimba, Niśā, Nimba, and Amṛtā (145).

This decoction of six ingredients, prepared with jaggery, removes headache, as well as pain in the eyebrows, temples, and ears, and afflictions of the lower head; it also cures sūryāvarta, śaṅkhaka, loose teeth, and their associated pain. (146)
It removes night-blindness, film over the eye, cataracts, and pain in the eyes.
(147) Regarding diseases of the eyes, a decoction of vāsā and others [is used]: vāsā, viśva, amṛtā, dārvī, raktacandana, and citraka.
A decoction made from bhūnimba, nimba, kaṭukā, paṭola, triphalā, ambuda, yava, kāliṅga, and kuṭaja destroys all eye diseases;
it also cures hoarseness of voice, chronic catarrh, dyspnea, and chest wounds. (148-149)
A decoction of *amṛtā* and the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), combined with powdered *pippalī* and honey, when consumed daily, conquers all eye ailments. (150)
A decoction of the five barks—
prepared from the Ashvattha, Udumbara, Plaksha, Vata, and Vetasa—
is traditionally known to destroy swelling and infections of ulcers when used for washing. 151
Now he describes the various types of decoctions (kaṣāya), beginning with *pramathyā*. Regarding that, the definition of *pramathyā* is as follows:
*pramathyā* is said to be [the preparation] made from one pala of the substance, ground into a paste and boiled.

In cases of blood-dysentery, they say that two *pala*s (8 *tole*s) of water constitute the drink for this preparation; a churned decoction (*pramathyā*) prepared with *mustaka*, *indrayava*, and other ingredients, measuring two *pala*s, is effective. 152. In cases of blood-dysentery, a churned decoction (*pramathyā*) prepared with *mustaka*, *indravāruṇī*, and *yava*, measuring two *pala*s, is recommended. They say that for this [decoction], the quantity of water is eight times the weight of the medicine, and the dose to be drunk is two *pala*s.

Very cold and mixed with honey, it destroys bloody diarrhea. (153) This is the general rule for preparing gruel (*yavāgū*): four *palas* of the medicinal substance should be cooked in sixty-four *palas* of water.
With half of that decoction remaining, one should prepare a thick gruel (yavāgū).
In cases of malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī),
the wise physician should cook [the gruel] in a decoction of the barks of mango, hog-plum, and rose-apple.
Having consumed that gruel prepared with *śāli* rice, one shall conquer *grahaṇī*.
Regarding the general rules for soups (*yūṣa*):
one *pala* of the paste-ingredient (*kalkadravya*) and half a *karṣa* each of ginger and long pepper.
One should cook it with one *prastha* of water; this is called *drava-yūṣa*.
In cases of *sannipāta* and other disorders, there is the *saptamuṣṭika-yūṣa*, prepared with *kulattha*, barley, *kola*, *mudga*, radish, and *granthika*.
A soup prepared with ginger and coriander removes phlegm and wind;
this "Saptamuṣṭika" formula conquers fever caused by the combination of all three humors (sannipāta), alleviates āmavāta, and purifies the throat, heart, and mouth. 157–158.
The preparation of drinks and so forth is well-established:

one pala of the substance should be cooked in six hundred and forty palas of water until half remains; that [decoction] should be administered for drinking or in the preparation of meals and the like. 159

The drinking of a decoction made from six ingredients—uśīra, parpaṭa, udīcya, musta, nāgara, and candana—destroys thirst and fever; likewise, water boiled with these and then cooled is to be drunk to eliminate thirst and fever. (160)
Regarding the procedure for hot water:
it is said that hot water is prepared when one-eighth, one-fourth, or one-half remains, or simply by means of boiling. 161
Drinking warm water at night destroys phlegm, undigested matter (āmā), wind, and fat; it cleanses the bladder, stimulates digestion, and removes cough, dyspnea, and fever. 162
The procedure for preparing medicated milk:

eight parts of milk and four parts of water are added to one part of the medicinal substance. When the preparation is reduced to the quantity of milk alone, drinking it overcomes colic arising from undigested food (āmadoṣaja). 163
Milk boiled with the five roots (*pañcamūlī*) is the supreme medicine for all chronic fevers; likewise, milk is the best remedy for dyspnea,
cough, headache, pain in the flanks, and catarrh.
One suffering from fever is liberated by drinking milk boiled with the five roots (pañcamūlī).
Milk boiled with trikaṇṭaka and others—
prepared with trikaṇṭaka, balā, vyāghrī, jaggery, and ginger— is likewise effective.
Milk cures the obstruction of feces and urine and removes fever caused by *kapha*.
(165) Now, regarding the preparation of food, the method for preparing gruel (*yavāgū*) and *kṛśara* is described;
here, the preparation of food itself is explained without excessive detail.
Yavāgū (gruel) prepared with six parts water becomes thick when it is cooked with rice, mung beans, black gram, or sesame;
it is wholesome, constipating, strengthening, satiating, and a destroyer of Vāta. (166–167)
The procedure for preparing *vilepī*:
*Vilepī* is a thickened gruel that has been cooked in four times its quantity of water;
it is nourishing, satiating, pleasing to the heart, sweet, and a destroyer of *pitta*. (168)
The method for preparing *peyā* and *yūṣa*:
*Peyā* is known by the wise as that which has a predominance of liquid, very few grains, and is cooked in fourteen times the amount of water; *yūṣa* is considered to be slightly thicker. (169)

The qualities of liquid gruel (peyā) and broth (yūṣa): Liquid gruel should be known as very light, constipating, and nourishing to the bodily tissues; broth is more strengthening than that, beneficial for the throat, easily digested, and dispels phlegm. 170
The method for preparing *bhakta* (rice gruel):
one should cook four *palas* of rice in fourteen parts of water; having strained off the scum (*maṇḍa*), that *bhakta* is sweet and light. (171)
The method for preparing *maṇḍa*:
*Maṇḍa* prepared with fourteen parts of water, free from froth and combined with ginger and rock salt, is an excellent digestive and appetizer. 172.
The eightfold *maṇḍa* consists of coriander, the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), rock salt, mung beans, and rice;
when these are combined and fried with asafoetida and sesame oil, that *maṇḍa* is known as "eightfold. (173)

Stimulating digestion, life-giving, cleansing the bladder, increasing the blood, overcoming fever, and destroying all the *doṣas*— this is called the eightfold benefit of *maṇḍa*. (174) This refers to *vāṭya-maṇḍa*.
A thick scum (*vāṭyamaṇḍa*) made from barley that has been well-cut and likewise fried,
removes phlegm and bile, is beneficial for the throat, and clarifies *raktapitta*.
(175) [This is] *lājamaṇḍa* (scum of parched rice).
Parched rice flour (lāja-maṇḍa) is proclaimed to be made from parched rice or parched grains;
it alleviates phlegm and bile, is astringent, and is considered to conquer thirst and fever.
(176) Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Preparation of Decoctions," in the Middle Section of the Śrī Śārṅgadharasaṃhitā.
The Preparation of Phāṇṭa and Other Decoctions; now, the third chapter, titled "The Preparation of Phāṇṭa and Other Decoctions," concerning the preparation of phāṇṭa.
When one pala of the powdered substance has been thoroughly crushed, one should properly pour in hot water measuring one kuḍava into an earthen vessel; then, having strained it through a cloth,
that liquid extract shall be the *phāṇṭa*, and its measure is two palas.
One should add sugar, honey, jaggery, and so forth, into that [decoction] as one would with other decoctions.
For fevers caused by Vāta and Pitta and similar conditions, there is the strong (bṛhat) *phāṇṭa* preparation of Madhūkapuṣpa and other ingredients:
Madhūkapuṣpa, Madhuka, Candana, and Parūṣaka.
One should place lotus stalks, lotus, lodhra, gambhārī, nāgakeśara,
triphalā, sārivā, drākṣā, and parched grain into lukewarm water;
this decoction (phāṇṭa) or cold infusion (himas) should be drunk mixed with sugar and honey.

It destroys fever caused by vāta and pitta, burning sensations, thirst, fainting, restlessness, vertigo, internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta), and intoxication; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
At the onset of fever, a decoction (phāṇṭa) made from mango and other fruits [is recommended].
A cold infusion (phāṇṭa) prepared with the tender leaves of the mango and rose-apple, the sprouts of the banyan tree,
and uśīra root, combined with honey, destroys fever; it overcomes thirst, vomiting, dysentery, and even difficult-to-cure fainting.
In cases such as burning sensations and disorders of *pitta*, a light decoction (*phāṇṭa*) made from *madhūka* flowers and other ingredients is used;
likewise, a cold decoction (*phāṇṭa*) prepared with *madhūka* flowers, *gambhārī*, sandalwood, *uśīra*, coriander, and grapes, combined with sugar, [is beneficial].
It is said to remove thirst and bile, and it conquers burning sensations, fainting, and vertigo.
(8) Regarding the method for *mantha*: *Mantha* is also a variety of *phāṇṭa*; therefore, it is described right here.
When four *pala* of cold water have been prepared, one should add one *pala* of crushed medicinal substance to an earthen vessel and stir it thoroughly; from that, one should drink two *pala*.
This is the *kharjūrādi-mantha* (stirred drink beginning with dates) for conditions such as alcoholism (*madātyaya*).
A *mantha* (a churned drink) prepared with dates, pomegranates, grape juice, *tintiḍīka*, *āmalaka*, and *parūṣaka* cures all disorders caused by wine.
In cases of vomiting, a *mantha* made of *masūra* and other grains [is recommended].

Barley flour mixed with honey and stirred with pomegranate juice quickly prevents vomiting arising from the three *doṣas*. In cases of thirst, burning sensations, and so forth, a churned drink (*mantha*) made of barley flour is recommended.
A *mantha* (churned drink) made with barley flour mixed with cold water and ghee,
neither too thick nor too thin, cures thirst, burning sensations, and blood-bile disorders.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Preparation of Phāṇṭas and Other Decoctions," in the Middle Section of the *Śrī Śārṅgadharasaṃhitā*.
The Chapter on the Conception of Snow; now, the fourth chapter, titled "The Conception of Snow.
The Conception of Snow.

One pala of crushed drug, properly saturated with six palas of water and dried overnight, constitutes a *hima*; it is likewise called a *śītakaṣāya*. Its measurement should be understood as being like that of a *phāṇṭa*; this is the rule in all cases.
In the case of *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorders), the *āmradihima* (ice-cold infusion of mango, etc. is prescribed:
having powdered mango, rose-apple (*jambū*), and *kakubha*, one should throw them into water;
one should drink that cold infusion in the morning with honey to conquer *raktapitta*. 2.
Sugar, *marīca*, *madhuyaṣṭī*,
the tender leaves of *kākodumbara*, blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), sugar, and its decoction alleviate thirst and vomiting. (3)
In fevers caused by vāta and pitta and other such conditions, there is a cold infusion (himā) of blue lotus and other ingredients:
blue lotus (nīlotpala), balā, raisins (drākṣā), madhūka, licorice (madhuka), uśīra, padmaka, kāśmarī, and parūṣaka. 4.
This cold infusion (śītakaṣāya) conquers fevers caused by vāta and pitta; it wards off delirium, vertigo, vomiting, fainting, and thirst.
In chronic fever, the cold infusion of *guḍūcī* is used, and in *raktapitta*, the cold infusion of *vāsā*.
The cold infusion (hima) of *amṛtā* is prescribed as a drink that cures chronic fever (*jīrṇajvara*).
The cold infusion of *vāsā* overcomes cough, hemorrhagic fever (*raktapitta*), and fever. In cases such as internal burning heat (*antardāha*), a cold infusion of *dhānyaka* is used.

In the morning, a cold infusion (hima) made from coriander (dhānyaka) mixed with sugar should be drunk; it overcomes internal burning sensations as well as thirst, and acts as a purifier of the channels. In cases such as raktapitta (hemorrhagic disorders), this coriander-based cold infusion is indicated.
The cooling preparation (Hima) made from coriander, emblic myrobalan, vāsā, grapes,
and parpaṭa destroys internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta), fever, burning sensations, thirst, and emaciation.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Preparation of Cooling Preparations," in the Middle Section of the Śrī Śārṅgadharasaṃhitā.
The Formulation of Pastes; now begins the fifth chapter, titled "The Formulation of Pastes.
The Formulation of Pastes.
The substance may be moist, ground on a stone, dry, or mixed with water; these are known as *prakṣepa*, *āvāpa*, and *kalka*. Their measure should be one *karṣa*.
In the case of a *kalka*, honey, ghee, or oil should be added in double the quantity.
One should give equal parts of sugar and jaggery, with four times as much liquid to be added.
Regarding the method for increasing the pippalī dose:
the *kaṇās* (pippalīs) may be increased by three, five, or seven at a time.
Having ground them, one should drink [the mixture] for ten days, and likewise reduce the dose over the same period.
Thus, perfected in twenty days is the *pippalī-vardhamānaka* (the increasing dose of long pepper).
By this, anemia, wind-blood disorders, cough, asthma, anorexia, and fever are cured.

Abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, wasting, phlegm, wind, and chest obstructions are destroyed. A paste of nimba leaves applied as a plaster cures wounds and vomiting; this paste of nimba leaves purifies and heals wounds.
By consuming it, one conquers vomiting, skin diseases, and worms caused by pitta and kapha. (5) A paste of the root of *mahānimba* is known to destroy sciatica (*gṛdhrasī*). (6)
Garlic paste is used for diseases of the wind (vāta), irregular fevers (viṣamajvara), and so forth.
Pure garlic paste mixed with sesame oil conquers severe diseases of the wind and destroys irregular fevers. (7)
The second formulation is a paste of garlic for wind-diseases:
one should take ripe garlic bulbs, remove the husks, split them open, and discard the central sprout. 8.
To destroy its pungent odor, one should place it in buttermilk at night;
then, having removed it from the midst of that, one should grind it on a stone slab.
After that, one should add a powder of these [other ingredients] into its midst in the proportion of one-fifth.
One should powder equal parts of sauvarcala salt, yavānī, fried asafoetida, rock salt, the three pungents (kaṭutrika), and cumin; then,
having combined all these, one should prepare a paste measuring one karṣa.
One should eat this while considering the strength of one's digestive fire and taking into account the season, the specific dosha, and other factors;

thereafter, one should take as a post-drink (anupāna) oil boiled with castor seeds every day for the treatment of vāta affecting the whole body or a single limb, including facial paralysis (ardita) and convulsions (apatantraka).
It conquers epilepsy, insanity, stiffness of the thighs, and sciatica; it overcomes pain in the chest, back, waist, sides, and abdomen, as well as worms,
indigestion, exposure to the sun, anger, excessive water, and the consumption of milk with jaggery.
A person who does not eat garlic should abandon these [other items] continuously;
he should always consume liquor, meat, and sour flavors.
(15) In cases of *ūrustambha* (stiffness of the thighs), a paste of *pippalī* and other such ingredients [is prescribed].
A paste made from long pepper (pippalī), long pepper root (pippalīmūla), and bhallātaka fruits,
taken with honey, cures thigh-stiffness (ūrustambha). A paste of viṣṇukrāntā is used for pain resulting from indigestion (pariṇāma-śūla).
A paste of *viṣṇukrāntā* and *ajaṭā*, combined with sugar, honey, and ghee,
destroys colic arising from the digestive transformation (*pariṇāma-śūla*) within seven days.
A paste of ginger (*śuṇṭhī*) [is likewise effective] for colic from the digestive transformation and for *āmavāta*.
One should administer a paste of ginger, sesame, and jaggery along with milk; this destroys colic arising from indigestion (pariṇāma-śūla) as well as āmavāta.
A paste of apāmārga is used for bleeding hemorrhoids (rakta-arśas).
A paste of Apāmārga seeds drunk with rice-water destroys hemorrhoidal piles; of this there is no doubt.
(19) A paste of Badarī roots [is used] for bloody diarrhea.

A paste of *badarī* root combined with sesame paste, along with honey and alkali, will effect the destruction of bloody diarrhea (raktātīsāra). A paste of lac (*lākṣā*) [is used] when there is a loss of blood.
One should drink two karṣas of lac mixed with the juice of *kūṣmāṇḍaka*;
this destroys loss of blood, chest pain, and the disease of consumption (*kṣaya*).
A paste of *taṇḍulīyaka* [is used] for *raktapradara*.
A paste of the root of *taṇḍulīya* mixed with honey and *rasāñjana*,
when drunk with rice-water, destroys menorrhagia (22).
A paste of the root of *aṅkola* is for the treatment of diarrhea and poisoning.
The paste of the root of *Aṅkola* mixed with honey and taken with rice-water is said to cure diarrhea and is also remembered as a remedy for poison.
(23) The paste of the roots of *Vandhyākarkoṭikā* and other such plants [is likewise used] for poison.
The root of Vandhyākarkoṭikā, as well as the root-fiber (jaṭā) of Pāṭalā,
or the root of Bilva with ghee— these two varieties will destroy poison.
A paste of Abhayā and others is for the destruction of the three doṣas, while a paste of Pathyā and others is for digestion and similar purposes.
A paste of *abhayā*, rock salt (*saindhava*), long pepper (*kaṇā*), and dry ginger (*śuṇṭhī*) destroys the three *doṣas*.
A paste of *pathyā*, rock salt, and dry ginger is an appetizer and a digestive.
(25) A paste of *trivṛt* and other [purgatives] is used in the treatment of worm infestations (*krimiroga*).

One should drink a paste made of equal parts of *trivṛt*, *palāśa* seeds, Persian barley (*pārasīkayavānikā*), *kampillaka*, *viḍaṅga*, and jaggery, mixed with buttermilk; this destroys hosts of worms. (26)

A paste of *tila*, *nāga*, and *keśara* is for hemorrhoids with blood; a paste of fresh butter (*navanīta*) and sesame is known as a conqueror of bloody hemorrhoids; and likewise, a paste of fresh butter, sugar, *nāga*, and *keśara* is also effective for that. (27)

The paste of *śuṇṭhī* and the rest, or the paste of *bṛhatī*, drunk with *masūra* soup, or the paste of *śuṇṭhī* and unripe mango fruits (*śalāṭu*), likewise conquers *saṃgrahaṇī*; similarly, the paste derived from *bṛhatī* taken with *takra* (buttermilk) achieves the same. 28.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, named "The Formulation of Pastes" (Kalkakalpanā), in the Middle Section of the Śrīśārṅgadharasaṃhitā.
Now begins the sixth chapter, named "The Formulation of Powders" (Cūrṇakalpanā).
Among these, first is the definition of powder (*cūrṇa*):
that substance which is extremely dry, well-ground, and strained through cloth is called powder, dust, or fine flour; its measure is equal to one *karṣa*. (1)
Regarding the proportions of jaggery and other ingredients in powders:
in a powder, an equal amount of jaggery should be added, while sugar should be double the amount.
In powders, fried asafoetida should be used so that it does not cause excessive moisture.
Regarding the determination of the dosage for the powder as a vehicle:
one should lick the powder with all types of liquids such as ghee and the like, measured at double the amount [of the powder];
or one should drink the powder stirred into liquids measured at four times the amount [of the powder].
The determination of the quantity of the adjunct liquid (anupāna) for powders and other preparations should be made according to the specific humor involved;
for powders, electuaries, pills, and pastes, one should take three, two, or one pala respectively when wind, bile, or phlegm is the cause of the affliction. (4)
The necessity of a post-prandial drink (anupāna) is as follows:
just as oil thrown into water spreads instantly, so too does the medicine spread through the body by the power of the anupāna. (5)
