Regarding the purpose of powdering, the instruction on the quantity of the infusion is as follows:
the measure for the infusion, as declared by the best of physicians, is that amount of liquid by which the entire powder becomes properly saturated. 6.
The powder of *āmalakī* and other ingredients—
namely *āmalaka*, *citraka*, *pathyā*, *pippalī*, and *saindhava*—
is to be known as this group of powders that destroys all fevers.

Pippalī powder is a laxative, appetizing, subdues kapha, and acts as a digestive stimulant and carminative. (7) One should lick pippalī powder with honey to alleviate hiccup, fever, cough, and other ailments.

The powder of Triphalā cures hiccup and dyspnea, is beneficial for the throat, destroys splenic disorders, and is suitable for children. (8) One Harītakī should be used for urinary disorders and similar ailments, while two Vibhītaka fruits should be employed.
These four *āmalaka* fruits together are proclaimed as *triphalā*.

*Triphalā* destroys urinary disorders (*meha*) and edema, cures irregular fevers (*viṣamajvara*), stimulates digestion, subdues phlegm and bile, destroys skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), and acts as a rejuvenative elixir (*rasāyana*).
Combined with ghee and honey, it conquers all eye diseases.
(11) The powder of the three pungents—pippalī, marica, and śuṇṭhī—is called *trikaṭu*; it is used for stimulating digestion and other such purposes.

The powder of the five pungent spices (pañcakola) stimulates digestion, destroys phlegm and fat, cures skin diseases and chronic cough, overcomes nausea associated with undigested matter (āmārocaka), as well as urinary disorders, abdominal tumors, and diseases of the throat. 12. [It is used] for loss of appetite and similar conditions.
Pippalī, cavya, viśvāhva, pippalīmūla, and citraka are known as the "pañcakola" (the five spices). It is appetizing, digestive, and carminative;
it destroys abdominal distension, splenic disorders, and gulma, and removes colic and disorders of the kapha-affected abdomen.
The qualities of the powders of *trigandha* and *caturjāta*: *Trigandha* consists of cardamom, cinnamon bark, and cinnamon leaves; *caturjāta* consists of these with the addition of nutmeg.
*Trigandha* along with *caturjāta* is dry, hot, light, and generates *pitta*.
This powder of black pepper and other ingredients is complexion-enhancing, appetizing, and sharp; it conquers diseases of bile and phlegm (pitta-śleṣma).
This powder of black pepper (kṛṣṇā), long pepper (aruṇā), mustaka, and śṛṅgikā, taken in equal parts with honey, [is used] for children in cases of fever, diarrhea, and similar ailments.
Fever, diarrhea, along with dyspnea, cough, and vomiting in children, are pacified by the Jīvanīya group [of drugs],
namely Kākolī, Kṣīrakākolī, Jīvaka, and Ṛṣabhaka. 16.
Medā, mahāmedā, jīvantī, and likewise madhuka;
mudgaparṇī and māṣaparṇī—this is the group known as the vitalizers (jīvanīya).
This group of vitalizers is sweet, promotes the healing of the fetus, and is heavy.
The group of eight (Aṣṭavarga) promotes the secretion of breast milk, is nourishing, aphrodisiac, unctuous, cooling, and relieves thirst;
it conquers internal hemorrhage (raktapitta), chest wounds, consumption (śoṣa), fever, burning sensations, and wind disorders.
19. Aṣṭavarga.
The two types of Medā, the two types of Kākolī, as well as Jīvaka and Ṛṣabhaka,
along with Ṛddhi and Vṛddhi— by all these together, the "group of eight" (aṣṭavarga) is proclaimed.
This group of eight, declared by the wise, is equal in its qualities to the life-promoting (jīvanīya) group.

The powder of the five salts— namely, *saindhava*, *sauvarcala*, *viḍa*, *sāmudrika*, and molasses— is known as the "five salts" (*lavaṇapañcaka*) when used in the sequence of one, two, three, four, and five parts respectively for the purpose of inducing the evacuation of feces, urine, and so forth. 22.
Among those, rock salt (saindhava) is the foremost; when no specific type is mentioned, one should employ it.
The five salts, beginning with rock salt and ending with romaka, should be known as follows:
[romaka] is sweet, promotes the discharge of feces and urine, is unctuous, subtle, and diminishes strength.
It is strong, hot, digestive, sharp, and increases *kapha* and *pitta*.
(24) The combination of alkalis— namely *svarjikā* and *yāvaśūka*— is declared to be the "pair of alkalis" (*kṣārayugma*).
The two alkalis derived from *svarjika* and *yavaśūka* should be known as equal to fire.
Other alkalis as well destroy abdominal tumors (*gulma*), hemorrhoids, and diseases of the *grahaṇī*; they are laxative, digestive, and destroy worms, virility, skin diseases, gravel, and stones.
Sudarśana powder is used for all types of fever and similar conditions;
[the formulation includes] Triphalā, the two types of Rajanī, the two types of Kaṇṭakārī, Śaṭī, Trikaṭu, Granthika, Mūrvā, Guḍūcī, and Dhanvayāsaka. (27)
Kaṭukā, parpaṭa, musta, trāyamāṇā, and bālaka;
nimba, puṣkaramūla, madhuyaṣṭī, and vatsaka (28);
yavānī, indrayava, bhārṅgī, śigru seeds, and surāṣṭrajā.
Vaca, tvak, padmaka, uśīra, candana, ativiṣā, balā,
29 śāliparṇī, pṛśniparṇī, viḍaṅga, tagara, as well as citraka, devadāru, cavya, and the leaf of paṭola. 30
One should likewise powder jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, lavaṅga, vaṃśalocanā, puṇḍarīka, kākolī, patraka, jātipatraka, and tālīsapatra in equal parts. 31.

The wise practitioner should add half a portion of *kairāta* to all the powder. This powder, named Sudarśana, removes the three humors (*doṣas*) and destroys all fevers; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
It destroys irregular fevers (viṣamajvara) arising from distinct dual combinations (dvandva), exogenous factors (āgantu), or located in the bodily elements (dhātu);
it also destroys those born of the combination of all three humors (sannipāta), as well as mental ones.
It cures cold-fevers (śītajvara), quotidian fevers (ekāhika), and others, along with delusion (moha), drowsiness (tandrā), vertigo (bhrama), and thirst (tṛṣā). 34.
It destroys dyspnea, cough, anemia, heart disease, and jaundice (35).
It removes pain in the sacrum, back, waist, knees, and sides;
the wise man should drink it with cold water for the cessation of all fevers (36).
Just as the Sudarśana discus is the destroyer of the Dānavas,
so too is this powder the destroyer of all fevers.
(37) The powder of Triphalā and Pippalī is [efficacious] for cough, dyspnea, and fever.

Triphalā combined with Pippalī, powdered and licked with honey, removes cough, dyspnea, and fever; it is a purgative and an awakener of the digestive fire. (38) The Kaṭphalādi powder is used for fever and other such conditions.
One should lick a powder of kaṭphala, mustaka, tiktā, śaṭī, śṛṅgī, and pauṣkara with honey or the juice of ginger;
this removes fever, is beneficial for the throat, and conquers cough, dyspnea, and anorexia. (39)
It dispels wind, vomiting, as well as colic and consumption (40).
This is the Bṛhatkaṭphalādi powder, used for colic, wind disorders, and so forth;
it contains kaṭphala, pauṣkara, śṛṅgī, mustā, trikaṭuka, and śaṭī.
One should have all these made into fine powders, either collectively or individually.
One should lick them with the juice of *ārdra* and honey; this destroys *kapha* and removes colic, wind disorders, loss of appetite, vomiting, cough, dyspnea, and consumption.
The second powder, beginning with *kaṭphala*, is for conditions such as dyspnea;
*kaṭphala*, *pauṣkara*, *kṛṣṇā*, and *śṛṅgī* taken together with honey constitute an excellent electuary that removes dyspnea, cough, and fever, and brings an end to *kapha*. 43.
The powder of Śṛṅgī and others, as well as the powder of Viṣā, should be given for cough, fever, and vomiting in children.
One should have the child lick the powder of Śṛṅgī, Prativiṣā, and Kṛṣṇā with honey;
or, for the pacification of cough, fever, and vomiting in the child, Viṣā alone may be used. 44
A powder of barley-alkali and other ingredients, when licked with honey, conquers the five types of cough in children;
this powder derived from barley-alkali, viṣā, śṛṅgī, māgadhī, and pauṣkara, when consumed with honey, overcomes the five coughs of the child. (45)
A powder of ginger and other ingredients for acute diarrhea:
A powder made from ginger, ativiṣā, asafoetida, musta, kuṭaja, and citraka, when drunk with warm water, destroys acute diarrhea (āmātīsāra). (46)
In the case of acute diarrhea (āmātīsāra),
one should drink a powder made of harītakī, prativiṣā, rock salt (saindhava), black salt (sauvarcala), vacā, and asafoetida (hiṅgu) with warm water. (47)
The light Gaṅgādharacūrṇa pacifies diarrhea caused by undigested matter (āmātīsāra), is constipating, and stimulates the digestive fire; likewise, for chronic diarrhea (pakvātīsāra),
one should use musta, indrayava, bilva, lodhra, and mocarasa.
The wise physician should powder dhātakī and administer it with buttermilk and jaggery.
This powder, named Laghu-gangadhara, is a supreme astringent that pacifies all types of diarrhea and stops dysentery. 48–49.
The Bṛhadgaṅgādharacūrṇa consists of mustā, aralu, śuṇṭhī, dhātakī, lodhra, and bālaka, along with bilva, mocarasa, pāṭhā, indrayava, and vatsaka; it is used for dysentery and similar ailments. 50
The powder of mango seed, *prativiṣā*, and *lajjālu*, when drunk with honey and rice-water, cures dysentery; all types of diarrhea and *grahaṇī* are swiftly pacified. 51.
The Vṛddhagaṅgādhara powder checks the forceful flow of the channels (52).
Regarding the Ajamodādi powder for diarrhea:
ajamodā, mocarasa, śṛṅgavera, and dhātakī flowers.
One could even block the flowing Gaṅgā with curd churned by a cow;

likewise, one who daily drinks the powder of black pepper and other ingredients with buttermilk for disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī) will find relief through this pepper-based powder. 53–54.

When combined with *citrasauvarcala* salt, it destroys *grahaṇī*; it also serves as a destroyer of abdominal enlargement, splenic disorders, weak digestion, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), and hemorrhoids (55).
This is the *kapitthāṣṭaka* powder, effective for *grahaṇī* and other such conditions.
Eight parts of wood-apple (kapittha) and six parts of sugar are prescribed;
likewise, pomegranate, tamarind, bilva fruit, and dhātakī, as well as ajamodā and long pepper, should each be three parts. 56.
Black pepper, cumin, coriander, granthika, and likewise bālaka; 57.
Sauvarcala salt, yavānī, the four spices (cāturjāta), citraka, and ginger—each of these should consist of one part, finely powdered. 58.
This powder known as Kapitthāṣṭaka dispels diseases of the throat, diarrhea, consumption, abdominal tumors, and malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī).
The Laghudāḍimāṣṭaka powder is used for loss of appetite and similar conditions, as well as for cough, fever, and other ailments.
Two palas of pomegranate (*dāḍimī*) should be taken, along with eight palas of sugar-candy (*khaṇḍa*),
one pala of the three aromatics (*trigandha*), and three palas of the three pungents (*trikaṭu*). All of this combined together shall constitute the "Eightfold Pomegranate Powder" (*dāḍimāṣṭaka*).
This Bṛhaddāḍimāṣṭaka powder stimulates the appetite, is digestive, beneficial for the throat, astringent, and cures cough and fever.
(61) For this, take eight palas of pomegranate and eight palas of sugar. In cases of diarrhea and other ailments, [this is used].
Pippalī, pippalīmūla, yavānī, and likewise marica;
dhānyaka, jīraka, and śuṇṭhī—one pala each of these; and one karṣa each of tugākṣīrī, tvak, patra, elā, and keśara.

Each [ingredient] should be the size of a jujube fruit; this powder, known as Dāḍimāṣṭaka, cures diarrhea, consumption, abdominal tumors, malabsorption syndrome, throat obstruction, weak digestion, chronic rhinitis, and cough. (64)
Pippalyādi powder is for vāta-type grahaṇī:
pippalī, bṛhatī, vyāghrī, yavakṣāra, kaliṅgaka, citraka, sārivā, pāṭhā, śaṭī, and the five salts (65).
One should administer that powder with curd, or even with wine or warm water;
it is supremely beneficial for pacifying the disorders of the *grahaṇī* caused by Vāta (Lavaṅgādi-cūrṇa, for loss of appetite and similar conditions). 66.
Lavaṅgādi-cūrṇa for anorexia and so forth.
Clove, pure camphor, cardamom, cinnamon, nāgakeśara, nutmeg, uśīra, ginger, black cumin, black agallochum, tugākṣīrī, māṃsī, blue lotus, and kaṇā. 67.
One should powder together sandalwood, tagara, bāla, and kaṅkola (68). All these should be in equal parts, and sugar should be half the amount of all of them.
This powder, beginning with cloves (lavaṅgādya), is worthy of kings and kindles the digestive fire (69).
It is clarifying, satiating, aphrodisiac, a destroyer of the three doṣas, and bestows strength; it cures heart disease, throat disorders, cough, hiccups,
chronic rhinitis (pīnasa), consumption (yakṣman), asthma with oppression (tamaka), dyspnea, diarrhea, and chest wounds.

This powder of nutmeg and other ingredients destroys urinary disorders (prameha), anorexia, abdominal tumors (gulma), and malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī). Regarding the nutmeg powder for malabsorption and related conditions:
it is prepared with nutmeg (jātīphala), cloves (lavaṅga), cardamom (elā), cinnamon leaves (patra), cinnamon bark (tvak), and nagakesara (nāgakeśara). 71–72.
With camphor, sandalwood, sesame seeds, *tvakkṣīrī*, *tagara*, and *āmalaka*;
with *tālīsa*, long pepper, *pathyā*, large cumin, and *citraka*;
and with ginger, *viḍaṅga*, and black pepper—all these ground into equal parts—73.
One should prepare all these ingredients in equal proportions and add sugar equal to the total weight of the powder;
then, the wise physician should administer one *karṣa* of this mixture, moistened with honey.
By its power, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), cough, dyspnea, anorexia, consumption, disorders of wind and phlegm, and coryza are swiftly pacified.
This is the Mahākhaṇḍava powder for conditions such as anorexia.

Marica, nāgapuṣpa, tālīsa, and the salts shall each have one part; likewise, pippalīmūla and citraka [shall have one part each], while tvak, kaṇā, tintiḍīka, and jīraka shall each have two parts. (77)
Dhānyāmla, vetasa, viśva, bhadra, elā, and badara fruits—each of these should be one-third part [of the total];
pomegranate fruit should be one-fourth part of all the medicinal herbs. 78–79.
Sugar should be added in half a mātrā to all these ingredients;
this powder, known as Mahākhāṇḍava,
is highly pleasing, promotes the digestion of fire, and cures cough and diarrhea.
This powder destroys diseases of the heart, the generative organs, the throat, the stomach, and the mouth;
it likewise dispels cholera, flatulence, hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors, worms, the five types of vomiting, and dyspnea. 81–82.
Nārāyaṇacūrṇa consists of citraka, triphalā, vyoṣa, jīraka, hapuṣā, vacā, yavānī, pippalīmūla, śatapuṣpā, and ajagandhikā, [to be used] for the abdomen and other ailments. (83)

Ajamodā, śaṭī, dhānyaka, viḍaṅga, sthūlajīraka, hemāhvā, pauṣkaramūla, the two types of kṣāra, the five salts (pañcalavaṇa), and kuṣṭha—these should be taken in equal parts; viśālā should be taken in two parts. (84)

Trivṛt should be known as three parts, and there should be three parts of dantī; śātalā shall be four parts. One should grind all these together into a powder for a patient whose digestive tract has been lubricated by means of digestive and oleating therapies. (85–86)
One should administer this powder as a purgative to destroy all diseases,
[especially] in cases of heart disease, anemia, cough, asthma, fistula-in-ano, weak digestion, fever, skin diseases, malabsorption syndrome, and throat obstruction. (87)

One should administer [the medicine] with appropriate adjuncts (anupāna): with wine and the like in cases of flatulence (ādhmāna); with jujube decoction in gulma; with whey from curd in diarrhea (viḍbheda);
with warm water in indigestion (ajīrṇa); and with sour tree-fruits (vṛkṣāmla) in cutting pains (parikartti). 88–89.
In cases of wind-diseases, one should administer camel's milk or cow's buttermilk;
in cases of hemorrhoids, pomegranate juice;
and for both types of poison, one should give an antidote with clarified butter. (90)
The powder named Nārāyaṇa removes hosts of malignant diseases.
(91) The Hapuṣādyacūrṇa is used for indigestion, abdominal enlargements, and other ailments;
it consists of hapuṣā, triphalā, trāyamāṇā, and pippalī.
One should powder together hemakṣīrī, trivṛt, śātalā, kaṭukā, vacā, nīlinī, rock salt (saindhava), and black salt (kṛṣṇa-lavaṇa);
[this powder is to be taken] with hot water, urine, or the juices of pomegranate and triphalā.
Likewise, a person should drink [this] with meat broth as appropriate in cases of indigestion, splenic enlargement, abdominal tumors, edema, hemorrhoids, and irregular digestion;
the *pañcasamacūrṇa* [is used] for colic and similar conditions. 94.
One should prepare fine powders of equal parts of ginger, chebulic myrobalan, long pepper, trivṛt, and black salt;
this powder known as Pañcasama is the supreme remedy for colic.
This is known as Nārāca-cūrṇa, which destroys flatulence, abdominal enlargement, hemorrhoids, and Āmavāta.
A dose of one Karṣa should be used for conditions such as flatulence and colic; in this formulation, Pippalī (Kṛṣṇā) should be one Karṣa and Trivṛt should be one Pala.
One pala of sugar candy should be known [as the ingredient], and one should prepare a powder by mixing them together.
One should lick this, measured at one karṣa, with honey; it destroys flatulence, hard stools, abdominal disorders, phlegm, and pitta-type colic. (97–98)
The powder beginning with the three salts is used for liver and spleen disorders;
[it consists of] the three salts, the two alkalis, the two types of *śatapuṣpā*, *vacā*, *ajamodā*, *ajagandhā*, *hapuṣā*, and the two types of *jīraka*. (99)
Black pepper, long pepper root, long pepper, elephant pepper, asafoetida, asafoetida leaf, *śaṭī*, *pāṭhā*,
*upakuñcikā* (100), dry ginger, *citraka*, *cavya*, *viḍaṅga*, and *amlavetasa*.
Pomegranate and tamarind; likewise, trivṛt, dantī,
śatāvarī (101), indravāruṇikā, bhārṅgī, devadāru, yavānikā, kustumburu, tumburu, pauṣkara, and jujube fruits (102).
One should have a powder made from equal parts of these, including Śivā, and then saturate it with the juices of Ārdra and Bījapūra.
One should drink that [powder] with clarified butter, or with aged wine, or with warm water. 103.

With kola-juice, or with buttermilk, camel’s milk, or whey, [it cures] diseases of the liver, spleen, waist, rectum, stomach, and heart; as well as hemorrhoids, constipation, weak digestion, abdominal tumors, splenic enlargement, and dropsy. (104–105)
One shall undoubtedly conquer hiccup, flatulence, dyspnea, and cough with these very drugs;
or the physician may properly prepare ghee with these same medicines.
This powder of *tumburu* and other ingredients is used for colic and similar ailments.
Tumburu, the three salts (trilavaṇa), yavānī, and that which is called puṣkara;
equal parts of yavakṣāra, abhayā, hiṅgu, and viḍaṅga;
and trivṛt, which should be known as three parts—these should be made into a fine powder. 107–108.
One should drink it with warm water or drink it with a decoction of barley;
it conquers all types of colic, as well as abdominal tumors, flatulence, and enlargement of the abdomen.
This is the Citrakādyacūrṇa, used for conditions such as weak digestion.
Take one *karṣa* each of *citraka*, ginger (*nāgara*), asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), long pepper (*pippalī*), the root of long pepper (*pippalī-jaṭā*), *cavya*, *ajamodā*, and black pepper (*marica*).
Then take *svarjikā*, barley alkali (*yavakṣāra*), rock salt (*saindhava*), black salt (*sauvarcala*), and *biḍa* salt. (110)
One should prepare sea salt and *romaka* salt in portions the size of jujube fruits (111).
Having combined the entire powder, one should saturate it with the juices of *mātuluṅga* or pomegranate, and then dry it in the sun (112).
This powder conquers abdominal tumors (gulma), malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī) caused by undigested matter (āmaja), and pain; it kindles the digestive fire, improves appetite, and destroys kapha.
This is the Vaḍavānala powder, indicated for weak digestion and similar conditions.

One should powder rock salt (*saindhava*), long pepper root (*pippalīmūla*), long pepper (*pippalī*), *cavya*, leadwort (*citraka*), dry ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), and chebulic myrobalan (*harītakī*) in increasing proportions.
This powder, named Vaḍavānala, is an inflamer of the digestive fire.
Ajmodādi powder for conditions such as āmavāta and swelling:
ajamodā, viḍaṅga, rock salt (saindhava), devadāru, citraka, pippalīmūla, śatapuṣpā, and pippalī. (115)
The wise physician should prepare one *karṣa* each of black pepper (*marica*) and [long pepper];
there should be five *karṣas* of yellow myrobalan (*pathyā*), ten of *vṛddhadāraka*, and likewise ten of ginger (*nāgara*). One should grind all these together into a powder.
One should drink this powder with warm water alone;
it destroys swelling (śvayathu), cures the pain of āmavāta, and overcomes the pain of the joints, sciatica (gṛdhrasī), as well as the pain located in the waist, back, anus, and calves. 117–118.
It overcomes *tūnī*, *pratūnī*, *viśvācī*, and diseases caused by *kapha* and *vāta*.
Alternatively, the physician should prepare pills (*vaṭaka*) for this with equal amounts of jaggery (*guḍa*).
This powder of *śuṇṭhī* and other ingredients [is used] for dyspnea (*śvāsa*) and similar conditions.
A powder of ginger, sauvarcala salt, asafoetida, pomegranate, and amlavetasa should be drunk with warm water for the pacification of asthma and heart disease;
this is the *hiṅgvādi-cūrṇa* used for colic and other ailments. (120)
Hiṅgu, pāṭhā, abhayā, dhānyaka, dāḍima, citraka, śaṭī,
ajamodā, trikaṭuka, hapuṣā, amlavetasa, ajagandhā, tintiḍīka, jīraka, pauṣkara, and vacā. (121–122)
One should powder cavya, the two types of alkali (kṣāra), and the five salts;
this powder should be administered either before or during a meal.
Alternatively, one may drink it with aged wine, buttermilk, or warm water. (123)
In cases of gulma arising from vāta and kapha, in cardiac oppression and aṣṭhīlikā; in pains of the heart, bladder, and flanks; in colic of the anus and vagina;
as well as in dysuria, abdominal distension, anemia, and loss of appetite. (124–125)
This powder is recommended for hiccup, liver disease, splenic enlargement, cough, dyspnea, throat obstruction, and disorders of the digestive tract and hemorrhoids;
it may be processed repeatedly with the expressed juice of *mātuluṅga*.
One should also prepare many pills that remove diseases caused by vāta and kapha (127).
Regarding the powder of *yavānī* and *khāṇḍava* for loss of appetite and other conditions:
*yavānī*, pomegranate, ginger, *tintiḍīka*, and *amlavetasa*.
One should prepare sour jujube (badarāmla) measuring four śāṇas;
black pepper, one and a half śāṇas; long pepper, ten śāṇas; cinnamon, sochal salt, coriander, and cumin, each two śāṇas. (128–129)
One should add sixty-four *śāṇa* measures of sugar to this;
the entire powder, mixed together, is called *yavānī-khāṇḍava*.
This powder conquers anemia (*pāṇḍuroga*), heart disease (*hṛdroga*), malabsorption syndrome (*grahaṇī*), and fever.

Tālīsādi powder [is used] for vomiting, grief-induced diarrhea, splenic enlargement, abdominal distension, constipation, anorexia, colic, weak digestion, hemorrhoids, and diseases of the tongue and throat. (131)
One should prepare the portions of tālīsa, marica, śuṇṭhī, pippalī, and vaṃśarocanā in one, two, three, four, and five karṣas respectively;
for elā and tvac, one should take half a karṣa as the portion for each.
Thirty-two karṣas of sugar should be added by the wise.
This powder, beginning with tālīsa, is known to be appetizing and digestive;
it removes cough, dyspnea, and fever, and destroys vomiting and diarrhea. (133–134)
This [preparation] removes emaciation and flatulence, conquers splenic disorders, malabsorption syndrome (agrahaṇī), and anemia;
having cooked sugar, one should add the powder, and from that, pills (guṭikā) may be made.
The powder of sitopalā and other ingredients is used for cough, wasting, Pitta-disorders, burning sensations, and so forth.

There should be sixteen *karṣas* of sugar candy (*sitopalā*), eight of bamboo-manna (*vaṃśarocanā*), four *karṣas* of long pepper (*pippalī*), and two *karṣas* of cardamom (*elā*). One *karṣa* of cinnamon bark (*tvac*) should be used; one should grind all of these together into a powder.
One should lick a powder of sugar, opium, and other ingredients combined with honey and clarified butter;
this removes asthma, cough, and consumption, conquers burning sensations in the hands, feet, and limbs, and cures weak digestion, numbness of the tongue, pain in the flanks, and loss of appetite.

The Lavaṇabhāskara powder quickly dispels blood and bile that have ascended to the head and cause fever. In cases such as malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī) and abdominal tumors (gulma), eight karṣas of sea salt should be prepared by the wise.
One should take five parts of sauvarcala salt, along with viḍa, rock salt (saindhava),
and coriander (dhānyaka) [139]; likewise, long pepper (pippalī), long pepper root (pippalīmūla), black cumin (kṛṣṇajīraka), cinnamon leaf (patrakam), nāgakeśara, tālīsa, and amlavetasa [140].
A wise person should have each of these made in the measure of two *karṣas*:
one *karṣa* each of black pepper (*marica*), cumin (*jīraka*), and ginger (*viśva*); four *karṣas* of pomegranate (*dāḍima*); and half a *karṣa* each of cinnamon bark (*tvak*) and cardamom (*elā*).
All this salt, named Bhāskara, should be ground into a powder; one *śāṇa* measure of it should be administered with whey (*mastu*), sour gruel (*takra*), wine (*surā*), or fermented liquor (*āsava*).
It cures abdominal tumors (*gulma*) arising from wind and phlegm, as well as splenic enlargement (*plīhāna*), abdominal dropsy (*udara*), and consumption (*kṣaya*).
This [preparation] destroys hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome, skin diseases, constipation,
fistula-in-ano, swelling, colic, asthma, cough, āmavāta, and heart disease;
it is an excellent digestive stimulant and carminative that cures weak digestion.
In ancient times, for the benefit of all the world, Bhāskara proclaimed this powder of cardamom and other ingredients for the treatment of vomiting:
cardamom, priyaṅgu, musta, the marrow of jujube fruit, and long pepper.
Likewise, one should lick a powder made of *śrīcandana*, parched grain (*lāja*), cloves (*lavaṅga*), and *nāgakeśara*, combined with sugar and honey;
this quickly destroys vomiting arising from *vāta*, *pitta*, and *kapha*. (146–147)
One should lick the powder of *vyāghrī*, *jīraka*, and *dhātrī* mixed with honey for conditions such as upward-moving wind (*ūrdhvavāta*) and severe dyspnea (*mahāśvāsa*).
One is instantly freed from upward-moving wind, severe dyspnea, and fainting (*tamaka*). 148

Regarding the powder of the five neem constituents: for the treatment of skin diseases (kuṣṭha) and other ailments, one should collect the root, leaf, fruit, flower, and bark of the neem tree; these should be ground into a fine powder using fifteen palas [in total]. 149
Iron ash, harītakī, cakramarda, citraka,
bhallātaka, viḍaṅga, sugar, āmalaka, niśā (150), pippalī, marica, śuṇṭhī, vākucī, and kṛtamālaka.
The wise one should have one *pala* each of *gokṣura* prepared;
having combined all these into a powder,
one should saturate it with eight parts of water from *khadira* and *āsana* trees, reduced to one-eighth.
Having processed it until it is completely dried, one should then drink a dose of one *karṣa* with water decocted from *khadira* and *āsana*, or with clarified butter, or with milk.
This elixir (*rasāyana*) destroys all types of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) within a month. (153)
This powder of the five neem ingredients destroys all diseases.
(154) Śatāvarī powder is for virilization;
[the formula consists of] śatāvarī, gokṣura, and the seeds of kapikacchu.
One should drink at night a powder made from *gāṅgerukī*, *cātibalā*, and seeds produced from *ikṣuraka*, all combined together with cow’s milk;
by the power of this powder, a man does not reach satiety with women. (155–156)

Regarding the powder of Aśvagandhā and other ingredients for aphrodisiac purposes: ten palas of Aśvagandhā and an equal amount of Vṛddhadāraka should be ground into a powder; the wise man should then cause both to be placed in a vessel of clarified butter. (157)
Having drunk one *karṣa* with milk, a man is never satiated by women;
even without approaching a woman, he shall become free from wrinkles and grey hair. (158) [This is] the powder of *musalī* and other ingredients for the treatment of impotence.

One should cause [the patient] to drink the powder of *musalī* root combined with the essence of *guḍūcī*, stirred with *vānarī*, *gokṣura*, *śālmalī*, sugar, and *āmalaka*, along with ghee and milk; this increases desire. 159

In the treatment of jaundice and other such ailments, one should take equal parts of powdered iron, *citraka*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *musta*, *viḍaṅga*, and the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*); these nine ingredients together should constitute nine parts of the total. (160)
One should lick this powder, combined as one and mixed with honey and clarified butter; cow’s urine or buttermilk is recommended as a post-drink (anupāna).
It conquers severe jaundice, heart disease, and fistula-in-ano. (161)
This powder of Ākārakarabha and others cures edema, skin diseases, abdominal enlargements, hemorrhoids, weak digestion, loss of appetite, and worms. (162) Regarding the stabilization [of the body],
the ingredients are Ākārakarabha, ginger, kaṅkola, saffron, and long pepper.

One should prepare one *karṣa* each by weight of nutmeg (*jātīphala*), clove (*lavaṅga*), and sandalwood (*candana*) (verse 163). One *pala* of *ahi-phaena* (opium) should be added; all these powders combined should be licked in a dose of one *māṣa* with honey (verse 164).
A lover should partake at night of this powder, which causes the retention of semen, brings joy to men, and generates pleasure in women;
furthermore, the powder of *bakula* bark [is used] for strengthening the teeth. 165.
One should rub the powder produced from *bakula* bark upon the rows of teeth;
the teeth will certainly become firmer than even a diamond, though they may have been previously unstable.
(166) Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Formulation of Powders," in the Middle Section of the *Śrī Śārṅgadharasaṃhitā*.
The Seventh Chapter: On the Formulation of Boluses (Vaṭaka-kalpanā). Names of Boluses.
Now, the *vaṭakas* (boluses) are described; they are called by these names: *guṭikā*, *vaṭī*, *modaka*, *vaṭikā*, *piṇḍī*, *guḍa*, and likewise *varti*.
[This is] the procedure for preparing *vaṭīs* that require heating over fire.
Just as jaggery, sugar,
or guggulu are processed over fire, one should likewise cast that powder into the fire;
this is the procedure for preparing pills (vaṭī) not processed by fire.
The wise man should prepare a pill (vaṭī) with guggulu processed without fire, or he may likewise make a bolus (guṭikā) with a liquid or honey.
Regarding the pill, there is no fixed rule concerning the amount of jaggery or sugar.
White sugar should be given four times the amount [of the powder] in pills; jaggery twice the amount of the powder;
guggulu should be made equal to the powder; honey should be equal to that; and the liquid should be given in double the amount for boluses (modaka) by the best of physicians. 4.
Regarding the instruction on the dosage of the pill:
its measure is one karṣa; it should be administered after considering the patient's strength.
This is the Śrī-Bāhuśāla-guḍa, beginning with the first part.
One should prepare two karṣas each of the following individual substances: indravāruṇikā, musta, śuṇṭhī, dantī, harītakī, trivṛt, śaṭī, viḍaṅga, gokṣura, citraka, and tejohvā.

Take eight palas of sūraṇa and four palas of vṛddhadāru; there should also be four palas of bhallātaka. One should boil all these together in one droṇa of water and take the excellent decoction when it has been reduced to one-fourth.
Having added treacle three times the quantity of the decoction ingredients, one should cook it again;
once it is known to be properly cooked, one should add this powder:
one pala each of citraka, trivṛt, dantī, and tejohvā.

One should prepare three *pala*s each of the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), cardamom (*elā*), black pepper (*marica*), and cinnamon bark (*tvac*). Once that has cooled, one should add one *prastha* measure of honey.
Thus prepared, this auspicious and glorious Bāhuśāla-guḍa becomes perfected.

This elixir conquers all types of jaundice, as well as abdominal tumors, wind-related abdominal enlargement, rheumatism, catarrh, malabsorption syndrome, consumption, chronic rhinitis, chlorosis, anemia, and urinary disorders. 12.
Regarding the Maricādi pill for cough and other ailments:
there should be one karṣa of black pepper (marica), one karṣa of long pepper (pippalī), half a karṣa of alkali of barley (yavakṣāra), and two karṣas of pomegranate (dāḍima). 13.
One should employ this powder mixed with eight *karṣas* of jaggery;
having formed pills the size of a *śāṇa*, one should hold them in the mouth.
By the power of this [preparation], all types of coughs indeed go to their complete destruction.
Regarding the use of jaggery boluses and the application of *bibhītaka* for dyspnea, cough, and other ailments:
one should hold a bolus made of jaggery, dry ginger, *harītakī*, and *musta* in the mouth for all types of dyspnea and cough; or even *bibhītaka* alone may be used. (16)

Regarding the *āmalakyādi-guṭikā* for thirst and other ailments: one should hold in the mouth a pill made from the powder of *āmalaka*, *kamala*, *kuṣṭha*, parched grain (*lāja*), and *vaṭarohaka*, mixed with honey.
This Sañjīvanī Vaṭī destroys increased thirst and severe dryness of the mouth;
it is used in cases of Sannipāta fever, snake bites, and the like.
Viḍaṅga, Nāgara, Kṛṣṇā, Pathyā, Āmalaka, and Bibhītaka [are its ingredients]. 17–18.
One should add vacā, guḍūcī, bhallātaka, and poison to these;
having taken these in equal parts, one should grind them with cow’s urine alone.
A pill the size of a guñjā seed should be made and administered with the juice of fresh arka leaves.
One pill should be administered for indigestion and abdominal tumors; two should be given for cholera;
three for snakebite; and four for diseases arising from the derangement of all three humors (sānnipātika).
This pill, named Sañjīvanī, restores life to a human being.
The Vyoṣādi pill for chronic rhinitis and similar ailments:
vyoṣa, amlavetasa, cavya, tālīsa, citraka, and likewise jīraka and tintiḍīka—one karṣa each of these [ingredients]. (22)

The three aromatics (trisaugandha) should be three śāṇas each, and there should be twenty karṣas of jaggery; this pill made from the three pungents (vyoṣa) and other ingredients conquers āma, chronic rhinitis, dyspnea, and cough. It is renowned for producing appetite and improving the voice, and it destroys catarrh. 23.

One should administer four types of pills made with jaggery (guḍa): in cases of undigested food (āma) and similar conditions, jaggery with ginger; in indigestion (ajīrṇa), jaggery with long pepper (pippalī); in urinary disorders (kṛcchra), jaggery with cumin (jīra); and in hemorrhoids (arśas), jaggery with chebulic myrobalan (abhayā). (24)

A bolus (modaka) prepared with the powder of *vṛddhadāru*, *bhallātaka*, and *śuṇṭhī*, combined with jaggery, destroys the pain caused by the six types of hemorrhoids when used in cases of hemorrhoids. (25)
Regarding the *śūraṇapiṇḍī* for the treatment of hemorrhoids (*arśas*):
one should take thirty-two parts of dried *śūraṇa* powder, sixteen parts of *citraka*, and four parts of ginger (*śuṇṭhī*). (26)
One should grind two parts of black pepper together with all the other ingredients into a powder;
one should then form a bolus with jaggery, which is the supreme destroyer of hemorrhoids (27).
This *śūraṇavaṭaka* is used for diseases such as hemorrhoids and others.
Śūraṇa and vṛddhadāru should each be taken in sixteen parts;
musalī and citraka are to be known as each measuring eight parts; and śivā, bibhītakī, dhātrī, viḍaṅga, nāgara, and kaṇā [are to be taken in four parts each]. 28–29.
Take four parts each of bhallātaka, pippalīmūla, and tālīsa, as well as two parts each of tvak, elā, and marica;
then grind them all together into a powder.
Then, the wise physician should have pills (vaṭakas) prepared with double the amount of jaggery.

These are powerful cleansers of the channels, as well as supreme destroyers of diarrhea; they cure dysentery caused by vāta and kapha, as well as asthma, cough, and the disease of consumption (kṣaya).
These medicinal elixirs (rasāyana), which promote intellect, destroy splenic disorders, elephantiasis, edema, hiccup, urinary disorders, fistula-in-ano, and premature graying of hair;
such is Maṇḍūravaṭaka, used for jaundice and other ailments. (33)

Take one *karṣa* each of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), *cavya*, the root of long pepper (*pippalīmūla*), *citraka*, *dāruharidrā*, honey-ore (*mākṣikadhātu*), cinnamon bark (*tvag*), *dārvī*, *musta*, and *viḍaṅga*; likewise, take double that amount of all [the other ingredients]. (34)
One should grind all the iron rust (maṇḍūra) into powder and throw it into eight times its quantity of cow's urine.

Having boiled this and formed it into boluses (vaṭaka), one should administer them with buttermilk as an after-drink (anupāna) for the cure of jaundice, anemia, urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, edema, skin diseases, and diseases caused by phlegm (kapha).
This Pippalī modaka also destroys stiffness of the thighs (ūrustambha), indigestion, and even splenic enlargement (plīhā). [In its preparation:
honey is twice the amount of ghee, and pippalī is twice the amount of ghee. 36–37.
Twice that amount of sugar and four times as much milk should be added;
having cooked it with an equal quantity of honey and the four aromatic spices (cāturjāta), one should prepare boluses (modakas).
These cure all fevers located in the tissues (dhātus), as well as dyspnea, cough, and jaundice.
The Pippalī-modaka conquers the depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātu) and sluggishness of the digestive fire (vahni). For urinary disorders such as prameha,
one should take Candra-prabhā-ṭī, which consists of vacā, musta, bhūnimba, amṛta, and dāruka.
Haridrā, ativiṣā, dārvī, pippalīmūla, citraka, 40 dhānyaka, triphalā, cavya, viḍaṅga, gajapippalī, vyoṣa,
mākṣikadhātu, the two kṣāras, and the three salts. 41
A wise person should have each of these made in the measure of a *śāṇa*:
trivṛt, dantī, patra, tvak, elā, and vaṃśarocanā (42).
A clever man should make each of these in the measure of one *karṣa*.
Two *karṣas* of processed iron (*hataloha*) should be used, and four *karṣas* of white sugar (*sitā*).
There should be eight *karṣas* of *śilājatu* and eight *karṣas* of *guggulu*.
With these thoroughly ground together, auspicious pills (*guṭikā*) should be prepared. (43–44)
Renowned as *Candraprabhā*, it destroys all diseases:

the twenty types of *prameha*, dysuria (*kṛcchra*), urinary obstruction (*mūtrāghāta*), as well as calculi (*aśmarī*), constipation, abdominal distension, colic, scrotal enlargement, glandular swellings, and tumors.
It likewise cures enlargement of the scrotum, anemia, jaundice, and halīmaka;
as well as intestinal hernia, pain in the waist, dyspnea, cough, eczema,
skin diseases, hemorrhoids, itching, splenic disorders, and fistula-in-ano.
It destroys diseases of the teeth, diseases of the eyes, and ailments arising from the menses in women;
likewise, it removes defects related to the semen in men, as well as weak digestion and loss of appetite.
It subdues Vāta, Pitta, and Kapha, and is strengthening, aphrodisiac, and a rejuvenative elixir.
In the *Candraprabhā*, four *śāṇa* are prescribed as one *karṣa*.
(49) The *Kāṅkāyana-guṭikā* [is used] for abdominal tumors (*gulma*) and other conditions;
it consists of *yavānī*, *jīraka*, *dhānyaka*, *marica*, and *girikarṇikā*.
Ajamoda and upakuñcī should each be four śāṇas;
hiṅgu should be made six śāṇas; and the wise one should prepare the two alkalis and the five salts with eight śāṇas each. 50–51.
A wise person should prepare pills from these— dantī, śaṭī, pauṣkara, viḍaṅga, dāḍima, śivā, citra, amlavetasa, and śuṇṭhī— using sixteen śāṇas of each and the juice of bījapūra. 52.
One should drink the pill proclaimed by Kāṅkāyana, which destroys abdominal tumors (gulma), with ghee, milk, wines, sour liquids, or warm water.
A vātika gulma is treated with wine, and a paittika gulma with cow’s milk.
One should ward off kapha-gulma with urine, and that born of the three doṣas with the ten roots (daśamūla).
One should eliminate women's rakta-gulma with camel’s milk; it destroys heart disease, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), colic, worms, and hemorrhoids. 55
Yogarāja-guggulu is for wind diseases, or for *āmavāta*, [the following are used]:
ginger, long pepper root, long pepper, *cavya*, and *citraka* (56);
as well as fried asafoetida, *ajamodā*, mustard, and the two types of cumin.
Reṇuka, indrayava, pāṭhā, viḍaṅga, gajapippalī (57),
kaṭukā, ativiṣā, bhārgī, vacā, and mūrvā— these twenty substances should each be one śāṇa in weight. 58.
Triphalā should be double the quantity of all these other ingredients;
to all these [ingredients] ground into powder, an equal amount of guggulu should be added. [Likewise, one should add] viḍaṅga, silver, lead, the essence of iron, and mica.
Take one *pala* each of iron filings (*maṇḍūra*) and mercury-cinnabar (*rasasindūra*); having prepared this in the consistency of boiled jaggery (*guḍapāka*), one should administer it as appropriate.
Then, having formed it into a single mass, one should store it in a vessel of clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
Having prepared pills of the measure of a *śāṇa*, they should be taken as appropriate;
this Guggulu is the king of formulations, a rejuvenator (*rasāyana*) that destroys the three *doṣas*.
In this case, there is no need for the renunciation of sexual intercourse, food, or drink.
It cures all wind-related disorders, leprosy, hemorrhoids, and diseases of the digestive tract (grahaṇī);

it also treats urinary disorders (prameha), gout (vātarakta), pain in the navel, fistula-in-ano, upward movement of gases (udāvarta), consumption (kṣaya), abdominal tumors (gulma), epilepsy, and chest congestion.

It destroys weak digestion, dyspnea, cough, and likewise loss of appetite; it removes seminal defects in men and menstrual defects in women. It generates offspring for men and bestows pregnancy upon barren women.
Combined with a decoction of rāsnā and other herbs, it destroys various types of vāta (66). Pitta is destroyed by a decoction of the kākolyādi group; kapha by that of the āragvadhādi group;
urinary disorders by a decoction of dārvī; and jaundice by cow’s urine (67).

One should take honey with *medā* for the increase of phlegm (*kapha*), with *kuṣṭha* boiled in *nimba* or with a decoction of *chinnā* for gout (*vātāsra*), and with a decoction of *kaṇā* for swelling and pain.
Combined with a decoction of *pāṭalā*, it overcomes poison born of rats.
Combined with a decoction of triphalā, it destroys severe eye pain; combined with a decoction of punarnavā and others, it cures all types of abdominal enlargements (udarā).
Kaiśoraguggulu is used for vātarakta and similar conditions.

Three *prasthas* of *triphalā* and one *prastha* of *amṛtā* should be crushed and cooked in an iron vessel with one and a half *droṇas* of water; knowing the water to be boiled down to half its original quantity, one should take it after filtering it through a cloth. (70–71)
Then, one should throw purified guggulu weighing one *prastha* into the decoction;
one should cook it again in an iron vessel, stirring it repeatedly with a ladle.
Having recognized that it has become thickened, resembling the consistency of boiled jaggery (*guḍa*), [one should remove it from the fire].
Then, having reduced these substances to powder, one should add them there:
triphalā is known to be two palas, guḍūcī is considered to be one pala,
the three pungents (yūṣaṇa) are declared to be six akṣas, and viḍaṅga is half a pala.
One karṣa of dantī should be prepared and one karṣa of trivṛt is prescribed;
then, having formed them all into a mass, one should place it in a vessel of ghee.
One should administer pills weighing one śāṇa each, according to the requirements of the bodily humors and other factors.

As a post-drink, the physician should administer lukewarm water or milk; alternatively, he may give water boiled with the Mañjiṣṭhādi group of drugs, applied according to the proper method. This will overcome all types of skin diseases (kuṣṭha) as well as vātarakta born of the three doṣas.

This elixir, when constantly employed, destroys all types of ulcers, abdominal tumors, urinary disorders, carbuncles, as well as those arising from urinary disorders, abdominal enlargements, weak digestion, cough, edema, and jaundice; it indeed cures all diseases.
This guggulu, known as Keśoraka, produces luster.

By means of a decoction of vāsā and other herbs, one may destroy eye diseases; by a decoction of varuṇa and others, one destroys abdominal tumors (gulma) and the like; and by a decoction of khadira, one destroys wounds and skin diseases (kuṣṭha). 79–80.

One who desires the excellence of the qualities of the city-physician should completely avoid sourness, pungency, indigestion, sexual intercourse, physical exertion, exposure to the sun, liquor, and anger. (81) Triphalā and guggulu are used for fistula-in-ano and similar conditions.
Three palas of Triphalā powder and one pala of Kṛṣṇā (Pippalī) powder, along with five palas of Guggulu, should all be ground together into a single mass. Then,
having formed pills from this, one should administer them according to the strength of the digestive fire.
It destroys fistula-in-ano, abdominal tumors, swellings, and hemorrhoids.
(83) Regarding the Gokṣurādi-guggulu for urinary disorders and other ailments: having taken twenty-eight palas of Gokṣura and so forth.
One should boil [the ingredients] in water with six times the quantity; the decoction should be taken when reduced to half.
Then one should cook it again, adding seven *pala* of *puṭa* (flour/cake); once it has reached the consistency of molasses (*guḍa*), one should add [the other ingredients] into it. 84–85.
One should take seven palas of the powdered *trikaṭu*, *triphalā*, and *musta*, and from this massed preparation, one should administer a pill (*guṭikā*).
It destroys urinary disorders (*prameha*), painful micturition (*kṛcchra*), menorrhagia (*pradara*), and urinary obstruction (*mūtraghāta*). (86)
The Triphalā modaka cures gout, wind diseases, seminal disorders, and likewise urinary calculi. For the treatment of skin diseases (kuṣṭha) and other ailments,
eight palas of Triphalā and four palas of Bhallātaka should be prepared.
Five palas of bākucī, four palas of viḍaṅga,
one pala each of hata-loha, trivṛt, guggulu, and śilājatu, and half a pala of pauṣkara. (88–89)
Half a pala of citraka, two śāṇas of marica,
and one śāṇa each of nāgara, pippalī, mustā, tvak, elā, patra, and kuṅkuma— these should all be powdered together as one.
Then, one should add that powder to an equal amount of cooked sugar-candy; having prepared boluses (modaka) weighing one pala each, one should administer them as appropriate.
These will destroy all types of leprosy (kuṣṭha) and diseases arising from the three humors (tridoṣa).

It destroys fistula-in-ano, splenic enlargement, abdominal tumors, diseases of the tongue, palate, and throat, as well as diseases located in the head, eyes, eyebrows, and even those situated in the back; it should be administered before a meal when the disease resides in the lower part of the body. (93)
Medicine should be taken in the midst of a meal when the disease is located in the stomach;
it should be taken after a meal in cases of diseases above the clavicle (ūrdhvajatrugada), such as those involving kāñcanāra, guggulu, gaṇḍamālā, apacī, granthi, and bhagaṃdara. 94.
Ten palas of gold-colored *āra* bark should be taken by the wise;

six palas of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) should be prepared, along with three palas of the three pungents (*trikaṭu*). One pala of *varuṇa* should be made, as well as one pala each of cardamom, cinnamon, and cinnamon leaves. 95–96.
Each one should be one *karṣa* in measure; one should grind them all together into a powder.
For as much as this entire powder is, there should be that same measure of *guggulu*. Having crushed everything together and formed it into a single mass, one should preserve it.
Pills the size of a *śāṇa* should be prepared and taken in the morning as appropriate.
They conquer severe *gaṇḍamālā*, scrofula (*apacī*), tumors (*arbuda*), glandular swellings, ulcers, abdominal lumps (*gulma*), skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), and fistula-in-ano (*bhagaṃdara*). 98–99.
A decoction of *muṇḍitikā* should be administered as a post-drink (*anupāna*),
as should a decoction of the heartwood of *khadira*, a decoction of *pathyā*, or warm water.
For nourishment, pills (*modaka*) weighing one *māṣa* or more may be given.

One should prepare one *pala* each of the following: dehusked *māṣa* flour, likewise flour derived from wheat, dehusked barley flour, and likewise flour produced from *śāli* rice, as well as fine *pippalī* powder. (101)
Having combined all of this together, one should fry it with cow’s ghee (102).
Then, having added sugar equal to half the total weight of all the ingredients,
and having added double the amount of water, one should cook it very slowly (103).
Then, having extracted the cooked [mixture], one should fashion round *modaka* boluses;
having eaten one at night, one should drink one *pala* of milk with four times as much water.
Furthermore, the two tastes of alkaline (*kṣāra*) and sour (*amla*) should be especially avoided.
Having acted thus, a man may enjoy many women and yet he does not waste away.
105. Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Preparation of Vaṭakas," in the Middle Section of the Śrīśārṅgadharasaṃhitā; [now follows] the Preparation of Avalehas (Linctuses).
Now begins the eighth chapter, titled "The Formulations of Linctuses" (Avaleha-kalpanā).
Herein is the definition, nomenclature, and dosage of the linctus; furthermore, that which attains thickness through the further cooking of decoctions and other ingredients is called *rasakriyā*.
That *avaleha* (lickable preparation) shall be a *leha* (linctus), and its measure should be one *pala*.
When no specific quantity is mentioned for sugar and other ingredients,
the sugar should be made four times the amount of the powder, and the jaggery (*guḍa*) should be twice the amount of the powder.
One should give four times as much clarified butter; this is the certainty everywhere.
Regarding the sign of successful preparation of an electuary (avaleha): when well-cooked, it should possess thread-like fibers and sink in water.
When it is pressed, the seal produces a pungent quality arising from fragrance, color, and taste.
The after-drinks for the electuary are milk, sugarcane juice, and soup prepared from a decoction of the five roots (pañcamūla).
A decoction of *vāsā* is recommended as a suitable post-medicine (*anupāna*).
Regarding the electuary of *kaṇṭakārī*: for cough, dyspnea, and other such conditions, one should boil one *tulā* of *kaṇṭakārī* in one *droṇa* of water to produce a decoction.
Having taken one quarter-portion of this, one should cause these powders to be added to it:
one pala each of *guḍūcī*, *cavya*, and *citraka*;
*musta*, *karkaṭaśṛṅgī*, the three pungents (*trivṛt*, *pippalī*, *marica*), and *dhanvayāsaka*. (5–6)
One should take twenty palas of sugar and eight palas each of bhārgī, rāsnā, and śaṭī; having cooked these with ghee and oil,
one should reduce them to the consistency of a linctus, and once cooled, add eight palas of honey.
Having added four palas of tugākṣīrī and four palas of pippalī,
one should place it in a beautiful, very sturdy earthen vessel;
this linctus destroys hiccup, asthma, and cough entirely.
The Cyavanaprāśa formulation is for those emaciated by wasting diseases and similar conditions;
it consists of Pāṭalā, Araṇikā, Aśmarī, Bilva, Āraluka, Gokṣura, the two Parṇīs, the two Bṛhatīs, Pippalī, Śṛṅgī, Drākṣā, Amṛtā, and Abhayā. (10)
Balā, bhūmyāmalī, vāsā, ṛddhi, jīvantikā, śaṭī, jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, musta, pauṣkara, kākanāsikā,
mudgaparṇī, māṣaparṇī, vidārī, and punarnavā.
The two types of *kākolī*, *kamala*, the two types of *medā*, *sūkṣmailā*, *agaru*, and *candana*— each of these medicinal substances measured at one *pala* and coarsely powdered—
are combined with five hundred *palas* of *pañcāmala* in a large vessel. (12–13)
Having cast pomegranate seeds into water containing one *droṇa* and boiled them until one-eighth remains,
then having removed the stones from those same *āmala* fruits and squeezed them with a cloth by a firm hand, one should then cast that [juice] along with ghee into it.

Having slightly fried those [drugs] weighing seven *palas* over a low fire, one should then add a decoction and half a *tulā* of sugar-candy (*khaṇḍa*) to it; having prepared it like an electuary (*leha*), one should cause these powders to be administered. 15–16.
Two palas of pippalī and four palas of tugākṣīrī should be given; likewise, three śāṇas each of tvak, elā, patra, and keśara should be used.
Then, once these have been combined, one should add six palas of honey.
Thus has been declared by Cyavana this electuary known as Cyavanaprāśa;
observing the strength of one's digestive fire, one who is emaciated should consume this elixir,
as should children, the elderly, those wasted by chest wounds, women who have become thin, and those suffering from consumption.
In men who suffer from heart disease and diminished voice, this [remedy] is applied;
it cures cough, dyspnea, thirst, hemoptysis, and constriction of the chest, and it destroys disorders of vāta and pitta, as well as defects of the semen and the urine. 20.

By the use of this, a man who avoids aged food attains intelligence, memory, joy toward women, luster, and clarity of complexion. This *kūṣmāṇḍāvaleha* is for [the treatment of] hemorrhagic disorders (*raktapitta*) and similar conditions.
Having deseeded one hundred palas of pumpkin pieces, one should cook them with two tulās of water until half remains;
these pumpkin pieces should then be pressed with a firm cloth. (22)
One should dry it slightly in the sun and repeatedly pierce it with the tips of needles (23).
Having placed it in a copper cauldron, one should add eight palas of ghee;
having fried it slightly in that, one should pour in the aforementioned water (24).
Having given one hundred palas of sugar-candy, one should cook it all together until well-cooked;

then add two palas each of long pepper (pippalī), dry ginger (śuṇṭhī), and cumin (jīraka), and half a pala each of coriander (dhānyāka), cinnamon leaves (patra), cardamom (elā), black pepper (marica), and cinnamon bark (tvac).
Having reduced it to powder, one should throw it therein and add half a part of ghee and honey.

One suffering from internal hemorrhage (raktapitta), consumption (kṣaya), fever, wasting, thirst, vertigo, vomiting, dyspnea, cough, or chest injury should eat this after observing the strength of their digestive fire.
This *kūṣmāṇḍaka-avaleha* is suitable for children and the elderly; it is considered to heal chest wounds, act as an aphrodisiac, promote nourishment, and increase strength.
(28) *Khaṇḍa-śūraṇa-avaleha* is used in cases of hemorrhoids.
A wise person should cook *śūraṇa* with pieces of *kūṣmāṇḍa* according to the proper method; this is suitable for those suffering from hemorrhoids, obstructed wind (*mūḍhavāta*), and weak digestion.
[This concludes] the *Agastyaharītakyavaleha*, used for wasting diseases (*kṣaya*) and other conditions.
One hundred *harītakī* fruits, one *āḍhaka* of barley,
ten *palas* of *daśamūla*, and twenty *palas* each of *citraka*, *pippalīmūla*, *apāmārga*, and *śaṭī* should be employed. (30–31)
One should boil *kapikacchū*, *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *bhārṅgī*, *gajapippalī*, *balā*, and *puṣkaramūla*— each in a quantity of two *palas*—
in five *āḍhakas* of water; once boiled, one should add it to the steamed barley.
Into that decoction, the wise physician should add one hundred palas of *abhayā*, eight palas each of ghee and oil, and likewise one *tulā* of jaggery;
having cooked it until it reaches the consistency of a linctus, once it is prepared and cooled, [one should add the following] separately: (33–34)
One should add one kuḍava measure of honey and powdered pippalī;
one should daily consume two harītakī fruits along with this electuary to [cure] consumption, cough, fever, dyspnea, hiccup, anorexia, and chronic rhinitis. (35)
This destroys the *grahaṇī* disorder and eliminates wrinkles and graying hair (36). This electuary (*avaleha*), a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*) that bestows strength and complexion upon men,
was prescribed by the sage Agastya as a destroyer of all diseases (37).
Regarding the *kuṭajāvaleha* (Kuṭaja electuary) for diseases beginning with hemorrhoids:
A wise person should boil one *tulā* of *kuṭaja* bark in one *droṇa* of water; when reduced to one-fourth, he should take the decoction after filtering it through a cloth. (38)
Having added thirty palas of jaggery to this, one should cook it again; once it has reached a thick consistency, one should add these powders:
rasāñjana, mocarasa, trikaṭu, and likewise triphalā. (39)
Lajjālū, citraka, pāṭhā, bilva, indrayava, tvak, bhallātaka,
prativiṣā, viḍaṅga, and bālaka— one pala of each, along with one kuḍava of ghee. (40–41)
Then, once it has cooled, one should add one *kuḍava* of honey;
this electuary (*avaleha*) will swiftly conquer all types of hemorrhoids (*arśas*), as well as diseases arising from hemorrhoids, diarrhea, and loss of appetite. 42.
For dysentery, anemia, internal hemorrhaging, jaundice, 43 acid gastritis, as well as edema, emaciation, and dysentery with tenesmus,
goat’s buttermilk, milk, and curd should be employed as a post-drink (anupāna).

Once [the medicine] has been digested, the person should consume ghee or water and eat wholesome food (pathya). 44. For diarrhea and similar ailments, one should boil one *tulā* of fresh *kuṭaja* bark in one *droṇa* of water; this is the *kuṭajāṣṭaka-ādyavaleha*.
Having reduced it to one-quarter of its original volume by boiling, one should cause these powders to be added:
*lajjālu*, *dhātakī*, *bilva*, *pāṭhā*, *mocarasa*, *musta*, and *prativiṣā*; each of these should be one *pala* in weight. (45–46)
Then one should cook it again until it reaches the consistency of a paste that adheres to the ladle;
when drunk with water, goat’s milk, or gruel (*maṇḍa*),
it conquers all severe types of diarrhea, even those of various colors and accompanied by pain.
It cures all types of menorrhagia, all hemorrhoids, and dysentery.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Preparation of Linctuses," in the Middle Section of the Śrī Śārṅgadharasaṃhitā; [followed by] the "Preparation of Oils."
Now begins the ninth chapter, titled "The Formulation of Unctuous Substances.
Regarding the formulation of ghee or oil:
one should take four times the quantity of paste (kalka) and [add] either ghee or oil.
It should be prepared in a liquid four times its quantity; the dose of that [medicine] is one pala.
Regarding the technical rule for decoctions used for preparing fats:
one should add water four times the amount of the substance to be decocted and then boil it.
Having taken one-quarter of the remaining oil, one should prepare it with that very [decoction].
Regarding the quantity of water for boiling soft substances, it should be fourfold;
for hard substances, the water should be eightfold.
Likewise, one should add eight times the amount of water to a medium-hard substance;
for an extremely hard substance, sixteen parts of water are prescribed.
This is the specific measurement according to another school of thought.
From one *karṣa* up to one *pala*, one should add sixteen times as much water;
beyond that, up to one *kuḍava*, the water should be eight times the quantity.
From one *prastha* onwards, one should add four times as much water, continuing until it reaches one *khārī*.
Where oil is prepared with water and other liquids,
the quantity of the paste (kalka) should be one-fourth; where the oil is prepared separately from water, decoctions, and juices, one should add the paste in a proportion of one-sixth or one-eighth.
The technical rule for cooking with milk and other liquids:
one-eighth part of a paste (kalka) should be added to milk, curd, juice, or buttermilk;
for the proper cooking of the paste, four times as much water is required here. 7.

Regarding unctuous substances, there is a classification of five types of liquids; for those unctuous substances in which five or more [qualities] exist, they are called "similar to unctuousness" (snehasamāna), and as before, they possess four qualities. 8.
Regarding the quantity for the cooking of oil with a single substance:
if the cooking of the oil is to be done with the substance alone, then the paste should be ground with water, and the water in this case should be four times the quantity [of the paste]. 9.
Regarding the quantity of a simple decoction for the purpose of cooking a medicated oil (sneha):
whenever a cooking process with a simple decoction alone is prescribed, the paste (kalka) of the same decoction-drug should also be employed therein in the oil. 10
The method for cooking medicated fats (sneha) without a paste (kalka):
However, that medicated fat which is devoid of a paste should be prepared with only the liquid extract.
The method for cooking medicated fats with a paste of flowers (puṣpakalka).
In a medicated oil where flower-paste is used, water should be four times the amount of the oil,
and the flower-paste should be applied at one-eighth the weight of the oil.
This is the characteristic sign of the successful completion of the oil.
When the paste of the medicinal fat (sneha-kalka), being rubbed with a finger,
becomes free of sound upon being cast into the fire like a wick, then that fat is considered perfected.
This is the description of the characteristics of perfection for the cooking of ghee and oil.
When froth arises from oil and the froth subsides in clarified butter (sarpiḥ), and when fragrance, color, and taste have developed, then the cooking of the fat (sneha) is accomplished. 14.
[This concludes] the varieties of the cooking of fats and their characteristics.
The cooking of medicated fats (sneha-pāka) is said to be of three kinds: mild (mṛdu), medium (madhya), and hard (khara).
When the paste (kalka) is still slightly moist, the cooking of the fat is considered mild. The completion of the medium cooking occurs when the paste has become moisture-free and soft.
When the paste is slightly firm, the cooking of the fat (sneha) becomes "hard" (khara);
beyond that, it would be a "burnt" cooking, which causes burning and is useless.
(16) These are the qualities of uncooked, cooked, and processed fats.
An uncooked preparation is devoid of potency, causes sluggishness of the digestive fire, and is heavy (17).
Regarding the rules for the cooking of fats such as clarified butter:
the cooking should be mild for the purpose of nasal administration (nasya), and moderate for all other procedures.
A donkey is prescribed for the purpose of massage; one should employ these [substances] in this manner as is appropriate.
(18) Regarding the timing for preparing ghee, oil, jaggery, and so forth:
one should not prepare ghee, oil, jaggery, and the like on the same day.
For when these have been consumed, they especially produce an accumulation of wholesome qualities (guṇasañcaya). Now follows the preparation of ghee:
"Kṣīraṣaṭpala-ghee" [is used] for irregular fevers (viṣamajvara) and other such conditions.

One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with one *pala* each of long pepper (*pippalī*), long pepper root (*pippalīmūla*), *cavya*, *citraka*, and dry ginger (*nāgara*), along with rock salt (*saindhava*),
adding four times as much milk; that ghee destroys splenic disorders (*plīha*).

This *cāṅgerī-ghṛta* is the supreme remedy for irregular fever (*viṣamajvara*) and weak digestion (*mandāgni*), and it promotes appetite; [it is also beneficial] in cases of diarrhea (*atīsāra*) and malabsorption syndrome (*grahaṇī*).
[The ingredients include] long pepper (*pippalī*), long pepper root (*pippalīmūla*), leadwort (*citraka*), and elephant pepper (*hastipippalī*).
Śvadaṃṣṭrā, nāgara, dhānya, pāṭhā, bilva, and yavānikā—
using these ingredients, each weighing one pala, a wise physician should add sixty-four palas of ghee and four times as much fresh juice of cāṅgerī.
Likewise, having added four times as much curd, one should cook it with ghee;
this excellent Cāṅgerī-ghṛta should be cooked very slowly.
That ghee destroys Kapha and Vāta, and cures disorders of the digestive tract and hemorrhoids.
It cures abdominal distension, prolapse of the rectum, dysuria, and dysentery.
(24) Regarding *masūra*-ghṛta for diarrhea and other ailments:
one should boil one hundred palas of *masūra* lentils in one droṇa of water.
Having reduced the decoction to one-quarter of its original volume and added eight *palas* of *bilva* leaves,
one should cook a *prastha* of ghee with it; this destroys all types of diarrhea, as well as *grahaṇī*, loose stools, and dysentery.
In the *kāmadevaghṛta* for conditions such as *raktapitta* (bleeding disorders), one *tulā* of *aśvagandhā* is prescribed, with *gokṣura* known to be half that amount;
along with *balā*, *amṛtā*, *śāliparṇī*, *vidārī*, and *śatāvarī*. (27)
One should boil ten *pala* portions each of the shoots of the *aśvattha* tree, lotus seeds, *punarnavā*,
the fruit of the *kāśmarya*, and likewise *māṣa* seeds,
in four *droṇas* of water.
When one *droṇa* of that liquid remains, one should cook an *āḍhaka* of ghee with *mṛdvīkā*,
*padmaka*, *kuṣṭha*, *pippalī*, red sandalwood,
*patraka*, *nāgapuṣpa*, and likewise the fruit of *ātmaguptā*.

One should collect one *karṣa* each of blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), the two types of *sārivā*, and the group of life-promoting drugs (*jīvanīya-gaṇa*), along with two *palas* of sugar and one *āḍhaka* of the juice of *pauṇḍraka* sugarcane. (31)
One should cook one āḍhaka of ghee with four times as much milk.
This ghee quickly destroys hemorrhaging (raktapitta), chest wounds (uraḥkṣata),
chlorosis (halīmaka), anemia (pāṇḍuroga), discoloration of the skin, and loss of voice.

This ghee cures dysuria, burning in the chest, and pain in the flanks; it should be administered to those living in large harems, to women who have not yet given birth, and to those whose bodies are weak. (34)
It is the best for increasing strength, improving the complexion, pleasing to the heart, nourishing, and an elixir;
it produces vitality and brilliance, is pleasing to the heart, promotes longevity, increases the life-force, and enhances the semen of a man with weak senses. (35–36)
Free from all diseases, like a tree sprinkled with water, this ghee of great virtue is called Kāmadeva;
it is known as Pānīyakalyāṇaka ghee for the treatment of epilepsy and other such conditions. 37.
Triphalā, the two types of niśā, kauntī, the two types of sārivā, priyaṅgukā, śāliparṇī, pṛṣṭhiparṇī, devadāru, elavāluka,
nata, viśālā, dantī, dāḍima, and nāgakeśara. (38)
Nīlotpala, elā, mañjiṣṭhā, viḍaṅga, kuṣṭha, padmaka,
jasmine flowers, sandalwood, tālīsa, and likewise bṛhatī—
using one karṣa of each of these as a paste, add four times the amount of water. 39–40.
The wise physician should cook one *prastha* of clarified butter for use in epilepsy, fever, consumption,
insanity, vātarakta, cough, weak digestion, as well as catarrh,
pain in the waist, and tertian or quartan fevers. (41)
It is employed in all cases of dysuria, erysipelas, itching, and anemia; it is likewise used for the two types of poisoning and urinary disorders.
It is known to grant sons to barren women and to destroy spirits, yakṣas, and rākṣasas.
One should cook clarified butter with the decoction and paste of *amṛtā*, along with milk, for use in cases of *kuṣṭha* and similar conditions;
it quickly conquers *vātarakta* and overcomes even the most difficult forms of *kuṣṭha*. (44)
Mahātiktaka-ghṛta is used for vātarakta, kuṣṭha, and other such conditions;
[its ingredients are] saptacchada, prativiṣā, śamyāka, kaṭurohiṇī, pāṭhā, musta, uśīra, triphalā, and parpaṭa. (45)
Paṭola, nimba, mañjiṣṭhā, pippalī, padmaka, śaṭī, candana, dhanvayāsa, the two types of viśālā, the two types of niśā, as well as guḍūcī, the two types of sārivā, mūrvā, vāsā, and śatāvarī. 46.
Trāyantī, indrayava, yaṣṭī, and bhūnimba should each be taken in one part (akṣa) measure.
One should add four times the amount of ghee, twice the amount of āmalaka juice compared to the ghee, and eight times the amount of water compared to the ghee. 47–48.
Once prepared, one should have this ghee drunk in all cases of vātarakta,

as well as for skin diseases (kuṣṭha), bleeding disorders (raktapitta), hemorrhoids with blood (raktārśas), anemia (pāṇḍutā), heart disease, abdominal tumors (gulma), erysipelas (vīsarpa), menorrhagia (pradara), and scrofula (gaṇḍamālā). 49.
This "Great Bitter" (Mahātiktaka) [decoction] overcomes minor diseases as well as fevers.
The Kāsīsādi-ghṛta [is used] for skin diseases (kuṣṭha), ringworm (dadrū), scabies (pāmā), eruptions on the head, and so forth.
[The ingredients are: green vitriol (kāsīsa), the two types of turmeric (niśā), nut-grass (musta), yellow orpiment (haritāla), and realgar (manaḥśilā).
Kampillaka, Gandhaka, Viḍaṅga, and likewise Guggulu;
51 Sikthaka, Marica, Kuṣṭha, Tutthaka, and Gaurasarṣapa;
Rasāñjana, Sindūra, Śrīvāsa, and Raktacandana. 52
One should powder one karṣa each of irimeda, nimba leaves, karañja, sārivā, vacā,
mañjiṣṭhā, madhuka, māṃsī, śirīṣa, lodhra, padmaka,
harītakī, and prapunnāṭa.
Then, having stirred that powder into thirty palas of ghee,
one should place it in a copper vessel and keep it in the heat for seven days.
By its application as an ointment, skin diseases such as kuṣṭha, dadru, pāmā, and vicarcikā are cured.
The disorders of the hair-follicles, erysipelas, eruptions born of vāta and rakta, boils on the head, venereal sores, fistulous ulcers,
swellings, fistula-in-ano, and spider-bites are pacified in embodied beings. (56)
Clarified butter (ghṛta) that performs purification, healing, and the restoration of natural skin color—
known as Jātyādi-ghṛta— is used for wounds;
it contains jasmine, neem, paṭola, the two types of turmeric, and kaṭurohiṇī.
A wise physician should properly cook ghee with a paste of mañjiṣṭhā, madhuka, siktha, karañja, uśīra, sārivā, and tuttha; by the application of this as an ointment,
even small sinus ulcers will heal.
Wounds that are located on vital points (marmas), are moist, deep-seated, and painful [should be treated with] *bindughṛta*. For the purgation of ascites (*jalodara*) and similar conditions,
[the drugs used are] *citraka*, *śaṅkhinī*, *pathyā*, *kampillā*, and the pair of *trivṛtās*.
Vṛddhadāru, śamyāka, dantī, as well as the fruit of dantī;
kośātakī, devadālī, nīlinī, girikarṇikā, sātalā, the root of pippalī, viḍaṅga, and likewise kuṭakī. (61–62)
A wise physician should cook one prastha of ghee with these paste ingredients measured at one picu each, along with six palas of snuhī milk and two palas of arka milk; once prepared,
this cures abdominal tumors (gulma) and skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
It destroys colic, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), swelling, flatulence, and fistula-in-ano; it pacifies the eight types of abdominal enlargements (udara) when administered in drops,
either with cow’s milk, camel’s milk, or boiled horse-gram soup.
Or, having drunk it with warm water, one should induce purgation by means of the force of drops;
this is called *bindughṛta*, and by applying it as an ointment to the navel, it induces purgation.
(66) *Triphalādya-ghṛta* is used for eye diseases such as *timira* and others.
One *prastha* of the juice of *triphalā*, one *prastha* derived from the juice of *vāsā*,

one *prastha* of the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*, and one *prastha* of goat’s milk are prescribed; having added these, one should add one *prastha* of ghee along with the medicinal pastes (*kalka*), each weighing one *karṣa*.
Triphalā, pippalī, drākṣā, candana, saindhava, balā, kākolī, kṣīrakākolī, medā, marica, nāgara, śarkarā, puṇḍarīka, kamala, and punarnavā. (68)
One should cook madhuka with the two types of niśā and all these [other] ingredients;
this conquers night-blindness, owl-like blindness, itching, pillaka, as well as ocular discharge, paṭala, timira, and cataracts (kāca).
Even other extremely severe eye diseases are pacified;
indeed, this Traiphala-ghṛta is recommended for drinking, as nasal drops (nasya), and so forth.
Gaurādya-ghṛta is used for wounds.
Two types of *haridrā*, *sthirā*, *mūrvā*, *sārivā*, the two kinds of *candana*,
*madhuparṇī*, *madhuka*, *padmakeśara*, *padmaka*, *utpala*, *uśīra*, *medā*, *triphalā*, and the five *valkalas*. 72.
One should cook one prastha of ghee with these pastes (kalka), each measuring one karṣa.

This ghee, renowned as Gaurādya, is the supreme destroyer of poison; it cures erysipelas (visarpa), spider bites (lūtā), eruptive boils (visphoṭa), wounds from poisonous insects, and other toxins. 73–74.
One should cook peacock-ghee with balā, madhuka, and rāsnā, along with the daśamūla and triphalā— each weighing two palas— using eight times as much water. (75)

Having properly boiled a peacock— excluding its feathers, bile, intestines, liver, feet, and head— until only the feet remain, one should add an equal quantity of milk and cook it with one *prastha* of ghee and one *picu* each of the *jīvanīya* (life-promoting) drugs.
Thus it is established that this [preparation] overcomes pain in the head, as well as stiffness of the neck and back,
facial paralysis (ardita), and diseases of the ears, nose, eyes, tongue, and throat;
it is employed for drinking, nasal administration (nasya), massage, and ear-filling.
This fruit-ghee is recommended during the winter, the cool season, and spring (79) for the condition of sterility;
it consists of triphalā, madhuka, kuṣṭha, the two types of niśā, and kaṭurohiṇī.
Viḍaṅga, pippalī, mustā, viśālā, kaṭphala, vacā;
the two types of medā, the two types of kākolī, the two types of sārivā, priyaṅgukā, śatapuṣpā, hiṅgu, rāsnā, candana, and raktacandana. (80–81)
One should add one karṣa each of the pastes (kalka) of jasmine (jātīpuṣpa), Tugākṣīrī, lotus (kamala), sugar (śarkarā), ajamodā, and dantī,
along with one prastha of ghee from a cow whose calf is living and which is of a uniform color. 82.
One should cook [the ingredients] with four times as much milk over a fire of wild cow-dung;
on an auspicious lunar day under the Puṣya asterism, it should be placed in an earthen or copper vessel.
Then, on a propitious day, either a woman or a man should drink it.
Having drunk this clarified butter, a man always acts like a bull among women;
the wise man procreates sons, and even a barren woman obtains a child.
She who gives birth to one who does not live long, or she who, having given birth, remains [unfertile] again—[by drinking this, she shall bear long-lived offspring]. 85.
That woman obtains a son who is intelligent and lives for a hundred years.
This is the remedy known as *Phalaghṛta*, spoken by Bharadvāja; the physician should add the root of *lakṣmaṇā*, which was not mentioned there, to it. (86–87)
In cases of gynecological disorders (yoniroga), [one should prepare] Laghuphalaghṛta using triphalā, the two types of sahacara, guḍūcī, punarnavā, śukanāsā,
the two types of haridrā, rāsnā, medā, and śatāvarī. 88

Having made a paste [of the aforementioned ingredients], one should cook one prastha of ghee with four times as much milk; once prepared, this should be administered to a woman afflicted by pain in the vagina—whether she is suffering, displaced, prolapsed, or dilated. 89.
Those born from a bile-based origin, those who are mentally deranged, and those known as eunuchs—
when they obtain this beneficial [mixture], they attain their proper place and conceive repeatedly.
This is the medicinal ghee named *Phalaghṛta*, which is supreme for removing defects of the female reproductive tract.
Ghee prepared with the five bitter herbs (pañcatiktaka), along with the decoction and paste of vṛṣa, nimba, amṛtā, vyāghrī, and paṭola, cures irregular fevers (viṣamajvara) and similar ailments.
It destroys leucoderma, skin diseases, erysipelas, worms, and hemorrhoids. (92) Now follows the preparation of oils:
*Lākṣādi-taila* (the lac-based oil) is used for intermittent fevers and other such ailments.
Having boiled one *āḍhaka* of lac with four *āḍhakas* of water, and having reduced it to a fourth part, one should pour it into one *prastha* of oil;
one should also add one *āḍhaka* of whey from cow's curd right there. 93.
One karṣa each of śatapuṣpā, aśvagandhā, haridrā, devadāru, kuṭakī, reṇukā, mūrvā, kuṣṭha, madhuyaṣṭikā,
candana, mustaka, and rāsnā [should be taken]. (94–95)
Having added [the ingredients] there, one should powder them and prepare the medicine over a mild fire.
By anointing with this, all types of irregular fevers (viṣamajvara) are pacified, as well as cough, asthma, catarrh, and stiffness of the sacrum and back. 96.
It conquers wind (vāta), bile (pitta), epilepsy, insanity, yakṣas, and rākṣasas;
it overcomes itching, pain, foul odor, and the twitching of the limbs.
Through frequent massage with this, a pregnant woman’s fetus will become well-nourished. 97–98.
Charcoal and oil [are used] for all fevers;
likewise, mūrvā, lac, the two types of haridrā, mañjiṣṭhā, indravāruṇī, bṛhatī, rock salt, kuṣṭha, rāsnā, māṃsī, and śatāvarī [are used]. 99
One should cook one *prastha* of oil with one *āḍhaka* of fermented rice-gruel (*āranāla*) therein;
this oil, named Aṅgāraka, liberates one from all fevers.
Or [one may use] Nārāyaṇa-taila for wind-diseases (*vāta-roga*) and the like. 100.
One should take ten palas each of aśvagandhā, balā, bilva, pāṭalā, the two types of bṛhatī, śvadaṃṣṭrā, atibalā, nimba, syonāka, punarnavā, prasāriṇī, and agnimantha. (101)
Having boiled four *droṇas* of *ūrṇa* in water until one-quarter remains, one should take that decoction;
then, having combined it with one *āḍhaka* of oil and one *āḍhaka* of the juice of *śatāvarī*, one should add cow’s milk there, which is four times the amount of the oil. 102–103.
One should slowly digest [the medicine] with these pastes (kalka), two palas each of the following:
kuṣṭha, elā, candana, mūrvā, vacā, māṃsī, and saindhava; as well as aśvagandhā, vacā, rāsnā, śatapuṣpā, indra, and dāru. 104.
One should prepare that oil with the four types of *parṇī* and *tagara*. It should be employed for nasal drops (*nāvana*), massage (*abhyaṅga*), oral intake (*pāna*), and enema (*basti*).
It cures hemiplegia (*pakṣāghāta*), lockjaw (*hanustambha*), stiffness of the neck (*manyāstambha*), and throat obstruction (*galagraha*).

Deafness, lameness, stiffness of the waist, emaciation of the limbs, loss of the senses, and the wasting away of blood, semen, and fever; 107 as well as hernia, scrotal enlargement, dental disease, and stiffness of the head.
