It conquers pain in the sides, lameness, loss of intellect, sciatica (gṛdhrasī), and other irregular disorders of Vāta located in all parts of the body.
By its power, even a barren woman gives birth to a son. 108–109.
Just as a mortal man, an elephant, or a horse may become happy through this oil, so too does the god Nārāyaṇa, the destroyer of wicked Daityas;
likewise, this excellent oil is the destroyer of wind-related diseases. 110–111.
For the disease of trembling (kampa), take three palas of crushed *vāruṇī* root and twelve palas of oil; boil them together in fire for a moment. 112.
One should consume three *niṣkas* of this [medicine] along with food; by this, trembling of the hands, trembling of the head, and trembling of the neck and vessels are destroyed.
This oil, beginning with *bala*, is for the treatment of wind-diseases (*vātavyādhi*).

One part of oil should be prepared with eight parts each of a decoction of *balā* roots, a decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūla*), a decoction of horse gram (*kulattha*), barley (*yava*), and jujube (*kola*), as well as milk.
With the group of vitalizing drugs (jīvanīya), śatāvarī, indradāru,
mañjiṣṭhā, kuṣṭha, śaileya, tagara, aguru, saindhava, vacā, punarnavā, māṃsī, the two types of sārivā, and patrakā— 115–116.
One should cook [this] with śatapuṣpā, aśvagandhā, and elā;
it is suitable for women desiring pregnancy, for men whose semen is depleted, for those whose limbs are wasted by physical exertion, and for women who have recently given birth. (117)
This oil is fit for kings and especially for those seeking comfort;
it is renowned as Balā-taila, which removes all diseases caused by Vāta.
Prasāriṇī-taila is likewise used for diseases arising from Vāta and Kapha, and so forth.
One hundred palas of *prasāriṇī* should be boiled in one droṇa of water;
when reduced to one-quarter, the decoction is to be taken, along with an equal amount of oil and curd.
The sour gruel (*kāñjika*) should be equal to the oil, and the milk should be four times the amount of the oil. (119)
One should add all the medicinal pastes (kalkas) in an eighth part of the oil.
These are: madhuka, pippalīmūla, citraka, saindhava, vacā, prasāriṇī, devadāru, rāsnā, and gajapippalī. (120–121)

One should cook this oil with bhallātaka, śatapuṣpā, and māṃsī; when properly prepared, this excellent oil conquers diseases of vāta and kapha, as well as kubja, lameness, limping, gṛdhrasī, and ardita. (122)
It destroys stiffness of the jaw, back, head, neck, and waist,
and quickly dispels all other various disorders of Vata.
This is Māṣādi-taila, used for Vata-related disorders and similar conditions.
One should take seven palas each of māṣa, yava, atasī, kṣudrā, markaṭī, kuraṇṭaka, gokaṇṭa, and tuṇṭuka;
having boiled these with four times as much water, one should reduce the decoction to one-quarter.
One should boil fourteen *pala*s each of cotton seeds, jujube fruit, hemp seeds, and horse gram in four times as much water;
when one-fourth remains, one should take that excellent decoction. (126–127)
The wise physician should place one *prastha* of goat meat into sixty-four *palas* of water and cook it until reduced to one-quarter; then,
he should add all these decoctions to one *prastha* of oil.
One should cook this with the pastes of amṛtā, kuṣṭha, nāgara, rāsnā,
punarnavā, eraṇḍa, pippalī, śatapuṣpā, balā, prasāriṇī, māṃsī, and kaṭukā.

One should prepare this oil by cooking these ingredients, each weighing half a *pala*, over a gentle fire; it quickly cures stiffness of the neck (*grīvāstambha*), *apabāhuka*, hemiplegia (*ardhāṅgaśoṣa*), convulsions (*ākṣepa*), and *ūrustambha* (stiffness of the thighs). 131.

This oil, beginning with black gram (māṣa), cures tremors of the limbs, tremors of the head, as well as viśvācī and ardita, and all disorders of vāta; it is known as śatāvarī-taila for [the treatment of] vāta and other such conditions. 132.
Śatāvarī-taila for vāta and related ailments.
One should take one and a half *pala* portions each of *śatāvarī*, the two types of *balā*, the two types of *parṇī*, *gandharvahastaka*,
*aśvagandhā*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, *bilva*, *kāśa*, and *kuraṇṭaka*,
and have them boiled together.
One should boil [the paste] with four times its amount of water until one-fourth remains;
having added a *prastha* of oil, one should pour in a *prastha* of milk, and add a *prastha* of *śatāvarī* juice and a *prastha* of water. 134–135.
Śatāvarī, devadāru, māṃsī, tagara, candana,
śatapuṣpā, balā, kuṣṭha, elā, śaileya, utpala, ṛddhi, medā, madhuka, kākolī, and likewise jīvaka. (136)

One should cook oil with the pastes of these [drugs] weighing one *karṣa* each over a fire of cow-dung. By means of that very oil, a man always acts like a bull among women, and a woman obtains a son; furthermore, pain in the womb is destroyed.

It cures aching in the limbs, headache, jaundice, anemia, poisoning, sciatica, splenic disorders, consumption, urinary disorders, tetanus, and vātarakta accompanied by burning sensations, as well as diseases afflicted by vāta and pitta. (139)
Menorrhagia, flatulence, and hemoptysis are likewise destroyed by this Śatāvarī oil,
which was spoken by Kṛṣṇātreya.
[Reciting] "Oṃ nārāyaṇyai svāhā," one should, facing north, dig with a stake of khadira wood.
*Oṃ sarvavyādhināśinyai svāhā* is the mantra for uprooting [the hemorrhoids];
*oṃ kumārajīvinyai svāhā* is the mantra for drinking. (142) Oil prepared with kāsīsa and other ingredients is used at the beginning of the treatment for hemorrhoids.
Kāsīsa, lāṅgalī, kuṣṭha, śuṇṭhī, kṛṣṇā, and saindhava;
manaḥśilā, aśvamāra, viḍaṅga, citraka, vṛṣa, dantī, the seeds of kośātakī, hemāhvā, and haritālaka. (143)
One should cook one *prastha* of oil with these pastes, each measuring one *karṣa*.
One should add two *palas* each of the milks of *snuhī* and *arka*, and having added four times as much cow’s urine, one should prepare it thoroughly. (144–145)
This oil, which destroys hemorrhoids, was described by Kharanāda;
like an alkali, it causes hemorrhoids to fall off when used for massage.
It does not damage the skin folds and is known to perform the function of an alkaline cauterization. 146

For vātarakta, one should prepare a medicinal oil known as *piṇḍa-taila* by cooking one pala each of mañjiṣṭhā, sārivā, sarja, yaṣṭīmadhu, and siktha; when used for massage, it destroys vātarakta. (147)

Sesame oil cooked with the juice of *arka* leaves and combined with a paste of turmeric cures skin diseases such as leprosy (*kuṣṭha*); likewise, mustard oil [prepared similarly] destroys ringworm (*pāmā*), scabies (*kacchū*), and eczema (*vicarcikā*). (148)
Maricādi-taila (the oil of black pepper and others) is used for skin diseases, ulcers, and similar conditions;
it contains black pepper, yellow orpiment, trivṛt, red sandalwood, musta, realgar, māṃsī, the two types of turmeric, and devadāru. (149)
One should take one *karṣa* each of *viśālā*, *karavīra*, *kuṣṭha*, the milky sap of *arka*, and likewise the juice of cow dung (150).
One should add half a *pala* of poison and one *prastha* of mustard oil.
One should add twice as much cow urine and twice as much water;
this oil, beginning with black pepper (marica), is supreme for removing sidhma and kuṣṭha.
It conquers all types of kuṣṭha, including puṇḍarīka and vicarcikā.
It destroys scabies, vitiligo, redness, itching, and itch-eruptions.
(152) Regarding *triphalādi-taila* for *arūṃṣikā*:
[the ingredients are] triphalā, ariṣṭa, bhūnimba, the two types of niśā, and red sandalwood.

Oil prepared with these [drugs] is beneficial for massage in cases of *aruṃṣi* (skin eruptions). For gray hair (*palita*), one should saturate nimba seeds with the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja* and then process them with oil from nimba seeds.
Likewise, that oil, when administered as a nasal drop with water from an earthen vessel,
immediately destroys premature graying for men who subsist on milk and rice.
[154–155] Yaṣṭīmadhuka oil is used for baldness.

Oil boiled with yaṣṭīmadhuka, alkali, and nine fresh āmalaka fruits, when administered as nasal drops (nasya), will cause hair and beard to grow in abundance. Karañja oil [is used] for the disease indralupta (alopecia).
Oil cooked with karañja, citraka, jātī, and karavīra, when applied as an oil massage, quickly destroys indralupta (alopecia).
This is the Nīlikādyataila, used in the section on hair treatments and the like.
Nīlikā, the bulb of the ketaka, bhṛṅgarāja, kuraṇṭaka, as well as the flowers of arjuna, the flowers of bījaka, black sesame seeds, tagara with its roots, and likewise the lotus (158).
One should cook one *karṣa* each of iron filings, *priyaṅgu*, pomegranate bark, *guḍūcī*,
the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and lotus mud as separate pastes with oil, combined with a decoction of the three myrobalans. (159–160)
Oil prepared with the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja* alone stabilizes the hair,
destroys premature graying, and cures even severe *upajihvikā*.
This is *bhṛṅgarāja* oil for the treatment of premature graying and similar conditions.

One should cook oil with the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*, iron dross (*lohakiṭṭa*), the three fruits (*phalatrika*), and *sārivā* as a paste; this destroys dreadful diseases, removes premature graying of hair, itching, and *indralupta*. (162)
Regarding the oil beginning with *irimeḍa* for diseases of the mouth, teeth, and so forth:
one should boil one hundred palas of crushed *irimeḍa* bark in one droṇa of water; from that, one should take the decoction when reduced to one-fourth. (163)
Having added half an āḍhaka of oil, one should cook it with paste-measures of one karṣa each of the following:
irimeda, cloves, red ochre, agallochum, padmaka, mañjiṣṭhā, lodhra, madhuka, lac, nyagrodha, and mustaka. (164)
Oil prepared with cinnamon, nutmeg, camphor, kaṅkola, and khadira, as well as pataṅga, dhātakī flowers, small cardamom, nāgakeśara, and kaṭphala, conquers diseases of the mouth. (165–166)

Putrid flesh, graying hair, decayed teeth, hollowing of the gums, blackened teeth, excessive hypersensitivity, abscesses, dental caries, loose teeth, halitosis, and pain arising in the tongue, palate, and lips. (167–168)
Oil made from *jāti* and other [fragrant] flowers is used for sinus ulcers (*nāḍīvraṇa*) and similar conditions;

[the paste consists of] the sprouts of *jātī*, *nimba*, and *paṭola*, along with *naktamāla*, beeswax, *madhuka*, *kuṣṭha*, the two types of *niśā* (turmeric and *dāruharidrā*), and *kaṭurohiṇī*. (169)
One should cause to be given mañjiṣṭhā, padmaka, lodhra, abhayā, blue utpala, tutthaka, the seeds of sārivā, and naktamāla;
having ground these in equal parts, one should cook oil [with them]. 170.
It is highly recommended for the occurrence of sinus ulcers, boils, and scabies;
indeed, it is beneficial for fresh wounds from weapons, as well as for burns and piercings, and for wounds on the body caused by nails or teeth, and for malignant ulcers. 171–172.
Regarding *hiṅgvāditaila*: one should cook mustard oil with asafoetida, *tumburu*, and dry ginger; by the mere filling of the ear with it, earache is destroyed. 173
Oil prepared from the *bilva* group of plants is used for deafness;
one should cook oil by grinding young *bilva* fruits in cow's urine along with goat's milk and water; filling the ears with this cures deafness. (174)

For diseases of the ear, alkaline oil (kṣārataila) should be used; likewise, the alkali of young radish and chickpea pods, the two types of alkali, the five salts, asafoetida, drumstick, and ginger. 175

One should cook one *prastha* of oil with one *karṣa* each of the pastes of *devadāru*, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, *śatapuṣpā*, *rasāñjana*, *granthika*, *bhadramusta*, and the seeds of *kadali* and *bījapūra*. 176.
With the two juices and honey-vinegar (madhuśukta) measured in a fourfold proportion,
this [preparation] destroys the discharge of pus, tinnitus, pain, deafness, worms, and other diseases of the ear as well as diseases of the mouth. (177–178)
One *prastha* of the fruit juice of *jambīra* mixed with honey (*madhuśukta*), one *kuḍava* of honey (*mākṣika*) should be added to it, and one *pala* of long pepper (*pippalī*) is prescribed. 179
All of this combined together should be placed in an earthen vessel, along with barley-water mixed with honey, ginger, and jaggery;
having remained for three nights in a heap of grain, it is called *madhuśukta*. 180
Oil prepared with pāṭhā and other ingredients is used for chronic rhinitis (pīnasa).
Oil duly processed with two types of pāṭhā, the two types of niśā, mūrvā, pippalī, jasmine buds, and dantī should be administered as a nasal drop (nasya) for malignant rhinitis. 181
Vyāghrī oil is used for rhinitis; a paste made of vyāghrī, dantī, vacā, śigru, tulasī, vyoṣa, and saindhava is a digestive agent, and this oil removes the affliction of putrid nose (pūtināsā). 182
For hiccups,
oil or clarified butter prepared with a paste and decoction of kuṣṭha, bilva, kaṇā, śuṇṭhī, and drākṣā, when used as a nasal drop (nasya), destroys the condition of excessive sneezing. 183.

Oil prepared with house-soot is beneficial for hemorrhoids of the nose; likewise, oil processed with house-soot, Kaṇā, Devadāru, alkali, Naktāhvā, Saindhava salt, and Śikharī seeds is beneficial for nasal hemorrhoids. 184
Vajrataila is used for skin diseases (kuṣṭha) and other ailments;
likewise, vajrīkṣīra, the juice of the sun-plant (ravikṣīra), the liquid derived from dhattūra and citra, the liquid produced from buffalo dung, and sesame oil in equal parts [are used]. 185.
Then, one should cook it until only the oil remains in four times the amount of cow's urine (186).
Having cooked that oil until only the oil remains, one should take one *prastha* measure of that oil along with sulfur, realgar, mica, orpiment, *viḍaṅga*, *ativiṣā*, and poison (187).
One should add one karṣa each of the powder of *tiktakośātakī*, *kuṣṭha*, *vacā*, *māṃsī*, the three pungents (*kaṭutraya*),
*pītadāru*, *yaṣṭyāhva*, *svarjikākṣāra*, *jīraka*,
and *devadāru* into the oil.
This is known as Vajrataila; by means of massage, it destroys all types of skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
Karavīra oil is for the purpose of removing body hair.
[The ingredients are] the root of Karavīra, Dantī, Trivṛt, and the fruit of Kośātakī.
Oil boiled with the alkaline water of *rambhā* (plantain) is recommended for removing body hair.
Oil prepared from sandalwood and other ingredients is used for diseases such as consumption (*kṣaya*).
[The group beginning with] sandalwood, water, nails, and *yāmya* (black pepper), along with *yaṣṭī*, *śaileya*, and *padmaka*, [is likewise employed].
Mañjiṣṭhā, sarala, dāru, sevya, elā, pūtikakesara (191), patra, elā, murā, māṃsī, kaṅkola, vanitā, ambuda,
haridrā, sārivā, tiktā, lavaṅga, aguru, and kuṅkuma (192).
A preparation consisting of *tvak*, *aguru*, *nalikā*, oil, and four parts of whey (*mastu*),

along with an equal amount of lac juice (*lākṣā-rasa*), when processed, destroys the influence of evil spirits (*graha*), increases strength, and eradicates epilepsy, fever, insanity, malevolent spells (*kṛtyā*), and misfortune (*alakṣmī*). 193.

This Vacādi oil promotes longevity and nourishment, is an excellent means of subjugation, and specifically destroys consumption (kṣaya) while being supreme for removing hemorrhaging (raktapitta). It is used in cases of glandular swelling (gaṇḍamālā). 194.
One should boil ten *pala* portions each of *vacā*, *śaṭī*, the two types of *haridrā*, *devadāru*, *mahauṣadhī*, *harītakī*, *ativiṣā*, *mustaka*, and *indrayava* in four *droṇas* of water. 195.
One should cook mustard oil with the juices of *cakramarda* over a gentle fire until one-fourth remains; then, having added vermilion (*sindūra*), one should remove it from the heat.
This oil quickly destroys even the most severe *gaṇḍamālā*.
Oil prepared with *lāṅgalī* for *gaṇḍamālā*:
oil cooked with the fresh juice of *nirguṇḍī* and a paste of *lāṅgalī* root, when used as a nasal drop (*nasya*), quickly destroys even the most severe *gaṇḍamālā*. (198)
Regarding *dhattūrāditaila* (oil of dhattūra and others) for diseases such as those caused by *vāta*:
having taken the juice of *dhattūra*, the juice of *hayamārāntikā*, the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*, *sāriṇī*, and *nimba* leaves. 199.
Śobhāñjana, Citraka, Aśvagandhā, Prasāriṇī,
Śirīṣa, Kuṭaja, Anantā, Śālmalī, Naktapatraka (200), Ravipriya, Mahānimba, Ḍiṇḍighoṣā, and Maheraṇā.
Balā, jyotiṣmatī, śyāmāka, and cakramardaka—
having taken the juice of these, an amount equal to the oil is added, along with devadāru, the two types of haridrā, māṃsī, kuṣṭha, and candana. 201–202.
Black pepper, trivṛtā, dantī,
yellow orpiment, realgar, kampillaka, sulphur, khadira, long pepper, vacā, 203 rasāñjana, vermilion, śrīvāsa, and red sandalwood.
Irimeda, likewise tumbī, mañjiṣṭhā, sinduvāraka (204), the root of karavīra, rāsnā, viśvā, śreṣṭhā, and pauṣkara; śaṭī, tālīsapatra, priyaṅgu, and likewise reṇukā (205).
One *pala* each of *cāturjātaka*, *mañjīra*, *kaṅkola*, *jātipatrikā*, and *jyotiṣmatī*, along with two *palas* of poison;
one *āḍhaka* of pungent oil (*kaṭutaila*) and four times that amount of cow's urine. 206.
One should cook [the medicine] slowly over a mild fire in an earthen or iron vessel.
It cures vāta residing in the marrow, located in the skin, and likewise situated in the bones;
it also treats stiffness of the thighs, āḍhyavāta, and the difficult-to-cure daṇḍāpatānaka.
Humpbackedness, swelling, hemiplegia,
as well as lockjaw, trembling of the head, fainting, disorientation of vision, epilepsy, insanity, and even convulsions (apatantraka). 209.

It destroys dislocations, fractures of the bones, and fractures of the joints. Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Formulations of Oleaginous Preparations," in the Middle Section of the *Śrī Śārṅgadharasaṃhitā*, concerning the formulation of fermented liquors (*āsava*), medicinal wines (*ariṣṭa*), and other compounding processes.
Now begins the tenth chapter, titled "The Formulation of Fermented Liquors (Āsava), Medicinal Extracts (Ariṣṭa), and Other Infusions.
Regarding the terminology of *āsava* and *ariṣṿa*: it is that substance which has been infused and has remained for a long period within liquids.

The distinction between *āsava* and *ariṣṭa* is stated as follows: that liquor which is prepared from uncooked medicinal herbs and water is called *āsava*. It is prescribed for medicinal purposes. (Note: The term *bheṣajocitam* means "suitable for medicine" or "medicinally appropriate.")
The *ariṣṭa* should be prepared as a decoction; the measure of those two [drugs] is one *pala*. Regarding the quantity of water and other ingredients in *ariṣṭas* where no measure is specified:
in *ariṣṭas* where no measure is stated, for every *droṇa* of liquid, there should be one *tulā* of jaggery (*guḍa*).
One should add honey equal to half the amount of treacle, and the additive (prakṣepa) should be one-tenth [of the total].
Sīdhu made with uncooked sweet liquids is known as *śītarasa* (cold-essence), while that prepared with well-cooked sweet liquids is *pakvarasa* (cooked-essence). 3–4.
Regarding the characteristics of the various types of intoxicants such as *surā* and *prasannā*, they declare that *surā* is produced from the fermentation of cooked food;
from it comes the scum (*maṇḍa*), which is *prasannā*, and from that, the thick *kādambarī*.
Below that is to be known as *jagala*; *medaka* is denser than *jagala*.
When it has been cooked and its essence extracted, it becomes *surābīja* and *kiṇvaka*.
These are the definitions of *vāruṇī* and *śukta*.

That which is prepared with the juices of dates and *yatta* is indeed called *vāruṇī*; whereas that liquid in which bulbs, roots, fruits, and the like, along with fats and salts, are fermented is designated as *śukta*.

That which has lost its characteristic mark, turned sour, or is fermented liquor that has become sweet and liquid, or that which has been spoiled and subsequently mixed [with other substances], is called *cukra*. (8)
The characteristics of *guḍaśukta*, *ikṣuśukta*, *drākṣāśukta*, and others:
that which is prepared with jaggery-water (*guḍāmbu*), oil, and tubers, roots, and fruits, and has attained acidity, is called *guḍaśukta*. (9)
In the same way, there may be sour gruel made from sugarcane, as well as that produced from grapes (mṛdvīkā).
Regarding the characteristics of *tuṣāmbu* and *sauvīra*:
*tuṣāmbu* is to be known as water infused with unhusked, split barley.
Sauvīra is prepared from cooked, dehusked barley grains mixed with water.
Regarding the characteristics of *kāñjika* and *saṇḍākya*:
they know *kāñjika* to be that which is prepared by mixing boiled grain-paste (*kulmāṣa*), rice-scum (*dhānyamanda*), and so forth.
Saṇḍākī is known to be prepared with a paste of radish, mustard, and other such ingredients.
Now, regarding the fermented liquors (āsava):
first among them is uśīrāsava, used for conditions such as raktapitta.
Uśīra, bālaka, padma, kāśmarī, nīlotpala, priyaṅgu, padmaka, lodhra, mañjiṣṭhā, dhanvayāsaka,
pāṭhā, kirātatikta, nyagrodha, udumbara, and śaṭī. (13)
Having made finely powdered portions of one *pala* each of *parpaṭa*, *puṇḍarīka*, *paṭola*, *kāñcanāra*, the resin of *jambū*, and *śālmali*, along with twenty *palas* of *drākṣā*. (14–15)
One should place sixteen palas of dhātakī into two droṇas of water,
add one tulā of sugar and likewise one tulā of honey; then,
having fumigated it with māṃsī and marica, one should let it sit in a vessel for one month.
This *uśīrāsava* is a destroyer of *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorders), as well as a remover of anemia, skin diseases, urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, worms, and swelling.
*Kumāryāsava* is used for urinary disorders and similar ailments.

One should carefully collect the leaves of the *kumārī* plant, which have been thoroughly purified by being well-boiled; having extracted the juice, one should place it along with a *droṇa* measure [of liquid] and a *tulā* weight of jaggery into a stone or earthen vessel, and then store it in a jar of ghee.
One should add half a *tulā* of honey and processed iron into that;
as well as the three pungents (*kaṭutrika*), cloves, the four aromatics (*cāturjātaka*), *citraka*, long pepper root, *viḍaṅga*, and elephant pepper (*gajapippalī*). (19–20)
Cavika, hapuṣā, dhānyaka, kramuka, kaṭurohiṇī, mustā, the three fruits (triphalā), rāsnā, devadāru, the two types of niśā,
mūrvā, madhurasā, dantī, and the root of puṣkara. 21.
Balā, atibalā, kapikacchu, trikaṇṭaka, śatapuṣpā, hiṅgupatrī, ākallaka, muṭiṅgaṇa,
the two types of punarnavā, lodhra, and mākṣika ore. 22–23.
Having added half a *pala* of these [ingredients] and eight *palas* of *dhātakī*,

[the quantities] are declared as one *pala*, half a *pala*, and two *palas* respectively; this [mixture], according to the measure of one's body and age, kindles strength, complexion, and the digestive fire.
It is nourishing, appetizing, aphrodisiac, and a remedy for digestive colic;
it destroys the eight diseases arising from the abdomen, severe consumption, the twenty types of urinary disorders, upward movement of gases (udāvarta), and epilepsy. 25–26.
It undoubtedly destroys dysuria, epilepsy, seminal disorders, urinary calculi, and blood-bile caused by worms;
this is the Pippalyādyāsavā for consumption and other ailments. (27)
Pippalī, marica, cavya, haridrā, citraka, ghana,
viḍaṅga, kramuka, lodhra, pāṭhā, dhātrī, elavāluka,
uśīra, candana, kuṣṭha, lavaṅga, and likewise tagara. (28–29)
Take half-pala portions each of māṃsī, tvak, elā, patra, priyaṅgu, and nāgakeśara; having finely ground these auspicious substances into powder,
one should place them into two droṇas of water and add three tulās of jaggery.
Ten palas of dhātakī and sixty palas of drākṣā should be taken;
having combined these together, one should place them in an earthen vessel.
Once it is known that all the essence has been extracted, one should administer it according to the patient's digestive fire.
This *pippalyādyāsava* quickly destroys consumption, abdominal tumors, emaciation, *grahaṇī*, jaundice, and hemorrhoids.
*Lohāsava* is used for jaundice and similar conditions.
One should take four palas each of iron powder, the three pungents (trikaṭuka), the three myrobalans (triphalā), yavānikā, viḍaṅga, mustaka, and citraka;
and one should add twenty palas of dhātakī flowers.
Then, having reduced [the ingredients] to powder, one should add sixty-four palas of honey;
one should put one *tulā* of jaggery and two *droṇas* of water into that,
place it in a vessel of ghee, and set it aside for about one month.
One who is intoxicated by this iron-fermented liquor (lohāsava), which is highly digestive, should drink it;
it cures anemia, edema, abdominal tumors, abdominal enlargements, the pain of hemorrhoids, skin diseases, splenic disorders, itching, cough, dyspnea, and fistula-in-ano. (37)
It destroys anorexia, malabsorption syndrome, and heart disease.
38 Now, regarding the *ariṣṭas*: first among them is the *mṛdvīkāriṣṭa*, used for diseases such as hemorrhoids (*arśas*).
One should boil one hundred palas of grapes with four droṇas of water; when it is reduced to one droṇa, well-cooled, and strained,
one should add two tulas each of honey and sugar-candy, as well as one prastha of dhātakī.
Kaṅkolaka, lavaṅga, and likewise the fruit of Jātī; four *palas* each of black pepper, cinnamon, cardamom, leaf-essence (*patra*), and saffron;
and pippalī, citraka, cavya, pippalīmūla, and reṇuka. (40–41)
Having placed it in a vessel of ghee and fumigated it with sandalwood and agallochum, this [preparation], scented with camphor, is indeed the supreme stimulant for the digestive fire (grahaṇī);
it is excellent for destroying hemorrhoids (arśas), and it cures upward-moving wind (udāvarta) and abdominal tumors (gulma). 42.
This Kuṭajāriṣṭa cures abdominal worms, skin diseases, and various types of ulcers,
as well as fevers and other ailments; it is prepared with one *tulā* of *kuṭaja* root and one and a half *tulās* of *mṛdvīkā*.

Having boiled ten *pala* portions each of *madhūka* flowers and *kāśmarya* in four *droṇas* of water until one *droṇa* remains, one should add twenty *palas* of *dhātakī* and one *tulā* of jaggery (*guḍa*). 44–45.
Remaining in a vessel for just one month, this preparation known as *kuṭajāriṣṭa* pacifies all fevers and acts as a sharp *dhanañjaya* (victory-giver).
*Viḍaṅgāriṣṭa* is used for abscesses (*vidradhi*) and other such ailments.
Viḍaṅga, granthika, rāsnā, the bark and fruits of kuṭaja,
pāṭhā, elavāluka, and dhātrī— one *pala* each of these—
should be boiled in eight *droṇas* of water until one *droṇa* remains. (47–48)
When it has been purified and cooled, one should add three hundred palas of honey,
twenty palas of dhātakī, two palas each of the three aromatics (trijāta),
and one pala each of priyaṅgu, kāñcanāra, and lodhra.
One should have eight palas of vyoṣa ground into a powder and administered;
having placed it in a vessel of ghee, one should let it remain for one month.
Then, drinking it according to the prescribed rule, one shall conquer even a powerful vidradhi.
The preparation known as Viḍaṅgāriṣṭa cures stiffness of the thighs, urinary calculi, urinary disorders, abdominal tumors, fistula-in-ano, scrofula, and lockjaw;
while Devadārvādyariṣṭa is used for urinary disorders and similar ailments.
Half a *tulā* each of *devadāru*, *vāsā*, and twenty *palas* each of *majjiṣṭhā*, *indrayava*, *dantī*, *tagara*, the two types of *rajanī*,
*rāsnā*, *kṛmighna*, *musta*, *śirīṣa*, *khadira*, and *arjuna*.
One should take ten-pala portions each of yava,
vatsaka, candana, guḍūcī, rohiṇī, and citraka;
having taken these eight-pala portions, one should boil them in eight droṇas of water.
When the decoction has been reduced to one-eighth, strained, and cooled,
one should add sixteen palas of dhātakī, three tulas of honey,
two palas of vyoṣa, and four palas of trijāta.
Take four palas of priyaṅgu and two palas of nāgakeśara;
having ground all these together, one should place them in a vessel of ghee.
After a month has passed, one should drink this; it destroys even difficult-to-conquer prameha.

The *ariṣṭa* made from *devadāru* and other ingredients destroys wind diseases (*vātaroga*), malabsorption (*grahaṇī*), hemorrhoids (*arśas*), and dysuria (*mūtrakṛcchra*); it is a destroyer of itching (*kaṇḍū*) and skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*).
The *khadira-ariṣṭa* is used for skin diseases and similar ailments.
One *tulā* (ten *prasthas*) of *khadira*, half that amount (*pañca-prasthas*) of *devadāru*, twelve *palas* of *vākucī*, twenty *palas* of *dārvī*,
and twenty *palas* of *triphalā* should be boiled in eight *droṇas* of water.
When the decoction has been reduced to one *droṇa*, strained, and cooled,
one should add two *tulās* of honey, one *tulā* of sugar,
twenty *palas* of *dhātakī*, as well as *kaṅkola* and *nāgakeśara*.
One should take one pala each of nutmeg, cloves, cardamom, cinnamon, and cinnamon leaves, and four palas of long pepper;
having placed these in a vessel of ghee, a person should drink it after a month has passed.
It conquers major skin diseases (mahākuṣṭha), heart disease, anemia, and arbuda;
it likewise overcomes abdominal tumors (gulma), glandular swellings (granthi), worms, cough, asthma, and splenic enlargement.
This indeed is the Khadirāriṣṭa, which wards off all skin diseases.

In the Babbūlāriṣṭa for consumption, cough, and other ailments, one should boil two *tulās* of *babbūlī* in four *droṇas* of water; when the liquid is reduced to one *droṇa* and cooled, one should add three *tulās* of jaggery. (66)
One should prepare sixteen palas of dhātakī, two palas of kṛṣṇā,
and one pala each of jātīphala, kaṅkola, elā, tvak, patra, keśara, lavaṅga, and marica.
This Babbūlāriṣṭaka, having remained in a vessel for one month,
conquers consumption (kṣaya), leprosy (kuṣṭha), dysentery (atīsāra), urinary disorders (prameha), asthma, and cough.
Drākṣāriṣṭa is used for nourishment and other such purposes.
A wise person should cook half a *tulā* (500 palas) of raisins in two *droṇas* (128 liters) of water until one-fourth remains; once the decoction is strained and cooled,
one should add two *tulās* of jaggery along with cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and *keśara*.
One should powder priyaṅgu, marica, kṛṣṇā, and viḍaṅga,
taking one pala of each part; then, having placed them in a jar and stirred them thoroughly on all sides, one should drink it whenever its juice has developed.
The *ariṣṭa* known as *drākṣā* destroys chest wounds, consumption, cough, dyspnea, and throat diseases; it bestows strength and purifies the impurities.
The *rohitakāriṣṭa* is used for hemorrhoids, disorders of the digestive tract (*grahaṇī*), and similar conditions.

One should boil one *tulā* of *rohitaka* in four *droṇas* of water until one-fourth remains; when the decoction has cooled and been strained, one should add two hundred *palas* of jaggery and sixteen *palas* of *dhātakī*. (73)

One should add the five pungents (*pañcakola*), the three aromatics (*trijāta*), and the three myrobalans (*triphalā*); having ground them in portions of one *pala* each, one should then place them in a vessel. After a month has passed, for those who drink it, hemorrhoids (*gudaja*) go to total destruction.
Known as Rohitāriṣṭa, it cures malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), anemia, heart disease, splenic disorders, abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, skin diseases, edema, and loss of appetite;
Daśamūlāriṣṭa is used for disorders of Vāta and other humors.
Parṇī, the two types of Bṛhatī, Gokaṇṭa, Bilva, Agnimantha, Aralu, Pāṭalā, and Kāśmarī— these are said here to constitute the Daśamūla (the ten roots).
One should prepare the Daśamūla using five palas of each individual root.
One should take twenty-five palas of citraka and likewise of pauṣkara;
one should take twenty palas of lodhra, and guḍūcī should be equal to that. Dhātrī should be sixteen palas, and durālabhā eighteen palas.
Khadira, bījasāra, and pathyā, each weighing one pala;
multiplied by eight [these], along with kuṣṭha, mañjiṣṭhā, devadāru, viḍaṅga, madhuka, bhārṅgī, kapittha, akṣa, and punarnavā. (80–81)
Cavya, māṃsī, priyaṅgu, sārivā, kṛṣṇajīraka, trivṛtā, reṇuka, rāsnā, pippalī, kramuka, śaṭī,
haridrā, śatapuṣpā, padmaka, and nāgakeśara. (82)
Musta, indrayava, śuṇṭhī, jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka,
as well as medā, mahāmedā, the two types of kākolī, and ṛddhi and vṛddhi—
one should take two palas each of these and boil them in eight times the amount of water. 83–84.
Having taken one-fourth part of the decoction, one should set it aside in an earthen vessel.
One should cook sixty-four *palas* of grapes in four times as much water;
when reduced to three-quarters and cooled, one should add it to the previously prepared decoction.
One should add thirty-two palas of honey for four hundred-fold potency (guṇa).
[Then there are] thirty palas each of dhātakī, kaṅkola, jalacandana, jātīphala, lavaṅga, tvak, elā, patra, and keśara. (86–87)

Having powdered long pepper (pippalī) and the other ingredients, taking two palas of each separately, one should add one śāṇa of musk and place everything together in a vessel buried in the ground; then, once the essence has developed, one should drink it. 88.
Having cast the fruit of *kataka*, one should bring the liquid to a state of clarity.

[This cures] malabsorption syndrome (*grahaṇī*), loss of appetite, asthma, cough, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), fistula-in-ano (*bhagandara*), wind disorders (*vātavyādhi*), consumption (*kṣaya*), vomiting, anemia (*pāṇḍuroga*), and jaundice (*kāmalā*). 89–90.
It conquers skin diseases, hemorrhoids, urinary disorders, weak digestion, abdominal enlargements,
gravel, stones, dysuria, and the depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātus). It generates nourishment for the emaciated and is the supreme bestower of offspring for the barren.
Ariṣṭa, known as Daśamūla, bestows vitality, semen, and strength.
(92) Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Preparation of Āsava, Ariṣṭa, and other Fermented Preparations," in the Middle Section of the Śrī Śārṅgadharasaṃhitā,
concerning the purification and killing of the [metallic] constituents.
Now begins the eleventh chapter, titled "The Purification and Killing of Metals.
Now follows the purification and killing of metals as a collective group;
therein, first, the enumeration and names of the metals.
Gold, silver, copper, lead, tin, iron, and mercury are to be known as the seven metals; therefore, the wise man should purify them.
(1) The procedure for the purification of metals.
One should heat the leaves of gold, silver, copper, and iron in fire,
and pour them while they are repeatedly heated into oil,
buttermilk, sour gruel, cow urine, and the decoction of *kulattha* beans— three times each.
In this way, the purification of gold and other metals is accomplished.
Regarding the procedure for purifying lead and tin:
one should heat and melt lead and tin, and then pour them out [into a cooling medium].
There should be a threefold, threefold purification, and likewise a threefold [purification] with mercury and milk. Now, regarding the killing of gold:
one should grind mercury, twice the amount of the gold, together with acid.
One should place the fragrance, equal in size to that ball, one above the other;
then, one should enclose the ball within a firm pair of bamboo-leaf covers and apply fourteen *puṭa* (roasting) treatments using thirty pieces of mica each time.
The ash becomes free of residue; fragrance should be applied again and again.
This is the second method for the killing of gold:
when the gold has been melted, one should add lead in the sixteenth part [of its weight]. 7.
Having powdered it and rubbed it with acid, one should form it into a ball; then,
placing an equal amount of sulphur (gandha) both below and above the ball,
one should place it in a sealed crucible (śarāva-sampuṭa) and heat it with thirty pieces of vanopalas.
In this way, after seven layers, the gold becomes ash-like *niruttha*.
This is the third method: having rubbed equal parts of mercury (*sūtaka*) and sulfur (*gandha*) with the juice of *kāñcanāra*.
One should coat gold leaves with kajjalī in equal proportions. A paste made from the bark of *kāñcanāra* should be used to construct a pair of crucibles (*mūṣā*).
Having placed the globule within that crucible assembly, one should then place it inside a clay crucible assembly.
Having applied a seal and closure, and having dried it with cow-dung, one should make the fire extremely intense; thus one should administer three *puṭas*.
The resulting ash becomes "irreversible" (*niruttha*) and may be employed in all ritual tasks. 12
The fourth method is by means of the *kāñcanāra* plant; *lāṅgalī* destroys gold, and just as *jvālāmukhī* would destroy it, so too does *manaḥśilā*. 13.
The fifth method:
one should give seven saturations of equal parts of the powder of realgar and vermilion with the milky juice of the *arka* plant, drying it again and again.
Then, once the gold has been melted, this paste (kalka) is added in equal measure.

One should heat it intensely again so that the paste dissolves; in this manner, one should add the paste three times, and the death of the gold [its transformation into pure essence] will occur. 15–16.
The sixth method: one should smear gold leaves with the excrement of pigeons or those produced by cocks, and apply them one above the other. 17.
Having added an equal amount of fragrant powder, one should apply a *kukkuṭapuṭa* (cock-pot) using a pair of shallow bowls joined together and heated with five cow-dung cakes.
In this manner, one should apply nine *puṭas*, and the tenth is the *mahāpuṭa*.
By thirty vanopalas, golden ash (hemabhasma) is produced.
The qualities of golden ash are that it is sweet, bitter, unctuous, cooling, and heavy. 19.
It bestows intelligence, knowledge, and memory, and is an elixir that destroys poison. (20) This is the first method for the killing of silver:
one part of *tālaka* (orpiment) should be ground with some kind of sour *jambha* fruit.
One should smear three parts of tāra leaves with that [mixture],
place them in a crucible (mūṣāpuṭa), seal it, and roast it with thirty pieces of vanopalas.
Having extracted [the product] and again added tāla, one should seal it and cook it in a crucible once more.
In this way, through fourteen applications, the ash of tāra is produced.
This is the second method: one should grind honey with the milky sap of snuhī and smear [the vessel] with it. 22–23.
A wise person should enclose silver leaves in the manner of a *tālaka* (copper-foil) within fourteen layers; thus, silver ash is produced.
This is the method for the killing of brass and bell-metal.

One should grind sulphur with the milk of *arka* and smear it onto clean copper leaves, repeatedly moistening them with acidic juices. Then, having placed them inside a crucible, one should roast them using the "elephant-heap" (*gajapuṭa*) method.
In this way, by means of exactly two layers, the reduction to ash is certain;
likewise, even brass (kāṃsya) that makes a ringing sound is definitely reduced to ash.
This is the procedure for the killing of copper, brass, and bell-metal.
Goat's milk should be like the milk of the *arka* plant, and likewise that of the *nirguṇḍikā*;
for the destruction of the sound of copper and tin, through the application of equal parts of sulfur—this is the procedure for the killing (*māraṇa*) of copper.
27. The Procedure for the Killing of Copper.
Having made thin copper leaves, the wise one should steam them with acid for three days; then he should place them in a mortar,
add mercury equal to one-fourth their weight, and grind them with acid for one *yāma*.
Then, having removed the leaves, one should coat them with double the amount of sulphur rubbed with acid; from that, one should form a ball.

Then, having ground either *mīnākṣī*, *cāṅgerī*, or *punarnavā*— 29–30. [One should apply this to the leaf-encased substance]. Then, having ground either *mīnākṣī*, *cāṅgerī*, or *punarnavā*— [one should proceed as follows].
One should coat the exterior of that sphere with its paste to a thickness of one finger-breadth;
having placed that sphere in a vessel, one should seal it with a shallow bowl,
then fill [the space] with sand, followed by ashes, salt, and water.
Having applied a seal over the mouth of the vessel,
one should then cook it on the hearth with a gradually increasing fire for exactly four *yāmas*.
Once it has cooled by itself, one should remove it and grind it with the juice of *sūraṇa* (yam).
One should prepare a ball for one day and coat it with half the amount of *gandha* mixed with clarified butter; then, having placed it in a crucible, one should cook it in a *gajapuṭa*.
Once it has cooled to the temperature of its own body, it should be extracted; the copper will then be auspiciously deadened (*mṛta*).
It never causes vomiting, dizziness, exhaustion, or fainting.
This is the first method for killing lead:
by repeatedly applying a paste of *śilā* (realgar) ground with the juice of *tāmbūlī* (betel leaf).
With thirty-two applications, the *nāga* [mercury] becomes immobile and turns to ashes.
This is the second procedure:
one should add the powder of the bark of the *aśvattha* and *ciñcā* trees in a fourth part [of the mercury].
When the snake [mineral] has melted in an earthen vessel, one should stir it with an iron ladle.
In one *yāma* (three hours), it becomes ash; then, having ground equal parts of that ash and realgar (*manaḥśilā*) with sour gruel (*kāñjika*), one should cook the mixture in a firm *puṭa*.

Having ground it again when cooled to its own temperature with a stone and with sour gruel (kāñjika), one should subject it to roasting (puṭa) using two earthen bowls; thus, through sixty such roastings, death [of the metal] occurs.
This is the procedure for the killing of tin.
Having thrown the powder of the bark of *ciñcā* and *aśvattha* into a molten tin vessel made of clay, one should stir it with a ladle consisting of a fourth part of that same powder;
then, in just two watches (six hours), the ash of tin is produced. (40–41)
Then, having added talc equal in weight to the ash, one should grind it with acid;
thereafter, having cooked it in a *gajapuṭa* fire, one should grind it again with acid. Then, with a tenth part of talc, one should cook it for one *yāma*. 42. Then one should apply the *puṭa* seal.
Thus, tin cooked in ten layers certainly dies [is killed]. This is the first method for the killing of iron: pure powder of iron, with the juices of *pātālagaruḍī*, [should be processed].
Having kneaded it, one should roast it in fire; thus one should give three *puṭas*.
Then one should give three *puṭas* with *kumārī* and the juice of *kuṭhāracchinnikā*; thereafter one should give six *puṭas*, whereby the sharp [iron] will undergo death.

The second method: one should add cinnabar (darada) in the twelfth part of the quantity of the sharp powder; then one should grind it with the juices of kanyā for two days and subsequently roast it in a *puṭa*. 46.

In this way, through seven layers, one may cause death by means of iron powder; likewise, death occurs for *tīkṣṇa* (arsenic) by means of the juices of *kuṭhāracchinnā*, the juices of *pātālagaruḍī*, breast milk, and the milk of the *arka* plant. 47

The third method: having added twice the amount of fragrance to the *sūtaka*, one should prepare a collyrium (*kajjalī*); then, one should grind an equal quantity of iron powder with the juice of *kanyā*. 48.
Then, having formed a ball from the pair [of substances] and placed it in a copper vessel,
the wise man should cover it with castor leaves while it is held in the heat;
after half a watch (yāma) has passed and it has become warm, he should then place it upon a heap of grain.
Having placed a shallow bowl on top, one should remove it at the end of three days;
having ground it and strained it through cloth, it will thus become water-soluble.
In this manner, one should "kill" all metals, including gold and the others.
The general procedure for the killing (calcination) of all metals:
all metals, such as gold and others, when smeared with stone-essence, fragrance, and the milk of the Arka plant, are killed in twelve crucibles; this is as true as the word of the Guru. 52.

Now, the methods for purifying and killing the minor metallic ores (upadhātu), and the enumeration of those minor metallic ores: honey-gold (mākṣika), blue vitriol (tutthaka), iron (abhra), antimony (nīlāñjana), realgar (śilā), and red arsenic (manaḥśilā).
And Rasaka—these are to be known as the seven minor metallic substances (upadhātus). 53.
The method for purifying Svarṇamākṣika:
take three parts of Mākṣika and one part of Saindhava salt.
Alternatively, one should cook it with the juices of *mātuluṅga*, *drākṣā*,
or *jambīra* in an iron vessel while stirring it, until the heated vessel becomes a beautiful red color; thus the *svarṇamākṣika* attains complete purification.
The method for its killing:
having rubbed it with a decoction of *kulattha* or with oil, one should roast it;
[thus] gold pyrite dies by means of buttermilk or horse urine. 56

The method for purifying silver pyrite: one should macerate it for a day in the juices of *karkoṭī* and *meṣaśṛṅgī* produced from *jambīra* fruits; when dried in the intense heat of the sun, it certainly becomes pure and stainless. 57
The procedure for purifying blue vitriol (tuttha):
One should grind the tuttha with the excrement of a cat and a pigeon;
then, having added one-tenth part of borax (ṭaṅkaṇa), one should cook it in a mild crucible (mṛdupuṭa). 58.
A sealed capsule (puṭa) with curd and honey should be given for the purification of tuttha.
This is the procedure for purifying mica:
one should heat black mica in fire and then cast it into milk.
Having made that [abhraka] into broken flakes, one should saturate it for eight watches (aṣṭayāma) with the juices of *taṇḍulīya* and sour gruel (*āmla*); thus the abhraka becomes purified.
This is the first method for the killing of abhraka.

Having prepared that *dhānyābhraka*, one should dry it and then grind it with the milky sap of the *arka* plant for one day in a mortar; one should then form it into the shape of a disc (*cakrākāra*),
wrap it with *arka* leaves, and cook it thoroughly in a *gajapuṭa* fire.
It should be rubbed again and cooked again with great care seven times.
Then, likewise, three *puṭa* applications should be given using a decoction of banyan-tree roots (*vaṭajaṭā*). It dies [is calcined] without doubt; one may employ it in all medicinal formulations.
The procedure for the immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) of dead mica:
One should cook an equal amount of ghee with dead mica in an iron vessel; once the ghee has been digested, that mica may be employed in all formulations. (64)
The qualities of processed mica:
processed mica removes death, destroys old age and graying hair, and when combined with appropriate adjuncts, it is the supreme remedy for various diseases. 65
The second method for the killing of mica:
Pure *dhānyābhraka* (grain-mica) combined with one-sixth part of *musta* and *śuṇṭhī* should be ground with *kāñjika* and with the juices of *citraka* for one day. (66)

Then one should give it a *gajapuṭa* fire; having extracted it from that, one should grind it with a decoction of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) and likewise subject it to *puṭa* treatment in this manner for three *puṭas*.
[One should then grind it] with the juices of *balā*, cow’s urine, *musalī*, *tulasī*, and *sūraṇa*.
When rubbed and heated in fire three times over three cycles, it shall go to death (i.e., be reduced to ash).
This is the method for the essence of *abhra* (mica):
one part of *dhānyābhra* and two parts of *ṭaṅkaṇa* (borax). 68–69.
Having ground it and sealed it in a blind crucible (andhamūṣā), one should cook it with a fierce fire;
once cooled naturally, the powder should be employed for all diseases. This is the procedure for purifying blue antimony (nīlāñjana).

Having powdered blue antimony and saturated it with the juice of *jambīra* for one day, it becomes pure when dried in the sun; one should employ it in its various applications. (71) This is the procedure for purifying red ochre, green vitriol, and other minerals.
In this way, red ochre, green vitriol, borax, cowrie shells,
*tūrī*, conch shell, and *kaṅkuṣṭha* certainly attain purification.
(72) This is the procedure for purifying realgar (*manaḥśilā*).
One should cook realgar for three days in goat urine using a *dolāyantra* (swinging vessel), and then saturate it seven times with goat bile; thus it attains purification. 73.
This is the procedure for the purification of *haritāla* (yellow orpiment).
Having reduced the mineral calamine (*tālaka*) into fine particles, one should throw that powder into fermented rice-water (*kāñjika*) and process it for one *yāma* in a *dolāyantra*. Then,
one should cook it for one *yāma* in the juice of *kūṣmāṇḍa* gourds, and for another *yāma* in the decoction of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*).
In this manner, the *rasaka* (calamine) should be cooked in the apparatus for four watches (*yāma*); thus the *tālaka* (orpiment) is purified.
This is the procedure for purifying *rasaka*.
Alternatively, one should cook the *rasaka* in human urine or cow's urine for seven days.
Purification by means of the swinging-oven (dolāyantra) shall take place; thereafter, one should employ it in various operations.
76. The procedure for precipitating the essence (sattva) of metals: lac, fish, milk, goat [milk], borax, and deer-horn.
One should grind together oil-cake, mustard seeds, *śigru*, *guñjā*, *ūrṇā*, jaggery, rock salt,
*yava-tiktā*, clarified butter, and honey as they are available (verse 77). All the metals, when mixed with these and subjected to intense heat, [are purified].
When blown in a crucible, they are born as liberated beings; of this there is no doubt.
(78) Now, the methods for purifying and killing the gems: first, the procedure for purifying the diamond (*vajra*).
One should cook the diamond (*vajra*) placed inside the bulb of *vyāghrī* in a dolāyantra using a decoction of *kulattha* and *kodrava* for three days; thus it attains purification.
This is the second method for the purification of diamond.
One should repeatedly heat that diamond and sprinkle it with donkey urine;
heating it again and sprinkling it again, one should perform this twenty-one times.
This is the first procedure for the "killing" (destruction) of the diamond.
Having ground talaka with bedbugs until it forms a ball, one should place a diamond within that ball and heat the ball in fire.
One should then sprinkle it with horse urine and cast it back into the ball once more. 81.
Having sealed it, it should be blown [with fire] and then sprinkled again; one should perform this twenty-one times (three times seven).
In this way, the vajra is killed; one should employ its powder in all applications. This is the second procedure.

One should repeatedly heat the diamond and throw it into a decoction of horse-gram (kulattha) mixed with asafoetida and rock salt; after doing this twenty-one times, it will become powder. This is the third method.
A wise person, having caught a frog in a vessel made of bell-metal, should place it there;
being terrified, it will urinate therein, and one should cast the diamond into that urine.
By heating the diamond repeatedly in this manner many times, its dissolution occurs. 85
The procedure for the purification and killing of vaikrānta:
Vaikrānta, whether blue or red, should be purified like a diamond; it should be sprinkled with horse urine, heated and then sprinkled again, twenty-one times in total. (86)
Then, one should place it in a ball (golaka) composed of five ingredients including the horn of a ram;
having sealed it in a crucible (mūṣāpuṭa), one should perform this process seven times. Thus, vaikrānta is reduced to ashes and may be employed in place of diamond (vajra). 87–88.
The method for purifying the remaining gems:
one should heat gems, pearls, and corals in a dolikāyantra with the fresh juice of jayantī; this constitutes a purification lasting for one yāma. 89.
The procedure for their very destruction is as follows:
one should sprinkle [the substances] with the milk of a maiden and with rice-water, each seven times, until they are entirely heated to the point of being intensely hot. 90.
Pearls, corals, and likewise all kinds of gems of various colors die in an instant; there is no doubt in this.
One should kill pearls and corals in the same manner as described for honey.
One should purify all gems like diamonds and likewise kill [the impurities].
92 This is the first method of purification for *śilājatu*:
having brought together *śilājatu* that has fallen from stones heated in the summer sun.
One should rub [the substance] with cow’s milk, decoctions of triphalā, and juices of bhṛṅgarāja for one day each in the sun; once dried, it attains purity.
This is the second method (93).
The wise person should place the primary stone of *śilājatu*, prepared in fine fragments, into very hot water and let it sit for one *yāma*;
then, having stirred it, he should take the liquid filtered through a cloth. 94.
Having placed it in an earthen vessel, the wise one should hold it in the sun;
whatever thick substance remains on top, he should pour that into another vessel. The intelligent one should hold it in the sun and take away what remains thick on top. 95–96.
In this manner, having processed it again and again for two months, the *śilājatu* becomes fit for its intended purpose; when thrown into the fire, it becomes like a phallus (*liṅga*).
Then, being smokeless, it is pure and may be employed in all ritual activities.
One should pour water into that which remains at the bottom;
having kneaded it, one should hold it in the heat and process it just as before.
This is the procedure for the purification and killing of *maṇḍūra*.

One should blow away the dross produced from iron using charcoal from axle-wood; then, having heated it repeatedly until it is thoroughly incandescent, one should sprinkle it seven times with cow's urine.
Then, having pulverized it, one should treat it with double the quantity of decoctions made from the three myrobalans (triphalā).
Having stirred it, one should roast it in the fire; thus excellent *maṇḍūra* is produced. (101) Regarding the preparation of alkali:
one should set fire to the dry wood of a milk-exuding tree (*kṣīravṛkṣa*).
Having taken that ash and placed it in an earthen vessel, one should grind it in four times the amount of water and let it sit overnight; in the morning, one should take the clear liquid.
That liquid should be boiled over fire until it has completely dried up.

Then, having scraped from the vessel, the white-shining alkaline substance should be collected; that which resembles powder should be used for rubbing (pratisāraṇa), while that which remains like a decoction should be drunk. Thus, the wise physician should employ these two types of alkali in the aforementioned procedures. (103–104)
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Purification and Killing of Metals," in the middle section of the *Śrī Śārṅgadharasaṃhitā*.
Now begins the twelfth chapter, titled "The Methods for the Purification and Killing of Mercury and Other Substances."
In that regard, first is the praise of mercury (rasa): Mercury is known as the conqueror of all diseases and the bestower of nourishment;
when prepared by one who is well-versed, it brings about the perfection of both the body and iron.
O King of Rasas! In the practices of alchemy (rasakarma), the names of mercury should be known as: pārada, sūta, haraja, sūtaka, rasa, and miśraka. 2.
The instruction on the presiding deities of the metals such as copper and so forth, beginning with the sun:
copper, silver, lead, tin,
gold, iron, bronze, and magnetite— these are remembered as the nine metals.
The planets, beginning with the Sun, have been described to you in order by their names.
(3) Regarding the procedure for purifying mercury:
having placed mercury in a crucible made of *rājī* and garlic, one should seal it.
One should steam the mercury in a dolikā apparatus with sour gruel (kāñjika) for four days;
then, one should grind the mercury for one day with juices derived from the kumārī plant,
and likewise grind it for one day with decoctions produced from the citraka plant.
Likewise, one should grind it for one day with the juices of *kākamācī* and similarly with decoctions of *triphalā*; thus the mercury should be diligently ground.
Then, one should separate the mercury from those substances, having washed it with *kāñjika*.
Then, having added mercury and half as much rock salt (saindhava) into the mortar,
one should grind it incessantly for one day with the juice of *nimbuka*.
Then, [add] *rājī*, garlic (*rasona*), *mukhya*, and *navasādara*.
Likewise, the mercury should be rubbed with these equal parts of juices and cold water;
then, having purified it, shaped it into a disc-like form, and smeared it with asafoetida,
one should place it between two vessels joined together and fill the space with salt.
Then, the wise one should place a very firm seal upon the vessel below;
having dried it and applied fire beneath, he should pour water on top,
and thereafter maintain an intense fire beneath that for three *praharas*.

In this way, the mercury, freed from defects, should be made to fall upwards; then that best of mercuries adheres within the middle of the upper vessel (ūrdhvapiṭharī). 12. This is the procedure for the purification of sulfur (gandhaka).
Having placed [the ingredients] in an iron vessel, one should heat the ghee over a fire;
when the ghee is heated, one should add an equal amount of powdered sulfur.
Once the sulfur is known to have melted, one should pour it into the midst of milk.
Thus shall be the purification of sulphur; one should employ it in all ritual operations.
(14) The procedure for purifying cinnabar:
vermilion is processed with ewe’s milk and the group of acidic substances.

If processed diligently seven times, it certainly attains purity. (15) This is the method for extracting mercury from cinnabar: [it should be treated] for one *yāma* with lime juice or with the juice of *nimba* leaves. (16)
Having ground cinnabar, one should cause it to fall [into mercury] according to the procedure for joining mercury;
then, having extracted the purified mercury from that, one should employ it in its various applications. (17) This is the method for opening the mouth of mercury (*pāradasya mukhakaraṇavidhiḥ*).
Kālakūṭa, Vatsanābha, Śṛṅgaka, Pradīpaka,
Hālāhala, Brahmaputra, Hāridra, Saktuka,
and likewise Saurāṣṭrika— these are declared to be the nine varieties of poison.
*Arka*, *sehuṇḍa*, *dhattūra*, *lāṅgalī*,
*karavīraka*, *guñjā*, and *ahi-phenā*— these are the seven species of secondary poisons (*upaviṣa*).
Mercury processed with these becomes "cut-winged" (*chinnapakṣa*).
And his mouth is produced, which swallows the minerals in an instant. (20) This is the second method for preparing the mouth and the organ of taste.
Alternatively, there are the three pungents, the two alkalis, black mustard, and the five salts. (21)
One should grind equal parts of garlic, saltpetre, and drumstick (śigru) together with mercury; then, using the juice of jambīra,
neem water, or sour gruel (kāñjika), one should rub them in a mortar with warm water.
Within three days and nights, the mercury becomes a mouth that consumes the metals; this is the third procedure for making the mouth of the mercury.
Alternatively, the mercury should be rubbed with *bindulī* insects for three days.
By means of salts and acids, his mouth becomes a devourer of the bodily constituents (dhātus).
(23) Now, the procedure for the digestion of sulfur using the tortoise-press (kacchapayantra) is described; next, the digestion of sulfur by means of the kacchapayantra is explained.
One should pour water into an earthen vessel and place a small bowl within it;
this [vessel] should resemble the lid of a large pit, be provided with a girdle in the middle,
and having smeared the interior of the girdle with powder, one should pour the mercury into it.
One should place an equal portion of powdered fragrance on top of the mercury;
having placed a shallow dish over it, one should apply the ash-seal (bhasmamudrā).
Then, one should apply a cover (puṭa) over that with four lumps of cow-dung.
In this manner, the wise practitioner should repeatedly digest the odor for six times its duration.
When the odor is digested, the mercury becomes a sharp-fire agent capable of performing all operations.
This is the procedure for the killing of mercury.
One should grind together equal parts of dhūmasāra, rasa, torī, gandhaka, and navasādara for one yāma with acidic juices; then,
having placed them in a glass flask, one should seal it with a soft cloth and clay.
Having smeared the mouth all around with mudrā and having applied it [to the neck], one should dry it;
then, one should place the *kūpī* (small flask) inside a perforated cooking pot (*piṭharī*).
Having filled the cooking pot up to the neck of the *kūpī* with sand... 31. ...[one should proceed].
Having placed [the crucible] on the hearth, one should kindle a fire beneath it very gradually (32).
One should then gradually increase the flame slightly more than that;
in this manner, after twelve watches (yāmas), the excellent mercury is killed (33).

When it has cooled to the temperature of one's own body, one should crack it open; then, one should discard the sulphur that has risen to the top and employ the mercury that remains at the bottom, which is now "dead," in all ritual operations.
(34) This is the second procedure for the killing of mercury.
One should prepare a pair of crucibles from the seeds of *apāmārga*; within that sealed crucible, one should place mercury mixed with the milk of *malayū*.
[Then add] the flowers of *droṇapuṣpī*, *viḍaṅga*, and *irimedaka*. 35.
Having administered this powder both above and below,
the wise one should properly seal that globule within a pair of earthen crucibles (mṛṇmūṣā-sampuṭa);
then, having applied the seal and purified it, one should cook it in a gajapuṭa fire.
In this way, the mercury (sūtaka) is reduced to ash in a single stage. This is the third method for the killing of mercury.
One should grind a small amount of the milky juice of *kākodumbarikā*. 38.
One should prepare a pair of crucibles using that milk and rubbed asafoetida;

having placed the mercury inside their joined lid, one should apply a seal (mudrā). Then, the wise person, holding that ball (golaka) within an additional clay crucible assembly, [should proceed]. 39.
One should cook it with a gentle fire alone, and the mercury (sūtaka) goes to the state of ashes.
This is the fourth method for the killing of mercury. [The mercury] should be rubbed with the juice of betel leaves and placed inside the bulb of *karkoṭī*.
Having been cooked in a closed crucible made of clay, the mercury indeed attains the state of ash. 41.
Now, the mercurial formulations for fever and other ailments are described;
therein is the *jvarāṅkuśarasa* (the "fever-hook" mercury).
Having sealed a broken deer horn together with the juices of *jvālāmukhī* inside a vessel, one should cook it on the hearth for two *yāmas*; thereafter,
one should add one-eighth part of the three pungents (*trikaṭu*) and consume a dose of one *niṣka*.
Together with the juices of *nāgavallī*, this removes fever caused by *vāta* and *pitta*.
This elixir named *Jvarāṅkuśa* (the Hook for Fever) removes all fevers—whether occurring every day, every two days, or every three days—without a doubt. (43–44)
Jvarārirasa consists of mercury,
green vitriol, orpiment, blue vitriol, borax, and sulphur— all these purified in equal parts and macerated for forty-five days with the juice of *kāravellī*.

The physician should rub it and smear that [substance] on the interior of a copper vessel to a thickness of half a finger-breadth; then, having sealed its opening, he should place it in a sand-oven (*vālukāyantra*) after putting grains inside its mouth and cook it. 46.
When the grains have burst open, then one should declare the preparation successful.

Thereafter, the physician should take the liquid from the interior of a copper vessel while it is still warm to the touch, and having powdered it together with an equal amount of black pepper, [administer] this remedy named Jvarāri. 47–48.
One should eat one *māṣa* of this with a leaf-fragment; it destroys fever—whether irregular, acute, or occurring every first, second, third, or fourth day—within three days.
This is the *Śītajvarāri-rasa*.

One karṣa each of talaka, tutthaka, copper, mercury, sulphur, and realgar should be taken and ground with the decoction of triphalā; one should then place the resulting ball inside a sealed crucible and apply a puṭapāka fire with great care. (50)
Then, having taken it, one should saturate it seven times with the decoction of *akadugdha* (vajrīdugdha),
and again seven times with the decoction of *dantī* and *śyāmā*.
Then, one should take a divine elixir (*rasa*) the size of a *māṣa* bean, combined with fifty black peppers.
One should devotedly consume one *gadyāṇaka* of jaggery along with a pair of *tulasī* leaves for three days; thereafter, the supreme enemy of cold becomes difficult to overcome.
As wholesome diet, milk and rice should be given, especially when the fever is irregular or preceded by cold.

This fever-destroying pill (jvaraghnī guṭikā) quickly removes fevers preceded by burning sensations, as well as tertian, quartan, bi-daily, and continuous fevers, and it also cures discoloration of the skin. 54.
One part of *rā* (turmeric) purified by means of *aila* (spikenard), *pippalī*, and *śivā* (myrobalan);
*ākārakarabha* and *gandha* (fragrant substances) purified with pungent oil (*kaṭutaila*); and these fruits of *indravāruṇī* (cucumber/gourd) measuring four parts—these [are the ingredients]. 55.
One should grind the powder together with the juice of *indravāruṇikā* (56).
Having formed pills (*guṭī*) of the measure of one *māṣa*, the wise physician should administer them for acute fever (*sadyojvara*).
This pill is considered a destroyer of fever when taken with a post-digestive drink of *chinnā* juice (57).
The essence of the Lord of the World (mercury), pure and hungry, should be two parts at the time of its depletion;
likewise, one should take two parts of sulphur and form a kajjalī from the two. (58)
One should place [the mercury] into four times as many beads of cowrie shell derived from cinnabar;
having added one part of borax, one should triturate it with cow’s milk.
Likewise, one should prepare eight parts of pieces of conch shell.

One should place everything inside the *puṭa* between two shallow bowls smeared with powder; having placed it in a pit measuring one cubit, one should perform the *gajapuṭa* roasting. Once it has cooled by itself, one should extract it and grind all of that together into a single paste.
A powder measuring six guñjās, when combined with twenty-nine purgatives (61),
should be administered there; as for the adjuncts, one should give it with ghee in cases born of vāta, and with fresh butter in cases born of pitta.

One should administer [this] with honey in cases of atisāra born of kapha, as well as in wasting (kṣaya), loss of appetite (aruci), disorders of the duodenum (grahaṇī), emaciation, and weak digestion; likewise, Lokanātharasa is beneficial in coughs, dyspnea, and abdominal tumors (gulma). 62–63.
Regarding the procedure for consuming that:
one should eat three mouthfuls of rice with ghee on top of it; then, one should lie face upward on a couch for a moment without any pillow. 64.
One should eat wholesome food that is not sour, along with ghee; sweet curd and, for the most part, meat from wild animals cooked in ghee should be served. 65

When the fire has been kindled during the evening meal, one should offer well-cooked rice with milk and include lentil dumplings with ghee among the side dishes. Regarding the rules for bathing therein: 66. [End of section].

One should bathe with a paste of sesame and *āmalaka*, or else anoint [the body] with clarified butter; the bath should be performed with lukewarm water. (67) Substances to be avoided during the period of practice:

In some cases, one should not take oil; nor should one consume bilva, kāravellaka, eggplant, śapharī fish, or tamarind. One should avoid physical exercise and sexual intercourse. [One should also avoid] liquor, fermented gruel, asafoetida, ginger, black gram, and lentils.
One should avoid the *kūṣmāṇḍa* gourd, black mustard, anger, and sour gruel (69). One should abandon improper sleep and eating from a bronze vessel;
one should renounce all vegetables, fruits, and the like whose names begin with the letter "ka" (70).

May this method of service toward the Lord of the World be beneficial! It should be performed on an auspicious lunar mansion and day, on a full moon day during the bright fortnight, and likewise when the Moon is in a state of strength. (71)
Having worshipped the Lord of the World, one should then feed a young maiden;
having given a gift, the best mercury (rasottama) should be taken within the interval of two ghaṭikās. This is the means for pacifying the burning sensation caused by mercury.
If a burning sensation arises from the taste, then one should take *sattva* combined with sugar (73), along with *guḍūcī* and *vaṃśalocana*. One should also administer dates,
pomegranate, grapes, and pieces of sugarcane (74).

According to the specific disease, one should provide appropriate after-drinks; in cases of anorexia, one should give dehusked grain fried in ghee with sugar; likewise, in fever, one should administer a decoction of coriander and *guḍūcī*. 75

One should administer a decoction of uśīra and vāsaka with honey and sugar in cases of raktapitta, kapha disorders, dyspnea, cough, and loss of voice. At night, the powder of jayā fried in fire should be given with honey.
In cases of insomnia, diarrhea, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), and weak digestion,
one should drink the powder of sauvarcala salt, abhayā, and kṛṣṇā with warm water. Similarly, kṛṣṇā mixed with honey is beneficial for colic, indigestion, and fever.
In cases of splenic enlargement, vātarakta, vomiting, anal polyps,
and bleeding from the nose and other sites, one should administer the juice of pomegranate flowers mixed with sugar as a nasal drop (nasya), or the fresh juice of dūrvā grass mixed with sugar.
One should have the patient lick a mixture of *kola* pulp, *kaṇā*, peacock-feather ash,
and sugar with honey for the pacification of vomiting, hiccup, and cough.
This procedure should be applied to all *poṭṭalī* decoctions.
In the *mṛgāṅka*, *hemagarbha*, and *mauktika* [preparations], as well as in these mercurial elixirs (*rasa*),
this elixir known as *lokanātha* shall conquer all diseases. (82) This is the *laghulokanātharasa*.
Having powdered cowrie-shell ash and iron rust (maṇḍūra), one should cook them in ghee;
this should be mixed with an equal amount of black pepper powder that has been processed with betel leaf.
This powder should be licked with honey or with fresh butter.

Eaten at every watch (yāma), even a measure of a single māṣa destroys consumption (kṣaya). This is indeed the Lokanātha-rasa; when taken from the maṇḍala, it conquers phthisis (yakṣman). For consumption and other such ailments, there is the Mṛgāṅkapoṭṭalī-rasa.
One should have thin leaf-like scales made from gold, as delicate as birch bark;
having placed equal amounts of these in a mortar with mercury, one should grind them together with the juice of *kāñcanāra* or the juice of *jvālāmukhī*. (86)
One should do this with the juices of *lāṅgalī* until a paste is formed (87).
Then, one should add borax equal to a fourth part of the gold,
as well as powdered pearls, and throw in twice the amount of gold (88).

Having thrown an equal amount of fragrance into each of them, one should grind them together in one place; then, having formed balls from them, one should wrap them with cloth. Afterwards, having coated them with clay and dried them, one should keep them.
One should place the *mudrā* inside a hollowed-out pair of earthen bowls (*śarāva-sampuṭa*). Having placed that bowl-pair into a vessel filled with salt and having applied the *mudrā*,
one should dry it and then roast it in a large quantity of cow-dung.
Then, once it has cooled, one should collect the fragrance and add an equal amount of mercury; having rubbed it in a mortar as before, one should roast it in a "gajapuṭa" (elephant-seal) furnace.
Once it has returned to its natural temperature, one should take two *guñjā* seeds' weight and employ it [medically].

Combined with eight black peppers, or else with three of long pepper (kṛṣṇā), it should be administered after examination; one *raktikā* of mercury should be given for each [ingredient], along with ghee or honey, according to the requirements of the humors (*doṣa*) and other factors. 93–94.
One who is pure and of sound mind should prepare this wholesome medicine equal to the Lord of the World;
this "Moon" elixir (Mṛgāṅka-rasa) destroys phlegm, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), cough, asthma, consumption, loss of appetite, emaciation, and weakness. (95)

In cases such as consumption and dyspnea, one should prepare a paste of gold with mercury in the proportion of one part mercury to four parts gold; to these two, an amount of sulphur twice their combined weight should be added, and the mixture should be rubbed with *kāñcanārī* juice. (96)
Having formed a ball, one should place it in a crucible-cup (mūṣā-sampuṭa) and seal it; then the wise man should cook it in a bhr̥ṅgī-yantra for three days.
Then, having extracted all of that, he should add an equal amount of sulphur.
One should grind [the ingredients] with the juices of fresh *karasa* and the fresh juice of *citraka*. Then, one should skillfully fill large yellow cowrie shells (*varāṭāḥ*) with this mixture.
From this medicinal preparation, one should add borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*) in an eighth part of its quantity. (98–99)
Having added half a *ṭaṅka* of poison and ground it with the milky sap of *sehuṇḍa*, one should seal the openings of the cowrie shells (*varāṭāḥ*) with that paste. Then,
having placed them in a vessel smeared with powder, one should apply the seal.
Having placed [the medicine] in a pit one cubit deep, one should perform a *gajapuṭa* roasting.
Once the mercury is known to have cooled to the temperature of one's own body, one should administer it like a Lord of the World (*lokanātha*).
The regimen (*pathya*) should be understood as being like that of the Moon (*mṛgāṅka*); one should avoid salt for three days.
When vomiting occurs, one should then give him *chinnā-śṛta* mixed with honey; likewise, in cases of provoked phlegm (*śleṣma-kopa*), one should give *guḍārdra*.
In the case of purging, fried *bhaṅgā* combined with curd should be administered.
It conquers cough, consumption, dyspnea, as well as malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī) and loss of appetite;
it makes the digestive fire brilliant and subdues kapha and vāta.
This supreme mercury, known as Poṭṭalikā, should be understood as Hemagarbha. 104–105.
The second [recipe] is the Hemagarbha-potṭalī-rasa:
four parts of mercury and as many parts of gold;
having made a paste of these two, twelve parts of sulphur [are added]. (106)
One should prepare a kajjalī (collyrium) from these, with sixteen parts of pearl,
twenty-four parts of conch shell, and one part of ṭaṅkaṇa;
all of this should be ground together with the juices of ripe nimbu fruits.
Then, having formed a ball (gola) of those [substances], one should place it within a pair of crucibles (mūṣā-sampuṭaka).
Having applied the seal (mudrā), one should then roast it in a pit one cubit (hasta) deep using cow-dung, specifically by means of the "elephant-roasting" (gajapuṭa) method.
Once it has cooled to the temperature of one's own body, one should extract it. 108–109.
Having ground four *mānas* of *guñjā*, one should administer it combined with cow’s clarified butter (*gavyājya*).
Twenty-nine *unmānas* of black pepper (*marica*) are added;
this should be licked from a silver, earthen, or glass vessel. (110)
With a tranquil mind, one should prepare this wholesome remedy equal to the Lord of the World (Lokanātha).
The *Poṭṭalī Hemagarbhikā* should be administered in cases of cough, asthma, consumption, wind-disorders, phlegm, disorders of the digestive tract (*grahaṇī*), and diarrhea. 111–112.
In the treatment of irregular fever (*viṣamajvara*) and similar ailments, there is the *Mahājvarāṅkuśa-rasa*:
purified mercury, poison (*viṣa*), and sulphur—each measured at one *śāṇa*;
*dhūrta* seeds should be three *śāṇas*, and [the remaining ingredient] should be double the amount of all these combined. (113)
One should carefully prepare a fine powder of these [drugs] called Hemāhvā;
this powder, in a dose of two *guñjā*s, should be administered with the marrow of *jambīra* or with the fresh juices of *ārdra*ka, and it destroys fever born of the three *doṣas*. (114)
It destroys quotidian, tertian, quartan, or irregular fevers; this is the renowned "Goad for Fevers" (Jvarāṅkuśa).
[This is] the Essence of Ānandabhairava for diarrhea and other ailments.
One should powder equal parts of darada, vatsanābha, marica, ṭaṅkaṇa, and kaṇā; this is indeed the Ānandabhairava rasa.
One should administer it in a dose of one or two guñjās, having ascertained the patient's strength.

One should then lick one karṣa of the powdered fruit and bark of *kuṭaja* with honey; this conquers diarrhea arising from the three doṣas. For wholesome diet, one should provide curd-rice, cow's ghee, and buttermilk.
In cases of thirst, cold water is beneficial, and Vijayā is beneficial at night.
(119) In the case of the three doṣas, the juice of Laghusūcikābharaṇa is used; one pala of mercury and one śāṇa of poison—one should powder these two together.
Having placed that powder inside a sealed vessel made of two earthenware bowls joined together,
and having applied the seal and dried it thoroughly,
one should then place it on the hearth and apply fire very gradually for a duration of two praharas.
Then one should open the seal situated above the crucible;
whatever mercury may be adhering to it, one should take it up very slowly.
One should place it in a vessel in such a way that it does not come into contact with air. 122.

One should administer a dose of the elixir (rasa) equal in measure to that which adheres to the point of a needle when it is drawn out with difficulty; this applies to one who has fainted due to a derangement of the humors (sannipāta).
When the head has been scarified with a razor, one should rub the area with a finger.

For just as one who has fainted recovers through contact with red medicinal herbs, so too does one bitten by a snake recover even when in a state of death. When a burning sensation occurs in him, sweet [substances] should be administered therein. 125–126.
In the combined mixture, there is a flavor like water and kinsman (jalabandhurasa);
one part of mercury ash, one-fourth part of sulfur, and realgar, honey, long pepper, and the three acrids (vyoṣa) each equal in quantity to the realgar. 127.

One should powder [the drug] and saturate it seven times with the bile of fish and peacock; once dried, two *guñjā* seeds should be administered as beneficial. Afterward, one should take the juice of *tālaparṇī* or a decoction of the five pungent spices (*pañcakola*).
The medicine named Jalabandhurasa cures *sannipāta*;
