furthermore, a water-based preparation (*jalayoga*) should be administered, by which potency will arise in the liquid.
In *sannipāta*, there is the Pañcavaktra-rasa.
One should grind purified mercury, poison, sulfur, black pepper, borax, and *kaṇā* with the juice of *dhūrtaja* for one day and then dry it.
This is the elixir named Pañcavaktra; two *guñjās* of it conquer *sannipāta*.

One should cause [the patient] to drink a decoction of *arka* root along with meat broth or vegetable soup (131). Curd-rice is wholesome when combined with this, and one should administer it with water;
by means of this juice mixed with honey, phlegm and other humors are pacified (132).
One should drink honey-moistened hand-juice (karasa) after [the meal] for the increase of the digestive fire;
by eating ghee and meat as desired, the digestive fire becomes capable.
In the case of *sannipāta*, the juice of *unmatta* [is used].
One should grind mercury with an equal portion of sulphur using the juice of *dhattūra* fruits for one day, and then add an equal amount of the three pungents (*trikaṭu*).
This mercury known by the name *unmatta* (the "intoxicated") conquers *sannipāta* when administered as a nasal drop (*nasya*). (134–135)
In cases such as *sannipāta*,
one should powder ten *niṣkas* of the seed of *jaipāla* (without its skin), and mix it with one *pratiniṣka* each of black pepper, long pepper, and mercury. (136)
This juice should be diligently processed for seven days with the juices of *jambīra* and *indravāruṇī*.
When applied as an ointment, this *nārāca-rasa* destroys *sannipāta* fever and other ailments such as colic. (137) *Nārāca-rasa*.
One should powder together equal parts of mercury and borax, double that amount of black pepper, two parts each of sulfur, long pepper, and ginger (138),
and the physician should add dehusked dantī seeds in an amount equal to the total of all these ingredients.
This great elixir, Nārāca, proven as a purgative in a dose of two guñjās,
destroys flatulence, constipation, and upward movement of wind (udāvarta).
[139] This is Icchābhedī-rasa, used for colic and similar ailments.

One karṣa each of darada, ṭaṅkaṇa, śuṇṭhī, and pippalī; one pala of hemāhvā, and an equal amount of dantī seeds—having powdered all these together, one should cause [the patient] to drink them with cow's milk alone. (140)
One should administer three *guñjā* of *recana* for those suffering from constipation and flatulence (141).
For all types of urinary disorders (*meha*), there is the *Vasantakusumākararasa*:
two parts of gold and mercury, and an equal amount of iron pyrite (*gagana*).
Three parts of iron ash and four parts of mercury ash, three parts of tin ash—these should all be ground together in one place;
one should add coral and pearl in quantities equal to the mercury. (142–143)
The purification (bhāvanā) is performed with cow's milk, by rubbing with the juices of *aṭaruṣaka*,
with water, with the juice of *mocakanda*, with the juice of the *śatapatra* lotus, and with the fresh juice of *mālatī*. 144.

Afterwards, camphor (mṛgamada) impregnated with the juice of *candratulasī*—this is called *kusumākara*, preceded by the word *vasanta*—one should take two *guñjā* of this with honey; it cures all urinary disorders. 145–146.
Combined with white sandalwood, it conquers diseases such as *amlapitta* (acid gastritis) and others. 147. In cases of consumption (*kṣaya*) and similar ailments, there is the *Rājamṛgāṅka-rasa*:
three parts of mercury ash and one part of gold ash.

Take one part of *mṛtābhra* (dead iron) and two parts each of purified *śilā*, *gandhaka*, and *tālaka*; having combined these and ground them into a fine powder, fill cowrie shells (*varāṭa*) with this mixture, along with *ṭaṅkaṇa* and goat’s milk. 148–149.
Having ground [the ingredients] with that [liquid], one should seal the mouth [of the vessel] and place it in an earthen pot.
Once dried, it should be cooked in a *gajapuṭa* fire; when cooled to the touch of one's own body, it should be powdered.
This *Rājamṛgāṅka* elixir, taken in a dose of four *guñjās*, destroys consumption (*kṣaya*).
One should administer ten *pippalī* fruits with honey and twenty-nine *ūṣaṇas*, along with clarified butter, as wholesome diet; one should avoid anger, fire, and physical exertion.
For the pacification of the king's disease, this wholesome regimen or light meats should be prescribed. (151–152)

In cases such as consumption and dyspnea, one should oneself prepare a kajjali by rubbing purified mercury and sulphur in equal parts with a mortar and pestle; then, one should grind an amount of sharp iron powder equal to those two with the juices of kanyākā. (153)

At the end of two watches (yāmas), one should place the prepared golaka into a copper vessel, cover it with an eraṇḍa leaf, and after half a watch has passed, it will become intensely hot. Afterwards, one should place it in a heap of grain and remove it after twenty-four hours (ahorātra).
Having crushed it, one should strain it through a cloth; truly, it will become water-pervading (vāritara).
One should then saturate it seven times with the juices of kanyākā, bhṛṅgarāja, kākamācī, kuraṇṭa, muṇḍī, and punarnavā.
It should be soaked separately seven times with Sahadevī, Amṛtā, Nīlī, Nirguṇḍī, and Citraja, and likewise dried in the sun;
for this is the renowned Siddhayoga, transmitted from the mouths of the Siddhas.
Truly, I have experienced this [remedy] which removes the entire host of diseases.
(158) One should indeed fix mercury with gold and other metals by reducing them to powder as one does with iron;
combined with the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) and honey, it should be employed for all diseases. (159)

Equal parts of the three pungents (trikaṭu), the three myrobalans (triphalā), cardamom (elā), nutmeg (jātīphala), and cloves (lavaṅgaka)—all these measured in identical proportions—should be combined with an amount of the aforementioned liquid (rasa) equal to their total weight.
Having powdered this, one should lick it with honey; the dose to be consumed is two niṣkas each.
This elixir, named Svayamagniras, destroys consumption and cough; it is an ocean of nectar for all types of cough. [It consists of] purified mercury, sulphur, dead metal (iron), and borax.

Rāsnā, viḍaṅga, triphalā, devadāru, the three pungents (kaṭutraya), amṛtā, padmaka, honey, and viśva—these should be powdered in equal parts. One suffering from all types of coughs should consume three guñjās of this "Ocean of Nectar" (Amṛtārṇava). 162–163.
In the *Śvāsasūryāvarta* formula, mercury (*rasa*) equal to half the quantity of lead (*sūta*), along with sulphur (*gandhaka*), should be ground for one *yāma* with the juice of *kanyākā*.
This mixture should be applied as a paste to copper leaves (*tāmrapatra*) equal in weight to the two [mercury and sulphur]. (164)
Having cooked Sūryāvarta for one day in a *sthālikā* vessel, one should grind it into a powder; this juice, taken in a dose of two *guñjā*s, will conquer asthma.
This is the *Svacchandabhairava-rasa* for wind diseases (*vāta-roga*).
Pure, dead mercury, dead iron, tutthaka, sulphur, and orpiment, along with harītakī,
agnimantha, nirguṇḍī, trikaṭu, ṭaṅkaṇa, and poison—
these should be taken in equal parts and ground in a mortar for one day with the juice of nirguṇḍī.

One suffering from wind diseases (vāta-roga) should eat one *vaṭakī* (pill) made from two *guñjā*s of *muṇḍī* root for a single day; it is known by the name Svacchandabhairava. [The decoction] of *rāsnā*, *amṛtā*, *devadāru*, *śuṇṭhī*, and *vātāri* should be boiled.
One should drink guggulu with lukewarm water as a post-drink (anupāna), which brings comfort. In cases of *grahaṇī* disease, one should take the juice of *haṃsapoṭṭalī*,
along with burnt cowrie shells, ground together with *tryūṣaṇa*, *ṭaṅkaṇa*, and *viṣa*.
One should grind equal parts of sulphur and purified mercury with the juice of *jambīra* fruit; one should eat a *māṣa* of this and afterwards lick black pepper with ghee.
This cures the disease of *grahaṇī*; as a wholesome diet, curd-rice is beneficial.
For the treatment of urinary calculi (aśmarī), there is the Trivikrama-rasa: dead copper should be cooked with equal quantities of goat’s milk until it has lost its fluidity;
then that copper, purified mercury, and sulfur, each in equal parts [are to be combined]. 171.

One should grind [the medicine] with the fresh juices of *nirguṇḍī* and form it into a ball (*gola*). This should be sealed and cooked for one day and one watch (*yāma*) in a *bālukāyantra*. It should be administered in a dose of two *guñjā*s.
Furthermore, one should take the root of *bījapūraka* with water as an after-drink (*anupāna*).
The mercury known by the name Trivikrama removes urinary calculi within one month.
(173) Regarding Mahātāleśvararasa for skin diseases and other ailments:
take cinnabar, pyrite, realgar, purified mercury, rock salt, and borax.
One should grind equal parts of mercury and twice that amount of sulfur in a mortar; then,

having added an equal amount of dead copper, it should be rubbed with *jambīra* fruits for five days and cooked in a *bhūdhara* furnace within a sealed crucible (*saṃpuṭa*) using six *puṭa* applications.
All of this—six palas in total—should be rubbed in each layer within a *puṭa* with *dru* (juice).
Two palas of processed copper and four palas of iron ash [are added].
All of that should be rubbed for one day with the sour juice of *jambīra* and then fired in a mild *puṭa*.
Having added a thirtieth part of poison to this, one should grind everything into a fine powder.
Mixed with buffalo ghee, one should always consume half a *niṣka* of it;
thereafter, one should lick one *karṣa* of *ākucī* powder with honey and ghee.
The Mahātāleśvara mercury quickly destroys all types of leprosy (179).
[This is] the Kuṣṭhakuṭhāra mercury:
sulphur equal to the ash of mercury, along with dead iron, copper, and guggulu.
One should prepare a powder of triphalā, mahānimba, citraka, and śilājatu, sixteen śāṇas each; one should likewise prepare sixty-four śāṇas of the powdered seeds of karañja. (180)
One should mix sixty-four parts of mercury with an equal amount of mica, stirred together with honey and clarified butter.
Kept in a greased vessel, one should consume two niṣkas of this; it is a "rasa" that destroys all skin diseases (kuṣṭha) and wards off even falling skin diseases.
This is the "Kuṣṭhakuṭhāra" (the axe for leprosy).
Regarding white leprosy and other ailments, the *Udayāditya* mercury [is prepared as follows]:
pure mercury and twice its amount of sulfur should be ground for one day with the juice of *kanyā*.
This ball should then be placed inside a crucible and sealed with a copper lid. (183)

With a clean vessel that is twice the size of the *sūtaka* and turned face-downward, one should place ashes on its side; then, adding small amounts of cow-dung and water to the top of the vessel, one should cook it over the stove for two watches (*yāma*).
Having extracted that with a fierce fire, one should grind it while it is still warm from one's own body.
One should then boil *kāṣṭhodumbarikā*, fire, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *rājavṛkṣaka*, *viḍaṅga*, and the seeds of *vākucī*, and saturate [the powder] with that decoction. 185–186.
One should administer two *guñjās* every day from the rising sun;
this will destroy *vicarcikā*, ringworm, leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), and gout (*vātarakta*). As a post-medicine (*anupāna*), a powder of *vākucī* fruit should be taken.
One should drink three *śāṇa* measures of that [powder] cooked with an equal amount of *khadira* decoction, along with cow's milk or *triphalā* decoctions;
at the end of three days, or within seven days, eruptions will appear in cases of *kilāsa*. 188–189.
Having ground together blue vitriol (*nīlādya*), *guñjā*, green vitriol (*kāsīsa*), *dhattūra*, *haṃsapādikā*, *sūryabhaktā*, and *cāṅgerī*,
one should apply it as a paste to the root [of the affliction] for seven nights, repeatedly, in order to pacify the site of the eruptions.
It quickly destroys white leprosy (śvetakuṣṭha), whether curable or incurable; of this there is no doubt.
(191) Furthermore, another ointment for vitiligo (śvitra) is described here by the best of physicians:
the powder of guñjā fruit and fire (agnimantha) applied as a paste removes white leprosy. (192)
Even ash from *apāmārga* stone, when applied, will destroy vitiligo (193).
Regarding leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) and other ailments, [one should prepare] Sarveśvararasa:
one *pala* of purified mercury and four *palas* of sulfur should be powdered together for one *yāma*.
One *pala* each of dead copper, mica, iron, and cinnabar;
ten *niṣkas* each of gold and silver;
one *māṣa* of dead diamond; and two *palas* of pure *tāla*.
It should be ground with *jambīra*, *unmatta*, *vāsā*, *snuhī*, *arka*, and *viṣamuṣṭi* (195), and with the juices of *hayārija* and *indravāruṇī*, each for one day.
Having been ground in this manner for seven days, that ball should be wrapped in cloth (196).
It should be sweated for three days in a sand-bath (*vālukāyantra*) over a mild fire;

then, having taken it, one should grind it into a fine powder. One *pala* of this should be combined with two *palas* of powdered long pepper (*pippalī*). This is the "Lord of All" (*sarveśvara*) elixir. 197.
Two guñjas should be licked with honey; this cures numbness, circular skin lesions, and leprosy.
(198) One karṣa each of vākucī and devadāru should be finely powdered; one should lick it smeared with castor oil as a pleasant after-drink. (199)
At the beginning of the period of sleeplessness and so forth, one should cook five *palas* of *hemāhvā* (turmeric) in the juice of *svarṇakṣīrī* in a jar of buttermilk;
once the buttermilk has been digested, it should be removed and cooked again in a jar of milk. 200.
When the milk has been digested, one should extract [the substance], wash it, and dry it thoroughly. Then,
having combined five *palas* of that powder with two *palas* of black pepper and one *pala* of mercury processed [with sulfur] (*mūrchita-sūta*), one should consume them together.
This juice of *svarṇakṣīrī* indeed cures one suffering from leprosy and skin diseases with a single *niṣka*;
it is the "diabetes-binding juice" for *prameha*.
[The ingredients are] calcined mercury, killed *kāntaloha*, calcined *muṇḍaloha*, and *śilājatu*.
One should purify mercury (tāpya), realgar (śilā), the three pungents (vyoṣa), the three myrobalans (triphalā), and the seeds of the jujube (kolabījaka);

then, having powdered wood-apple (kapittha) and turmeric (rajanī), one should saturate these with the juice of bhṛṅgarāja twenty times and dry them. Afterward, one should always lick this mixture combined with honey.
One niṣka of this great mercury, bound by the *meha* [medicinal] process, removes urinary disorders (*meha*).
Having ground six *māṣas* of the seeds of great nimba with water from one *pala* of rice and two *niṣkas* of ghee, [one should administer it]. (205)
Having combined these, one should drink them after [the meal]; this cures even chronic urinary disorders (meha). 206.
For dropsy (jalodara) and other ailments, there is the "Great Fire" (Mahāvahni) preparation:
four parts of mercury (sūta), eight parts of sulphur (gandha), turmeric, triphalā, and harītakī (śivā).
Trivṛt, jaipāla, and citraka should each be two parts;
trikaṭu, danti, and jīraka should each be three parts;
and [the remaining ingredients] should each be eight parts. Having combined these, one should grind them into a powder. (207–208)
It should be processed seven times each with the juices of *jayantī*, *snuk*, *bhṛṅga*, *vahni*, *vātārī*, and oil, separately and in sequence.
This is called *mahāvahnirasa*; one should drink one *niṣka* of it with warm water.
By this, purgation occurs; one should administer curd-rice with rock salt at the end of the day as the wholesome diet, while avoiding cold water.
This is said to cure all types of abdominal enlargement and is supreme for removing obstructed wind (mūḍhavāta). 210–211.
For disorders such as abdominal tumors (gulma) and splenic enlargement (plīha),
one should take equal parts of sulfur, orpiment, mica, killed copper, realgar,
and purified mercury; these should be ground together and macerated for twenty-one days.
One should saturate half a niṣka [of the powder] with a decoction of pippalī and the milk of *vajrī*;
by consuming it with honey, one conquers abdominal tumors, splenic disorders, and other ailments.
This elixir is named Vidyādhara; one should drink cow’s urine as an after-drink. (213–214)
For colic pain (pakti-śūla),
one should grind mercury, borax, the horn of a deer, gold, copper, and dead mercury for one day with the juice of Ārdra-kadru; then, having sealed it in a crucible, one should cook it in a puṭa fire.
One should lick one *māṣa* of the elixir called *Trinetrā* with honey and clarified butter (215).
Thereafter, one should lick rock salt, cumin, and asafoetida with honey and clarified butter;
this is renowned as a cure for colic caused by indigestion (*pakti-śūla*) within just one month—of this there is no doubt (216).
In the *Śūla* [chapter], the *Śūlagajakesarī-rasa*:
one should grind purified mercury and twice its amount of purified sulfur firmly for one *yāma*;
then, adding an equal amount of purified copper, one should seal it within a *sampuṭa* (a double-vessel). 217
Having placed salt above and below it in an earthen vessel, the physician should keep it there;
then, having cooked it in a *gajapuṭa* fire, he should remove it once it has cooled to body temperature.
He should then grind the contents into a fine powder in a mortar and administer two *guñjā* seeds' weight on a leaf-fragment.
One suffering from all types of colic should consume asafoetida, ginger, and cumin;
one should drink a powder made of *vacā* and black pepper in a dose of one *karṣa* with warm water.
This elixir, "The Elephant’s Mane," destroys even incurable colic. 219–220.
In cases such as impaired digestion (agnimāndya) and the like, there is the Agnituṇḍīvaṭī-rasa:
purified mercury, poison, sulphur, ajamodā, the three fruits (triphalā), svarjika alkali, yavakṣāra, citraka, rock salt, and cumin. (221)

One should grind equal parts of sauvarcala salt, viḍaṅga, sea salt, and the three pungents (trivṛt, pippalī, and marica), along with an amount of viṣamuṣṭi equal to the sum of all these, with the acidic juice of jambīra fruit.
One should then swallow pills the size of black pepper to pacify sluggish digestion.

For cholera (viṣūcikā), one should powder purified mercury, poison, and sulphur in equal parts; then add black pepper in an amount equal to all of them, and mix with the juice of the fruits of *kaṇṭakārī*. (224)
One should rub and saturate everything twenty-one times;
one should eat three *guñjā* seeds of this pill for the pacification of all types of indigestion.
This elixir, known as *Ajīrṇakaṇṭaka*, destroys cholera (*viṣūcikā*). 225
In the treatment of phlegm diseases (kapha-roga), the Manthānabhairava-rasa is prepared as follows:

one should powder together equal parts of dead mercury (mṛta-sūta), dead copper (mṛta-tāmra), asafoetida (hiṅgu), Puṣkara root, rock salt (saindhava), sulfur (gandhaka), orpiment (tāla), and Kaṭukī. (226)
One should grind Punarnavā, Devadālī, Nirguṇḍī, Taṇḍulīyaka,
Tiktakośātakī, and Drākṣā together firmly for one day.
One should lick a *māṣa*-measure of this "Manthānabhairava" juice with honey.
For the purpose of pacifying diseases of phlegm (kapha), one should subsequently drink a decoction of nimba.
In diseases of wind (vāta), there is the Vātanāśana-rasa,
consisting of mercury, gold, diamond, copper, iron, and honey.
One should grind together equal parts of *tāla*, blue vitriol (*nīlāñjana*), *tuttha*, and opium,
along with one part each of the five salts; having rubbed them for one day with the milk of the *vajrī* plant, one should seal the mixture and cook it in a *bhūdhara* (earth) furnace.

One should have the patient lick one *māṣa* of fresh *kadrava* to destroy vāta; or one should administer a decoction of long pepper root (*pippalīmūla*) with black pepper as a post-drink. This destroys all disorders of vāta, such as convulsions (*ākṣepaka*) and others. 231–232.
In the *Sannipātādi* [treatment], the *Kanakasundara* elixir consists of eight *śāṇas* of gold; the mercury is considered to be twelve [parts],
the sulphur is also said to be twelve, and the copper is measured at two *śāṇas*.
There should be four *śāṇas* of mica (*abhraka*) and two *śāṇas* of *mākṣika*;
two *śāṇas* of tin (*vaṅga*), three *śāṇas* of *saubīra*, and eight *śāṇas* of iron;
having made the poison (*viṣa*) three *śāṇas*, there should be one *pala* of *lāṅgalī*.
One should rub it for one day with juices extracted from sour fruits, then place it in a mild crucible and heat it in fire; thereafter, one should grind it into a fine powder.
A dose of one *māṣa* of this mercury should be administered in cases of most severe *sannipāta*.
With the juice of *ārdra* itself, or with the juice of garlic (*rasona*),
this disease-curing elixir conquers *kilāsa*, all types of *kuṣṭha*, *visarpa*, *bhagaṇḍara*, fever, artificial poison, and indigestion. (236–237)

One karṣa each of the mercury from Sannipātabhairava, the mercury, and the sulphur should be used to prepare a collyrium (kajjalikā) from those two; then, one karṣa each of silver, mica, copper, tin, and the essence of snake-venom [should be added]. (238)

One should perform a separate maceration for one *yāma* each with the fresh juices of *śigru*, *jvālāmukhī*, *śuṇṭhī*, *bilva*, and *taṇḍulīyaka*. Having formed a ball [of the medicine], one should wrap it in cloth and place it inside a vessel filled with salt.

Then, one should place the glass flask into a vessel made of glass; having filled it with sand, the fire should be maintained for two yāmas. Then, having extracted that globule and ground it into powder, one should mix it.
One should likewise saturate it twice with one karṣa of coral powder, with poison in the measure of a śāṇa, and with the venom of a black cobra;
[and add] tagara, muśalī, māṃsī, hemāhvā, vetasa, and kaṇā. 242.
One should grind together *nīlinī*, *padmaka*, *cailā*, *citraka*, *kuṭheraka*,
*śatapuṣpā*, *devadālī*, *dhattūra*, *agastya*, and *muṇḍikā* with the juices of *madhūka*, *jātī*, and *madana*. (243–244)

Then, having dried each one individually for a single period, one should preserve it with sixteen parts each of bījapūra, ārdra, kaṭvarī, and marica. This elixir, measuring two guñjās, is administered in cases of *saṃnipāta*.
This well-known rasa is named Bhairava of Sannipāta (246). For diarrhea and other ailments, there is the Grahaṇī-kapāṭa-rasa:
silver, pearl, gold, and *sāra* [copper], each in one part.

Two parts of sulphur and three parts of mercury—one should grind these together firmly with the juice of *kapittha* fruit; then one should place them in a deer horn and roast them in a medium-sized *puṭa*. Having then extracted [the contents], one should grind them again. (247–248)
It should be processed seven times with the juices of *balā* and three times with the juice of *apāmārga*.
Then, there should be a triple maceration for each of the following— *lodhra*, *prativiṣā*, *mustā*, *dhātakī*, *indrāyava*, and *amṛtā*— using their respective fresh juices, three times for each.
One *māṣa* of this meat-juice (*rasa*), given with honey and black pepper, likewise destroys all types of diarrhea and even that caused by *grahaṇī*.
This *kapāṭa-rasa* is a digestive stimulant for the disease of *grahaṇī*. (250–251)
The wise physician should take mercury, mica, sulphur, barley-alkali, borax, *agnimantha*, and *vacā*, each of these being equal in quantity to the mercury. (252)
Then one should grind it with *jayantī*, *jambīra*, *bhṛṅga*,
and *drākṣā* for three days; thereafter, having formed a ball and dried it thoroughly, one should keep it in an iron vessel, place a shallow bowl (*śarāva*) over it, and seal it.
One should slowly cause the fire below to flow for half a watch (yāmārdha), and then extract [the substance].
One should add a quantity of ativiṣā equal to mercury, as well as mocarasa; one should then saturate it seven times separately with the juices of kapittha, vijayā, and āmrātaka. (254–255)
Having impregnated *dhātakī*, *yava*, *mustā*, *lodhra*, *bilva*, and *guḍūcī* with their juices, one should dry each [ingredient] for one day.
One should lick one *śāṇa* of this juice, known as *vajrakapāṭa*, with honey. (256)
One should powder equal parts of *vahni*, *śuṇṭhī*, *viḍa*, *bilva*, and salt (257).
One should drink this with warm water afterwards; it conquers all types of *grahaṇī*.
This is the *madanakāmadeva* elixir for aphrodisiac purposes (258).
One should take mercury, diamond, gold, copper, mercury-oxide (sūtaka), sulphur, and iron, increasing these substances in successive order according to their proportions;
having ground them with the juice of kanyākā, one should place them in a glass jar.
Having removed [the vessel] from the middle of the *piṭharī*, one should place the *saindhava-amṛta* inside;
one should seal the *piṭharī* properly and then set it upon the hearth.
One should apply the fire very gradually for one day, and then take it out. 260–261.
Having powdered [the ingredients] while they are still warm from one's own body,
one should saturate them three times each with the milks of *arka*, and with the juices of *aśvagandhā*, *kākolī*, *vānarī*, *musalī*, and *kṣurā*, as well as with the juice of *śatāvarī*.
One should saturate [the powder] with the juices of lotus stalks, kaseru, and kāśa.
Then, one should mix this powder with musk, the three pungents (vyoṣa), camphor, kaṅkola, cardamom, and cloves, each being one-eighth part of the previous powder. 263–264.
Having added an equal amount of sugar to all [the ingredients], one who follows a sweet diet should drink [this] in a dose of one *śāṇa* with two *palas* of cow's milk.
By its power, beauty, strength, and splendor increase. (265)
A young woman may delight many men without any loss of semen occurring.
In this aphrodisiac (vājīkaraṇa) known as Kandarpa-sundara-rasa, the ingredients are mercury, diamond, snake, pearl, silver, gold, and black mica.
One should grind these [ingredients] in one-karṣ portions with the juices of *irimedaja*;
then, one should mix two karṣas each of coral powder and sulfur, and subsequently grind them with the fresh juice of *aśvagandhā* inside a deer horn. 267–268.
Having placed it in a soft pouch and cooked it, one should saturate it with the juice of dhātakī and with kākolī, madhuka, māṃsī, the three types of balā,
viśa, iṅguda, drākṣā, pippalī, vandāka, śatāvarī, and the four types of parṇī.
Having infused *parūṣaka*, *kaseru*, *madhūka*, and *vānarī* with their own juices, one should dry them and reduce them to powder;
[then add] *elā*, *tvak*, *patraka*, *māṃsī*, *lavaṅga*, *aguru*, and *keśara*. 270–271.

One should mix Musta, mṛgamada, kṛṣṇā, water, and moon (karpūra); with these powders, each measured at one śāṇa, one should prepare a juice as beautiful as Kandarpa. One should consume one śāṇa of this at night, along with sugar, āmalakī, and vidārī.
One should take one karṣa of the powder of these [herbs] combined with one karṣa of ghee;
thereafter, with a steady mind, one should drink two palas of milk. Thus, one may enjoy many women, and no loss of semen occurs. (273–274)

One part of purified mercury, the lord of essences (rasendra), and two parts of purified sulfur should be added; one should prepare a kajjalī from them, and then add the powder derived from *tīkṣṇa* iron. (275)
Having added an amount equal to collyrium, one should grind it for one *prahara*;
thereafter, one should grind it with the juices of maiden plants (*kanyādrava*) for three days in the heat of the sun.
Then, a great, hot emission of smoke arises from it.
Having thoroughly compressed it into a mass, one should place it in a copper vessel (277).
The wise person should keep it for three days inside a single grain of paddy;
then, having extracted it from there and placed it in a mortar, one should set it out in the sun (278).
One should repeatedly saturate [the powder] three times with the juices of *kuṭhāracchinnā*,
dry it in the sun, and then saturate it three times with decoctions of the three pungents (*trikaṭu*).
It should then be saturated in succession three times each with the juices of *vāsā*, *amṛtā*, and *citraka*.
Then, having placed it in an iron vessel, one should steep it with the decoction of triphalā,
and with the juices of nirguṇḍī, the bark of dāḍima, bisa, bhṛṅga, and kuraṇṭaka,
as well as with the boiled juice of palāśa, kadalī, drākṣā, and bījaka.
One should saturate [the powder] three times each with the juices of nīlikā, alambuṣā, drākṣā, babbūla, and phalikā, and then with the juice of nāgabalā.
Then, in the morning, one should lick a portion the size of a jujube fruit (kola) with honey and ghee.
One should drink one *pala* of the decoction of the best [drug] as an after-drink (*anupāna*).
When practiced for three months, it destroys wrinkles and graying hair, as well as weak digestion, asthma, cough, jaundice, phlegm, and wind. (283–284)

Combined with long pepper and honey, this undoubtedly destroys vātarakta (gout), urinary disorders, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), and pain from hemorrhoids; it also conquers scrotal enlargement when saturated with chinnā, asatva, and honey. 285.
This iron elixir (lohara-sāyana) is known as the supreme means for increasing strength and complexion, an aphrodisiac, and life-prolonging; it conquers all diseases over time.
One should avoid pumpkin, sesame oil, black gram, and mustard.
One who uses iron should avoid liquor and sour tastes.
(288) Here follow summary verses on topics not previously mentioned; therein is the purification of *jayapāla*.
Jaipāla seeds, stripped of their husks and sprouts, are placed for three days in buffalo urine;
then, purified by hot water,
they are ground with *vāsā* in a mortar, smeared onto fresh earthen vessels, and, once devoid of oiliness, become like dust.
When repeatedly processed with lime juice, the poison becomes pure, rich in its qualities,
and fit for detoxification. Having cut the poison into small pieces, one should bind it with a piece of cloth.
Having placed it in the midst of cow urine, one should set it in the sun for three days.
Wise ones should provide fresh cow urine every day.
When the three days have passed, one should take it out, dry it gently, and grind it finely.
Thus purified, that poison becomes fit for use and overcomes disease;
or else,
having cut the poison into pieces and bound it with cloth, one should suspend it on a swing.
One should cook it with goat's milk until it is thoroughly steamed; thereby it attains purity. However, in the absence of goat's milk, one should purify it with cow's milk.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Purification and Killing of Mercury and Other Substances," in the Middle Section of the Śrī Śārṅgadharasaṃhitā.

Thus ends the middle section; the procedure for the internal administration of oleaginous substances. Now begins the first chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Internal Administration of Oleaginous Substances."
Now, regarding the classifications of oleaginous substances (sneha) and the time for their consumption:

oleaginous substances are said to be of four kinds—clarified butter (ghṛta), oil (taila), muscle fat (vasā), and marrow (majjā). One should drink them when the sun has slightly risen above the horizon.
Regarding the two-fold nature of oleaginous substances according to their origin:
"Oleaginous substance is said to have two origins: the immobile and the mobile.
This is the designation of the names of the superior oleaginous substances among the immobile and the mobile.

Sesame oil is the best among stationary substances, while ghee is the best among moving ones. (3) The names for combined unguents are formed by two, three, or four of these; when they are mixed, it is called *yamaka*, *trivṛt*, or *mahat*. (4)
Regarding one accustomed to oleation, the duration for drinking it is three days, four days, five days, or likewise six days;
beyond seven nights, the oil becomes fully integrated when used.
Regarding the dosage for the internal administration of unctuous substances (sneha),
a wise physician should administer the small, medium, or large dose after having observed the strength of the doshas, the season, the digestive fire, and the age. 6

The complications arising from oleation (sneha) consumed in improper quantity, at the wrong time, or through improper diet and lifestyle, as well as the remedies for them: Oleation taken in excessive quantity, at the wrong time, or due to improper diet and conduct,
causes edema, hemorrhoids, drowsiness, sleepiness, and loss of consciousness.
In that case, one should administer fasting, followed by sudation, and once [the patient's condition] is known, purgation; the doses of oleaginous substances should be given,
and for one with a stimulated digestive fire, the dose of oil is measured at one pala.
For one of medium constitution, it should be three karṣas; for one of inferior constitution, two karṣas. These are other variations regarding the dose of drinking fats;
alternatively, there are three other generally accepted measures for the dose of fats.
A large dose is digested in a full day and night; a medium dose is digested during the day;
and a small dose is known to be digested in half a day and brings comfort. These are the benefits of drinking medicated fats according to the different measures.
The smallest dose is digestive and aphrodisiac, and is honored for minor disorders;
the medium dose is known as emollient, nourishing, and a remover of vertigo.
The largest dose destroys skin diseases, poisons, insanity, seizures, and epilepsy.
The determination of the post-drink (anupāna) for the consumption of ghee according to the [specific] dosha is as follows:

ghee alone should be drunk in cases of Pitta; it should be taken with salt in cases of Vata; and it should also be combined with the three pungents (vyoṣa) and alkali (kṣāra) when Kapha is predominant. 12.

The drinking of ghee is recommended for those fit for its consumption, as well as for those afflicted by dryness, wounds, or poison, for those suffering from disorders of vāta and pitta, and for those with diminished intellect, wisdom, and memory. (13)
Persons fit for oil-drinking—those afflicted by worms in the stomach, by wind (vāta), and by increased phlegm (kapha) and fat (medas);
those accustomed to oil; and those who desire firmness—should drink oil. 14.

Persons fit for the consumption of muscle fat (vasā) are those exhausted by physical exercise, those with depleted semen and blood, those suffering from great pain, and those whose digestive fire, wind, and vital breath are powerful; such men are traditionally considered fit for muscle fat. 15

Those people who are fit for drinking marrow—those of cruel disposition, capable of enduring hardship, afflicted by wind, or possessing a blazing digestive fire—should drink marrow, or even ghee; this is beneficial in every respect. (16)
The time for drinking medicated fats (sneha) is during the cold season; one should drink the fat by day in the cold season, or at night in the hot season;
when vāta and pitta predominate, one should drink it at night, and when vāta and kapha predominate, by day. 17
The specific indications for the application of oil and ghee:

one should employ either oil or ghee for nasal drops (nasya), massage (abhyañjana), gargles (gaṇḍūṣa), and the filling of the head, ears, and eyes (mūrdha-karṇākṣi-tarpaṇa), after having observed the relative strength or weakness of the doshas. 18
Regarding the variations of post-drink liquids according to the type of unctuous substance:
with ghee, lukewarm water should be drunk; with oil, vegetable broth is recommended; and with muscle fat or marrow, one should drink the scum of boiled rice as a pleasant post-drink liquid. (19)

One should administer warm food, fats, and drinks to those who dislike fats, as well as to infants, the elderly, the delicate, and the emaciated, even during the hot season, along with their meals. 20
A formulation for immediate oleation is a lukewarm gruel (yavāgū) made with plenty of sesame seeds and very few grains of rice; when consumed, it produces an immediate oleating effect. 21.

Immediately after the application of an oleation treatment, one should milk a cow into clarified butter that has been heated with powdered sugar; drinking the warm milk from this is called "instantaneous oleation" (sadyaḥ-snehana). 22
Regarding the management of undigested fat (sneha-ajīrṇa):
For one whose fat is not digested due to improper conduct or excessive quantity, or if it is digested with flatulence, one should induce emesis with warm water. (23)
Remedy for the indigestion of oleaginous substances: When there is suspicion of the indigestion of an oleaginous substance, a person should drink warm water;
by that, eructation becomes purified and likewise an appetite for food arises. (24)
Treatment for thirst resulting from the drinking of oleaginous substances:
When the digestive fire of one who has undergone oleation (sneha) is made excessively sharp, it then excites thirst; such a person should vomit the oleaginous substance with warm water.

One should drink cold water, for by that thirst is quenched. (25) Men who are unfit to drink unctuous substances— namely those with indigestion, those suffering from abdominal enlargement, and those with acute fever— should avoid unctuous substances.
One who is weak, suffering from anorexia, obese, afflicted by fainting, or oppressed by intoxication; one who has been administered an enema, purged, or vomited; one afflicted by thirst or fatigue;
a woman who has had a premature delivery, or one during foul weather—one should avoid these cases [for bloodletting]. 26.

Persons fit for the internal administration of oleaginous substances (sneha-pāna) include those who require sudation or purification therapies, those addicted to wine, women, or physical exercise, those given to anxious reflection,
the elderly, children, the emaciated, the dry, those with diminished blood, and those with depleted semen.
For those afflicted by Vāta and those afflicted by Timira (visual impairment), oleation is the supreme treatment. (27) The description of the signs of being well-oleated and dry:
Downward movement of Vāta, a stimulated digestive fire, and stool that is unctuous and not hard. (28)

Softness and smoothness of the limbs, absence of fatigue, a surge of oleation, lightness, and clarity of the sense organs—these are the signs of proper oleation; in the case of dryness, the opposite occurs. (29) These are the characteristics of one who has been excessively oleated.
Aversion to food, salivation, burning in the anus, dysentery,
drowsiness, diarrhea, and extreme pallor are the signs of one who has been excessively oleated (30).
The remedy for both the dry and the excessively oleated states [is as follows].

The oleation of the dry with unctuous substances, and the drying of the excessively unctuous with *śyāmāka*, *caṇaka*, and the like, as well as with buttermilk, oil-cake, and parched grain flour—these are the benefits of employing oleation. 31. The virtues of the practice of oleation.

A person who consumes fats (sneha) becomes one with a kindled digestive fire, a purified gastrointestinal tract, nourished tissues, firm sense organs, freedom from disease, and an abundance of strength and complexion. (32) Those to be avoided in the consumption of fats:

During the administration of oleation therapy (sneha), one should avoid physical exercise, exposure to cold, suppression of natural urges, staying awake at night, sleeping during the day, foods that cause internal secretions (abhiṣyandi), and dry foods (rūkṣa). Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Administration of Oleation Therapy," in the Uttarakhanda of the Śrī Śārṅgadharasaṃhitā.
The Procedure for Fomentation:
Now begins the second chapter, titled "The Procedure for Fomentation.
In this regard, first are the classifications of fomentation.
Sudation is said to be of four types: tāpa (heat), ūṣma (warmth), sveda (actual sweating), and upanāha (poultice). All of these alleviate the afflictions caused by vāta.
The application of sudation varies according to the specific *doṣa*.
Sweats arising from heat and steam are generally declared to destroy *śleṣman* (phlegm);

however, poultices (*upanāha*) destroy *vāta*, while a liquid application is beneficial when there is an association with *pitta*. This is the instruction on the three types of sudation according to the disease, the strength of the patient, and other factors.
In cases of great strength and great disease, strong sudation is prescribed;
in those who are weak, mild sudation is used; and in those of moderate strength, moderate sudation is considered appropriate.
This is the instruction regarding specific types of sudation according to the specific nature of the *doṣas*.
In cases of *balāsa* (catarrh), drying sudation is indicated; in cases of *kapha* and *vāta*, sudation that is both drying and oleating is used;
and when *vāta* is obstructed by *kapha* and *medas*, one should certainly stay in a slightly warm room with sunlight, engage in wrestling, walk on foot, and wear heavy clothing.

Those who suffer from the burdens of anxiety and mental exertion should resort to these for liberation from disease; indeed, among those people who are first to be treated with sudation, nasal therapy (nasya) and enema (vasti) should also be administered to embodied beings.

Whosoever are to be purified (śodhanīya) are considered by me to have been previously treated with sudation (svedya). Those persons who require both [purification and sudation] should be sweated first;
likewise, those suffering from splenic enlargement, fistula-in-ano, and hemorrhoids are to be sweated first.
A person suffering from urinary calculi should undergo sudation at the time of surgical intervention;
likewise, people should be sweated after the foreign body has been removed,
as well as those with cases of retained fetus or disease.
Whether delivered in due time or prematurely, the woman with broad hips should subsequently undergo sudation (sveda).
The proper time for sudation is when all those requiring it have been treated; one should administer it in a windless place and once the food has been digested.
The fruit of sudation is that,

through the application of sweat, the morbid humors (doṣas) residing within the bodily tissues of a person whose body has been moistened by oleation reach a state of liquidity and, having entered the digestive tract, undergo purgation. 10

The protective procedure for one who has undergone sudation: one should touch the heart of the person whose body is being sweated with cool [substances]; and for one whose body has been anointed with oil, one should cover the eyes with cool [substances]. 11.

Persons unfit for sudation therapy include those with indigestion, the weak, those suffering from urinary disorders (mehin), those emaciated by chest wounds, the thirsty, those with diarrhea, those with hemoptysis (raktapitta), those with anemia (pāṇḍuroga), and likewise those with abdominal diseases (udarī). 12.
One who is afflicted by intoxication and a pregnant woman should not be subjected to sudation by a wise physician;
however, even these individuals, if they are curable by sudation, should be treated with mild sudations.
[13] Those parts of the body that are suitable for mild sudation—
One should apply mild sudation to the heart, the scrotum, and the eyes.
Diseases born of excessive sudation include pain in the joints,
burning sensation, thirst, exhaustion, and vertigo.
In cases where there is an aggravation of pitta, blood, and pustules (piṭikā), one should treat them with cold measures.
Regarding the characteristics of sudation (sveda), among those types, that called *tāpa* (heating) is performed with sand, cloth, or the hands.
The procedure for steam-sudation (ūṣmasveda) is as follows: it should be applied appropriately using a skull, a ball, or charcoal;
steam-sudation should be administered using iron balls, bricks, or stones.
It should be prepared with heated [substances] sprinkled with sour liquids and wrapped in a cloth;
or else, having filled a bell-metal vessel with the decoction or juice of drugs that destroy wind (vāta), one should place a hole on its side.
One should employ a seal-less [vessel] that is three-segmented, made of metal, wood, or bamboo,
six finger-breadths wide at the mouth, shaped like a cow’s tail, and two cubits in length.
[The patient] should be seated comfortably, well-anointed, and covered with the teacher’s upper garment.
One should apply sudation to a patient suffering from wind disorders using a tube shaped like an elephant's trunk.

Alternatively, having dug a pit in the ground measuring one man’s length, burned it with khadira wood, and then sprinkled it with milk, fermented grain-water (kāñjika), and water; [one may then apply sudation]. 19–20.
One should cause a person lying down, covered with leaves that destroy wind (vātaghna), to undergo sudation;
likewise, one should administer sudation to the person while they lie down using boiled beans and other such substances.
This is the procedure for poultice-sudation (upanāha-sveda).

Then, one should apply poultice-fomentation (upanāha-sveda) using Vata-alleviating herbs; having smeared the body of the patient afflicted by Vata with these herbs ground with sour liquids, mixed with salt, combined with fats, and applied lukewarm along with milk and meat broth. 22
The procedure for the great fomentation with śālvaṇa involves the meat of domestic and marshy animals, the group of vitalizing (jīvanīya) drugs,
sour curd, sauvīraka, alkali, and likewise the vīrataru group.
With horse gram, black gram, wheat, linseed, sesame, and mustard;
with dill, devadāru, śephālī, and large cumin;
and with castor root-seeds, rāsnā, radish, and śigru. (24–25)
With *miśī*, black *kuṭhera*, and salts combined with sour substances;
with *prasāriṇī*, *aśvagandhā*, *balās*, and the ten roots (*daśamūla*);
and with *guḍūcī* and the seeds of *vānarī*, gathered as they are available—(26).
One should cause the person to sweat by binding crushed and heated substances with a cloth.
(27) Regarding the characteristics of *dravasveda*: *Dravasveda*, moreover, consists of [the application of] a decoction of Vata-subduing substances that has been filled [into a vessel].

Seated comfortably in a cauldron or even a chamber, one should immerse oneself up to six finger-breadths from the navel while being bathed by a stream of decoction; this is the procedure for sudation (dra-sveda). 28–29.
A person whose body has been made unctuous should remain with lukewarm water poured over his shoulders;
in this manner, one should cause a person to undergo sudation with oil, milk, or clarified butter. This is the rule regarding the duration of immersion.
An oil bath (avagāhana) with oil applied at intervals of one or two days is appropriate;
the fruit of this oil bath is that it satisfies [the body] through the openings of the channels, the pores of the hair, and the arteries.
Oil applied during immersion-baths bestows strength upon the body;
it is the cause for the increase of the bodily constituents (dhātus) in one who has been anointed with oil,
just as the sprouts of a tree flourish when its roots are moistened with water.
For in this way, an increase of the bodily elements occurs when one is sprinkled with oil;
there is no other means superior to this for the destruction of Vāta. (33) This is the instruction on the stage of ceasing the sudation therapy.

When coldness, pain, and other such symptoms have subsided, when stiffness and heaviness are restrained, when the digestive fire has been kindled, and when softness has arisen, cessation from sudation is prescribed. (34) Procedures to be performed after sudation:

Once properly sweated and massaged, one should bathe slowly with warm water, eat food that does not cause internal secretions, and should not engage in physical exercise. Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Procedure for Fomentation," in the Uttarakhanda of the Śrī Śārṅgadharasaṃhitā.
The Procedure for Emesis:
Now begins the third chapter, titled "The Procedure for Emesis.
In this regard, [the following is] the timing for emesis and purgation.
In autumn, spring, and the rainy season, a skilled physician should administer emesis and purgation to embodied beings;
these are the persons who are fit for emesis.

One should induce emesis in a person who is strong, afflicted by kapha, suffering from nausea and pain, accustomed to vomiting, and possesses a steady mind. Diseases that are curable by emesis [should be treated thus].
In cases of poisoning, diseases of the breast milk, weak digestion, elephantiasis, scrotal enlargement, heart disease, leprosy, erysipelas, urinary disorders, indigestion, and vertigo;
and in cases of vidārikā, apacī, cough, asthma, chronic catarrh, and hernia.
In cases of epilepsy, fever, insanity, as well as blood-dysentery;
in inflammations of the nose, palate, and lips; in ear-discharge, double-tonguedness, uvulitis, diarrhea, and likewise in diseases of bile and phlegm.

The physician should administer emesis in cases of jaundice and indigestion. People unfit for emesis are those suffering from cataracts (timira), abdominal tumors (gulma), abdominal enlargement (udara), and those who are emaciated. One should not induce emesis in these individuals.
One who is not excessively old, nor pregnant, nor obese, nor afflicted by a wound or disease, nor suffering from intoxication,
nor a child, nor emaciated, nor hungry, should be given a nirūha enema. Likewise,
those suffering from upward-moving wind (udāvarta), upward flow of blood, difficult vomiting, or disorders of pure vāta should be treated with it.

One suffering from jaundice, one infested with worms, and one who impairs the voice [are excluded] from recitation. Furthermore, even those for whom emesis is otherwise unsuitable may be administered emetics if they are afflicted by indigestion or tormented by poison.
Those [patients] whose [stomachs] are pervaded by *kapha* should be induced to vomit by drinking a decoction of *madhuka*.
One should not induce vomiting in those who are delicate, emaciated, young, old, or timid; nor in one who has drunk gruel up to the throat, or milk, buttermilk, or curd.
When the bodily humors of a person have been aggravated by unwholesome and phlegm-increasing foods,
emesis administered after the body has been treated with oleation and sudation proceeds effectively.
[11] This concludes the sequence of beneficial substances for emesis and purgation.
In all emetic procedures, rock salt or honey is beneficial;
one should administer a loathsome emetic, whereas a purgative should be the opposite. (12) This is the method for preparing decoctions for the purpose of emesis.
Having boiled one *kuḍava* of the medicinal substance in one *āḍhaka* of water until one-half remains, one should administer it for emetic purposes;
this is the dosage for drinking a decoction according to the opinion of Bhela. (13)
In the drinking of decoctions (kvātha), nine prasthas is proclaimed as the maximum dose;
the medium is said to be six [prasthas], and the minimum is three prasthas.
(14) This is the dosage for the paste (kalka) and other preparations when taken by the left hand.

Three palas each of paste (kalka), powder (cūrṇa), and electuary (avaleha) constitute the superior dose; one should know that two palas each are the middling dose, while one pala each is the inferior dose.
(15) Thus, according to the distinctions of superior and so forth, there are differences in the number of emetic bouts.
In emesis as well, there should be eight urges; those ending with bile are considered excellent, six urges are middling, and four urges are regarded as inferior.
At the beginning of the emesis, the measure is one *prastha*.
In cases of emesis, purgation, and likewise bloodletting,
the wise say that thirteen and a half palas constitute one *prastha*.
[This is] the specification of particular substances for emesis according to the specific nature of the *doṣas*.
One should conquer *kapha* with pungent, sharp, and hot substances; *pitta* with sweet and cold ones;
and *kapha* associated with *vāyu* with very sweet, salty, sour, and hot substances.
(18) One should drink long pepper (*kṛṣṇā*), *rāṭhaphala*, and rock salt (*sindhu*) with lukewarm water for *kapha*.
In cases of Pitta, one should drink cold water with *paṭola*, *vāsā*, and *nimba*.
When afflicted by Kapha and Vāta, one should drink *madana* with milk.
In the case of indigestion (*ajīrṇa*), a wise person should drink *sindhuvāra* with lukewarm water and induce vomiting.
The recommended procedure for emesis:
Having administered the emetic, the physician should cause the patient— who is seated on a stool reaching up to the knees and touching his throat with an eranda stalk— to vomit.
One should administer two [applications] on the sides of a person who vomits from the forehead.
(21) The symptoms of one who has vomited poorly are salivation, a sense of constriction in the heart, skin eruptions, and itching; these arise from improper vomiting. (22)
The symptoms of excessive vomiting are as follows: thirst, hiccups, belching, loss of consciousness,
protrusion of the tongue, retraction of the eyes, and clenching of the jaw.
Vomiting of blood, spitting, and pain in the throat arise.
(23) Regarding the treatment for diseases produced by excessive vomiting: if there is indeed an excess of vomiting, one should administer mild purgation. (24)
When the tongue has entered deep during vomiting,
gargling with pleasant, unctuous, sour, and salty substances, or with ghee, milk, and meat-broths, is beneficial. Furthermore, other men should eat sour fruits in front of him.
Once it has emerged, one should apply a paste of sesame and grapes and then insert it back.
When the eye has turned outward, one should lubricate it with ghee and press it slowly and gradually.
For jaw-lock (hanumokṣa), fomentation is prescribed, as well as nasal medication that removes phlegm and wind.

One should treat vomiting of blood according to the procedure for *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorders), administering a churned drink (*mantha*) made with the juice of *dhātrī* (myrobalan), *añjana*, *uśīra*, parched rice (*lāja*), and water infused with *candana*,
mixed with ghee, honey, and sugar. 28.

By this, thirst and other afflictions arising from vomiting are pacified. (29) The signs of one who has vomited properly are the cleansing of the heart, throat, and head, as well as a stimulated digestive fire and lightness of body.

The destruction of *kapha* and *pitta*, as well as the proper conduct of one who has vomited correctly, [should be observed]. Then, in the afternoon, wholesome foods for the one who has vomited— such as *mudga* beans, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, and *śāli* rice— should be given to one whose digestive fire is kindled.
One should prepare a soup with heart-pleasing meat juices from wild animals and have him eat it.
When his vomiting has been well-controlled,
there may still be drowsiness, sleepiness, foul odor, itching, and disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī).
For one who has properly vomited, these never cause any affliction: unwholesome food, indigestion, cold water, physical exercise, and likewise sexual intercourse. (32)
A wise person should avoid oil massage and [excessive] provocation for one day.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Procedure for Emetic Therapy," in the Uttarakhanda of the Shri Sharngadharasamhita. Now begins the procedure for purgative therapy.
Now begins the fourth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Purgation.
Regarding the subject of purgation:
one should administer a proper purgative to a person who has been oleated, sudated, and has undergone emesis. (1)
If purgation is administered without prior emesis, the defects of purgation occur;
moreover, in one who has not vomited, the phlegm (kapha) displaced downward may cover the duodenum (grahaṇī), causing weak digestion, heaviness, or dysentery (pravāhikā).
Alternatively, one should digest undigested phlegm (balāsa) with digestive (pācana) remedies;
for one who has been oleated, oleation should be administered; for one who has been sweated, purgation (recana) should be given after sweating.
This is the time for purgation.
In the autumn and spring seasons, one should administer purgation for the purification of the body;
at other times, during an emergency, the wise person should practice purification. Purgation is the best method for the destruction of the *doṣas*.

The doshas that have been conquered by fasting and digestive treatments may sometimes become aggravated again; however, for those that have been purified by cleansing therapies, there is no recurrence. These are the diseases for which purgation is indicated.

One should employ purgation in cases of pitta, as well as in diseases arising from āma, in abdominal enlargement (udara), and especially in flatulence (ādhmāna) for the purpose of cleansing the digestive tract (koṣṭha). [Now follow] those persons who are unfit for purgation.
The child, the elderly, those who are excessively unctuous, those emaciated by chest wounds, those overcome by fear, the fatigued, those afflicted by thirst, the obese, the pregnant woman,
one suffering from acute fever, a woman who has recently given birth, and those with weak digestion or alcoholism [should avoid excessive unctuousness].
One afflicted by a foreign body (śalya) or one who is emaciated and harsh should not be given purgatives by a wise physician.

Those persons who are fit for purgation include: one suffering from chronic fever (jīrṇajvarin), one affected by poison (garavyāpta), one with gout (vātaraktin), and one with fistula-in-ano (bhagandarin).
Those afflicted by hemorrhoids, anemia, abdominal enlargements, tumors, heart disease, and jaundice;
those suffering from vaginal disorders, urinary diseases, abdominal lumps, splenic disorders, and ulcers;
and those afflicted by abscesses, vomiting, eruptive skin lesions, cholera, and leprosy—[should take this].

Men afflicted with diseases of the ears, nose, head, mouth, anus, or penis; those suffering from splenic enlargement, swelling, or eye diseases; those emaciated by worms or afflicted by Vāta; those with colic or urinary obstruction—these persons are considered fit for purgation.
Regarding the classifications of the digestive tract (koṣṭha) for the purpose of purgation: one with a predominance of pitta has a soft bowel; one with a predominance of phlegm has a medium bowel;
and one with a predominance of wind is said to have a hard bowel, which is difficult to purge. 12
The instruction on the dosage of purgatives according to the nature of the digestive tract:

a mild dose is prescribed for a mild digestive tract, a moderate dose for a moderate digestive tract, and a sharp dose is considered appropriate for a harsh digestive tract, using substances that are mild, moderate, or sharp respectively. (13)
Instruction on mild and other types of purgative substances:
one is purged even by mild drugs such as *arka*, *kṣāra*, milk, and *cañcu* oil;
those of moderate strength are purged by *trivṛt*, *tiktā*, and *rājavṛkṣa*.
The cruel [purgative] consists of the latex of *snuk* (euphorbia) along with the fruits of *hemakṣīra*, *dantī*, and others.
Regarding the prescription of the dosage according to the number of purgations:
the highest dose for purgation consists of thirty urges that end with the expulsion of *kapha*.
Those with twenty urges are called medium, while those with ten urges are said to be inferior.
(15) Regarding the dosage of decoctions and other preparations for purgation:
two palas is declared the best, and one pala is the medium.
In the latter half of the day, a *karṣa* of decoctions (*kaṣāya*) constitutes the mildest purgative (16).

For medicinal pastes (*kalka*), boluses (*modaka*), and powders (*cūrṇa*), the dose is one *karṣa* when taken with honey, ghee, or as a linctus; however, it may be two *karṣas* or even a *pala*, depending on the patient's age, disease, and other factors (17).
The administration of purgative medicines should be determined according to the state of the digestive tract (koṣṭha).
In cases where pitta is predominant, one should drink the powder of trivṛt with a decoction of drākṣā and other such liquids;
one afflicted by kapha should drink vyoṣa with a decoction of triphalā and cow’s urine. (18)

A person afflicted by Vāta should drink the powder of Trivṛt, Saindhava, and Śuṇṭhī with sour liquids or with the meat-broth of wild animals for the purpose of purgation. (19) This is the application of castor oil.
Castor oil, taken with double the quantity of a decoction of triphalā or with milk, causes purgation before long.
These are the six formulations for purgation, applied sequentially during the six seasons beginning with the rainy season.

Trivṛt, kuṭaja seeds, pippalī, and viśvabheṣaja (ginger), along with drākṣā juice and honey, constitute a purgative for the rainy season. Trivṛt, durālabhā, mustā, sugar, udīcya, and candana [are also used]. 21–22.

At the end of the rainy season, one should drink cold water boiled with *drākṣā* (grapes) and *yaṣṭīmadhu* (liquorice); in the winter, one should drink the powder of *trivṛt*, *citraka*, *pāṭhā*, *ajājī*, *saralā*, *vacā*, and *hemakṣīrī* with warm water.
One should lick long pepper, ginger, rock salt, black turpeth, and trivṛt together with honey during the cold season and spring as a purgative;
in the summer season, equal parts of trivṛt and sugar serve as a purgative.
A purgative formulation suitable for all seasons:
having powdered *trivṛt*, *hapuṣā*, *dantī*, *saptalā*, *kaṭurohiṇī*,
and *svarṇakṣīrī*, one should macerate them in cow’s urine for three days.
This *abhayādi-modaka* is a formulation suitable for all seasons; it removes unctuousness and the defects of impurities.
(26) Abhayā, marica, śuṇṭhī, viḍaṅga, and āmalaka. (27)
Long pepper, long pepper root, cinnamon bark, cinnamon leaves, and musta—these should be taken in equal parts; danti should be double that amount;
trivṛt is known to be eight times that; and sugar should be six times [the amount of] these.
Having prepared sweetmeats (modakas) with honey in the measure of one karṣa each,
one should eat them one by one in the morning and drink cold water afterwards; the person will continue to purge as long as they do not consume anything warm.

One should always remain free from restraint in matters of food, drink, and recreation; [this cures] irregular fever, weak digestion, anemia, cough, fistula-in-ano, hemorrhoids, leprosy, abdominal tumors, piles, goiter, vertigo, and abdominal diseases.
It conquers burning sensations, splenic disorders, urinary diseases, consumption, and eye ailments; likewise,
it overcomes wind-related diseases, flatulence, dysuria, urinary calculi, and pains in the back, sides, thighs, hips, calves, and abdomen.
By the constant practice of these, one may destroy gray hairs;
for these are known as the best elixirs, consisting of *abhayā* and *modaka*.
(34) This is the instruction on the procedure to be performed at the conclusion of purgation.
Having drunk the purgative, a person should sprinkle their eyes with cold water,
smell a fragrant scent slightly, and then use betel leaf; remaining in a windless place, one should not suppress natural urges nor sleep.
One should never touch cold water; one should repeatedly drink lukewarm water. (36) The signs of one who has been properly purged:
just as wind carries away phlegm, medicine, and bile after they have been vomited, so should [the doshas] be expelled.
By means of purgation, impurities, bile, and phlegm likewise pass out along with the medicine. (37) The signs of insufficient purgation:
stiffness of the umbilical region and pain in the abdomen in one who has been insufficiently purged.
In one who has been inadequately purged, obstruction of feces and flatus, itching, circular patches, heaviness, burning sensation, loss of appetite, flatulence, vertigo, and vomiting arise.
(38) This is the treatment for inadequate purgation.

Furthermore, having cooked that [oil] with digestive (pācana) and unctuous (sneha) substances, one should administer an unctuous enema and then purge; by this, his complications subside, the digestive fire becomes kindled, and lightness is attained. (39) These are the signs of one who has been excessively purged.

From excessive purgation, fainting and prolapse of the rectum may occur (40). There may be colic and an excess of phlegm; blood resembling the washings of meat, or like fat, or appearing like water, is also purged out (41).
Regarding the treatment for one who has been excessively purged:
having sprinkled his body with cold water and rice-water mixed with honey, one should likewise induce a mild emesis with other cold substances. 42
In that regard, an application to the navel of a paste made from mango bark ground with either curd or *sauvīraka* vinegar cures even severe diarrhea by means of this navel-ointment. 43
In that regard, the dietary regimen consists of goat's milk or meat broth from birds or deer; one should feed [the patient] sparingly with *śāli* rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, or even lentils. 44
In that case, the physician should employ another method: he should effect a consolidation [of the humors] with cooling and astringent substances.
This is the characteristic of one who has been well-purged.

When there is lightness, satisfaction of the mind, and the downward movement of the wind (vāyu), one should recognize that the person has been well-purged by emetics; then, at night, one should have them drink a digestive (pācana) decoction. This is the fruit of purgation.

Through the practice of purgation (virecana), there arises strength of the senses, clarity of the intellect, stimulation of the digestive fire, stability of the bodily constituents (dhātus), and stability of youth. 47.
Prohibited acts regarding purgation:
One who has undergone purgation should not resort to exposure to strong winds, cold water, oil massages, indigestion, physical exercise, or sexual intercourse (48).
For the sake of what is wholesome for one who has been purged, substances such as thin gruel (*peyā*) and others [should be used].

One should feed [the patient] gruel prepared with *śāli*, *ṣaṣṭika*, mung beans, and other grains; or rice (*śālyodana*) is beneficial when served with the meat broths of wild animals or gallinaceous birds. (49) Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Purgation," in the Uttarakhanda of the *Śrī Śārṅgadharasaṃhitā*.
The Procedure for Oleaginous Enemas (Snehabasti-vidhi).
Now begins the fifth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Enemas" (Basti-vidhi),
concerning the classification and etymology of the enema.
Enema (basti) is of two kinds: that called oil enema (anuvāsa) and thereafter the decoction enema (nirūha).
It is known as basti because it is administered by means of a bladder (vasti). [This concludes] the definition of the oil enema and the decoction enema.
That which is administered with unctuous substances (snehas) is called *anuvāsana*; that which is administered with decoctions (*kaṣāya*), milk, or oils is declared to be *nirūha*.
This is the sequence for the *bastis*, beginning with *anuvāsana*.
Among those, that which is called the *anuvasana* enema is described here first; thereafter, the enema known as *nirūha* will follow,
and after the *nirūha*, there shall be the enema named *uttara*.
The specific type of non-unctuous enema (anuvāsana) is declared to be the measured enema (mātrābasti). In the measured enema,
the quantity of oil should be two palas, or it may even be half of that.
People who are fit for non-unctuous enemas (anuvāsana) are as follows: one who is dry, one with a sharp digestive fire, and one afflicted by vata alone;
such persons are suitable for non-unctuous enemas.
One suffering from leprosy (kuṣṭha), urinary disorders (meha), obesity, or abdominal enlargement (udara) should not be given an unctuous enema (anuvāsya).

Those afflicted by indigestion (ajīrṇa), insanity (unmāda), thirst (tṛṣ), grief (śoka), fainting (mūrchā), anorexia (aruci), fear (bhaya), dyspnea (śvāsa), cough (kāsa), or consumption (kṣaya) should neither be given a non-unctuous enema (āsthāpya) nor an unctuous enema.
Regarding the materials for making the enema nozzle:
the nozzle should be fashioned from metals such as gold, or from trees, bamboo, reeds, ivory, the tips of horns, or gems. (8)
The differences in the measurement of the eyes according to the divisions of lifespan are as follows:
from one year up to six years, the measurement is six finger-breadths;
from there up to twelve years, the measurement should be eight finger-breadths.
Beyond that, the length of the nozzle is twelve finger-breadths (9).
The measurement of the opening of the bladder-nozzle is as follows:
the opening may be like the hole of a mung bean, like a pea, or like the size of a jujube stone.
The nozzle should be smooth and shaped like a cow’s tail according to the respective measurements;
it is prescribed to be thick at the base with the size of the patient’s thumb, while its circumference at the tip is that of the little finger, ending in a globular opening.
At its base, two pericarp-like structures (*karṇikā*) should be made from the fourth part [of the width];
there, one should attach the bladder according to the two methods of binding. 12.
Specification of the substances to be used for the bladder pouch (*bastipuṭaka*).

The bladder may be made from the urine-bladder of a deer, goat, boar, cow, or even a buffalo; in the absence of these, one made from skin is suitable—a bladder that is well-dyed with decoctions, very soft, unctuous, and firm is beneficial. (13)
Regarding the characteristics of the ulcer-cleansing enema (vraṇabasti):
its nozzle should be eight finger-breadths in length, with an aperture the size of a mung bean, and its circumference should be equal to that of a tube made from a vulture’s wing feather. 14.

When properly administered, the enema (basti), through its qualities of using appropriate substances, brings about the nourishment of the body, complexion, strength, health, and the full increase of lifespan. 15

Instruction on the appropriate timing for enema therapy: An oil enema (snehabasti) should be administered during the day in the cold season and spring; whereas an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) should be given at night during the summer, the rainy season, and autumn. 16.
Regarding the rules for eating at the time of administering an enema:
one should not administer an oil enema (anuvāsana) after having the patient eat food that is excessively unctuous.
[Verse 17] The result of administering an enema when the dietary regimen is contrary [to these rules].
If unctuous therapy (sneha) is administered in two ways—either insufficiently or excessively—it may produce intoxication (mada) and fainting (mūrchā).
If it is given to one who has eaten very dry food, strength and complexion are diminished. There is a prohibition against administering an enema (vasti) that is either deficient or excessive in dose.
Both enemas that are deficient in dose are considered ineffective;
likewise, those that are excessive in dose cause abdominal distension, exhaustion, and diarrhea. (19) [The dosage of the enema]

The appropriate dose for an oil enema (anuvāsana) is six palas for a superior patient, three palas for a middling one, and reduced by half a pala for an inferior one; in this oil enema, the quantity of rock salt (saindhava) and śatāhvā powder to be added is as follows.
A powder of *śatāhvā* and rock salt (*saindhava*) should be added to the oil; its dosage is classified as superior, middling, and inferior, consisting of six, four, and two *māṣakas* respectively.
This is the rule for administering an unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*) immediately after a purgative (*virecana*).
When seven nights have passed since the purgation and the patient has regained strength and begun to eat solid food, an oil enema (anuvāsana) should be administered as an unctuous enema.
This is the procedure for the application of enemas.
Then, having anointed the patient well, having fomented him with warm water,

and having fed him according to the scriptures, one should subsequently have him perform gentle walking exercises; once his flatus, feces, and urine have been evacuated, one should administer an unctuous enema (sneha-basti).

While the patient is asleep on his left side, with the left leg extended and the other leg flexed, one should apply the nozzle to the lubricated rectum; having secured the opening of the enema bag, one should hold it steady with the left hand using straps.
The wise physician should press [the bladder] with the right hand using moderate force.
At the time of administering an enema, one should not perform yawning, coughing, or sneezing.
(26) This is the instruction regarding the timing for pressing the enema.

A period of time measuring thirty mātrās is prescribed for the pressing of the enema bag; thereafter, once the oil has been introduced, the patient should remain lying on his back while reciting a hundred verses.
This is the definition of a *mātrā*.

Wrapping around the kneecap while accompanied by a snap of the fingers constitutes one *mātrā*; this is the settled rule for all cases. (28) This is the procedure following the application of the enema and the subsequent treatment of the body.
With all his limbs extended, he crawls according to his strength;
one should strike him gently three times with the palms of the hands.
Then, in the same manner, one should strike his buttocks and hips, and thereafter lift him up from the bed.
Once the procedure has been performed, one should then sleep as comfortably as possible.
The characteristic of one who has been properly oleated is that the unctuous substance, along with the flatus and feces, is expelled.

If there are no complications, he has been properly administered the unctuous enema quickly; once the oil has returned, the regimen for when food is digested is as follows: in the evening, when the oil has returned again, [the procedure is repeated].

If a person has a stimulated digestive fire, one may at will feed them light food. As for the remedy for complications arising from an oil enema (anuvāsana), lukewarm water should be given to the patient on the following day.

Alternatively, a decoction of coriander and dry ginger destroys complications arising from the improper administration of oleation (sneha). Regarding the number of enemas (basti) to be administered according to the specific doshas:
by this method, six, seven, eight, or even nine may be given.
Enema treatments should be administered to them, and at the conclusion of these, a non-unctuous enema (nirūhaṇa) should also be given.
Regarding the number of unctuous enemas (snehavasti) and their benefits:
the first enema that has been administered provides oleation to the bladder and the groin region.
The second [type of] correctly administered [breath control] conquers the wind located in the head;
the third, when employed, generates strength and complexion;
and the fourth and fifth, when administered, lubricate the lymph-chyle and the blood.
The sixth [day] oleates the flesh, the seventh the fat alone,
and the eighth and ninth likewise the marrow in due order;
thus, one who is twice-born should properly treat the defects residing in the semen.
He who employs eighteen sets of eighteen enemas will possess the strength of an elephant, conquer even a horse, and become equal in splendor to the immortals.
For one who is dry and has an excess of wind, an oil enema (snehabasti) should be administered day after day.

The physician should administer [therapies] for others in such a way as to remove other afflictions. (39) For those who are dry, a small dose of unctuous substance over a long period is without harm; likewise, a small dose of non-unctuous enema is recommended for those who are already unctuous. (40)
The procedure to be performed when the oil administered by enema returns immediately, or when the oil exits as a pure liquid at that time:
another [dose] should be given to such a person, for [the oil] does not remain if it does not become viscous. 41
Regarding the complications arising when the oil of an anuvāsana enema does not flow out, and their treatment:
When the oil, mixed with impurities, does not emerge from one who has not been properly cleansed, then laxity, flatulence, colic, and dyspnea arise. (42)

If there is heaviness in the colon (pakvāśaya), one should administer a strong non-unctuous enema (nirūhaṇa) combined with sharp medicinal substances; likewise, suppositories made from *āphala* are beneficial, so that the wind, waste matter, and unctuousness are restored to their natural downward movement.
Likewise, one should administer a strong purgative, and a sharp nasal medication (nasya) is also recommended.
Even when a fatty enema (snehabasti) has not been expelled, one should perform the necessary actions to prevent complications; for a retained fatty enema may cause adverse effects.
Whether it be large or small, if the oil remains due to dryness (raukṣya), it should be disregarded by the wise.
If the oil has not been eliminated after a day and night, there is a remedy;
however, if the oil has not returned even after a day and night, one should remove it with purificatory (saṃśodhana) measures.
If the unctuous enema (snehabasti) has not taken effect, no other unctuous substance is prescribed;
for the purpose of an oil enema (anuvāsana), one should use the oil of *guḍūcī* and other ingredients:
*guḍūcī*, castor, *pūtīka*, *bhārgī*, poison, and *rohiṣa*.
One pala each of śatāvarī, sahacara, and kākanāsā;
one prasṛta each of barley, māṣa, atasī, kola, and kulattha—having boiled these in four droṇas of water until one droṇa remains, and with that decoction... 47–48.

One should cook one āḍhaka of oil with one pala each of the life-promoting (jīvanīya) drugs as a paste; this is indeed an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) that cures all disorders of vāta. This concludes the instruction on the number of complications arising from the application of enemas (basti) and their treatment.

Seventy-six complications may arise from the administration of enema therapy when it is improperly performed; these should be treated collectively according to the teachings of Suśruta. (50) The regimen of wholesome diet for the oil enema (anuvāsana-basti).

The drinking, eating, and movement, as well as all prohibitions, should be performed exactly as they are for the internal administration of medicated fats (sneha-pāna); there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
(51) Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Oleaginous Enemas (Sneha-basti)," in the Uttarakhanda of the Śrī Śārṅgadhara Saṃhitā.
The Procedure for Nirūha Enema:
Now begins the sixth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Nirūha Enema.
In this regard, he states its classifications:

The nirūha enema is divided into many types according to various causes, and the preeminent sages have assigned names to it based on those very factors. Furthermore, the wise have stated that another name for the nirūha is āsthāpana.
