Establishing the doshas and dhatus in their own natural locations is considered "establishment" (sthāpana). The doses of nirūha enemas, depending on the state of the doshas and other factors, range from one prastha as the minimum to one and a quarter prasthas as the maximum.
A medium dose is specified as one *prastha*, while for a low dose, three *kuḍavas* are prescribed.

(3) Persons unfit for the non-unctuous enema (*āsthāpana-basti*) are those with excessively unctuous constitutions, those with aggravated *doṣas*, those with chest injuries, and those who are emaciated.
One afflicted by flatulence, vomiting, hiccups, cough, or dyspnea; one suffering from swelling of the anus or diarrhea; one afflicted by cholera or leprosy;
a pregnant woman; one with diabetes mellitus; and one with ascites—these should not be subjected to non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana).
Persons suitable for non-unctuous enemas (nirūhaṇa-basti) are those suffering from diseases of Vāta, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), gout (vātāsṛj), irregular fever (viṣamajvara),
fainting (mūrchā), thirst (tṛṣṇā), abdominal distension (udara), flatulence/distension of the bowels (ānāha), dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra), and urinary calculi (aśmarī).

A wise physician should administer a non-unctuous enema (nirūhaṇa) according to the prescribed rules in cases of menorrhagia, weak digestion, urinary disorders (prameha), colic, acid gastritis (amlapitta), and heart disease.
This is the procedure for administering a nirūha-basti.
After the patient has voided flatus, feces, and urine, and has been treated with oleation and sudation but not yet fed,
the wise physician should administer a *nirūha* enema at midday inside the house according to the appropriate procedure, following the method prescribed for an oil enema (*snehabasti*).
Once the non-unctuous enema (nirūha) has been administered,
the patient should then sit in a squatting posture (utkaṭaka-āsana) for about a muhūrta, remaining there with the desire for the nirūha to come out.
If the nirūha does not emerge after a muhūrta, one should expel it by means of purificatory (śodhana) measures.
The wise physician should administer non-unctuous enemas (nirūhas) containing alkali, urine, sour substances, and rock salt.
The signs of a well-administered enema are those in which feces,
bile, phlegm, and flatus pass out in succession.
Lightness also arises; one should designate that as a well-administered non-unctuous enema (sunirūha).
As for the characteristics of a poorly administered enema (durnirūḍha):
the enema (vasti) occurs with very slight frequency, and the feces and flatus are deficient.
One should designate that as a difficult non-unctuous enema (durnirūha) which causes fainting, pain, stupor, and anorexia.
This is the instruction regarding the procedure for administering a non-unctuous enema;
one who knows how to administer enemas should employ the non-unctuous enema according to this method.
The second, third, or fourth meal, as appropriate, follows this sequence:
for one afflicted by bile, phlegm, and wind, [the diet] proceeds respectively with milk, vegetable broth, and meat broth.
After having the patient fed with a non-unctuous enema (nirūha), one should then administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana).
People who are suitable for mild enemas— such as the delicate, the elderly, and the young— benefit from a mild treatment.
If a sharp enema is administered to them, it may destroy their strength and lifespan.
Regarding the instruction on the timing for the administration of enemas such as the *utkleśana* (provocative) and others:
one should first administer the *utkleśana* enema, and thereafter the *doṣahara* (purificatory) enema in the middle.

Thereafter, the wise physician should administer a pacifying enema (saṃśamanīya-basti). The substances for the enema that induce nausea (utkleśana) are castor seeds, licorice, long pepper, rock salt, and sweet flag.
A decoction enema (basti) made from the paste of *hapuṣā* fruit is known to cause excitation of the doshas.
The substances for a dosha-eliminating enema are *śatāhvā*,
*madhuka*, *bilva*, and the fruit of *kauṭaja*.
An enema containing sour gruel (kāñjika) and cow’s urine is known to remove the [bodily] humors (doṣa).
The substances for pacifying enemas (śamana-basti) are priyaṅgu,
madhuka, mustā, and likewise rasāñjana.
An enema containing milk is recommended and is known to pacify the doṣas.
This is the procedure for the purificatory enema (śodhana-basti),
prepared with decoctions of purifying substances, their pastes, fats, and rock salt.
Enemas churned with a churning-stick (khaja) according to the prescribed method are known as purificatory (śodhana).
The substances for scraping enemas (lekhanabasti) consist of a decoction of triphalā combined with cow’s urine, honey, and alkali.
Enemas prepared with additives such as ūṣaka and others are known as scraping (lekhanā) enemas.
Enema substances for nourishing (bṛṃhaṇa) consist of decoctions and pastes of nourishing drugs combined with those of the sweet (madhura) group.
Enemas (bastis) containing ghee and meat broth are known as nourishing (bṛṃhaṇa).
The substances for slimy enemas (picchila-basti) include jujube (badarī), airāvatī, śelu, śālmalī, dhanvana, and ginger (nāgara).
Those prepared with milk and mixed with honey are known by the name Picchila;
they should be administered by the wise along with the blood of goats, sheep, and deer.
The dosage for Picchila enemas is considered to be twelve palas.
Regarding the prescription of substances for the purpose of a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) according to their measurements:
having first administered one akṣa of rock salt and two prasṛtas of honey, and having stirred them together, one should then add three prasṛtas of unctuous substance (sneha). 25.
Then, when the oil has become unified, one should add one *prasṛta* of paste;
once it has thickened, the physician skilled in his craft should add a decoction measuring four *prasṛtas*, stir it thoroughly, and administer the non-unctuous enema (*nirūha*).
In the case of Vāta, one should add four palas of honey and six palas of unctuous substance (sneha).
In the case of Pitta, one should add four palas of honey and three palas of sneha.
And in the case of Kapha, one should add six palas of honey and four palas of sneha.
The procedure for the Madhutailika enema:
eight *palas* of honey and oil, with an equal portion of castor-plant decoction,
combined with half a *pala* of *śatapuṣpā* and half a *pala* of rock salt.

This enema, known as *madhutailika*, when stirred with a churning-stick, destroys fat-tumors (*medogulma*), worms, splenic disorders, impurities, and upward movement of gases (*udāvarta*); it bestows strength and complexion, is aphrodisiac, and acts as a digestive stimulant and nourisher. (30–31)
The procedure for the digestive (dīpana) enema:
one prasṛta each of honey, ghee, milk, and oil should be used;
with an addition of one akṣa each of hapuṣā and rock salt, this enema is an excellent stimulant of digestion. 32
The procedure for the Yuktaratha enema:
A decoction of castor root with honey, oil, rock salt, vacha, pippali, and madana fruit—this is the Yuktaratha enema. (33)
The procedure for the Siddha-basti is as follows: a decoction of the five roots (pañcamūla), oil, Māgadhikā, honey, rock salt, and Madhuka—this is known as the Siddha-basti. 34.

One should follow the regimen of wholesome and unwholesome foods, bathe with warm water, and avoid sleeping during the day and indigestion; one should avoid everything else and practice [the remaining measures] as in the case of an oil enema (snehabasti). 35.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Nirūha-basti," in the Uttarakhanda of the Śrīśārṅgadharasaṃhitā.
Now begins the seventh chapter, titled "The Procedure for Uttarabasti."
In this regard, I shall first describe the nature of the uttarabasti; hereafter I will explain the enema known as uttara.
Its nozzle should be twelve finger-breadths long, with a constriction (karṇika) fashioned in the middle.
The opening [of the nozzle] should resemble the stalk of a *mālatī* flower, and the aperture should be like a mustard seed.
For those aged twenty-five years, the dose of oil for the urethral enema (*uttarabasti*) is two *karṣas*. Below that age, the dose is two *karṣas*.
Beyond that, the best of physicians have stated that the quantity of oil should be one *pala*.
Now follows the procedure for the urethral enema (*uttarabasti*): for one who has been purified by the non-unctuous enema (*āsthāpana*), is satiated, and has performed bathing and eating.
While standing on a seat that reaches up to the knees, one should search for the opening of the penis with a smooth probe and then slowly insert the nozzle,
which has been smeared with ghee, into the urethral opening to a depth of six finger-breadths.
Then one should press the enema bag and slowly withdraw the nozzle;
once the oil has returned, the procedure for an oil enema (snehabasti) is beneficial.
This is the method for administering enemas to women.
One should make the nozzle for women as thick as the little finger and ten fingers long;
it should be joined with an opening the size of a mudga bean, four fingers deep inside the vagina,
and one should employ a fine nozzle two fingers deep in the urinary passage.
The procedure for administering an enema to children:
In cases of urinary disorders such as dysuria, a wise physician should gently and steadily insert a fine nozzle into the child to a depth of one finger-breadth.
The quantity of oil for women and children in the vaginal canal is two *pālikas*; in the urinary tract, it is one *palam* for women and two *karṣas* for children. (9)
The method for administering the urethral enema (uttara-vasti) to women:
A wise physician should administer it to a woman lying on her back with her knees raised, provided that the enema known as *uttara-vasti* does not return. 10.
Furthermore, the physician should administer a vaginal enema (basti) with groups of purifying substances,
or he should insert a firm medicinal suppository (phalavarti) into the vaginal canal,
fashioned from threads, lubricated, and composed of purifying ingredients.
Likewise, when the bladder is being burned, the expert physician should administer an enema with a decoction of milk-yielding trees or with cold milk;
this enema cures seminal disorders in men and pain arising from the menses in women.
The urethral enema (uttarabasti), however, should never be administered to those suffering from urinary disorders (mehin).
[This section covers] the benefits and defects of the urethral enema, the signs of its correct administration, complications, and the sequence of treatment.
The characteristics of the *phalavarti* (medicated suppository) for one designated as having a "bladder-like" (*basti*) upward movement are the same as those for an oil enema (*snehabasti*).
It should be smooth, similar in size to one's own thumb, and inserted into the anus after it has been lubricated with clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
The wick that causes the impurity to flow is known as the *phalavartī*.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Upper Enema (*uttarabasti*)," in the Uttarakhanda of the *Śrī Śārṅgadharasaṃhitā*;
[followed by] the procedure for nasal therapy (*nasyavidhi*).
Now begins the eighth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Nasal Administration" (Nasyavidhi).
Regarding that, the etymology and definition of *nasya* are stated by the wise: it is that medicinal substance which is to be taken through the nose.
Nāvana and nasyakarma are considered its two names. Regarding the classifications of nasya:
the classification of nasya is said to be twofold, namely recana (purificatory) and snehana (oleating).
Recana (evacuation) is declared to be karṣaṇa (depleting), while snehana (oleation) is considered to be bṛṃhaṇa (nourishing).
The proper time for the administration of nasal therapy (nasya-karma) is during the forenoon, midday, and afternoon, respectively, for the destruction of kapha, pitta, and vāyu.
Nasal medication (nasya) should be administered during the day, or even at night if the disease is severe.
Those who are unfit for nasal medication include pregnant women;
one should also avoid nasal medication after eating, on cloudy days, or when there has been insufficient fasting.
Likewise, one suffering from acute catarrh, a pregnant woman, one poisoned by another,
one with indigestion, one who has received an enema, one who has drunk oil, water, or fermented liquor,
one who is angry, one overcome by grief, one afflicted by thirst, and the elderly or the young.
One who suppresses natural urges, one who has already bathed, and one who intends to bathe should avoid [nasal therapy].
One should perform the procedure of nasal therapy for a child who is eight years old, regardless of whether they are fit or unfit for it.
After eighty years of age, nasal drops (nāvana) are never to be administered. Furthermore,
purgative nasal therapy (virecana-nasya) should be employed using extremely sharp oils.
Or, with unctuous substances (snehas), decoctions, or meat broths prepared with sharp medicinal drugs,
the dosage for nasal administration (nasya) as a head-purgative (śirovirecana) is eight, six, or four drops in each nostril.
In each exhalation, [the breath] should be joined with the primary, middle, and final measures.
Regarding the dosage of medicine for nasal therapy (nasya-karman):
for nasal therapy, one *śāṇa* of sharp medicine should be administered.

One should take a measure of *hiṅgu* (asafetida), one *māṣa* of rock salt (*saindhava*), eight *śāṇas* of milk, and three *karṣas* of water; one should employ one *karṣa* of sweet substance for the administration of nasal therapy (*nasyakarma*). 9–10.

The varieties of *śirovirecana* (head-purgation) and *nasya* (nasal therapy) are as follows: *avapīḍa* and *pradhamana* are recorded as two other varieties; these two should be administered here according to their respective indications. (11)

The nature of *avapīḍana* (pressed-out extract) and *nasya* (nasal medication): the juice extracted by pressing medicinal substances such as pastes (*kalka*) and the like is designated as *avapīḍa*; it is produced from sharp (*tīkṣṇa*) substances. (12)
The nature of blowing-nose therapy (*pradhamanana*) is as follows:

a tube (*nāḍī*) six finger-breadths long and having two bends should be used to blow medicinal powder through it; using sharp [powder] in the measure of a jujube fruit (*kola*), blown by means of the breath from the mouth—that indeed is *pradhamana*. 13.
Persons who are fit for recana and nasya [therapies] are those suffering from diseases above the clavicle caused by kapha, loss of voice, anorexia,
coryza, headache, and chronic rhinitis.

In cases of swelling, epilepsy, and skin diseases, purgative nasal therapy (virecana-nasya) is beneficial. (14) People suitable for oleaginous nasal therapy (sneha-nasya) include those who are timid, women, the emaciated, and children; for them, nasal therapy is administered with unctuous substances. (15)

Persons who are fit for the administration of *avapīḍana* (nasal drops) include those suffering from throat diseases, *sannipāta* disorders, sleepiness, intermittent fevers (*viṣamajvara*), mental afflictions, and parasitic infestations; in these cases, *avapīḍana* is employed. 16.

People who are suitable for insufflation (pradhamana-nasya) are those with extremely aggravated doshas and those who have lost consciousness; the powder is administered as an insufflation by the wise, because it is indeed more potent. 17.
Now, some formulations for avapīḍana and pradhamana:
Nasya (nasal medication) should be prepared from jaggery and dry ginger, or from long pepper and rock salt, ground with water; by that, diseases of the eyes, ears, nose, and head are cured. (18)

Those [afflictions] arising from the neck, throat, and chest, as well as those born on the back of the arms, are destroyed by this nasal medication (nasya) made from the pith of *madhūka* and the others;
[specifically] with the pith of *madhūka*, black pepper (*kṛṣṇā*), *vacā*, black pepper, and rock salt (*saindhava*). 19. Madhūkasārādinasyam. *Madhūkasārakṛṣṇābhyāṃ vacāmaricasaindhavaiḥ*.
One should administer nasal drops (nasya) ground with lukewarm water to restore consciousness in cases of epilepsy,
insanity, *sannipāta*, and *apatantraka*; likewise,
a nasal drop consisting of rock salt (*saindhava*) and other ingredients is used for excessive drowsiness (*tandrā*).
Saindhava salt, white pepper, mustard seeds, and kuṣṭha,
ground with goat’s urine and used as a nasal drop (nasya), removes drowsiness.
In that same context, there is also the inhalation therapy (pradhamana-nasya) using black pepper and other ingredients.

Rock salt (*saindhava*), *vacā*, black pepper (*marica*), long pepper (*pippalī*), ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), *kaṅkola*, garlic (*laśuna*), and *kaṭphala*— this powder, processed with the bile of a rohita fish, should be administered as a nasal insufflation (*pradhamana*) by the wise. (22–23)
The Procedure for Oleaginous Nasal Therapy (Bṛṃhaṇanasya):
Now, the preparation for oleaginous nasal therapy is described;
two types are recognized as oleating: the Marśa and the Pratimarśa. (24)
The primary satiating dose of marrow (marśa) is recorded as eight śāṇas;
the middling is four śāṇas, and the inferior is recorded as one śāṇa.
This dose should be administered by the wise into each nostril individually.

Having observed the strength or weakness of the *doṣas*, the wise physician should administer nasal medication (*nasya*) once every other day or once every two days, either twice or three times a day, for three days,
five days, or seven days, while remaining well-restrained. (26–27)
Various complications are recorded to occur during massage (*marśa*) and head-evacuation (*śirovireka*);
these should be understood as arising respectively from the provocation of the *doṣas* and from depletion (*kṣaya*).
In cases caused by the provocation of the *doṣas*, one should employ purification through emesis (*vamana*).
Now, in conditions caused by wasting (kṣaya), nourishing therapy (bṛṃhaṇa) appropriate to each case is beneficial.
This applies to diseases of the head, nose, and eyes; in sūryāvarta and ardhabhedaka; in dental diseases; when strength is diminished; and in disorders of the neck (manyā), arms, and shoulders.

In cases of dryness of the mouth, ringing in the ears, diseases of vāta and pitta, premature graying of hair, and excessive falling out of the hair on the head and beard, nourishing nasal therapy (nasya) with unctuous substances or sweet juices is indicated. (31)
In that case, saffron ground with sugar and milk, and fried in clarified butter,
when used as a nasal drop (nasya), destroys the pains arising from vāta-rakta. 32.

[One should treat] the eyebrows, temples, eyes, head, ears, sūryāvarta, and ardhabhedaka [with these]; furthermore, there may be another nourishing nasal medication (nasya), or a nasal medication with aṇutaila or nārāyaṇa oil.

Alternatively, one may administer an errhine (nasya) with ghee prepared with black gram (māṣa) and other such substances, processed with the appropriate medicinal drugs according to the specific dosha. Regarding the application of unctuous substances (sneha),
oil should be used for kapha, while muscle fat (vasā) should be used for pure vāta.

One should always administer nasal drops (nasya) of ghee and marrow when pitta is predominant; in cases such as hemiplegia (pakṣāghāta), one should use a nasya of black gram (māṣa) and other ingredients, namely black gram, *ātmaguptā*, *rāsnā*, *balā*, *rubūka*, and *rohiṣa*.
A decoction of *aśvagandhā* prepared with *hiṅgu* and rock salt,

when applied lukewarm as a nasal drop (*nasya*), conquers hemiplegia accompanied by tremors, as well as facial paralysis (*ardita-vāta*), torticollis (*manyā-stambha*), and the *apabāhuka* syndrome. (36–37)
The dosage for the nasal massage (pratimarśa) is determined to be two drops of oil for each nostril. This is the established rule regarding the quantity of the massage. 38.
The characteristic of a *mātrā* consists of a single drop (*bindu*).
When two knots have been submerged in the oil and then withdrawn, that which causes a drop to flow from the index finger is the *mātrā* known as a *bindu*. (39)
Eight drops of this kind are called a *śāṇa*;
that should be given for the *marśana*, while the *pratimarśa* consists of two drops. There are fourteen occasions for the *pratimarśana*.
The wise have declared fourteen occasions for self-reflection:
at dawn, after using the tooth-stick, upon leaving the house, after physical exercise, walking, sexual intercourse, voiding feces or urine, and after applying collyrium.
Pratimarśa is administered at the end of a mouthful of food, at the conclusion of a meal, upon rising from daytime sleep, after vomiting, and likewise in the evening.
This is the characteristic sign of the administration of pratimarśa.

When a slight amount of oil, drawn up by the breath, reaches the mouth, one should know that it has been administered in the quantity prescribed for *pratimarśa* when poured as a nasal drop (*nasya*).
One should not swallow this while drawing it up; rather, having reached the mouth, one should spit it out.

Persons suitable for nasal medication (pratimarśana) are those whose thirst has subsided and who suffer from headache; it is also applied to children and the elderly. By means of nasal medication, diseases of the supraclavicular region are pacified.
There shall be the destruction of wrinkles and graying hair, and strength born of the senses will arise.
(45) For the disease of graying hair, the nasal medication (*nasya*) consists of *bibhītaka*, *nimba*, *gambhārī*, *śivā*, *śelu*, and *kākinī*.
By the application of each oil as a nasal drop (nasya), gray hair is certainly destroyed. (46) Now,
for the purpose of administering the nasal drops, I shall describe the procedure for taking a nasya.
In a place free from wind and dust, having performed the rubbing of the teeth, being purified by the inhalation of medicated smoke, and likewise having the forehead and throat fomented,
the man should lie on his back with his head slightly extended. (47–48)

The two physicians should administer the nasal medication (*nasya*) to one whose hands and feet are firmly supported, whose eyes are covered with a cloth, and whose tip of the nose is slightly raised,
using vessels made of gold, silver, or other metals, with the liquid being lukewarm and poured in an unbroken stream. (Verse 49)
One should administer nasal therapy (nasya) using either a horn, a tube, or a cloth-wick.
At the time of administering nasal therapy, one must avoid sensory objects;
while the nasal drops are being poured, one must not shake the head at all.
One should not become angry, one should not speak [harshly], one should not uproot [the object of affection], and likewise, one should not laugh.
For when affection is governed by these [restraints], it does not reach its end; thus, diseases born of negligence do not arise.
Thereafter, the occurrence of cough, catarrh, headache, or eye disease may arise;
having caused the *śṛṅgāṭaka* (the junction of the nasal passages) to overflow, one should stop [the flow] and not swallow the liquid. This is the measure for administering nasal drops (*nasya*).
There should be five, seven, or ten measures for the retention of the nasal medication (nasya).
After the retention of the nasal medication, the subsequent action to be performed is as follows: having sat down, one should then spit out the liquid that has entered the nose and mouth.
One should spit from the left or right side, but certainly not in front.
After the administration of *nasya*, one should abandon activities that must be avoided;
once the *nasya* has been applied, one should cast off mental distress, passion, and anger.

Having abandoned sleep, a person should lie down on their back and recite a hundred words; likewise, at the conclusion of a purgative (virecana), smoking or gargling is beneficial. (56) [The following is] the three-fold characteristic of nasal therapy (nasya).

Regarding the application of nasal therapy (nasya), three signs have been taught by those who contemplate the scriptures: deficient administration, excessive administration, and [proper] purification; these are specifically the signs of head-purification (śiraḥśuddhi). 57. Sign of Head-Purification.

Lightness of mind, purity, the diminution of diseases in the channels, and clarity of the intellect and senses are the signs of successful purification of the head; [the opposite] are the signs of deficient purification. 58. Signs of deficient purification.
Itching, burning sensations, heaviness, and the discharge of phlegm from the channels are proclaimed as the signs of insufficient purification of the head (59).
The signs of excessive purification are as follows:

When the head is strongly purged, there may be the appearance of brain matter, an increase in wind (*vāta*), confusion of the senses, a sense of emptiness, and even pain in the head; these are the results of insufficient, excessive, or correct purification. 60.
If the head is insufficiently purified, one should apply treatments that subdue *kapha* and *vāta*;
once the head is properly purified, one should administer medicated ghee as a nasal drop (*nasya*). (61) [The symptoms and treatment for one who is excessively oleated.]

Excessive salivation, heaviness of the head, and confusion of the senses are the signs of excessive unctuousness; in that case, one should administer dry (non-unctuous) measures, feed the patient with non-obstructive food, and prescribe the regimen for nasal therapy. 62
The names of the five therapies are emesis, purgation, nasal medication, non-unctuous enema, and unctuous enema; these five therapies have been described by the lords of sages. 63

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Nasal Administration," in the Uttarakhanda of the glorious Śārṅgadharasaṃhitā. Now begins the ninth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Inhalation of Smoke."
Regarding the enumeration of medicinal smokes:
smoke is said to be of six types— namely, pacifying (śamana), nourishing (bṛṃhaṇa), purgative (recana), cough-alleviating (kāsahā), emetic (vāmana), and for fumigating wounds (vraṇadhūpana).

The synonyms for pacification (*śamana*), nourishment (*bṛṃhaṇa*), purgation (*recana*), and medicated smoking (*dhūma*) are as follows: the synonyms for pacification are *madhya* (intermediate) and *prāyogika* (habitual); the synonyms for nourishment are *snehana* (oleating) and *mṛdu* (mild).
The synonyms for *recana* (purgative) are also *śodhana* (cleansing) and *tīkṣṇa* (sharp).
Those persons who are unfit for the inhalation of smoke (*dhūmapāna*)— namely,
those who are exhausted, frightened, or suffering— are indeed those for whom smoke is prohibited.
One who has been administered an enema, one who has undergone purgation, one who has stayed awake at night, one who is thirsty, one suffering from burning sensations, one with dryness of the palate,
one suffering from abdominal diseases, one with headache, one with blurred vision, and one afflicted by vomiting and flatulence— [these should not be treated with emetics].
One with an injured chest, one afflicted by urinary disorders (prameha), one suffering from jaundice (pāṇḍuroga), and a pregnant woman;

one who is dry, one who is emaciated, one who has consumed milk, honey, ghee, or fermented liquors (āsava); one who has just eaten food, curd, or fish, as well as a child, an elderly person, and one who is thin.

The fault of inhaling smoke at the improper time and its remedy: Smoke that is inhaled at the wrong time or in excess causes complications; in such cases, the drinking of ghee, nasal drops (nasya), collyrium (añjana), and eye-salve (tarpaṇa) are desired. 7.
For pacification, one should administer ghee, sugarcane juice, grapes, milk, sugar-water, or even sweet and sour juices.
[This concludes] the proper time for smoking and its benefits.

Smoking (dhūma) should be practiced from the twelfth year until the eightieth; it destroys cough, dyspnea, catarrh, and pain in the neck, jaw, and head, as well as disorders of wind (vāta) and phlegm (śleṣman), when properly administered.
Through the practice of fumigation, a person becomes one whose senses, speech, and mind are serene,
whose hair, teeth, and beard are firm, and whose face is fragrant.
(10) This is the procedure for the smoking pipe.
In that case, the smoke-tube should be divided into three sections and possess three joints;
it should have the circumference of the little finger and a width equal to a *rājamāṣa* bean.
For the pacification of a patient's ailments, the smoke-tube should be long by as many finger-breadths [as the age of the patient].

Likewise, it is considered that for a mild [patient], it should be forty finger-breadths (aṅgulas) long, for a sharp [patient] thirty-two, for one who suppresses cough twenty-four, and sixteen for one who reduces [excess fluids]. For emesis, it should be ten finger-breadths long, and the same applies to a wound-probe (vraṇanāḍikā).

A tube for the inhalation of smoke should be made from a hollow pea-stalk, as thick as a *kalāya* bean and twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) long; one should then smear this reed-like tube very smoothly.
A plaster made from the paste of *dhūmadru* wood is prescribed for a length of eight finger-breadths (15).
Having applied a paste measuring one *karṣa*, one should allow it to dry in the shade; then, carefully removing the stalk, one should prepare a wick soaked in oil with care (16).
Having ignited [the resin] with charcoal and held it at the opening of the eye, one should inhale the smoke through the mouth and expel it through the mouth alone;
then, having inhaled through both nostrils, the wise person should exhale through the mouth alone. 17.17–18a.

Having placed the medicinal paste inside a hollowed-out earthenware bowl and ignited charcoal within it, one should insert the nozzle into the opening and fumigate the ulcer with that very [smoke]. 18.
[The following are] the substances for the various types of pacifying (śamana) and other fumigations.
For pacification, one should administer a paste of cardamom and other ingredients; for mild purgation, resin of *sarja* tree;
and for sharp purgation, a pungent paste that cures cough. For minor ailments, *koṣaṇa* should be used.
For inducing vomiting, one should give sinews, skin, and so forth, as a substance to be inhaled as smoke.
For wounds, fumigation with *nimba*, *vacā*, and other ingredients is highly recommended (20).
Against infantile seizures and similar afflictions, the *aparājita* incense is used;
furthermore, other types of incense should be prepared in the home for the pacification of diseases (21).
Peacock feathers, nimba leaves, the fruit of bṛhatī, black pepper, asafoetida, māṃsī, seeds produced from cotton (22),
goat’s hair, a snake’s slough, and likewise the excrement of a cat—
And that powder of elephant tusk, mixed with a little ghee and offered as incense in the houses, conquers all child-seizing spirits (bālagraha).
Having conquered the piśācas and rākṣasas, it shall become a remover of all fevers.

In the administration of medicinal smoking (dhūmapāna), eye-salves and other ophthalmic substances are beneficial; however, regarding the inhalation of smoke, one should observe the same precautions as for purgative nasal therapy (recananasya).
It is said that eyes are produced from the bodily elements (dhātu), as well as from substances such as lac and bamboo. 25.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Inhaling Medicinal Smoke," in the Uttarakhanda of the venerable Śārṅgadharasaṃhitā.
Now begins the tenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Gargling, Holding in the Mouth, and Rubbing with Medicinal Powders."
Regarding the distinction between *gaṇḍūṣa* (mouthful) and *kavala* (gargle):
there are four types of *gaṇḍūṣa*, namely oleating (*snaihika*), pacifying (*śamana*), purifying (*śodhana*), and healing (*ropaṇa*); *kavala* is likewise of these same four kinds.
The types of its classifications are as follows:
in Vata, it is oleating with unctuous and hot substances; in Pitta, it is pacifying with sweet and cold substances;
and in Kapha, it is purificatory with pungent, sour, salty, and hot substances.
A gargle (gaṇḍūṣa) and a mouthful (kavala), which are of four types— bitter, astringent, sweet, and slightly warm— are declared to be healing for ulcers.
[Now follows] the definition of the gargle and the mouthful.
When the mouth is full, it is called *asañcārī*; a *gaṇḍūṣa* (mouthful) is mobile, while a *kavala* (bolus) moves about.
Among these, a *gaṇḍūṣa* is known to be used with a liquid, whereas a *kavala* is used with a paste (*kalka*).
This is the medicinal dosage for *gaṇḍūṣa* and *kavala*.
The wise should administer powder in the form of a liquid, a quantity of one kola in a gargle (gaṇḍūṣa), and a paste (kalka) measuring one karṣa for use as a mouth-wash (kavala).
This is the appropriate state for a gargle and the measure for its retention.
Gargles, mouthfuls, and other such treatments should be administered starting from the fifth year of age.
One who is well-positioned, with the forehead and throat area warmed, should perform gargles three, five,
or seven times for the destruction of the *doṣas*.
The retention of gargle-water should continue until the mouth is filled with phlegm, until there is a discharge of the morbid humor, or until there is a flow from the eyes and nose;
for wind (vāta), an unctuous gargle is prescribed.
Oil-cake paste, water, milk, or an unctuous substance are beneficial for oleation; likewise,
a gargle consisting of sesame seeds, blue lotus, ghee, sugar, and milk serves to destroy burning sensations.
A gargle containing honey, held in the jaws and mouth, destroys burning sensations (9).
A honey-gargle for mouth ulcers and similar conditions produces clarity in the mouth and heals oral wounds.

Holding honey in a mouthful (gaṇḍūṣa) pacifies burning and thirst. In cases of burns from poison, alkali, or fire, a mouthful [of honey] should be held; or else, clarified butter or milk should be held in the mouth.
In cases of loose teeth,
a gargle of oil and rock salt is recommended;
in cases of dry mouth and phlegm, a gargle of fermented rice-gruel (kāñjika) is beneficial.

Gargling with *kāñjika* (fermented rice water) overcomes dryness of the mouth and a bad taste; it is beneficial for phlegm when combined with *sindhulavaṇa*, the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), *rājī*, and *ārdraka*.
This gargle destroys phlegm and blood-bile (*raktapitta*).
A gargle of Triphalā with honey destroys Kapha, blood, and Pitta disorders.
A gargle of Dārvī, Guḍūcī, Triphalā, Drākṣā, and the tender leaves of Jātī cures mouth ulcers.
The decoction of *yavāsa* combined with honey in a sixth part,
when held cold in the mouth, destroys facial inflammation (*mukhapāka*) caused by the three *doṣas*.
(15) In procedures such as gargles (*gaṇḍūṣa*), there is mutual identity of the substances.
The wise should know that for whichever medicinal substance a gargle (gaṇḍūṣa) is prescribed, that same substance is to be used for rubbing (pratisāraṇa) and as a mouthful (kavala) as well.
This kavala destroys loss of appetite caused by kapha and vāta.
The filaments of *mātuluṅga* combined with rock salt (*saindhava*) and black pepper (*uṣaṇa*), when used as a gargle (*kavala*),
destroy numbness and anorexia caused by *kapha* and *vāta*.
(17) [This describes the application of a rubbing agent (*pratisāraṇa*).]

The varieties of application for rubbing (pratisāraṇa) consist of three types— paste (kalka), electuary (avaleha), and powder (cūrṇa)— which are applied with the tips of the fingers according to the specific disease of the mouth. 18.
For diseases of the teeth, mouth, and throat, a powder for rubbing (pratisāraṇa-cūrṇa) should consist of kuṣṭha, dārvī, samaṅgā, pāṭhā, tiktā, pītikā,
tejanī, musta, and lodhra; this powder is to be used as a rubbing agent.
It destroys bleeding from the gums, toothache, swelling, and burning sensations.

(19) Defects arising from deficient or excessive application of gargles and similar treatments: from deficient application, there is provocation of kapha, as well as loss of taste perception and anorexia.
From excessive application, there occurs inflammation of the mouth, dryness, thirst, and exhaustion.
(20) The signs of successful gargling are the cleansing of the disease, its reduction, satisfaction, clarity, and lightness of the mouth.
Clarity of the sense organs is the sign of purity in gargling.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Gargling and Other Rinses," in the Uttarakhanda of the Śrī Śārṅgadharasaṃhitā.
[Now follows] the procedure for medicinal pastes, head-massage oils, and ear-drops.
Now begins the eleventh chapter, titled "The Procedure for Application" (Lepavidhi).
The names of application (lepa) and its classifications, as well as the names of topical application (ālepa), are: *lipta*, *lepa*, and *lepana*.
Facial application (mukhalepa) is considered to be of three types: it destroys defects (doṣaghn), neutralizes poison (viṣaha), and improves the complexion (varṇya).
The dosage for this application is of three measures: one-fourth, one-third, or half an aṅgula in thickness.
Fresh [punnāga] is a remover of disease; when dried, it impairs the complexion.
Furthermore, a paste of punarnavā, devadāru, ginger, siddhārtha, and śigru destroys swelling.

A paste made by grinding [the aforementioned substances] with rice-wash water is a remedy that conquers all types of swelling (3). A paste made from the marrow of the *bibhītaka* fruit destroys burning sensations; it is an application that eliminates the pain of burning (4).
For conditions such as erysipelas, swelling, and ulcers, there is this ten-ingredient paste: *śirīṣa*, liquorice (*madhuyaṣṭī*), *tagara*, red sandalwood (*raktacandana*),
cardamom (*elā*), spikenard (*māṃsī*), the two types of turmeric (*niśāyugma*), costus (*kuṣṭha*), and *bālaka*.
Having thus ground these ingredients, this paste— mixed with one-fifth part clarified butter and prepared with water by the wise— is known as *Daśāṅga*.
It conquers erysipelas (*visarpa*), toxic eruptions (*viṣavisphoṭa*), swellings (*śotha*), and malignant ulcers (*duṣṭavraṇa*).
An ointment made from *āruṣkara* destroys swelling;
likewise, an ointment of sesame seeds mixed with goat’s milk and fresh butter destroys swelling caused by *āruṣkara*, or an ointment made from black earth [is effective]. (7)
An insecticide ointment:
an application made from the roots and seeds of *lāṅgalī*, *ativiṣā*, *alābu*, and *jālinī*, ground with rice-water, destroys insect bites and eruptions. (8)
A facial ointment consisting of red sandalwood, mañjiṣṭhā, lodhra, kuṣṭha, priyaṅgu,
banyan sprouts, and lentils removes freckles and bestows radiance upon the face. (9)
Another ointment that produces facial luster consists of *mātuluṅga* root-fiber, clarified butter, realgar, and the juice of cow dung;
this application produces facial luster and conquers pustules, freckles, and discoloration. 10
An ointment of *lodhra*,
*dhānyaka*, and *vacā* removes pimples of youth;
likewise, black pepper combined with *gorocanā* applied as a facial ointment removes them.
An ointment consisting of *siddhārthaka*, *vacā*, *lodhra*, and rock salt is a plaster that removes freckles (*vyaṅga*).
For freckles,
an ointment of *arjuna* bark, or *vaca*, or *mañjiṣṭhā* mixed with honey may also be used.
An ointment of fresh butter or soot from the hoof of a white horse [applied] results in blackness of the face; likewise,
by rubbing with the milk of the *arka* plant and *haridrā*, and applying it as a plaster, the same result is achieved.
The blackness of the face that has arisen over a long period will certainly subside;
in that very context, another ointment consists of the pale leaves of the *vaṭa* tree, *mālatī*, and red sandalwood. 13–14.
One should apply a medicinal paste made from kuṣṭha, kālīyaka, and lodhra; this destroys eruptions of youth, facial freckles, dark spots, and the like.
This is the paste for aruṃṣikā (scaly skin lesions).
An ointment made from old oil-cake (piṇyāka), cow dung, and chicken droppings ground with urine, when applied as a plaster, will quickly destroy aruṃṣikā.
In that same context, another plaster is as follows:
Alternatively, a plaster made from the barks of *khadira*, *ariṣṭa*, and *jambu* combined with urine,
or a plaster of *kuṭaja* bark and rock salt, will destroy *aruṃṣikā*.
This is the plaster for *dāruṇaka*.

In the case of *dāruṇaka*, a plaster composed of *priyāla* seeds, *madhuka*, *kuṣṭha*, black gram (*māṣa*), and rock salt (*saindhava*), mixed with honey, should be applied to the head. (18) Therein, two other plasters [are also prescribed].
By applying a paste of *khākhasa* seeds with milk, one conquers severe [pain].
Furthermore, a paste made from the powder of mango seeds mixed with an equal amount of *śivā* powder, ground with milk and applied as an ointment, destroys even the most formidable disease. 19.
In cases of *indralupta* (alopecia),
an ointment made from the bitter leaves of *paṭola* applied as a plaster will certainly bring about the subsiding of the condition within just three days. 20.
In this very context, there are other ointments as well:
an ointment that removes Indra-lupta consists of honey and the juice of *bṛhatī*, or the root or fruit of *guñjā*, or even the juice of *bhallātaka*. (21)
A paste consisting of *gokṣura*, sesame flowers, and equal parts of honey and clarified butter, when applied as a head-ointment, is the supreme means for promoting hair growth. 22.
A hair-generating ointment:
having prepared ink from elephant tusks, with goat’s milk and *rasāñjana*, hairs grow by this application even on the palms of the hands. (23)
Indraluptaghna is another ointment:

through the application of a paste of licorice (yaṣṭī), blue water-lily (indīvara), raisins (mṛdvīkā), oil, clarified butter (ājya), and milk, Indralupta is pacified and the hair becomes thick and firm. 24.
Another hair-increasing ointment:
an application made with the ashes of the skin, hair, nails, horns, and bones of quadrupeds, together with oil, is a supreme means for the generation of body hair. 25.
A paste for blackening the hair:
one should perform an oil massage daily with the seed-oil of *indravāruṇikā*; by that, locks of hair arise resembling the color of a bumblebee. 26.
A hair-restoring ointment:
iron filings, *bhṛṅgarāja*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and black earth, kept for a month in sugarcane juice; by applying this as an ointment, one conquers graying hair. 27.
Another ointment consists of the three *dhātrī* fruits, the two types of *pathyā*, one *bibhītaka*, five kernels of *āmravṛntaka*, and one *karṣa* of iron is administered. 28.
Having ground [these ingredients], one should place them in an iron vessel and let them sit overnight;
this ointment quickly destroys even great premature graying of the hair. 29.
Another ointment for blackening the hair:
Triphalā, nīlikā leaves, iron, and bhṛṅgarāja in equal parts,
ground together with goat’s urine, are known to turn the hair black when applied as a paste. This is the procedure for the preparation that destroys premature graying (palita).
A wise person should prepare a powder consisting of triphalā, iron filings, pomegranate bark, and lotus stalks, five palas each;
he should also provide six prasthas of bhṛṅgarāja juice.
Having placed it in an iron vessel, one should bury it in the ground.
Then, for one month, one should apply a plaster made of goat's milk; at night, having wrapped the head in a tuft of hair and encircled it with castor leaves.
One should sleep [with it] and then perform a bath in the morning; by that, the destruction of gray hair occurs through three applications, without a doubt.
This is the application that destroys the hair.
Two parts of conch powder, one part of yellow orpiment (haritāla),
half a part of realgar (manaḥśilā), and one part of natron (svarjikā)— this paste, ground with water, is applied after the hair has been pulled out. 35–36.
And by applying this ointment-technique seven times, the place where the hair grows will be eradicated completely, just like the head of a *kṣapaṇaka*. 37.
Another ointment:
Two *śāṇas* of *tālaka* (mica), six *śāṇas* of conch-shell powder,
and two *śāṇas* of *palāśa* ash should be added and thoroughly rubbed together with the juice of plantain stalks or the sap of *ravipatra* leaves. 38.
For this [condition] as well, there is an excellent application for the removal of hair using seven coatings:
*suvarṇapuṣpī*, *kāsīsa*, *viḍaṅga*, and *manaḥśilā* is a plaster that destroys *śvitra* (leucoderma). 39.
Rocanā and rock salt, when used as an ointment, destroy the affliction of *śivatrana*.
Another ointment consists of a pill (*guṭikā*) made from *vāyasī*, *iḍagaja*, *kuṣṭha*, and *kṛṣṇā*.
Ground with goat's urine, this plaster destroys skin diseases. 41.
Another plaster:
one *śāṇa* of *tālaka* (orpiment) and four *śāṇas* of *vākucī* (seemingly a corruption for *vākucī*, i.e., *pruṣkaravardhinī*).
That powder, ground with cow’s urine and applied as an ointment, destroys tinea versicolor (śikthin).
This is an ointment that removes all types of vitiligo (śvitra):
vākucī, vetasa, lākṣā, kākodumbarikā, and kaṇā.

Take the powder of *rasāñjana* and black sesame seeds; having ground these together and kneaded them with the bile of cows, a pill (*guṭikā*) is formed. By applying an ointment of this, even severe swellings (*śivatrāṇi*) are destroyed with extreme speed.

A plaster for removing *sidhma* (vitiligo) consists of *dhātrī*, *sarjarasa*, and powdered *yavakṣāra*; this application should be used with *sauvīra* (sour gruel) for the destruction of *sidhma*. 45.
Another ointment consists of one karṣa each of dārvī, mūlakabīja, tālaka, suradāru, and tāmbūlapatra, taken separately. 46.
One should combine one *śāṇa* measure of conch powder with all [the other ingredients] in one place;
this plaster, ground with water, is the supreme destroyer of *sidhma* (vitiligo) and removes eye diseases when applied as a paste. 47. This plaster removes eye diseases.
Harītakī, rock salt (saindhava), red ochre (gairika), rasāñjana,
and viḍālaka ground together with water remove all eye diseases.
This is another ointment.

Rasāñjana mixed with the three pungents (vyoṣa), ground together and made into pills, destroys itching accompanied by inflammation when applied as an ointment; this is known as the collyrium [formula] for itching and other skin diseases such as ringworm. 49.
This is an ointment for ringworm, itching, and similar conditions.

Having ground together the seeds of *prapunnāṭa*, *vākucī*, mustard seeds, sesame, *kuṣṭha*, the two types of *niśā* (turmeric and *dāruharidrā*), and *musta*, and applying this paste with buttermilk as an ointment, ringworm, itching, and eczema are destroyed. 50.
For ointments against scabies and similar ailments, one should grind together in a single vessel *hemakṣīrī*, *viḍaṅga*, *darada*, *gandhaka*, *dadrughna*, *kuṣṭha*, and *sindūra*. (51)
By merely applying a plaster made from the fresh juices of *dhattūra*, *nimba*, and *tāmbūlī* leaves separately, scabies, ringworm,
herpes zoster, itching, and *rakasa* are swiftly pacified. (52–53)
Regarding itching, scabies, and similar conditions, there is another ointment:
dūrvā, abhayā, rock salt (saindhava), cakramarda, and kuṭheraka; an ointment made from these mixed with buttermilk destroys itching and scabies. 54
In that same context, there is another ointment:
an ointment combined with dūrvā and niśā is known to destroy itching and scabies, as well as to remove worms and skin eruptions, and to alleviate śītapitta. 55
An ointment consisting of white mustard, turmeric, kuṣṭha, prapunnāṭa,
and sesame seeds, mixed with pungent oil (kaṭutaila), is a proven application that destroys ringworm. 56
This ointment destroys Vata-visarpa (erysipelas caused by Vata): an application of Rasna, Nilotpala, Daru, Chandana, Madhuka, and Bala, combined with ghee and milk, is a destroyer of Vata-visarpa. 57
An application of lotus stalks, sandalwood, *lodhra*, *uśīra*, *kamala*, blue lotus,
*sārivā*, *āmalakī*, and *pathyā* is a plaster that destroys *pitta*-type erysipelas (visarpa). 58
An ointment consisting of triphalā, padmaka, uśīra, samaṅgā, karavīraka, the root of nala, and anantā destroys kapha-visarpa; this ointment is a destroyer of phlegmatic erysipelas. (59)
This plaster destroys bile, wind, and blood: māṃsī, sarjarasa, lodhra, madhuka, along with reṇuka,
mūrvā, blue lotus, red lotus, together with the flowers of śirīṣa.

A plaster soaked in *śatadhauta* ghee is for [disorders of] pitta, vāta, and blood; it stops bleeding from the nose. Furthermore, *āmala* fruit fried in ghee and ground with *kāñjika* and water [serves the same purpose].

By applying this as a plaster on the head, blood flowing from the nose is conquered; this plaster, consisting of *kuṣṭha* ground with *eraṇḍa* oil and *kāñjika*, removes headache caused by *vāta*. (61)
One should apply the flower of the *mucukunda* tree to cure headache caused by Vata (62).
Another plaster consists of *devadāru*, *nata*, *kuṣṭha*, *nalada*, and *viśvabheṣaja*.

An application of oil mixed with fermented gruel (kāñjika) cures headache caused by Vāta. An application made of sandalwood, uśīra, yaṣṭyāhva, balā, vyāghranakha, and utpala removes headache arising from blood and bile (raktapitta).
An ointment made from these ground with milk will overcome bleeding disorders (raktapitta) and headache.
An ointment that cures raktapitta consists of āmalakī, kaseru, hrīvera, padma, padmaka, and candana.
One should prepare a paste with the roots of *dūrvā*, *uśīra*, and *nalada*;
this application destroys headache born of *pitta* as well as the pain of *rakta-pitta*,
and it is a plaster that removes headache caused by *kapha*.
A lukewarm paste made from *hareṇu*, *nata*, *śaileya*, *mustā*, *elā*, *agaru*, *dāru*, *māṃsī*, *rāsnā*, and *arūka* removes pain caused by *kapha*. Another paste [is as follows]: 67.
Another paste.
A lukewarm paste made from ginger, kuṣṭha, prapunnāṭa, devadāru, and rohiṣa, ground with urine, removes phlegmatic headaches;
it is also a plaster for sūryāvarta and ardhāvabhedaka. 68.
An ointment consisting of sārivā, kuṣṭha, madhuka, vacā, kṛṣṇa, and utpala,
combined with sour gruel (kāñjika) and oil, is a remedy for both sūryāvarta and ardhabheda;
it is an ointment that removes all types of headache.
A paste of *varī*, blue lotus, *dūrvā* grass, black sesame, and *punarnavā* is a cure for all types of headache, including those caused by *śaṅkhaka* and *anantavāta*.
There are two varieties of this paste.
Now, another method of application (lepa-vidhi) is declared, which is approved by the wise;
it has two stated varieties, known as pralepa and pradeha. Their characteristics [are as follows]: 71. Their characteristics...
Just as a fresh buffalo hide is highly elevated, such is the measurement for those two;
a cold and drying application is prescribed as *pralepa*. A thick, warm application is *pradeha*, which destroys *kapha* and *vāta*. (72)
Regarding the procedure for medicinal pastes:

the two types known as *pralepa* (external application) and *pradeha* (plaster), when applied facing the hair follicles, cause their potency to enter properly and swiftly through the pores of the skin and the openings of the vessels. (73)
Regarding the prohibition of applying ointments at night:
one should not apply an ointment at night, nor should one keep it on while it is drying; one should disregard the drying of the medicinal paste with respect to its compressing effect. (74)
The reason for the prohibition against applying ointment at night is as follows:

"For the heat residing in the openings of the pores of the skin escapes during the night when it is shrouded by darkness even without an ointment; therefore, one should not apply ointment at night. (75)
Regarding specific diseases, the instruction for medicinal pastes at night is as follows:
even at night, the procedure for applying plasters and the like should be performed by the wise in cases of deep-seated, unripened swellings arising from blood and phlegm. 76
Regarding the treatment of wounds, the instruction on the sequence of applications is as follows:
first is an application that removes swelling; second is bloodletting;
third should be poulticing; and fourth is the procedure for incision. (77)

The fifth stage should be purifying, the sixth is considered healing, and the seventh effects the restoration of color; these are regarded as the successive stages of a wound. (78) This is an ointment that removes swelling caused by Vāta in a wound.
A plaster composed of *bījapūra*, *jaṭā*, *hiṃsrā*, *devadāru*, *mahauṣadha*, *rāsnā*, and *agnimantha* destroys swelling caused by *vāta*.
This plaster also cures swelling and ulcers arising from *pitta*.
Madhuka, candana, mūrvā, nalamūla, padmaka, uśīra, bālaka, and padma constitute an ointment for inflammatory swelling caused by pitta;
this application destroys swellings of ulcers born of kapha. (80)
Black soot, old oil-cake, the bark of *śigru*, and sand, ground with urine and applied as a lukewarm paste, destroy swelling caused by *kapha*;
this ointment also cures traumatic wounds and swellings arising from blood. (81)
One should apply a medicinal paste consisting of two types of *niśā*, sandalwood (*candana*), the two types of *śivā*, *dūrvā*, *punarnavā*,
*uśīra*, *padmaka*, *lodhra*, *gairika*, and *rasāñjana* for swellings caused by external trauma or blood disorders. 82–83.

An ointment consisting of the roots of *śaṇa*, *mūlaka*, and *śigru*, along with the fruits of these, sesame, mustard, *vacā*, yeast (*kiṇva*), and *atasī*, is known as a digestive application (*pācana*) for ulcers. 84
Regarding ointments for incising ulcers:
therein is the dantyādi-ointment— dantī, the bark of the root of citraka, the milky sap of snuhī and arka, and jaggery.
Bhallātaka, asthi, kāsīsa, saindhava, and dāraṇa are prescribed [as a paste]. 85.
A plaster consisting of cirabilva and others—namely cirabilva, agnika, dantī, citraka, and hayamāraka—is [also used].
The excrement of pigeons, herons, and vultures, when applied as a paste, causes bursting [of tumors]. Svarjikā and the like, and the application of *hemakṣīrī*,
as well as alkaline substances such as *svarjikā* and *yavaśūka*, cause bursting when applied as a paste.

Likewise, a plaster made of *hemakṣīrī* is an excellent ulcer-dissolver (87). A plaster composed of sesame, rock salt, *yaṣṭyāhva*, nimba leaves, and the two types of *niśā* cleanses and heals ulcers.
An ointment made from the three pungent spices (trivṛt) ground with ghee purifies ulcers (88). An ointment composed of nimba leaves, ghee, honey, dārvī, and madhuka both purifies and heals ulcers.
A plaster combined with sesame seeds is both purifying and healing (89). A plaster of karañja, ariṣṭa, and nirguṇḍī destroys worms in ulcers.
Alternatively, an application of garlic, or an application derived from asafoetida and nimba leaves,
is a healing ointment that pacifies malignant ulcers.
[Likewise,] nimba leaves, sesame seeds, danti, trivṛt, rock salt, and honey [are used for this purpose].
This plaster pacifies wounds that have been seen [to fester], and it is both purifying and healing.
This plaster destroys the pain arising from internal abscesses (antarvidradhi), prepared by grinding the fruit of *madana* and *tiktā* with sour gruel (*kāñjika*) and water. 91.
One should apply a lukewarm plaster to the navel; from this, the pain will be pacified.
This plaster, made from *śigru*, *śephālikā*, castor, barley, wheat, and mung beans, cures Vata-type abscesses (*vātavidradhi*).
A thick, lukewarm plaster should be applied in the case of a Vāta-vidradhi.
For a Pitta-type abscess, a plaster that removes Pitta should be used,
consisting of parched grain (lāja), madhuka, and sugar, mixed with ghee.
Alternatively, one should apply a plaster of *payasyā*, *uśīra*, and *candana* ground with milk;
this is a plaster that removes *kapha*-type abscesses (*kaphavidradhi*).
[One may also use] brick, sand, iron slag, and cow dung together.
This lukewarm poultice made with [cow's] urine should be applied in the case of a Kaphaja Vidradhi (95).
A plaster composed of red sandalwood, mañjiṣṭhā, niśā, madhuka, and gairika removes traumatic abscesses (āgantukavidradhi).
An application of milk is for a Vidradhi caused by blood or external factors (96). An application of Nicula, Śigru seeds, or Daśamūla removes Vāta-type Gala-gaṇḍa.
A lukewarm poultice is applied for swellings caused by Vāta.
A plaster of Devadāru and Viśālā removes swellings of the throat and cheeks caused by Kapha; it is a poultice for Kaphaja Gaṇḍa.

A plaster for destroying *apacī* (scrofula): having burnt mustard seeds and *ariṣṭa* leaves together with *bhallātaka* fruits, this paste, ground with goat’s urine, is an application that destroys *apacī*. 99
For conditions such as gaṇḍamālā, one should grind mustard seeds, drumstick seeds, hemp seeds, linseed, barley,
and radish seeds with sour buttermilk to form a medicinal paste.

By this ointment, *gaṇḍamālā*, *arbuda*, and *gaṇḍa* are pacified. For those afflicted solely by wind (*kevalānila-pīḍita*), one should apply an ointment of vulture fat and other such substances after first scarifying the limb with a razor.
In that case, one should apply a plaster made from ground guñjā seeds (101).
By this, pain arising in the upper arms, as well as viśvācī, gṛdhrasī,
and other pains born of vāta, quickly comes to an end (102).
An ointment that removes the disease of elephantiasis:
an application made of *dhattūra*, castor, *nirguṇḍī*, *varṣābhū*, *śigru*, and mustard seeds destroys elephantiasis, even that which is long-standing and severe. (103)
A plaster for curing kuraṇḍa:
cumin, hapuṣā, kuṣṭha, eraṇḍa, and badara, ground together with kāñjika, is an ointment that destroys kuraṇḍa. 104
By applying a plaster made from the root of *karavīra* ground with water during an *upadaṃśa*, even an incurable pain arising in the penis comes to an end through this external application. 105
In that regard, another ointment:
one should burn *triphalā* in a cauldron; this soot, combined with honey, as an application for *upadaṃśa*, heals the ulcer instantly. 106
Another ointment consisting of *rasāñjana* combined with *śirīṣa* and *pathyā*, applied as a plaster with honey, should be employed to remove the disease of *upadaṃśa*. 107
For burns caused by fire,
the physician should apply an ointment consisting of *tugākṣīrī*, *plakṣa*, *candana*, and *gairika*, along with *amṛta*, mixed with unctuous clarified butter (108).

Alternatively, one should apply a plaster mixed with ghee using decoctions of *tindukī* bark; likewise, having burnt barley, one should prepare a charcoal powder and apply it with oil as a plaster for all fire-burns to promote wound healing. 109

An ointment for contracting the vagina is made from the fruits of the *palāśa* and *udumbara* trees combined with sesame oil and honey; one should smear this upon the vagina, as it is an excellent means for making it firm. 110

In that very context, there is another ointment: by applying an ointment of madhuka mixed with the fruit of the *mākanda* and camphor, the female organ of women becomes firm even when their youth has passed. 111
For the enlargement of the genitals, breasts, and so forth, the following is an ointment:
black pepper, rock salt, long pepper, *tagara*, the fruit of *bṛhatī*, *apāmārga*, sesame, costus, barley, black gram, and mustard seeds. (112)

One should combine aśvagandhā with its powder and honey (113). By the continuous application of this and by massage, there occurs an enlargement of the penis, the swelling of the breasts, and the thickening of the arms and ears (114).
An ointment that causes the enlargement of the penis:
one should cook ghee with sugar, *aśvagandhā*, rock salt, and goat’s milk; from applying this as a paste and massaging it, a supreme enlargement of the penis is produced. (115)
One should rub mercury with the juice of the leaves of *indravāruṇikā* and apply a paste of *yonidrāvakara*; this should be done repeatedly using a stick of red oleander wood.
From contact with a liṅga smeared [with these], the vaginal discharge of women is produced. This ointment removes foul body odor;
it consists of the powder of betel leaves and the powder derived from kuṣṭha and śivā.
One should apply a plaster with water to eliminate foul odors from the body;
a plaster of *kuḷittha* groats, *kuṣṭha*, *māṃsī*, and the powder of sandalwood removes perspiration and foul odor. (117–118)
One should prepare a paste by mixing the flour of chickpeas with their skins in one place;
from the smearing of this, perspiration and foul odor are destroyed.
This is the ointment for subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*). (119)
Vacā, sauvarcala salt, kuṣṭha, the two types of rajanī, and marica—by the power of an ointment made from these, there is supreme subjugation (vaśīkaraṇa). 120.
Now, the procedure for head-oil (mūrdhataila).
In that regard, the varieties of head-oil (mūrdhataila) are, in order: massage (abhyaṅga), pouring (pariṣeka), poultice (picu), and enema (basti);
thus head-oil is fourfold, each subsequent one being more strengthening than the previous. 121
The statement of the reason for describing the procedure for the exclusive head-poultice (śirobasti):

The three [therapies] beginning with massage (abhyaṅga) have been previously established and are remembered as being applicable everywhere; now, the procedure for the head-poultice, which is approved by the wise, is being declared here. (122)
Now follows the procedure for the head-pouch (śirobasti):

the head-pouch should be made of leather, two-faced, twelve finger-breadths in length, and equal in size to the head; having bound it over the head with a paste of black gram (māṣa), [one should proceed].

Having first performed the occlusion of the joints, one should fill [the head] with lukewarm unctuous substances. Regarding that, the instruction on the duration and procedure for maintaining the *śirobasti* is as follows:
it should be maintained for as long as there is discharge from the nose, eyes, and mouth.
Or else, there may be a subsiding of pain, or [the patient may feel] a thousandfold [strength].
This is the instruction on the time and procedure for the application of the head-poultice (śirobasti);
in this case, the head-poultice is recommended even without food.
The head-poultice (śirobasti) should be applied for five or seven days;
after releasing the head-poultice, one should grasp the upper part of the body all around.

Then, one should cause the upper body to be bathed with lukewarm water. (126) The benefits of the head-fomentation (śirobasti): by this, diseases born of vāta that are difficult to conquer go to their destruction.
Therefore, shaking the head and other such actions are appropriate at all times.
Regarding the procedure for filling the ears:
one should slightly warm the region of the ear while the patient lies on their side.
Then, one should fill the ear with lukewarm urine, fats, or meat broths.
Regarding the duration for which the medicinal substance should be retained in the ear,
one should protect the filled ear for either one hundred or five hundred [muhūrtas].
Even a thousand measures may be applied for ailments affecting the ears, throat, and head. The characteristic of the measure (mātrā) is as follows:
one should rotate the hands around one's own knees, accompanied by the snapping of the fingers.
This shall be one *mātrā*; this is the certainty in all cases.
(130) The specific timing for filling the ears according to the [qualities of] taste and so forth is as follows:
filling the ears with tastes and such is recommended before eating.
When the sun has set, filling the ear with oil and other such substances [is beneficial].
A juice that removes earache [is prepared as follows]:
one should heat in fire a leaf of the *arka* plant smeared with clarified butter (*ājya*) after it has been soaked in [the juice].
When that essence is poured into the ear, it is the supreme remedy for removing earache.
Regarding the application of goat's urine for earache:
for one suffering from earache, lukewarm goat's urine mixed with rock salt [should be used].
By applying this, pains such as those from a piercing or an abscess are pacified. (133) Regarding earache, there are other applications:
ginger, licorice, honey, rock salt, and emblic myrobalan. (134)
The juice of *tilaparṇī*, oil, borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*), and the juice of lime—these, when applied lukewarm to the ears, remove pain; this is another application for that same condition. 135.
Therein is yet another method.
To alleviate earache, one should fill the ear with the auspicious, pleasantly warm juices of *kapittha*, *mātuluṅga*, and *amlashṛbera*.
In that same context, there is also the application of *arkāṅkura* (Arka sprouts).
One should place sprouts of *arka* ground with sour liquids, smeared with oil, and mixed with salt,
inside a *snuhī* stem that has been covered with its own leaves;
having performed the procedure for *puṭapāka*, one should fill it with those juices.
By means of these lukewarm [applications], even most severe earaches are pacified.
In that very same manner, oil from a lamp and the eight-finger-long stalks of the great *pañcamūla* [are used].

Having wrapped it in linen cloth and sprinkled it with oil, one should then set it on fire. The oil that drips from those [wick-cups] should be collected while lukewarm; this is known as *dīpikā-taila*, which immediately subdues pain.
In this manner, oil from a lamp wick [is used] for leprosy (kuṣṭha), as is oil from the Devadāru tree; likewise, in that same case,
oil from the Syonāka root is cooked over a mild fire.
This quickly removes earache arising from the three doṣas through filling [the ear].
In the case of tinnitus (karṇanāda), [one should use] the fat of yaṣṭī along with the paste and decoction of yaṣṭīmadhu, kākolī, māṣa, and dhānyaka.
Having cooked the fat of a pig, it destroys pain from ringing in the ears (142).
Regarding ear diseases, there is the oil of *svarjikā* and other ingredients:
*svarjikā*, dried radish, asafoetida, combined with black pepper (143).
Oil cooked with *śatapuṣpā* and four times its quantity of sour gruel (*śukta*) cures ear-ache, deafness, and discharge from the ear. For deafness, oil prepared with the alkali of *apāmārga* is used.
One should throw that alkaline paste into water containing the alkali of *apāmārga*;
oil cooked with this overcomes deafness and tinnitus.
For ear-canal disorders, *śambūka-taila* [is used].
One should cook mustard oil with the flesh of a śambūka;
by merely filling [the ear] with it, the ear-canal disorder is pacified.
This is the formulation that destroys ear-discharge.
The powder of the five astringents (pañcakaṣāya) and the juice of *kapittha* mixed with honey are praised for filling the ear in cases of otorrhoea (karṇasrāva). 147.
The five astringents.
Tinduka, abhayā, lodhra, samaṅgā, and āmalakī are to be known as the five decoctions (kaṣāya) to be employed by the best of physicians in this procedure [for ear-disease],
such as ear-discharge (karṇasrāva) and others; [furthermore] there is the application of svarjikā and other substances.
One should pour the juice of *bījapūra* mixed with the powder of *svarjikā*;
ear discharge, pain, and burning sensations will undoubtedly perish.
(149) Regarding putrid ears (*pūtikarṇa*), [there is] *āmra*-oil.

Oil prepared with the tender shoots of the mango, the rose-apple, the madhūka, and the banyan tree brings about the pacification of *pūtikarṇa* (foul-smelling ear disease). These two formulations are destroyers of ear-worms (*karṇakīṭa*). 150.
Filling [the ear] with yellow orpiment mixed with cow's urine,
or alternatively, mustard oil is an excellent remedy for removing insects from the ear.
(151) Another formulation for insects in the ear:

Having combined the fresh juice of *śigru* root, the juice of *sūryāvarta*, powdered *trikaṭu*, and the juice of the roots of *kapikacchū* into one, one should pour it into the ear; this is the supreme remedy for removing insects from the ear. 152
Two other formulations immediately and swiftly destroy the most dreadful ear-worm:
asafoetida indeed quickly destroys the most dreadful ear-worm.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Procedure for Ointments, Head-Oils, and Ear-Drops," in the Uttarakhanda of the Śrī-Śārṅgadhara-Saṃhitā.
Now begins the twelfth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Bloodletting."
In that case, having carefully examined the disease of the person, one should cause the flowing blood to be drained—
either a *prastha*, or half a *prastha*, or even half of that half.
The time for bloodletting is during the autumn season; by its very nature, a person should undergo the flow of blood,
because skin diseases, tumors, swellings, and the like do not occur when there is a discharge of blood.
The description of the nature of blood: Blood that is red in color, neither cold nor hot, and heavy; it should be unctuous and have a fleshy odor, and its burning sensation is like that of pitta. (3)
In blood, there are the qualities of the five great elements: foul odor, fluidity, passion, mobility, and likewise dissolution;
these are remembered as the qualities of blood belonging to the five elements, beginning with earth. 4.
The symptoms of vitiated blood:
when the blood is vitiated, there occurs pain, suppuration, and a burning sensation; there is the appearance of red circular patches, itching, swelling, and the eruption of pustules. 5

The symptoms of increased blood (raktavṛddhi) are as follows: when blood increases, there occurs redness of the limbs and eyes, distension of the vessels, heaviness of the body parts, sleepiness, intoxication, and a burning sensation. (6)
The symptoms of diminished blood (rakta) are:
a craving for sour and sweet things when [blood] is depleted, fainting, dryness of the skin, flaccidity of the vessels, and the movement of vāta into its improper pathways. 7
Blood vitiated by Vāta has the following characteristics:
it is reddish, frothy, dry, rough, thin, flows rapidly, does not coagulate, and causes pricking and stinging sensations; such blood is known as vitiated by Vāta. 8.
The characteristics of blood vitiated by bile (pitta) are:
it is yellow, green, blue, or dark-brown; it has a fleshy odor; it is not clotted; it is warm; and it is undesirable to flies and ants. 9.

The characteristics of blood vitiated by phlegm (kapha) are: it is cold, thick, unctuous, resembling water mixed with red ochre, has the appearance of a piece of flesh, flows in clots, and moves slowly—such blood is vitiated by phlegm. 10

The characteristics of blood vitiated by two or three doṣas: that which is vitiated by two doṣas is combined [in its symptoms], while that vitiated by three is foul-smelling; it arises possessing all the symptoms and resembling fermented gruel (kāñjika). (11)

The characteristics of blood vitiated by poison are as follows: it becomes dark-brown, flows through an abnormal path of the nose, has a fleshy odor, resembles sour gruel (kāñjika), and in great quantity, it causes all types of skin diseases (kuṣṭha). 12.

Pure red blood should be known as having the characteristics of an *indragopa* insect, appearing like its luster; it is natural, unagitated, and indicates that diseases caused by the discharge of blood are curable. 13. Diseases treatable by the flow of blood.
In cases of swelling, burning, inflammation of the limbs, and redness, as well as in the discharge of blood;
likewise in vātarakta, skin diseases (kuṣṭha), difficult-to-conquer wind disorders (anila) accompanied by pain, hand diseases, elephantiasis (ślīpada), and blood vitiated by poison. 14.

In cases of cysts, tumors, apacī, minor diseases, blood-disorders, adhimanthi, vidārī, and diseases of the breasts; in cases of lassitude and heaviness of the limbs; and when there is excessive discharge of blood, drowsiness, or a foul odor from the nose, mouth, and body.
In cases of spreading inflammation of the liver and spleen, abscesses, and the eruption of carbuncles;
in the suppuration and burning of the ears, lips, nose, and mouth; in headache, syphilis, and internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta), the discharge of blood is recommended.
Regarding the procedure for bloodletting in these diseases: a person should effect the drainage of blood by means of horn-cups, leeches, or gourd-sculptures, or else by venesection. 18.

One should not perform venesection on persons unfit for bloodletting: those who are emaciated, those who have overindulged in sexual intercourse, the impotent, the timid, pregnant women, those recently delivered, and those suffering from anemia. (19)
For those with hemorrhoids who have undergone purification through the five purificatory therapies (pañcakarman) and have consumed oleaginous substances (sneha),

for those suffering from swelling of all the limbs, abdominal enlargement (udara), dyspnea, cough, vomiting, diarrhea, or bodily corruption, and even for those whose bodies have been excessively subjected to sudation (atisvinna)— 20—
Bloodletting by venesection is not recommended for one under sixteen years of age, for one over seventy, or for one whose blood flows from a wound;
in these cases, if there is an emergency illness, one should instead extract the blood using leeches.
The method of bloodletting for blood vitiated by poison, as well as the venesection of vessels affected by poison, is likewise recommended (23).
The method of bloodletting according to the specific doshas such as vāta and others.

A wise physician should drain blood vitiated by wind, bile, and phlegm—either individually or in combination—in three ways: using a cow's horn, leeches, or even a gourd. Blood corrupted by two of the humors, as well as that afflicted by all three, should likewise be drawn out.
One should cause the blood to flow by means of skillful venesection at the appropriate sites; furthermore,
regarding the measurement for extracting blood with horns and other instruments,
a horn forcibly draws out blood to the extent of ten finger-breadths.
The leech (*jalaukā*) is one cubit (*hasta*) in length, while the gourd (*tumbī*) is twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
A single application (*pada*) of the size of one finger-breadth purifies the vessels of the entire body;
this is the stage for obstructing the flow of blood.
In cases of cold weather, lack of food, fainting, excessive sleep, or those afflicted by fear, intoxication, or fatigue, blood does not flow;
likewise, it does not flow for those with retention of feces and urine (27). This is the treatment when there is no discharge of blood.

If the blood does not flow, one should rub the opening of the wound with *kuṣṭha*, the three pungents (*tri-kaṭu*), and rock salt (*saindhava*); by this means, the blood will flow properly. This is the time for bloodletting.

Therefore, a wise person should cause blood to flow from one who has been satiated by drinking gruel— not when it is cold, nor when it is excessively hot, nor when the body is perspiring, nor when it is over-heated.
This is the reason for excessive discharge of blood.

In one who has been excessively fomented during the hot season, or likewise due to excessive venesection, blood flows out in excess; in that case, one should administer the appropriate treatment. (30) This is the treatment for excessive hemorrhage of blood.
When the blood flows excessively, one should apply *lodhra*, resin of *sarja*, and *añjana*;
or the powders of barley and wheat; or *dhava*, *dhanvana*, and *gairika*; or the powder of the sloughed skin of a snake; or the ashes of linen cloth and cotton.
Having bound the opening of the ulcer, one should treat the ulcer with cold applications.
In that same case, as another treatment,
one should pierce the upward-pointing vein or cauterize it with alkali or fire.

Astringent (kaṣāya) heals a wound; cold (hima) causes the blood to coagulate; alkali (kṣāra) ripens the opening of a wound; and cauterization (dāha) contracts the vessels. Diseases that are curable by fire-cauterization [should be treated thus].
In that regard, for swelling of the scrotum, the application of cauterization to the thumb is prescribed:
for swelling of the left testicle, one should cauterize the vein at the base of the right hand's thumb;
however, in the case of the opposite (swelling of the right), one should cauterize the vein of the left thumb.
By the power of the burning sensation in the vessels, swelling of the scrotum is destroyed.
(35) In the case of visūcī, the condition of burning in the heels occurs;
through the burning in the heels in visūcī, there arises an intensification of the digestive fire.

Because of that, the vessels carrying lymph and phlegm contract (verse 36). When there is an increase in blood-born enlargement of the spleen and liver, there is a localized burning sensation at those sites;
this occurs when an enlargement of the liver and spleen arises in a child due to [an excess of] blood.
Then, by the burning of that site, the blood-carrying vessels contract.
(37) Prohibition against excessive bloodletting: Even if some corrupted blood remains, the disease will not be provoked.
Therefore, blood should be drained until a residue remains; it is not beneficial to exceed this limit.
(38) The complications arising from excessive bloodletting include blindness, convulsions, thirst, blurred vision, and headache.
It causes hemiplegia, dyspnea, cough, hiccup, burning sensation, and jaundice;
it may cause excessive bleeding or even death. (39) This is the great danger of blood [letting].
The body originates from blood, and the body is sustained by that very [blood];
without it, the life-force would depart. Therefore, a wise person should protect the blood.
Even when blood has flowed out, there is a remedy for the provocation of the humors (*doṣa*).
When vāta has become aggravated after bloodletting,
one should sprinkle the painful swelling with lukewarm ghee as a cooling treatment.
This is the regimen for one whose strength is depleted by the loss of blood.

For one whose blood has been depleted, a broth made from the meat of deer, rabbit, sheep, antelope, or goat is appropriate for drinking; alternatively, milk or *ṣaṣṭika* rice is beneficial. (42) [This concludes] the signs of properly bled blood.

When blood has been properly drained, the signs are the alleviation of pain, lightness, the subsiding of the upward movement of the disease (udreka), and the restoration of mental composure. After the bleeding, one should avoid the following contraindications: 43. [The verse continues: ...the cessation of pain, lightness, the subsiding of the upward movement of the disease, and mental composure; these are the signs when the blood has been properly drained.
Following the flow of blood, the prohibited conditions are as follows: [verse 44].
One should avoid physical exercise, sexual intercourse, anger, cold baths, and exposure to strong winds;

likewise, one should abstain from eating only once a day, sleeping during the day, consuming alkaline, sour, or pungent foods, grief, debate, and indigestion until signs of recovery are observed. (44–45)
