Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Bloodletting," in the Uttarakhanda of the *Śrīśārṅgadharasaṃhitā*. Now begins the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Treatment for Clarifying the Eyes."
In that regard, first, one should treat the eye with these formulations: its names are *sekam*, *āścyotanam*, *piṇḍī*, *biḍālaka*, *tarpaṇam*, as well as *puṭapāka* and *añjanam*. (1)

The procedure for sprinkling: sprinkling with fine streams is beneficial for all eyes; it should be administered from a distance of four finger-breadths to one whose eyes are closed and who is intoxicated. 2.

The different types of irrigation (sekā) are determined according to the specific dosha; that [irrigation] should be oleating (snehana) for vāta, healing (ropaṇa) for blood and pitta, and scraping (lekhana) for kapha. Its dosage is now being described.

In the case of oleation, sprinkling should be performed with six hundred words; in the case of healing, with four hundred words; and in the acts of sprinkling and scraping, it should be done with three hundred words. 4.
The time for the consecration (sekasamaya) should be performed during the day; however, the consecration may take place at night in the case of an urgent illness.
The arrangement of the consecration follows the specific nature of the affliction.
Goat's milk boiled with castor bark, leaves, and roots is beneficial; when applied lukewarm as a wash to the eyes, it destroys vāta-abhiṣyanda.
These two types of irrigation (sekas) are indicated for vāta-abhiṣyanda, māruta-paryaya, and śuṣka-akṣi-pāka.
For one whose eyes have been affected by Vata-abhishyanda, a lukewarm eye-wash with milk,

rock salt (saindhava), and turmeric (rajanī) and deodar (dāru), or milk prepared with turmeric and deodar and combined with rock salt, is beneficial for pacifying Vata-abhishyanda and is wholesome in cases of Māruta-paryaya.
This irrigation is always beneficial for dry ophthalmia (śuṣkākṣipāka).
This sprinkling removes eye pain caused by pitta, blood, or injury;
it consists of equal parts of *sāvara* and *madhuka*, finely powdered and fried in ghee.
Ghee prepared with goat’s milk, when used as a wash, conquers pitta-blood disorders and injuries from trauma (9).
For the condition of blood congestion (raktābhiṣyanda), a wash should be made with triphalā, lodhra, yaṣṭīmadhu, sugar, and bhadramusta.
An irrigation with a paste ground in cold water destroys red congestion (raktābhiṣyanda).
In that same context, there is another irrigation:
lac, madhuka, mañjiṣṭhā, lodhra, and kālānusārivā.
An irrigation (seka) containing white lotus destroys red congestion;
an irrigation that destroys eye pain consists of white *lodhra* fried in ghee, powdered, and strained through a cloth.
Massaged with warm water and applied as a wash, it destroys pain in the eyes (12). Now follows the procedure for eye-drops; therein, the proper time for the act of administering eye-drops:

Now, the procedure for eye-drops (āścyotana) should never be performed at night. Regarding the method of application: when the eyes are open, it is beneficial to apply drops two finger-breadths from the center of the vision.
The number of drops to be applied is specified according to the specific quality [of the treatment]:
eight drops for scarifying applications, ten drops for emollient applications, and twelve are prescribed for healing applications; these are to be administered in either cold or warm form.

And in heat, they should be cold in nature; this is the certainty in all cases. (15) The description of substances for instillation according to the distinction of wind and other humors: in the case of wind, [the substance] should be bitter and unctuous; likewise, in the case of bile, it should be sweet and cold.
For phlegm (kapha), eye-drops that are bitter, hot, and dry are beneficial in successive order. Regarding the determination of the dose for eye-drops:
for all types of eye-drops, a dose of one hundred words is considered beneficial.
The closing and opening of the eyes, the snapping of a finger by men, or the pronunciation of a heavy syllable— this is considered by the wise to be merely a measure of time (vāṅmātra).
[This] eye-drop (āścyotana) removes wind and ocular congestion.
A lukewarm decoction made from the five roots beginning with *bilva*, along with *bṛhatī*, *eraṇḍa*, and *śigru*, used as eye-drops (*āścyotana*), destroys *abhiṣyanda* caused by *vāta*.
This is the remedy for *abhiṣyanda* arising from *vāta*, *rakta*, and *pitta*.

One should apply a paste of Nimba leaves ground with water and Lodhra bark; having heated this over a fire and then ground it again, filling the eyes with its juice destroys Abhiṣyanda arising from Vāta or arising from Raktapitta. 19.

The *āścyotana* (eye-drop) made from the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) destroys all types of ocular congestion (*abhiṣyanda*); it is an eye-drop that eliminates all forms of ocular congestion and relieves eye afflictions arising from blood and bile (*raktapitta*). 20.

The dripping of a woman’s breast milk into the eyes overcomes the afflictions of *rakta-pitta* and *vāta*; likewise, milk-boiled ghee (*kṣīra-sarpiḥ*) or plain ghee (*ghṛta*) shall conquer the pain of *vāta-rakta*. (21) This is the procedure for the medicinal bolus (*piṇḍikā-vidhi*).
The *piṇḍī* is called a bolus; it is bound with strips of cloth and is suitable for ocular inflammation (*netrābhiṣyanda*), yet it is also applied to wounds.
For both ocular inflammation and *adhimantha*, head-purgation (*śirovirecana*) is indicated.
When *abhiṣyanda* and *adhimantha* have arisen from *śleṣman*, one should administer strong head-purgatives (*śiro-virecana*) to a person whose upper body has been treated with oleation and sudation.
In cases of *adhimantha*, venesection and thermal cauterization (*agnidāha*) are also indicated.

In all cases of *adhimantha*, one should pierce the vein on the forehead; if the *mantha* is not pacified by any means, one should apply cauterization above the eyebrows. For all types of *abhiṣyanda*, the application of *piṇḍikā* [is prescribed].
In all cases of *abhiṣyanda*, the wise physician should apply a medicinal poultice (*piṇḍikā*).
Regarding the application of the poultice for *vātābhiṣyanda*:
for the purpose of pacifying *vātābhiṣyanda*, the poultice should be unctuous and warm.
A preparation made from the leaves, roots, and bark of the castor plant (eraṇḍa) destroys Vāta. For the two types of Pitta-abhiṣyanda,
a bolus of Āmalakī (dhātrī) is easily administered to destroy Pitta-abhiṣyanda.
A bolus prepared from the fruit of the great nimba tree destroys bile (pitta). A bolus made from the leaves of the śigru tree destroys the congestion of phlegm (kapha). (27–28)
In cases of ophthalmia caused by *kapha* and *pitta*, two types of medicinal pastes are used:
a paste made from *nimba* leaves removes *śleṣma* and *pitta*, while a paste of *triphalā* is likewise declared for the destruction of *śleṣma* and *pitta*. (29)
In cases of red-colored *abhiṣyanda*,
a paste of *lodhra* ground with *kāñjika* water and fried in ghee quickly removes the *abhiṣyanda* arising from blood. (30)
In cases of swelling, itching, and similar conditions,
a paste made from ginger and neem leaves, mixed with a small amount of rock salt and applied lukewarm to the eye, removes swelling, itching, and pain through its application. (31)
The procedure for *biḍālaka*:
*Biḍālaka* is an external application that excludes the eyelashes;
its dosage should be understood as being like the procedure for facial applications. 32.
For all eye diseases,
an external application of equal parts of liquorice (*yaṣṭī*), red ochre (*gairika*), rock salt (*sindhūttha*), *dārvī*, and *tārkṣya*, ground with water, removes all ailments of the eyes. (33)
In that very context, there are six other ointments:
an ointment with *rasāñjana*, or with *pathyā*, *viśva* leaves,
or *kumārikā* and *agnipattra*, or even with pomegranate sprouts.
Alternatively, a paste made of vacā, haridrā, and nimba, or likewise with nāgara and gairika,
removes eye pain immediately.
Having burnt lodhra together with rock salt (saindhava) and mixed it with beeswax and ghee, [it should be applied].

Ground [with water], it removes eye pain instantly when applied as an ointment or a paste (verse 35). A paste that relieves eye affliction is the juice extracted from nimba fruit, rubbed in an iron vessel.
A certain thick paste, applied as an external ointment, removes irritation of the eyes;
it is a remedy for destroying *arman* (eye-films) when black pepper is powdered and rubbed with the fresh juice of *keśarāja*.
This king of applications brings about the destruction of diseases through application;
having incised and squeezed the swollen *añjananāmikā* when it has burst, one should apply [the remedy] over the *añjananāmikā*.
One should rub [the eye] with realgar, cardamom, natron, and rock salt, mixed with honey.
Now follows the procedure for *tarpaṇa* (eye-satiation); first, the characteristics of an eye suitable for *tarpaṇa*.
Now I shall describe the *tarpaṇaka* (eye-irrigation), which is supremely satisfying to the eyes;
it is for when the eye is parched, distorted, turbid, 39 with decayed lashes, a discharge from the head [of the eye], and accompanied by painful opening.

That eye which is afflicted by *timira*, *arjuna*, *śukra*, and other such conditions, as well as by *abhiṣyanda* and *adhimantha* (40), by *śuṣkākṣipāka* and swelling (*śotha*), and by disorders arising from the vitiation of *vāta*, should be treated with *tarpaṇa* by those experts in ophthalmology.
Regarding the contraindications for tarpaṇa:

tarpaṇa is not recommended when the weather is cloudy, excessively hot, or cold; nor during states of anxiety, exhaustion, or confusion; nor when there is no subsiding of secondary complications in the eye. (41)
The procedure for saturation (tarpaṇa) is as follows:
in a place free from wind, sun, and dust, the patient should lie supine;
two circular supports made of moistened black gram flour are placed beneath [the eyes]. 42.
The two eye-sockets should be made even, firm, and free from obstruction;
one should fill them with the scum of clarified butter (ghṛtamaṇḍa) mixed with lukewarm water, or with clarified butter washed a hundred times, or with that produced from milk. 43.
One should fill [the breath] only as long as the eyelashes remain submerged in the fullness; once the eyes are closed, one should then open them slowly. 44.
In the case of *tarpaṇa*, the wise physician should apply the measures for retaining oil; in diseases of the eyelids (*vartma-roga*), one should retain it for one hundred *vāṅmātrās*.
In cases of clear phlegm (*svaccha-kapha*) or diseases of the joints (*sandhi-roga*), five hundred *mātrās* are beneficial.
In cases of white [disorders], six hundred [drops] are prescribed; for black diseases, seven hundred are considered appropriate.
For eye diseases, eight hundred; for adhimantha, one thousand;
and for wind diseases, one thousand—thus indeed should the *tarpaṇa* be administered. 46–47.
After the satiation (tarpaṇa), the procedure to be performed is as follows:
one should then clear away his kapha with the inhalation of appropriate medicinal smoke, following the application of steamed barley flour mixed with unctuous substances. 48
The duration for the rite of libation (tarpaṇa) is desired to be one day, or three days, or at most five days;
this is the characteristic sign of complete satisfaction in the libation.
In the case of satiation, one should observe these signs of satisfaction in the eyes:
pleasant sleep and waking, clarity, proficiency of color, the cessation [of secretions], the alleviation of disease, and lightness of movement. (50)
Now, the characteristics of over-saturation: an eye that is tearful, heavy, and glossy would be characterized as over-saturated (51). The characteristics of under-saturation:

An eye that is dry, turbid, and painful is one that has been under-nourished (hīnatarpita). The treatment for both under-nourishment and over-nourishment (atitarpita) consists of dry and unctuous therapies respectively; such is the remedy for these two conditions. 52–53.
Hereafter, I shall explain the procedure for *puṭapāka* and the method for accomplishing it:
two well-kneaded, smooth lumps of meat, each the size of a *bilva* fruit [54].
One *vilva*-measure of solid substances and one *kuḍava* of liquids are considered the standard quantity;
having mixed these together, wrapped them well with leaves,
and cooked them by the *puṭapāka* method, the wise physician should extract that juice.
For one who always lies on their back, the [medicine] should be poured into the middle of the eye.
There are three types of *puṭapāka*: the emollient (*snehana*), the scraping (*lekhana*), and the healing (*ropaṇa*). (55–56)
The objects for the three types of *puṭapāka* are as follows:
the first is beneficial and unctuous for those who are excessively dry; the second is indeed scraping (*lekhana*) even for those who are unctuous;
and the third is for the sake of strengthening the vision and alleviates pitta, blood disorders, wounds, and vāta. (57)

The *snehanapuṭapāka* (oleating cupping) prepared with ghee, meat, fat, marrow, muscle fat, and sweet medicinal herbs is oleating; this *puṭapāka* should be applied to the eyes for two hundred words [of recitation]. 58.
The *lekhanapuṭapāka* (scraping poultice) is prepared with the liver and meat of wild animals combined with scraping substances, along with iron filings,
copper, conch shell, coral, and rock salt.
With sea-foam, kāsīsa, srotoja, and whey from curdled milk, it is a scraping agent (lekhana); it should be retained for a hundred recitations, and its retention is of this extent. 59.
This is the ropaṇa-puṭapāka.

A *puṭapāka* cooked with breast milk, meat from arid regions (*jāṅgala*), honey, clarified butter, and bitter substances is three times more effective for scraping; it should be retained as a healing agent for wound closure.
This is the instruction regarding what must be done upon observing complications.
One should perform the procedure for *tarpaṇa* as prescribed when a complication (*vyāpatti*) is observed. (61) Now follows the procedure for collyrium (*añjana*).
First, the appropriate times for the application of collyrium are as follows:
Now, one should apply collyrium when the humors have fully ripened;
collyrium is recommended at midday during the late winter and early spring seasons,
while it is recommended in the forenoon and afternoon during the summer and autumn seasons.
Indeed, during the rainy season, when it is not cloudy, and always during the spring,
there are various types of collyrium:
the scraping, the healing, and likewise the lubricating collyrium.
There are four types of collyriums (añjana): scraping (lekhana), healing (ropaṇa), clarifying (prasādana), and scraping-healing (lekhana-ropaṇa).
A scraping collyrium is desired to be prepared with alkaline, pungent, and sour tastes;
a healing collyrium is considered to be combined with astringent and bitter tastes along with unctuous substances.
The sweet, the oily, and the clarifying—these are the three types of collyrium (añjana). Furthermore, there are three kinds of collyrium preparations: pills, liquids, and powders.
One should apply [the collyrium] with a probe or a finger, using progressively smaller amounts for those who are unfit for collyrium—
namely, those who are fatigued, weeping, frightened, intoxicated by liquor, or suffering from acute fever. (66)

Collyrium is not recommended when indigestion is present or when the natural urges have been suppressed. In the case of a sharp collyrium, the physician should prepare a wick with a thickness equal to a grain of *hareṇu*.
The dosage for the medium type should be one and a half [karṣas], while for the mild type it should be double that.
68. Regarding the dosages for *rasakriyā*, the *rasakriyā* should be excellent when measured at three *viḍaṅgas*, which is beneficial.
The medium dose consists of two *viḍaṅga* fruits, while the inferior dose consists of one;
the quantity for powdered collyrium (*cūrṇāñjana*) is prescribed as two *śalākā* measures of purgative powder.

In the mild [application], there should be three probes; in the unctuous (*snaihika*) application, four. (70) Regarding the nature of the probe for the collyrium: it should be blunt at both ends, smooth, and eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length.
It may be made of stone or derived from minerals, and should be as round as a pea (kalāya). The form of the stylus depends on the specific task;
a stylus produced from copper, iron, or stone is intended for engraving.

The wise consider a probe made of gold or silver to be intended for lubrication, while a finger, due to its softness, is prescribed for healing. (72) This is the instruction regarding the timing for applying collyrium.
One might apply collyrium in the evening or in the morning, but one should never do so at all times.
It is highly recommended during a season that is neither too cold nor too hot, nor when there is wind or clouds;
the collyrium should be applied below the black portion of the eye, reaching as far as the outer corner.
Candana, dayā, vartī, śaṅkhanābhi, the marrow of bibhītaka, pathyā, manaḥśilā, pippalī, marica, kuṣṭha, and vacā— these should be taken in equal parts. (75)
Having ground [the ingredients] with goat's milk and made a wick the size of a barley grain,
one should rub it with water in the measure of a *hareṇu* seed and apply it as a collyrium (*añjana*).
This cures cataract (*timira*), fleshy growths, cataract-like opacity (*kāca*), film over the eye (*paṭala*), and tumors (*arbuda*).

O King! Night-blindness, seasonal blindness, flowers, a wick, and the moon—these would be conquered by a wick made of *karañja* [oil] that has been repeatedly saturated with the fresh juice of *palāśa* flowers. (77)
A wick made from *karañja* seeds destroys the vision;
a wick made from sea-foam and other substances [is prepared] with sea-foam (*samudraphena*), rock salt (*sindhūttha*), conch-shell (*śaṅkha*), *dakṣāṇḍa*, and bark.
A wick made from *śigru* seeds will cut the semen and other fluids like a surgical instrument (79).
A "tooth-wick" is made from the teeth of elephants, boars, camels, cattle, horses, goats, and donkeys.

A smooth tooth-wick (dantavarti) made from all these substances—conch-shell, pearl, and sea-foam—pulverized together, is a supreme destroyer of seminal fluids (śukra); it is a wick that destroys lethargy (tandrā). 80.
It is a wick that destroys lethargy.
A wick made from the paste of blue lotus, drumstick seed, and likewise nagakeshara removes excessive sleep; this is the "Flower Wick. 81. Puṣpavarti.
Eighty sesame flowers, sixty grains of rice,
fifty jasmine blossoms, and sixteen black peppercorns— having ground these finely in water, a wick is made known as "Kusumikā. 82–83.

This Rasāñjana-wick destroys cataracts (*timira*), *arjuna*, and *śukra* disorders, and removes the growth of flesh; for its application as an ointment (*añjana*), the prescribed measure is one and a half parts of *hareṇukā*. (84) Rasāñjana-wick.
A wick made of *rasāñjana*, the two types of *haridrā*, and the tender leaves of *mālatī* and *nimba*,
combined with the liquid of cow dung, destroys night-blindness.
This is the *dhātrī-ādi-varti*.

O Dhātrī! Having ground one, two, or three times the quantity of *yakṣa-pathya* seeds with water, one should prepare a wick; this collyrium, containing two parts of *hareṇuka*, quickly removes eye discharge as well as the pain of *vāta-rakta*. (86)
One should powder together rasakriyā, tuttha, mākṣika, sindhūttha, sugar, conch-shell, manaḥśilā, gairika, sea-foam, and black pepper. (87)

Having mixed it with honey, one should prepare this medicinal extract (*rasakriyā*) for use as a collyrium; it is the supreme remedy for diseases of the eyelids, cataracts, darkness of vision, opacities, and corneal ulcers. (88) This is the *puṣpaharī* medicinal extract.
A primary particle of camphor combined with banyan-milk, when used as an ointment,
quickly destroys two-month-old *kusuma* [mold] and removes excessive sleep. (89) This is the "sleep-removing ointment."
One should apply collyrium to the eyes made from black pepper rubbed with honey and dog saliva;
excessive sleep is then pacified, just as darkness vanishes at the rising of the sun.
This is *prabodhāñjana*.

Jātī flower, young sprouts [of mango], black pepper, kaṭukī, vacā, and rock salt, ground together with goat's urine, is an ointment that destroys drowsiness; another is the awakening ointment (prabodhāñjana). 91. Another is the awakening ointment.

An eye-salve for awakening [the vision] should be prepared from śirīṣa seeds, cow’s urine, kṛṣṇā, marica, saindhava, sarala, na, śilā, and vacā; this is a medicinal extract (rasakriyā) made from the decoction of dārvī and other herbs. 92.

One should boil these—dārvī, paṭola, madhuka, nimba, padmaka, utpala, and prapauṇḍarīka—in four times the quantity of water; having boiled them until reduced to one-fourth, one should take the decoction and boil it again. 93–94.
In that cold [season], a person should add one-quarter part of honey and sugar;
this medicinal extract (rasakriyā) removes burning sensations, lacrimation, redness, and pain.
This is the *rasāñjanādi-rasakriyā*.
Rasāñjana, sarjarasa, jasmine flowers, realgar, sea-foam, salt, red ochre, and black pepper— these,
taken in equal parts and ground with honey, [are applied] in the case of a moistened eyelid (praklinnavartman).

This collyrium (rasāñjana) made from *guḍūcī* and other ingredients destroys moisture and itching and promotes the growth of eyelashes. (97) One *karṣa* of the fresh juice of *guḍūcī* and one *māṣaka* of honey [should be used].

One should take equal parts of rock salt (saindhava) and honey and grind them all together into a paste. By applying this as an eye-salve (añjana), one conquers pilla, arma, timira, kāca, itching (kaṇḍū), liṅganāśa, and diseases located in both the white and black parts of the eye.
Rasāñjana from *punarnavā* and other herbs [applied] with milk cures itching; with honey it cures ocular discharge; with clarified butter it cures [inflammation of the] cornea;
with oil it cures blindness caused by *timira*; and with sour gruel (*kāñjika*) it cures night-blindness.

Punarnavā quickly conquers [the disease], just as the sun dispels darkness. 100. From the decoction of babūla leaves, once it has been reduced to a linctus, the application of that collyrium [is effective].

This [ointment], combined with honey, undoubtedly conquers eye discharge (netrasrāva). [One should apply] *añjana* made from the juice of *hijjala*; having ground the fruit of *hijjala*, one should daily apply it as an ointment to the eyes with water.
This great medicine should be prepared for the purpose of pacifying the discharge from the eyes.
*Kataka* and other *rasāñjana* preparations clarify the vision;
having ground the fruit of the *kataka* tree with honey, one should apply it as an eye-salve.
That which contains a small amount of camphor is remembered as a clarifier of the eyes (103).
In the case of *śirotpāta*, a medicinal preparation of mercury (*rasakriyā*),
clarified butter, and honey should be used as a collyrium for the pacification of *śirotpāta* (104).
The preparation of a medicinal extract from the fat of a black cobra,
along with conch shell, *kataka* fruit, and collyrium—
this extract quickly bestows sight upon the blind. 105
This collyrium formulation for scraping consists of *lekhanāñjana* (scraping ointment), the skin of a hen's egg, realgar, glass, conch-shell, sandalwood, and rock salt;
this application of collyrium scrapes away *puṣpārma* and other such [ocular lesions]. 106
O King! Kanā, having been cooked within a goat's liver and applied as an ointment to both eyes, quickly destroys night-blindness; likewise, it does so when combined with honey and musk. 107
For the collyrium powder used at night to cure night-blindness,
take half a *śāṇa* of black pepper, two half-*śāṇas* each of long pepper and sea-foam (*arṇavaphena*),
half a *śāṇa* of rock salt, and nine *śāṇas* of antimony collyrium (*sauvīrāñjana*). (108)
This auspicious medicinal powder, ground very finely under the asterism Citrā, is a collyrium that purifies the impurities of those afflicted by itching, cataracts, and phlegm;
it is a healing collyrium and a soft powder-collyrium. 109.
Having ground the *rasaka* on a stone slab and thoroughly saturated it with water,
one should take all that liquid and discard the powder that has settled at the bottom.
When all that water has dried, it becomes like a thin wafer (*parpaṭī*).
Having powdered it, one should thoroughly saturate it three times with the juices of triphalā.
One should then add camphor powder equal to one-tenth part of that; by applying this as an ointment to the eyes, all defects are indeed removed.
This powder removes all diseases and brings comfort to the eyes. For the *prasādana-añjana*: heat *sauvīrāñjana* over a fire and then pour it into the juice of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*).

Likewise, having been sprinkled with the breast milk of women seven times and ground into powder, one should apply it as an ointment to the eyes every day; this is beneficial for the eyes and will undoubtedly destroy all eye disorders.
The probe named *dṛṣṭiprasādanī* [is prepared] with the juices of *triphalā*, *bhṛṅga*, and *śuṇṭhī*, and likewise with clarified butter (115).
A serpent, sprinkled with cow’s urine, honey, and goat’s milk, is then heated.
That medicinal stick (tacchalākā) certainly removes all diseases arising in the eyes;
when applied as a collyrium (pratyañjana), one sees clearly in water, free from defects and with tears gone. (116)

After washing the eye according to the specific disorder, an after-collyrium (pratyañjana) should then be applied. Regarding the prohibition of washing the eyes during collyrium application: one should not employ washing while the morbid humors (doṣa) have not yet been expelled from the eye.
For the counter-collyrium, a powder applied to the eyes when they are heated with a sharp flame serves as a clarifier.
This is the collyrium "Nayanāmṛta.
When pure lead has been melted, one should cast an equal amount of pure mercury into it.
One should grind black collyrium equal in quantity to those two together into a single powder (119).
One should add camphor amounting to one-tenth part of that powder;
this counter-collyrium (pratyañjana) conquers eye diseases and is nectar for the eyes (120).
One should saturate the marrow of *jayapāla* twenty-one times with the juice of *nimbuka*; from that, one should then prepare a medicinal wick (*varti*). 121.
Having rubbed human saliva, one should then apply it as collyrium to the eyes; having conquered the poison of one bitten by a serpent, this restores the human to life.
(122) This is the instruction for increasing the radiance of the eyes.

If, after eating, one rubs the palm of the hand and applies it to the eyes, any diseases that have arisen, as well as cataracts (timira), are destroyed. This is the method for improving vision. 123. Method for increasing sight.

That person who, having filled his mouth with cool water, sprinkles his two eyes with water three times every day, will certainly never suffer from the affliction of eye disease. (124) A humble submission by the author of this work.
Having understood the collection of jewel-like hidden meanings within the ocean of Āyurveda, various compendia have been composed by certain wise men;
taking a small portion of that meaning, this compendium has been made by me.
May the virtuous cast a glance of compassion upon this work,
which, like the beloved of Hari, destroys the poverty of various afflictions through its jewels of yoga— the fruit of studying this treatise.
May that *Saṃhitā* of Śārṅgadhara shine within the hearts of people, which are as pure as lotuses. (127) Conclusion:
For those of short lifespan and limited intellect, this has now been composed according to the capacity for reciting the entirety of the scriptures.
Therefore, in this matter, it is proper that one should diligently practice even a single remedial seed-remedy for the sake of one's own welfare.
(128) Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Clarifying the Eyes," in the Uttarakhanda of the Śrī Śārṅgadharasaṃhitā.
The Śārṅgadharasaṃhitā is hereby completed.
The first supplement;
therein, the first supplement: now begins the section on liver disease (yakṛdroga). 1.
The location of the liver is to be known as below and to the right of the heart; the liver is situated there,
and diseases pertaining to that region are characterized by an abundance of suffering.
In that state, many diseases arise that cause great suffering;
when that [stool] is withered, the signs of the patient are the non-passage of feces and a deficiency of bile.
Pallor, a muddy appearance [of the skin], turbid urine, suppression of eructations, flatulence, vomiting, nausea,
a bitter taste in the mouth upon waking in the morning, hardness of the veins, and dullness of the digestive fire [are the signs].
The body appears like clay, and the tongue is covered with impurities;
these are the signs that arise there, along with pain similar to that of being pulled,
and symptoms of illness when the liver is enlarged.
When the *yakṛt* has increased, pain arises there; likewise,
when it is in the right ribcage, the right shoulder, or the right thigh,
there will be numbness in the right arm and a bitter taste in the mouth.
Discoloration of the feces, cough, blood in the urine, restlessness, loss of strength, fever, constipation with scanty stools,
yellowing of the eyes, and the patient lying on his left side— these are the signs.
In this condition, piercing pain, tearing sensations, burning, jaundice,
loss of sleep, thirst, swelling, and the depletion of the vital essence (sattva) arise; thus, liver abscess (yakṛt-vidradhi) is difficult to cure.
This [disease] generally occurs in the liver and is usually fatal;
by the power of fortune alone, some single creature among living beings is liberated from it.
This is the diagnosis of liver disease (*yakṛdroga*).

From excessive drinking of intoxicants, from the consumption of very hot and heavy food, from the suppression of natural urges, from sleeping during the day and staying awake at night, from excessive sexual indulgence, carrying heavy loads, traveling on foot, and from injury;
Likewise, indeed, due to other terrible karmas, liver diseases (yakṛdroga) arise; one should perform all the treatments prescribed for splenic enlargement (plīhoddiṣṭa) in cases of liver disease.
In that case, as in the treatment for splenomegaly, fomentation with morning urine is desired;

one should drink, according to one's digestive fire, an alkaline preparation extracted from *pūtika* wood along with *viḍaṅga* and *kṛṣṇā* in the morning for the pacification of liver and spleen disorders.

One should extract the blood with leeches or apply an alkaline solution (kṣāra) there; furthermore, a plaster made of the powder of *śigru* bark and mustard seeds is appropriate for that area. Then, one should take one karṣa of *mahādrāvaka* with a measure of one *prastha* of water.
Then, having massaged that area, one should rub it with the feet and thighs;
[the patient] should be made to purge with yellow myrobalan (*haridrā*), *ābhayā*, *dhātrī*, *drākṣā*, *āragvadha*, and rock salt, along with powdered iron and either sesame oil or castor oil.
Regarding the treatment of liver abscess (*yakṛt-vidradhi*): having diagnosed an abscess in the liver by means of symptoms such as hiccup, dyspnea, and pain,
a physician skilled in surgery should apply the *trikūrcaka* instrument there.
Having first made him drink wine that is effective for strength and vitality, and having collected water and other items prescribed as the foremost of requisites,
he comforted the patient with words, whether true or even false.
Having meditated upon the Lord, the warder-off of all calamities,
the physician should be quick-handed, strong, steadfast, firm-minded, discerning, one who has witnessed many procedures, one who has performed his duties, and fearless.

Having taken up a surgical instrument endowed with the qualities of a weapon and a triple-pronged probe, one should cut through the skin— along with its pain and swelling— and together with the blood,
quickly insert it deep inside so that the abscess may be opened.
Then one should draw the weapon out from that [wound] by means of its own channel and without hesitation; otherwise, the vital air (anila) might enter within,
causing distress from the pain of the weapon's impact, which can then be alleviated by sprinkling with water and other such measures.
Having comforted the patient, one should lay them down on their left side;
then one should apply a paste of *atasī* seeds mixed with milk and clarified butter,
and properly administer a measured dose of *ahiphena* extract.
One should have the patient drink milk and meat broth, which restore strength; then, for two months, once the patient has regained life,
he may live comfortably, casting aside all fatigue and consuming light, nourishing food.

A wise physician should apply a large lancet with a blade like an utpala petal to a large abscess (*vidradhi*), but he should not attempt to treat a patient whose abscess has already developed into various types.
Now begins the section on heart disease (*hṛdroga*). 2.
The characteristics of heart diseases such as *āvaraṇika* and others are as follows:
*āvaraṇika* arises from *āmavāta*, from disorders of the kidneys (*vṛkkadoṣa*), or from indulgence in cold and damp conditions.
In one who has not disciplined the self, the covering of the cardiac region is quickly afflicted;
there occurs burning, heat, swelling, heaviness, great pain,
trembling of the abdomen, cough, weakness, and difficulty breathing.
The flow of blood through the nasal passages, dullness of the digestive fire,
swellings in the extremities, and the vessels becoming irregular in their course—
this disease is called *āvaraṇika* by the learned.
As soon as it arises, this [disease] must be treated and never neglected—
whether it be caused by internal wind (āmavāta), injury, or a disease characterized by obstruction (āvaraṇika)— so says Kauṣṭhika.
Swelling arises in the cavity of the heart; this is indeed the Kauṣṭhika disease.

Fever, burning sensation, loss of appetite, trembling, discoloration, diminution of digestive fire, dyspnea, cough, consumption (rājayakṣmā), and the accumulation of pus in the abdominal cavity [are its symptoms].
Fainting, convulsions, and delirium; the pulse flows irregularly—
by some stroke of fortune, this child may perhaps be liberated from this most terrible disease.
When the movement of blood into the uterus is obstructed due to the lack of self-control and through improper diet and lifestyle, that fetal mass becomes enlarged; there,
one experiences cardiac tremors, pain, weakness, and labored breathing.
Dislike, vertigo, and delusion are the symptoms of the two types of *pṛthuka* and *gada*.
A spreading affliction in the region of the heart is known by the name of the disease *āyāmikā*.
Dyspnea, edema, vertigo, fainting, cardiac tremor, dullness of the digestive fire, ascites, insomnia, and the wasting away of strength and flesh—
by these and other such signs, the disease of āyāma (tetanus) is to be recognized.
From wasting (kṣaya) arises a terrible condition known as parikṣaya;
it is the wasting of the muscles of the abdominal cavity, characterized by dyspnea, debility, exhaustion, and vertigo.
Trembling of the heart, dullness of the digestive fire, and swelling arise in succession;
by these and other such signs, the disease known as *parikṣaya* (wasting) is to be recognized. This concludes the section on fat (*medas*).
A mass of fat within the ligaments of the muscle of the cardiac cavity is called *medaḥ-sūtra* by the sages who know the truth;
it is a disease in which the pulse moves very slowly and there is a trembling of the heart.
Despondency, delusion, fainting, and the loss of strength in the tendons occur;
furthermore, due to the rupture of the heart's function, death may happen suddenly.
This most dreadful disease must be treated as soon as it arises.
The disease known as Vikṣepikā is considered to be one that causes tossing about;
when this great disease has arisen, it affects the region of the visceral cavity, specifically below the chest bones.
In the bone of the left shoulder, the left arm, the neck, and the region of the back,
a sharp pain arises that afflicts the vital organs and the life-force; therein piercing, tearing, pulling, and burning sensations are produced.
Repeated obstruction of breath, coldness of the skin, emergence of perspiration, flatulence, distension of the abdomen, delusion, discoloration, emaciation, loss of appetite,
gradual destruction of the sense organs, and death— these are the signs of one who lacks self-mastery.
Those who drink the powder of *kakubha* bark with clarified butter, milk, or molasses-water, having destroyed heart disease,
indigestion, fever, and internal hemorrhaging, shall become long-lived.

A powder derived from *harītakī*, *vacā*, *rāsnā*, *pippalī*, *nāgara*, *śaṭī*, and the root of *puṣkara* destroys heart disease. One should drink the powdered horn of a deer, roasted in a closed vessel (*puṭapāka*) and mixed with cow’s ghee.

Even the most agonizing pain in the heart and back quickly finds relief from this powder made of wheat and *pārtha* (Terminalia arjuna), cooked with sesame, ghee, and molasses; the man who drinks it while subsisting on milk alone becomes a conqueror of all heart diseases.
The Pippalyādi powder consists of long pepper (pippalī),

cardamom (elā), sweet flag (vacā), asafoetida (hiṅgu), alkali of barley (yavakṣāra), rock salt (saindhava), black salt (sauvarcala), dry ginger (śuṇṭhī), and ajamoda, all ground together into a powder.

For a patient whose body has been purified, one should have them drink curd, wine, fermented liquor (āsava), sour gruel (kāñjika), or ghee, in cases of heart disease caused by Vāta. When the heart is afflicted by Pitta, cooling plasters, affusions, and purgation are likewise indicated.
In the case of vomiting caused by bile, one should drink a decoction of *drākṣā*, *kṣitā*, honey, and *parūṣaka*; or, once purified, one should consume food and drink that increases bile.
Alternatively, having ground *yaṣṭyāhvaya* (liquorice) and *tiktakarohiṇī*, one should drink them with water and sugar;
or, when vomiting arises from phlegm in the heart, one should drink a decoction of *vacā* and *nimba*.

One should administer the Pippalyādi powder for heart disease caused by Vāta; in cases arising from all three Doshas, fasting (laṅghana) should be performed first. Furthermore, food that is beneficial in all cases should be prescribed, and the three types of therapeutic measures should be applied according to whether the condition is mild, moderate, or severe.

One should drink asafoetida, ugragandhā, viḍa salt, viśva, kṛṣṇā, kuṣṭha, abhayā, citraka, and yavaśūka, enriched with sauvarcala salt and puṣkaramūla, along with barley-water; this destroys colic and heart disease.
[Likewise, one may take] pāṭhā, vacā, yavakṣāra, abhayā, and amlavetasa.
One should have Durālabhā, Citraka, Trikaṭu, the three types of Balā, Śaṭī, Puṣkaramūla, Tintiḍīka together with pomegranate,
and the roots of Mātuluṅga made into a fine powder.
One should cause these to be drunk soaked in warm water or with wines;
this quickly subdues hemorrhoids, colic, heart disease, and abdominal tumors.
In cases of worm-infestation, one should drink urine combined with *viḍaṅga* and iron.
Thus, worms residing in the heart of men fall downward;
thereafter, one should give him barley-food along with viḍaṅga.
Now follows the section on the chest and water (3).
The accumulation of water in one side of the chest, or in both sides,
is known as the disease *urastoya* (chest-water), which generally destroys life.
Its symptoms are labored breathing, expectoration of phlegm, bluish lips, swelling of the face,
and a small, uneven, earth-like flow of urine that comes with great force.
There will also be scantiness of urine, and that man is unable to lie down;
while sitting, he attains some slight relief in this great disease.
[This concludes] the diagnosis of *urastoya* (water in the chest) from another treatise.

The breathing is extremely difficult, there is a discharge of phlegm, and both lips, the face, and the eyes are blue. There is no perspiration, and the stool and urine are scanty. Distressed by dyspnea, the patient is unable to lie down;
his senses are dull, his strength, digestive fire, and luster are diminished, and the pulse is feeble and rapid.
Pain in the heart and swelling in both feet— these are the symptoms that arise in this disease;
the treatment consists of medicines that eliminate phlegm (kapha) and promote the flow of urine.
In cases of chest afflictions and edema, the physician should always administer [medicines] after careful discernment; thirst must be restrained, cold water should be consumed,
and one should diligently avoid everything that causes internal secretions (abhiṣyandi).
One should drink a small amount of that water which remains after the feet have been washed when thirsty;
or, one should always bring relief from thirst by drinking milk that has been boiled and then warmed,
or even the fresh juice of Varṣābhū mixed with Yava-kṣāra.
One who is free from sloth should drink this water regularly every morning and evening for swelling,
dysuria, cough, asthma, and heart disease;
whatever medicine has been prescribed [elsewhere] should be employed here as well.
If this disease were not to be pacified even by all ritual acts,
then a physician of light hand would perform surgical intervention either in the midst of the ocean, or between the earth and the mountains.
Having inserted the instrument called *trikūrcaka* between the two rib bones in the direction of the shoulder-blade,
one should carefully protect the liver and spleen while draining the fluid completely;
in this way, the disease is pacified.
Now begins the section on secondary (aupasargika) and incidental (upadaṃśa) diseases, number four.
Their causes, symptoms, and so forth are as follows:
[this disease] arises in the male organ through the consumption of many mixed [substances].
This wound is most painful and terrible, manifesting as various diseases;
it is described as being caused by poison or by sin, and is likewise called "supervening" (aupasargika) by the ancient sages.
This disease spreads from woman to man, and from him likewise to her, and it may arise even among their offspring; this hereditary condition is truly dreadful.
Upadaṃśa is said to be of two kinds, distinguished as primary (mukhya) and secondary (gauṇa).
The first defect of the organ is the primary one, while the other is burning;
starting from the time of the procedure and within the interval of three weeks,
a wound caused by the bite of a poisonous creature arises in the generative organ.
That which persists for an exceedingly long time, having passed through such duration,
would likewise be most difficult to endure and a source of much suffering;
due to the two-fold nature of the secondary affliction of sin, the wound may be either hard or soft.
The first type is transmissible, difficult to treat, and causes a burning sensation throughout the entire body;
the other is not transmissible and does not afflict the whole body.
This latter is said to be more easily curable and is not as painful as the first.
In men, pustules arise on the penis and the glans; likewise, in women, they appear all around the covering skin of the vulva, at the vaginal opening, and in the labia majora—
hard, and when burst, they discharge lymph.
Deep-rooted and depressed in the middle, causing fever, scrotal enlargement, and other ailments—
this is known as the primary form of Upadaṃśa (venereal disease). Even when this has subsided, the poison residing within the body may indeed cause various disorders once again.
Secondary venereal disease (gauṇopadaṃśa) is characterized by skin disorders, eye diseases, loss of hair on the head and body,
glandular swellings, chronic catarrh, and leprosy.
Skin disorders and the like are indicated by the term "gauṇopadaṃśa";
"viṣopadaṃśa" refers to poison; and [the condition] associated with the accumulation of phlegm in glandular swellings is that of "pāpopadaṃśa."
It produces a disease of the penis accompanied by fever and great suffering;
the treatment for this ulcerative sore (piḍikā) of upadaṃśa should be performed by applying caustic alkali (kṣāra).
By that, the disease is pacified; no other calamities arise.
One should carefully grind the purified mercury with the two [substances] until the mercury is no longer visible due to its hardness.
One should consume two *guñjā* seeds of this [preparation] daily, held in the mouth for three *puṭas*;
it should be abandoned in cases of pain in the gums and excessive salivation.
This is due to the consumption of the mercury-powder and the essence of camphor.
By this very method, that terrible disease is pacified;
having thrown a powder measuring half a *pala* into five *śarāva*s of water and having stirred it thoroughly, [one should wait] until the end of four watches (*yāma*s).
One should very carefully collect its clear upper portion;
this powder-water destroys acidity and heals wounds and urinary disorders.
To two palas of this powder-water, one māṣaka of the medicinal juice-powder should be added.
One should throw [the ingredients] in and mix them until the liquid becomes black in appearance;
this supreme great medicine, used for washing with this black extract, removes wounds and is especially recommended for upadaṃśa (venereal sores).
Into this [mixture] measuring two and a half palas, one should add nine rattis of camphor essence; having prepared this yellow medicinal liquid with it,
one should wash the ulcer caused by the infection of a wound with that water.

This is indeed declared by the wise to be the supreme medicine here; whatever treatment is prescribed for Vidradhi is also beneficial in Bradhna, as well as in Gaunopadamsha and Vishama-jvara, along with pitta-alleviating measures and blood purification.
One should prescribe sugar, medicine, food, and drink;
[specifically] Anantādyam Ghr̥ta, as well as Anantā, Āmalakī, Drākṣā, the pair of Kākolīs, and Varī.
The two types of cardamom, vidārī, madhūka, madhuka, murā,
triphalā, svarṇaparṇī, seeds of gokṣura,
the ten roots (daśamūla), the pair beginning with tālamūlī, trivṛt, and indravāruṇī.
Having ground one karṣa each of nīlinī, śūkaśimbī, and its seeds into a paste, one should cook it with a prastha of ghee and water from the sārivā plant;
this ghee, beginning with anantā, destroys upadaṃśa.
This supreme elixir is aphrodisiac, a destroyer of the defects of the heart,
a medicine that pacifies skin diseases (kuṣṭha) and likewise removes vātarakta;
it should be applied appropriately to both secondary and primary cases of upadaṃśa.
In particular,

one suffering from pāpameha, one with vātarakta, one with leprosy (kuṣṭha), or one afflicted by a venereal disease (pāpopadaṃśa) should avoid women; nor should a woman who suffers from such diseases approach a man.
Now begins the chapter on hemiplegia caused by external factors (5).
Hemiplegia is known to be of two types, distinguished as being born of the *doṣas* or from external causes.
That which is born of the *doṣas* has been described previously; now hear about that which is born of external causes.
The exogenous form is also of two types:
hemiplegia is described as being first produced by mercury (*pārada*) and secondly by lead (*nāga*).
The etiology of the mercury-induced hemiplegia is as follows:
Due to the constant contact with the taste [of mercury] and the consumption of its properties,
that which results in hemiplegia (pakṣāghāta) should be known as arising from pārada; such is the symptom of pārada-induced hemiplegia.
First there is the destruction of strength in the arms, then trembling arises;
thereafter both thighs and the entire body tremble. The wielder of the mace moves as if dancing, and indeed he cannot firmly hold his weapon.
He is unable to speak clearly or even to chew;
consequently, he suffers from aversion to food, sleepiness, delirium, and loss of strength.
There is nausea, loss of digestive fire, decay of the teeth, and occasionally discharge.
There is a pacification of trembling when the elixir is held in the hand;
now hear from me briefly the symptoms of the "serpent-ailment" caused by the blow of mercury's wings,
and the treatment for it.

The primary treatment for this is the avoidance of its causes; for a disease that follows its etiological factors does not subside through medicine alone. All sudation, diuretics, and purgatives [should be employed].
In this case, a medicine that removes blood disorders and bestows comfort is considered appropriate;
they say sulfur is the supreme medicine for diseases of mercury (pārada),
and iron should be consumed with water from the Nimba tree of Nepal for its pacification.
The cause of the wing-stroke of the Nāgas is this:
for those headed by Citrakṛt who perform work for the Nāgas, or those who trade with their vessels, from that [act] comes their affliction.
Its characteristic is this:
beginning from the fingers and extending all the way to the wrist, the disease spreads throughout; weakness therein is one major symptom.
Pain in the shoulders, the forearms, and the arms, discoloration, and inflammation of the gums— these are indeed the signs of this [disease]; now follows its treatment.

All treatments for leprosy (kuṣṭha), including sudation (svedana) and purgation (bhedana), as well as whatever other medicines are curative of leprosy, should be employed here after having first avoided the causes; thus ends the sixth chapter on the agitation caused by disease.

The nature of "fear of disease" (gadodvega) is defined as the apprehension of disease in the absence of actual disease; because it lacks the status of being a real entity, it is called an "entityless disease" (apadārthaga).
For one who has fallen into a state of distress and agitation regarding what is not an actual object, the primary causes are excessive physical and mental exhaustion, grief, loss of strength,
despair, loss of self-respect, great agitation, and great fear.
Poor vision, defects in the seed, and the absence of the vital essence (sattva)— these are declared by the wise to be the causes of the disease known as apadārtha;
its symptoms are as follows:
Regarding these wondrous symptoms of this marvelous disease,
and these inconceivable, unthinkable portents of great calamity,
someone might surely think that a serpent has entered his belly.
"He wanders constantly within my stomach; whatever I eat, he consumes.
By what path will he exit? By what means will he perish? What will he do to us? Or shall I be devoured by this evil-minded one? I do not know."
Or someone might think, "A single frog is perched upon my head;
he is crushing my brain and will surely kill me.
Someone else might likewise think, "How strange! My body is made of glass!"
"Since this [self] has been born, it must therefore be protected with great effort from injury"—
thus, agitated by such manifold and futile anxieties,
one who speaks of non-existent things will always wither away, ever fearful and ever miserable.
Though awakened in many ways and repeatedly consoled,
he is unable to remove this delusion from his mind nor his fear; moreover,
he always shows hostility toward anyone who points out his error.

One who is distressed by disease is pleased when someone speaks of the reality of that disease; for one afflicted by illness, an extremely intense pain is generally experienced within the abdominal cavity, particularly in the region of the digestive tract.

The tongue becomes coated with phlegm, the mouth is foul-smelling, and breath exits with a putrid odor; there is nausea as well as vomiting—such are the symptoms of indigestion (jīrṇa). Furthermore, there is numbness of the sense of touch, loss of luster, and redness of the face.
Trembling of the heart and belly, paleness, abdominal disease,
and a chronic ailment in the chest— by whom else, afflicted by such maladies, has the destruction of manhood been experienced?
A continuous fever is indeed difficult to treat by other means; what wonder is there that trembling and other symptoms arise from time to time?
Thus, diseases of many forms are created by the imagination.
These arise in the form of delusions for those who are devoid of strength and lacking in intelligence;
these diseases cannot be described in their entirety,
but they must be identified by the wise according to their respective characteristics and the signs of the *doṣas*.
Generally, this disease is observed to occur before the age of sixteen and not beyond fifty; its cause is the state of the mind.
Every month, through the flow of the menses, all the bodily constituents (dhātus) are purified.
Therefore, this disease that afflicts the ligaments generally does not arise in women;
its treatment consists of soothing, consolation, oleation, cheering, and nursing during times of distress from the ailment.
One should treat that which is afflicted by the onset of symptoms not yet manifest with thirst-quenching measures;
one should employ here such medicine as is digestive, kindles the digestive fire, promotes the downward movement of vāta, removes pitta, and does not excessively increase kapha.

In this regard, a wise physician should skillfully employ oils and ghees prescribed for wind-diseases (vātavyādhi), as well as medicinal elixirs (rasāyana). The physician should never say to such a patient that his ailment is false.
One should listen attentively to whatever account he relates.
Now begins the section on the eligibility for renunciation in childhood (śaiśava-saṃnyāsa).
[This includes] the cause and the characteristics of renunciation in childhood.
Furthermore, by drinking corrupted breast milk, by constantly staying in a cool room,
or in one devoid of wind and sunlight yet vitiated by foul air, and by various harmful drinks, foods, and activities, the infant [is afflicted].
Afflicted by the disease known as saṃnyāsa, he is likewise tormented by worms; his eyes are turned upward, his limbs are convulsed, and being unconscious,
he falls to the ground like a log, his body rigid and resembling one who is dead.
This disease is named *śaiśava-saṃnyāsa*; it afflicts children.
In this case, purgation (*recana*) is considered beneficial, as it yields immediate results.
This is the treatment for *śaiśava-saṃnyāsa*.

In cases of disease or renunciation during childhood, one should exert every effort to eliminate the underlying causes; likewise, one should perform actions that remove karmic defects by means of *rubūta* oil or medicinal powders.
In the case of a child’s *saṃnyāsa* (failure to thrive), purgation is indicated, and fomentation (*sveda*) is beneficial for that abdomen.
One should have a healthy woman who nurses the child drink pure breast milk,
or one should perform purification of the milk for whichever woman’s milk the child drinks.
In the case of a child's abandonment due to worms, the removal of the worms is beneficial;
in a state of fainting (mūrchā), the physician should administer mercury mixed with long pepper and honey.
Now begins the section on epilepsy in women (yoṣā-apasmāra-adhikāra).
A woman is the primary cause of epilepsy (apasmāra),
as well as [its onset] due to the depletion of blood, its excess, indigestion (ajīrṇa),
obstruction of the abdominal cavity (koṣṭha), mental distress, extreme agitation, and grief.
Due to the absence of *rajas* in women, as well as the transformation of the fetal membrane (*jarāyu*), lack of capacity, harshness, lack of affection from the husband,
and the affliction arising from widowhood, there occurs that which is known as female epilepsy (*yoṣāpasmāra*).
A difficult-to-cure disease arises that torments both the mind and the body;
because this disease occurs predominantly in women,
it is considered to be designated by the name "Apasmāra" (epilepsy).
The time for this disease of youth is not before twelve years,
nor does this disease arise after fifty; this is its prodromal symptom.
Heartache, yawning, and a sense of exhaustion in both the body and the mind will occur;
these are the symptoms that will appear when a woman suffers from the disease known as apasmāra (epilepsy).
Agitation, confusion of the intellect, laughter, and weeping;
loud crying out, delirious speech, aversion to light, as well as vertigo, arrogance, labored breathing, and pain in the throat and stomach.
There is always an intensity of the power of touch in a certain part of the body, constant pain,
the appearance of false circular spots extending from the belly up to the neck,
diminished intellect, and fainting; such are the symptoms that arise in this disease.
Its treatment consists of whatever drink, food, and medicine nourishes the bodily constituents (dhātus),
as well as that which purifies the digestive tract; all such things should be employed here.
In a state of fainting (mūrchā), one should apply a sprinkling of cold water on the head and eyes,
or even administer head-purgation (śiro-virecana) to bring it to an end;
in this case, one should employ every medicinal treatment prescribed for fainting and epilepsy (apasmāra).
One should remedy all the defects of the womb according to the prescribed rules;
forgetfulness in a woman is pacified through conciliatory words and the giving of pleasant gifts, and here also the "Great Bhūta-Bhairava" elixir should be administered.
Now begins the ninth chapter, "The Intoxication of Reality.
As for its essential nature:
"Oh, how great is my fortune, that I have obtained the grace of Brahman!"
Thus, this delusion born of error is called "madness regarding reality" (tattvonmāda).
This madness regarding reality, which consists of joy and delusion, is known as "delusion concerning Brahman" (brahmamoha); this disease, arising from futile thought, has been described by the wise.
"What is the nature of Brahman, or where does it reside? Alas, no one knows this!
Even through the ancient philosophical systems, the vision of Brahman has not been attained;
some declare the universe to have a creator, while others say it is without a Lord."
The cosmic egg is confounded by various futile speculations of the Brahma-tarka; its existence is difficult to comprehend, let alone such qualities as compassion;
it is thus indeterminate and incapable of being determined—understand it in this way.
"O Brahmins, act for my sake; abandon this enemy of mine!
Give me wealth, burnish my fame, and grant me a kingdom free of thorns—a woman with wide eyes, beautiful teeth, and full, elevated breasts."

Grant me that beautiful woman, who has shapely hips and a slender waist, who is skilled in the arts of amorous play, ever fond of jesting, slim-limbed, a mistress of aesthetic delight, devoted to my vows, eternally contented, and full of charm.
O man of deluded intellect, do not think that Brahmā, merely upon hearing these words, will become afraid and act with such haste as to fulfill your request;
perhaps some prayer of yours might eventually bear fruit.
Know that to be "like the crow and the palm fruit" (a chance occurrence); in that regard, Brahman is not the cause.
Brahman does not rejoice in praises, nor does it feel aversion toward blame.
One who asserts existence is not dear to it, nor is one who asserts non-existence unloved.
He has no disregard for the fool, nor excessive respect for the scholar;
he feels no fear toward the wealthy, nor does he inflict punishment upon the poor; whether it be a dog-cooker, a Yavana, or even a Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas, [he treats them all alike].
Whether in one who drinks liquor, one attached to a courtesan, or one who wears garlands and forehead marks;
whether in a pure person or an impure one; in a virtuous woman or a prostitute; and in both the young and the old—everywhere indeed is the same Brahman, the universal form, the eternal.
"This work is mine" is the thought of one who has become such as this;
for he whose mind is intoxicated by reality suffers from the very disease of madness.
Indeed, for the wicked and base-minded who lack intelligence, madness is generally their only recourse.
This disease may arise even for the great;
it is the cause of a delusion regarding reality, resulting from an excessively intense mental attachment to phenomena and the like.
A disease called *tattvonmada* arises from the provocation of *vāta*;
its symptom is extreme delusion regarding reality and a fixed, motionless gaze of the pupils.
The opening of the eyes, sleep, obstruction of movement, eloquence of speech, deceitful and fierce dispositions, agitation, laughter, drunkenness, and weeping—
such indeed are the signs that occur in the madness of the *tattvas*.
Whatever medicine, drink, or food stabilizes the tendons, cures the intoxication of reality, and likewise facilitates the downward movement of the bodily winds (vāta),
that should be employed here.
Anointing with ghee purified a hundred times, and the equal application of honey and ghee,
as well as ghee mixed with water, are the supreme remedies for *brahmamoha*;
sometimes *brahmamoha* is also pacified through beating and other such means.
When that [state] has become unnatural, a blow is indeed the remedy;
furthermore, everything such as clarified butter and oil— which removes epilepsy and likewise cures wind-diseases— is recommended for the delusion caused by Brahman.
Now begins the chapter on disorders of the brain and the tendons (mastiska-snayu-vikara-adhikara).
Due to dry, scanty, or light food, excessive exposure to heat, grief, travel, anxiety, and indulgence in women,
the collection of tendons in the brain of men undergoes desiccation and weakness.

There may occur various disorders such as weakness of strength, impairment of all the sense organs, loss of luster, dejection of mind, loss of sleep, and trembling in the heart. Now begins the section on the pain of the sinews (snāyu-śūla). 11.
That which is extremely terrible, characterized by pain in the sinews, and which occurs either in the limbs or even in the sinews themselves,
is known as *snāyu-śūla* (sinew-pain); it is a tormentor of life.
The site of the disease may be in the arms, the head, the thighs, or indeed any other limb; furthermore,
the disorder occurs specifically within the veins situated beneath the skin.
This *śūla* (piercing pain) occurs in all the limbs and causes intense agony;
it also receives specific names based on the particular limb in which it arises,
such as *ūrdhvabheda*, *ardhabheda*, and likewise *adhobheda*.
The names for the various types of baldness (*muṇḍa*) are, in order: *muṇḍa*, *ardhaka*, *sphija*, and *jagada*.
Among these, the primary cause of the upward-ascending type (*ūrdhvabheda*) is either the depletion of strength and blood or a disorder of the kidneys and brain.
From indigestion and dental disease, a disorder characterized by upward displacement may arise;
its symptoms appear on the forehead, the eyelids, the hollows of the cheeks, the nose, and the lips.
When there is pain like a piercing ache or a burning sensation on the sides of the tongue, the lower lip,
or the teeth— generally on one side of the face—
it is called *ūrdhvabheda* by the experts in medicine (*agadaṅkāra*). This is the description according to the sequence [of symptoms].
The disease increases through contact with cool breezes and from trembling of the body;
it becomes a disorder characterized by the breaking of tendons and the splitting of the limbs.
The cause of hemiplegia (ardhabheda) is as follows:
it arises from residing in a damp place, exposure to cold, loss of strength,
and the influence of vitiated wind and water.
The definition of *ardhabheda* (hemiplegia) is as follows:
that intense pain which, having pervaded half [the face], occurs in the region of the mouth and generally on the left side, is proclaimed as *ardhabheda*.
Like a head pierced by an arrow, it throbs with extreme and most dreadful pain; sometimes, by adopting a gradual approach, there may be a great cessation here,
yet for women, this disease generally arises in abundance.

The manifestation [of hemorrhoids] in one established in youth is considered excessive during adolescence; it is the primary cause for the downward displacement [of the humors] due to suppression of stool,
fatigue, cold, debility, and āmavāta.
Due to the defect of the embryo remaining in a moist place, there occurs a fissure in the lower part; the symptoms of this lower fissure appear on the buttocks,
the thighs, the joints of the knees, and sometimes on the back of the feet.
The pain that occurs in the calf is called *adhobheda*;
this pain usually occurs in one leg and is strong at night;
it generally arises only in mature adulthood.
The treatment for ligament pain (snāyuśūla) consists of whatever medicine serves to kindle the digestive fire, or that which increases strength,
or that which facilitates the downward movement of Vāta.
To pacify the partial manifestation of the poison of wood,
this iron powder known as *madirāmṛtasāra*, along with the ash of *kupīlu* fruit, should be administered; it must never be used when the poison is in full fury.
These [remedies] should be employed according to the prescribed method for the pacification of pain in the tendons;
one should apply fomentation, affusion, and medicinal pastes to tendon-pains,
and in cases of an accumulation of morbid humors, one should administer a strong purgative.

Clarified butter, oil, and other such substances that destroy diseases of the wind (vāta) should be applied; they are the medicine for all types of ligament pain and are a rejuvenative elixir (rasāyana).
Now begins the chapter on the disease Tāṇḍava.
On a delightful peak of the Himalayas, frequented by hosts of perfected ones and seers, adorned with fragrant flowers, beautified by many fruit-bearing trees,
echoing with the sweet warbling of birds, and filled with numerous peaceful wild beasts.
As soon as Ātreya, the ocean of knowledge, the great teacher of Ayurveda, whose body was radiant with asceticism, had sat down at the foot of the banyan tree,
a devoted goat addressed him from before, with palms joined in reverence.
"How does the disease of *tāṇḍava* arise, what are its symptoms, and how may it be remedied? Out of compassion, tell me all of this.
Having heard this request from his wise disciple, he who is affectionate toward his disciples [spoke].
The lord of sages began to speak with words of clear meaning:
"O devoted child, I am pleased; I shall tell you that which you wish to hear regarding the primary cause."
That which Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds, previously declared regarding Dakṣa:
even from affliction, excessive anger, excessive joy, loss of strength, emaciation, suppression of sleep, constipation, and the accumulation of worms.
From the frustration of hopes, from violent blows, from the irregularity of women's menses, and from the excessive consumption of *kaśerukā* (a type of grass),
there arises a disease named *Tāṇḍava*, which causes supreme suffering to living beings.
Because of the dancing of its limbs, this condition is termed "Tāṇḍava" by the wise;
it generally arises in youth, especially in women,
and also in the elderly due to the loss of strength.

The symptoms of the disease of *tāṇḍava*: beginning with the left arm, and generally first [the right], then the other [arm], then the feet, and then the limbs—one should move them; such is the affliction of *tāṇḍava*.
Unable to grasp any object properly with his fist,
nor even to place edible food into his mouth,
this man moves about like one dancing a *tāṇḍava*, with loathsome facial contortions.
One who is restless should remain constantly free from trembling during sleep;
this is the treatment for *tāṇḍava*,
consisting of nourishing and purgative therapies that increase the strength of the digestive fire.
Medicine, drink, and food should be administered in the case of *tāṇḍava* disease; when it arises from an accumulation of worms, the destruction of the worms must be effected;
and in a disease born from the obstruction of the *rajas* humor, the flow of the *rajas* must be set in motion.
Having boiled *śyāmā*, *anantā*, *madhuka*, *trivṛtā*, the two types of *candana*,
the two types of *elā*, and *dhātrī* together, one should drink the water; by this,
the disease known as *tāṇḍava* will certainly be pacified.
Tāṇḍavāri-lauha should also be administered.
Now begins the section on the disease of the kloma (13):
[The kloma] is situated between the spleen and the small intestine, and its function consists of the digestion of food and so forth.
The *kloma*, which is named after sesame seeds (*tila*), occupies the space adjacent to its companion [the liver].
Its increase and softening are caused by heavy, excessively unctuous foods, as well as by non-restraint and similar factors; therein occurs the accumulation of blood.
In that case, there may be hemorrhage or other terrible diseases;
when the *tilaka* has thus undergone such a transformation, there occurs a depletion of digestive fire (*vahni-saṃkṣaya*),
as well as nausea, vomiting, emaciation, pallor, lassitude, and vertigo.
In ūrdhvodara, there is intense pain, hardness, and heat, along with colic, flatulence, and excessive salivation; in vidradhi, there is great thirst,
and even a stone-like calculus (aśmarī) arises here, which is extremely difficult to treat.
Regarding the treatment of *kloma*:
whatever food, drink, or medicine stimulates the digestive fire (*vahni*) and promotes the downward movement of the wind (*māruta*), all of that is beneficial for one afflicted with *kloma*.
Whichever disease may take refuge in the *kloman*, having observed each one, the physician should accomplish the treatment according to the specific *doṣa* and the relative strength [of the patient],
using decoctions of *abhayā* and others, *surendramodaka*, the elixirs of *śaśiśekhara*, and *surendrābhravaṭī*.

And likewise, medicines that pacify *vāta* and *pitta* should be employed for the alleviation of *kloma* disease. Now begins the section on kidney disease (14): its premonitory symptoms (*pūrvarūpa*).
The skin becomes rough and hot, the vessels become prominent and hard,
and there is loss of sleep, dullness of the digestive fire, and swelling in the eyes, face, and feet; these, the best of physicians say, are the premonitory symptoms of kidney disease.
The symptoms of kidney disease (vṛkkāmaya) are as follows: due to the deficiency of blood, there is paleness of the face,
pain in the waist, dryness of the skin, absence of perspiration, and a rapid pulse.
There is weakness of the digestive fire, indigestion, aversion to food, pain in the abdomen, sour eructations, vomiting, trembling of the heart, labored breathing,
and scanty urine; furthermore, there is a constant urge to urinate, which arises especially at night.
At the time of urination, a slight burning sensation is experienced at the tip of the penis; furthermore, in this disease, a disorder of the kidneys specifically arises,
and it always occurs in conjunction with disorders of the liver, spleen, and heart as well.
Tinnitus, impairment of vision, pain in the head, neck, and shoulders,
heaviness in the limbs, and fainting are the symptoms of kidney disease;
this is the etiology of kidney disorders.
Indeed, from the transformation of blood, a disorder of the kidneys arises;
its treatment consists of that which promotes urination, purifies the blood, provides nourishment, and increases the digestive fire.
In cases of kidney disease, a physician who is knowledgeable in the prescribed methods should administer it after observing the strength of the disorder;
he should increase the patient's nutritional essence (rasa) but should not employ it with oil,
nor should he employ the medicinal herbs mentioned in the section on rejuvenation (rasāyana).

And there is no specific medicine prescribed for its pacification; however, *sarvatobhadrā* pills should also be administered. This concludes the section on secondary types of urinary disorders (*upasargika-meha*). 15.
Even though it is fouled by the discharge of many impurities, when a man unites with a woman, he becomes deluded and incurs a terrible disease;
for the skin situated within the urinary canal is a channel for phlegm.
Or, when it draws out the moisture from a wound, it is called *vraṇameha*; *aupasargikameha* is considered another name for it,
and by some it is also recited as *āgantukameha*.
Starting from the night of sexual union, on the seventh day—
or at some time thereafter— a disease generally arises;
there is itching at the tip of his penis, which occurs again and again.

Or, due to intense pain, there may be frequent urination, swelling of the penis, redness, and pain in the scrotum and the glans; occasionally, because the passage is obstructed by discharge, it may flow with excessive pain.
Due to a terrible burning sensation, the urine flows out in two streams,
or blood may sometimes flow from the penis at the time of urination;
first a thin discharge flows continuously, and thereafter it becomes thick.
If that [undigested matter] is again quickly reabsorbed, it leads to a sense of well-being; however, at the [wrong] time, it may cause slight pain and a disease difficult to treat,
and complications such as *āmavāta* and eye diseases are to be known as its sequelae.
The treatment for Aupagrika-meha:
A patient suffering from Vraṇameha should carefully avoid sexual intercourse, because it is harmful and would cause that same disease to arise in the woman with whom he has consorted.
One should consume medicine, drink, and food that are soothing,
heal the ulcer, and promote urination; one should avoid harsh treatments and immerse the penis in a lukewarm decoction of *jātī* or *varā*.
Through that, there is the subsiding of pain and the depletion of the strength of the disease;
one should drink a decoction of *ābhā* mixed with barley-alkali (*yavakṣāra*) and water,
or raw milk, for the cessation of ulcerative urinary disorders.
Or one should drink a decoction of śārivā together with alkali and the juice of narasāra;
or having boiled water with śyāmā, anantā, kaṭvī, and the seeds of gokṣura, along with gandhāśman and the juice of narasāra, one should drink it.
One *surapriya* fruit should be used to remove the discharge of urine;
for the cessation of wounds and urinary discharge, one should diligently administer an *uttarabasti* (urethral/vaginal enema) using a decoction of *varā*, *abhā*, and *pippalī*.
The Mahābhravaṭika and Kandarparasa should also be employed here.
Now begins the chapter on diseases of the head and the eyes (Śīrṣāmburogādhikāra), section 16: Etiology and Pathogenesis.
Due to excessive drinking of alcohol, exposure to extreme cold, consumption of incompatible foods, vitiation of the bodily wind (vāyu),

drinking contaminated water, physical trauma, and likewise the presence of worms within the intestines, an excessively large quantity of water gradually accumulates when the fatty tissues (sneha) located in the head are obstructed.

This remedy known as Śīrṣāmbu was proclaimed by the ancients; it is a disease considered most difficult for physicians to treat, occurring generally in childhood due to the indulgence in various unwholesome things,
and it arises most frequently from the eruption of teeth.
Its premonitory symptoms will be a coated tongue, excessive sleepiness, weakness, foul breath,
and constipation; these shall indeed occur in that condition.
Its symptoms are:
severe pain in the head, acuteness of hearing and vision, scanty urine, black stools, and the pulsation of the arteries with great force.

The skin is rough and hot; likewise, there is vomiting, and the pupils are irregular. There is irritability, discoloration of the face, sleepiness, grinding of the teeth, itching of the lips, twitching of the nose, and redness of the eyes.
Hemiplegia, delirium, and the symptoms of head-disease (śīrṣāmbu-gada) are described;
furthermore, in another treatise, the etiology of head-disease states that corrupted water—
extremely cold, vitiated, and windy— [is the cause].
In children who consume unwholesome or incompatible food,
and due to injuries from falling or the presence of parasites, a considerable amount of fluid accumulates within the head.
The premonitory symptoms (pūrvarūpa) of this disease are excessive sleep, loss of strength,
foul-smelling breath, and hardness of the stool.
Its symptoms are constant, intense pain in the head,
as well as scanty urination, vomiting, and heat.
Discoloration of the face, blackness of the impurities,
and even a reddish tint to the pair of eyes;
itching of the nose and lips, flapping of the wings [or eyelids], convulsions, and grinding of the teeth.
The pulse flows excessively through the vessels; this is the symptom of head and eye diseases. The treatment consists of medicinal purgation and whatever promotes the flow of urine.
Whatever [remedy] removes blood disorders is beneficial for diseases of the head;
having shaved the head, one should cover it with a warm cloth and also cause [the patient] to drink coconut oil continuously.
The wise physician should administer a small dose of this powder to one who has drunk *trivṛt* from the dark variety (*śyāmā*), along with *pathyā*, *āmalakī*, *śaṭī*, *anantā*,
*madhuka*, *mustā*, *dhānyaka*, and *kaṭurohiṇī*.
Having boiled the two types of *haridrā* and *trijāta* according to the prescribed method,
one should administer it along with *yavakṣāra* for his relief;
[one should also use] the powder that dries up the fluids and the *ghṛta* beginning with saffron (*kuṅkuma*).
In this case, oil extracted from *rasa* should be applied along with substances that are bright and fiery; however,
as long as the disease has not subsided, a skilled physician should carefully extract fluid from the brain using a small *trikūrcaka* instrument.
Now begins the chapter on tremors of the brain (mastīṣkavepana), number 17.
As for its etiology and symptoms: when the head is struck by various [injuries], fainting, nausea, and vomiting occur.
Inertness, throbbing, decline, weakness, mental instability, trembling, ringing in the ears, impurity of the face,
dilation of the pupils, and the loss of strength in the arteries.
Coldness of the body and likewise of speech, as well as hemiplegia and trembling of the head— this is the disease [Śīrṣavepana]; its treatment [is as follows].
One should perform actions that produce steadiness of mind; when there is trembling of the brain or heat in the head, sprinkling with very cold water is beneficial;
and purgation with the oil of *dantī* destroys the trembling of the brain.
To obtain strength, wine that restores the dead should be administered in the proper measure, along with other strengthening medicines;
a skilled physician should thus remove the coldness of the limbs by means of great heat.
Having decocted trivṛt, svarṇapatrī, mustaka, madhuka, balā,
the two types of haridrā, nāgara, triphalā, and kaṭurohiṇī,
it should be administered for the alleviation of tremors of the head.
Sindūra (vermilion) with a decoction of *balā* destroys headache and shivering;
