it removes all wind-related diseases (*vātavyādhi*) and brings about his pacification.
Now begins the chapter on the increase and decrease of the brain matter (*mastiska*). 18.
The brain matter and the skull of children as well as of youths sometimes increase due to their physical constitution and through destiny.
If there is growth of both the brain and the skull,
no sign is generally visible due to their simultaneous enlargement;
however, if there is growth of the brain alone and not of the skull, [then signs appear].
Then, from that oppression, various ailments arise:
intense and acute pain in the head, debility, vertigo, fainting, hemiplegia, convulsions, and ultimately even death.
The brain undergoes atrophy due to bodily defects or from past karma (*adṛṣṭa*). If it atrophies on only one side, there will not be a swift loss of life;
however, if it atrophies on all sides, the end of one's life will occur with great haste.
The treatment for old age is the growth of the brain; indeed, that leads to death. If a medicine were to be used there, it would nevertheless be an elixir (*rasāyana*).

In this case, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) mixed with ghee and honey should be drunk; such is the treatment for the wasting away of the brain, though if the wasting occurs, it leads only to death.

Nevertheless, in this condition, nourishing medicine should always be used; likewise, the oils and clarified butters prescribed for wind-disorders (vātāmaya) and those prescribed for the disease of epilepsy (apasmāra) should be employed at all times.
Likewise, a decoction of sandalwood and other such ingredients should be employed.
Now begins the nineteenth chapter on the section of "Aṃśughāta" (sudden injury),
including its etiology and symptoms.
When the head is scorched by the fierce rays of the sun,
there arises in living beings a disease called *aṃśughāta*, which afflicts their vital breaths;
it is characterized by most terrible thirst, parched skin, dizziness, and redness of the eyes.
Urinary retention, fainting, nausea, irregularity of the pulse,
labored breathing, loss of tactile sensation, and convulsions may occur;
these symptoms generally arise in soldiers confined within prisons.
A bluish tint of the hands and feet, the momentary disappearance of the pulse,
and the twitching of the limbs indicate death for one who strikes with a weapon; this is its treatment.
Having carefully cast aside his ornaments, garments, and clothing far away, he should sit in a pleasant place that is well-shaded,
with a flowing breeze, rich in fragrance, and agreeable to the mind.
In a secluded place where the sky is visible and filled with the songs of flocks of birds,
one should quickly lay the sun-scorched person upon a comfortable bed;
then, one should remove his exhaustion with breezes produced by palm-leaf fans.
The skilled physician should apply a sprinkling of cold water and cause the patient to drink sandalwood water; he should not suddenly give excessive amounts of water,
but should cover the entire body with a cloth moistened with cold water.
Bathing with a thousand-streamed [shower] removes diseases caused by the striking of rays;
purgation with oil derived from the *dantī* plant is said to be beneficial.
A broad cloth made of wool, when sprinkled with very hot water, [is used for fomentation].

Then, having removed the water and covered it with fragrant pastes and spots, one should place it while still warm upon the neck; it should be wrapped with another dry cloth or even with plantain leaves, but not too tightly.
Having bound it, one should protect it with extreme care until the excessive burning subsides;
by this method, fainting indeed ceases quickly,
provided there is no loss of heat in the limbs and no derangement of the vessels.

Sudation should be administered and the "reviving the dead" liquor (mṛtasañjīvanī) should be applied; in the case of a sunstroke (aṃśughāta), the procedure for alleviating fainting (mūrcchā) should be performed. Even when the sunstroke has subsided, for one who engages in improper diet and lifestyle...
Many diseases, such as epilepsy and others, generally arise from that;
therefore, once freed from it, one should constantly practice what is beneficial for the sake of regaining strength,
and should continuously perform actions that bring joy to the mind.
The *Ratneśvara-rasa* is to be employed here as a very cooling beverage; now follows the section on diseases caused by women, the twentieth chapter on diseases, concerning their symptoms.
Blood, moisture, the sixth [day], the sprout, and the water-child—
these four are the obstructors that hinder the production of offspring. Blood and moisture are their characteristics.
Moist with blood due to the *pradoṣa* disorder, she then becomes devoid of menses;
the symptoms of the sixth [day] appear in the eyes and hands, and especially in the vagina.

Due to the influence of the malefic conjunction with Śanaiścara (the Sixth Lord), blood mixed with saliva will flow; likewise, due to the influence of the malefic conjunction with Śanaiścara, there will be two menstrual periods within one month, and she will have a stained vagina.
The symptom of the *aṅkura* [demon] is agitation and heaviness in the body; there is profuse discharge of blood and pain below the navel,
for that *aṅkura* is indeed harmful.
If she remains without menstruation for four or three months,
becomes emaciated in body, and if a flame-like eruption appears on her hands and feet due to the conjunction of the *aṅkura* [sign], these are the characteristics of a *jalakumāra*.
Accompanied by pain and accompanied by pregnancy, with a withered body and scanty menses,
fruitlessness arises due to the defect of Jalakumāra; likewise, she who was thin-bodied becomes stout, and her menstrual period occurs after a long time.
If the breasts are large and the blood is scanty due to the affliction of Jalakumāra,
there will be a miscarriage even when conception has occurred; this is the treatment for such an obstacle.
Having drunk *rasāñjana*, *viḍaṅga*, and *citraka* together with cold milk,
a woman is immediately freed from obstructing disease;
likewise, the root of *prajāvatī* taken with black pepper and cold water [achieves the same].
Indeed, having drunk this, a woman becomes free from obstacles and conceives a fetus; for all obstacles arising from the womb vanish within her during times of distress.
Therefore, the physician should treat these women according to this prescribed method.

A woman suffering from gynecological disorders should not set her mind excessively on sexual intercourse, for she will certainly produce a further morbid alteration of the womb; thus begins the section on vaginal itching (yonikaṇḍū). 21.
The etiology [is as follows]:

when *balāsa* (phlegm) is provoked in the womb, or likewise from a deformity of the placenta, or when an *arbuda* (tumor) arises at the opening of the bladder, or even from the disease known as *durnāma* (hemorrhoids).
In a woman with an excess of channels in the genital tract and an abundance of wind (vāta),
itching of the vagina arises due to excessive sexual intercourse by the man at the time of the onset of menstruation, or even during the initial stages of conception.
In women, this condition occurs most frequently in old age;
its symptoms are itching in the vagina, pricking pain, roughness, and dryness.
Physicians know these to be the characteristics of vaginal itching and discharge (yoni-kaṇḍūgada): the disease is relieved by heat, whereas cold provides relief; this indeed is its treatment.
When itching occurs in the vagina, one should first administer an unctuous purgative;
then, a medicine that destroys blood disorders, provides strength, and acts as a rejuvenative (rasāyana) should be given— namely, sārivā, lodhra, trivṛt, and ibhapippalī.

One should drink water boiled [with these herbs] for the pacification of vaginal itching. When vaginal itching has affected the vagina, one should perform affusion with cold water, as well as oleation, sudation, and the enema known as *uttara-vasti*.
One should apply here the medicinal remedies prescribed for gynecological disorders (*yonivyāpad*),
as well as the *śivakarī vaṭī* and the powder of *ṭaṅkaṇa* and other ingredients.
Now begins the chapter on the provocation of the womb (yonyākṣepādhikāra), number twenty-two.
When the wind (māruta) is deranged, the etiology and symptoms are as follows: there is an excessive sensitivity to touch within the womb.
Her mouth is distorted and she experiences intense pain upon being touched;
such a woman, afflicted by *yonyākṣepa*, cannot endure sexual intercourse. If her husband should approach her by force, she will become exceedingly distressed.
Constantly overwhelmed by trepidation, she does not approach her husband;
rejected by her husband, she desires death for herself due to her suffering.
Furthermore, agitation, loss of appetite, and a decrease in sleep follow in succession.

Burning pain in the vagina, pain in the back, inability even to walk, weakness, loss of complexion, and the depletion of vitality— these, according to the wise, are declared to be the symptoms of the disease known as *yonyākṣepaka*.
A disease that cannot be cured by medicine is to be successfully treated with surgery; therefore,
a physician skilled in surgery should employ the surgical instrument in this case.
Having made her drink strong, intoxicating liquor, and having laid her on her left side or turned her supine, one should insert the instrument into the vagina; then,
quickly cutting through the modesty of the woman and tearing open the opening of the vagina—
The physician with light hands should plug and bind [the urethra] with cotton;
once the urine is obstructed, the doctor should insert a probe and alleviate the pain by the application of *phaṇiphena* (spider venom).

Again, at the end of two days, having made her drink that liquor and having extracted the cotton from within the vagina, the physician should open the vaginal opening and perform an incision below it measuring half a finger-breadth in size.
Thus, by such [remedial] action, the disease resulting from the projection into the womb is pacified.
Now begins the section on diseases of the placenta (jarāyu), chapter 23: Diagnosis.
Due to the continuous formation of the fetus, its discharge, coldness, damp clothing, as well as the addition of sin, excessive sexual intercourse,
and union with one who has urinary disease (pāpamehin), [the semen becomes vitiated].
The disease of the placenta may arise;
observe its symptoms: fever, dullness of the digestive fire, blueness of the mouth, and pain in the three regions [of the back].
There is pain in the lower abdomen, heat, and heaviness in the bladder, frequent urination, discharge of moisture from the vagina,
excessive passage of feces, and subsequently, their obstruction.
In the case of *jarāyu-roga* (placental disease), symptoms such as bad odors, weakness, headache, and vomiting arise;
such are the signs,
and this is the treatment.
In cases of diseases of the uterus (jarāyu-roga), an unctuous purgative should first be administered;
an uttara-basti (urethral/vaginal enema) is also beneficial here, as is immersion of the lower body in warm water.
An application of a *puṭapāka* plaster made from heated *atasī* seed paste along with clarified butter is declared by the wise to be beneficial below the abdomen; likewise,
the consumption of *rasasindūra* with coconut oil is recommended.
One should pacify diseases of the placenta through wholesome conduct, and one should consume the *pramadānanda* elixir and the powder of the *śārivādi* group.
Now begins the chapter on diseases of the testes (24).
The disease of the testicles arises from excessive sexual indulgence, coldness, injury, poison, and the consumption of unwholesome food; it is difficult to cure.
The symptoms are pain in the abdomen and thighs, difficulty in urination, scantiness and redness of the urine, fever, loss of appetite, nausea, restlessness, and depletion of strength.
Dhamanī, Veginī, Kṣudrā, Jihvā, and Raktojjvalā— these are declared by the wise to be the forms of the disease Aṇḍādhāra-gada; [now follows] its treatment.
Whatever increases strength and is conducive to the downward movement of the *vāyu* should be administered by the best of physicians for diseases of the scrotum;
a decoction of *paṭolādi*, the *rasa* called *yoṣidvallabha*, and the powder (*cūrṇa*) known as *candanādya* should also be given.
Poison should be administered with honey; this is beneficial for the disorders of the seminal vesicle and the prostate.
Now begins the section on *ojomeha* (Chapter 25):
etiology and symptoms.
Due to trauma, weak digestion, āmavāta, indigestion, choleraic disorders (viṣūcikā),

irregular fevers, swellings, and so forth, as well as from consumption (yakṣman), cough, and other ailments, and from the vitiation of the blood channels of the kidneys due to the disorder of the blood (asradōṣa).
When the urine of men is mixed with lymph, semen, pus,
or blood, and likewise in women during conception, [these conditions arise] from eating excessively sweet and vitalizing substances while avoiding pungent and alkaline ones.
From eating food kept overnight by a guru, from overeating, from the excessive consumption of new grains, wheat, and *haṃsaḍimba*,
and from bathing, drinking, or immersing oneself in water that is contaminated or cold;
Due to these and other causes, one becomes afflicted with diminished *ojas*; that condition is to be recognized as *ojomeha*, which destroys longevity and strength,
arising from physical exhaustion as well as other factors.
Due to the rapid circulation of blood and its abnormal flow,
the *ojas* undergoes a morbid transformation and, like the white part of a swan's egg or like flour and rice grains, flows out together with the urine.
In that condition, there occurs a wasting of the fat (medas) as well as fever and loss of appetite;
when swelling and impaired digestion (agnimāndya) arise, the disease is undoubtedly incurable. Otherwise, it is difficult to cure, and the person survives only with great effort.
Having deliberated upon the treatment, one should avoid the etiological factors such as the humors (doṣas) and the affected tissues (dūṣyas),
and should treat the patient afflicted by disease in accordance with those humors and tissues.
An elixir (agada) primarily composed of iron is especially beneficial here;
one desiring well-being should avoid medicines derived from mercury (rasa),
and should diligently eliminate the weakness caused by the loss of vital energy (ojas).
A decoction of sandalwood and other ingredients, a powder of ajamoda and others,
and a fermented liquor (āsava) of sandalwood and so forth should be administered; for example, sandalwood, nalada, drākṣā, guḍūcī, madhuka, and śaṭī.
A decoction of these, including dhātrī, pacifies disorders of ojas and medas;
likewise, it is declared by the compassionate Śambhu to be the supreme medicine for diseases such as hāridramēha and māñjiṣṭhamēha, even when accompanied by complications.
The *dāḍimādya* ghee, the pill named *candraprabhā*,
as well as *muktāvaṅgeśvara*, *vasantakusumākara*,
the *candanādya* āsava, and the *ariṣṭa* derived from *devadāru*.

One desiring well-being should always employ Pramehamihira oil, as well as the remedies pertaining to the section on urinary disorders (meha), and the anti-venom (agada) mentioned here; this concludes the chapter on the growth of the sprouts of the womb (yony-aṅkura). 26.
The cause is corrupted wind and the vitiation of blood, along with the action of karma;
from these, the growth of the sprout of the womb arises most intensely.
Having rendered the patient unconscious for the sake of treatment, one should excise the growth of the female organ;
one may also bind it with a ligature and sustain her with wholesome diet.
Now begins the section on Lasikāmeha (Chapter 27):
the etiology and symptoms of [the types of] meha arising from sweet fruits, roots, and products of molasses.
Due to the excessive consumption of heavy substances, as well as from over-exertion,
and for those habitually engaged in mental labor— provided physical labor is avoided—
from eating food that has been kept overnight by a teacher, or is moist, putrid, or causes internal secretions;
From the consumption of marshy fish, meat, and the like, as well as from overeating— by these causes, the liver and the colon become vitiated;
having produced a widespread injury in the two kidneys and the urinary bladder, [the disease arises].
Through the urinary passage, it repeatedly causes men to discharge a liquid resembling pus, blood, and the like, accompanied by fat and semen; it makes the urine flow properly,
appearing like milk mixed with lac-dye.
Sometimes urine is produced thick with pus, blood, and other such substances,
resembling coarse threads; consequently, greater pain arises due to the decrease or increase of the urine through the various combinations of the *doṣas*, *dūṣyas*, and other factors.
Likewise, a variation in color always arises in the one who voids urine; this is the characteristic of the Vata-born Lasikameha, which is sour-smelling and contains blood.
When a person passes urine frequently like curdled milk mixed with water,
and because the joints are loosened, the waste matter does not exit properly,
it is called the Pittaja type.
In the Pittaja type, there is thick, purulent urine that is excessively foul-smelling; furthermore, a bad taste in the mouth and a burning sensation in the hands and feet arise.
[Now he] describes the Kaphaja type:
In the case of *lasikāmeha* caused by *śleṣman*, the urine is white and turbid;
likewise, when it has stood overnight, it becomes clear on top and thick at the bottom.
Loss of appetite and pain in the groin and waist arise fully.
Regarding that arising from two or three doṣas, he says: in a prameha born of two or three doṣas, mixed symptoms are observed; it may be curable or incurable.

A disease that has arisen recently is easily curable for young people; otherwise, it will undoubtedly become incurable or difficult to treat. However, it may sometimes subside after having become severe through the observance of wholesome regimens.
Then, as it increases further, one should bring it under control through time;
the treatment consists of *tinduka*, *bilva*, *viḍaṅga*, *vyāghrī*, *dhātrī*, and *jāmbavī*.
A decoction of babūla, lohitaka, khadira,
and red sandalwood removes the most dreadful type of meha known as lasikāmeha, as well as various complications such as māñjiṣṭhamēha and others.
Somanātharasa, Hemanātha, Vaṅgeśvara, the pill known as Candraprabhā, likewise the liquor known as Candanāsava,
the oil named Pallavasāra, and that which is called Śrīgopāla.
One should apply [treatment] with effort in this disease according to the proper method.
Now begins the section on Somaroga (gonorrhea), concerning its etiology and symptoms.
Due to excessive indulgence with women, or from grief, or from the avoidance of fatigue,
as well as from the fault of malevolent magic and the fault of administering poison,
the waters within all bodies become agitated and flow forth.
Therefore, having fallen from their place, they move toward the urinary passage;
they flow excessively— clear, stainless, cold, sweet, painless, and white—
and there is weakness and loss of mobility.
Looseness of the head and dryness of the mouth and palate should be known as *somaroga*, which occurs in men due to the depletion of *soma* in the body;
it causes urine to flow excessively and repeatedly in an abnormal manner.
This condition, characterized by excessive urination and diarrhea, is called balanāśana; overcome by thirst due to it, the patient drinks water in excess,
and suffers from fainting, yawning, delirium, and extreme dryness of the skin.
One never attains satisfaction with various kinds of foods, edibles, and drinks;
[the remedy is] a treatment involving ripe plantain fruit, the juice of *dhātrī* fruit, and honey.
Drinking sugar-water is the supreme method for retaining water;
one should also cause [the patient] to drink ripe plantain fruit, vidārī, and śatāvarī with milk in the morning— this is the supreme method for retaining water.

One should always drink the juice of the *dhātrī* fruit with honey; it cures excessive urination and emaciation. Likewise, one may take the ash of *vāsaka*, fresh *tālakaṇḍa*, dates, and plantain fruit.
One should administer a powder of black gram (*māṣa*) along with licorice (*madhuka*), *vidārī*, sugar, and honey with milk in the morning; this destroys dysuria and urinary disorders.
One should administer [the same] with milk in the morning to destroy *somaroga*.
Through the use of opium (ahiphena), urinary retention will certainly occur;

however, in such cases, the following remedies should be employed: ghee prepared with plantains and other ingredients, ghee from the *dhātrī* tree, *pramehamihira-taila*, *pallavasāra-taila*, as well as the medicinal formulations known as *somanātha*, *hemanātha*, *tārakeśvara-rasa*, and the *vasantakusumākararasa* and others.
Now begins the twenty-ninth chapter: An Exposition on Diseases Arising from Sins as Spoken by Śātātapa.
Diseases arising from great sins (mahāpāpa) are leprosy (kuṣṭha), consumption (rājayakṣmā), urinary disorder (prameha), and malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī).
Dysuria, urinary stones, cough, diarrhea, fistula-in-ano, malignant ulcers, scrofula, hemiplegia, blindness,
and diseases such as these are known to arise from great sins.
Diseases arising from minor sins include dropsy, liver disease, splenic disorders, colic, ulcers, asthma, indigestion,
fever, vomiting, vertigo, delusion, and throat-obstruction.
Diseases such as red tumors (raktārbuda) and erysipelas (visarpa) arise from secondary sins;
diseases arising from major sins include hemiplegia (daṇḍāpatānaka), various bodily deformities, tremors, and scabies (vicarcikā).
Diseases such as skin eruptions (valmīka) and leprosy (puṇḍarīka) arise from sin;
diseases such as hemorrhoids (arśas) and others arise from extreme sin; indeed, these diseases of men originate from excessive wickedness.
The teaching on the origin of diseases from sin:
Since there is no suffering without sin, and diseases are givers of suffering,
therefore all diseases indeed arise solely from sin.
Now begins the section on the breaking of the banner (Dhvajabhaṅga).
Verse 30: The definition and types of the eunuch (klība): one who is incapable of sexual intercourse is a eunuch; that state is called klaibya (impotence/eunuchism).
That [desire] is said to be of seven kinds; its etiology is now described.
Regarding the mental [cause], it is said that when the mind of one desiring sexual pleasure is wounded by various unpleasant objects, [desire arises].
From this, the flag falls for men and impotence arises;
and from union with a loathed woman, mental impotence is said to occur.
He now describes that which is born of the [physical] humors (doṣaja).
Through the excessive consumption of pungent, sour, hot, and salty substances, a depletion of semen caused by pitta is observed; from that, impotence arises.
He now describes that which is born from the depletion of semen:

One who is habitually addicted to excessive sexual intercourse and does not resort to aphrodisiacs suffers from the failure of the penis (dhvajabhaṅga), which he says is caused by the depletion of semen and arises from diseases of the penis.
The fourth type of impotence arises from a severe disease of the penis; he describes that which is born from the cutting of vessels:
from the cutting of the semen-carrying vessels, there occurs a lack of elevation in the penis.
Regarding the cause of seminal obstruction, he says:
"Indeed, due to the suppression of the strength and the agitated mind of a strong man,
that which is known as the sixth type of impotence is caused by seminal obstruction."
He speaks of the innate [impotence]:
that which is innate from birth is indeed the seventh;
innate impotence is incurable, as is that which arises from injury to a vital organ.
The characteristics of women and eunuchs may also occur in women: there may be impotence characterized by the obstruction of seminal emission;
such eunuchs do not reach satisfaction through union with women, nor do women [reach it] through union with men.
In another treatise, the etiology of impotence is described:
"Impotence arises from injury to the seed and the penis, or from old age due to the depletion of semen;
hear now its general symptoms."
One who is constantly intent on sexual desire does not approach even his own beloved and submissive wife due to the flaccidity of his organ; or, if he does approach her at some time,
he does so afflicted by labored breathing and with perspiring limbs, his efforts and intentions rendered futile.
With a flaccid penis and lacking virility, this is the characteristic of impotence (klaibya).
Impotence arises from grief, anxiety, fear, and terror; from excessive indulgence with women; and from the imbalance of the bodily humors such as wind (vāta) and the others.
Impotence occurs due to approaching a four-footed animal, injury to the penis,
or obstruction of the semen;
this is the treatment for impotence.
For those afflicted by impotence who are curable, the reversal of the cause must be applied, since the primary medical treatment is the avoidance of the etiological factors.
[The ingredients are: mercury, snake-gall, iron, mica, tin powder, gold, vijayā, yaṣṭī, śālmalī, and betel leaf.
Clarified butter, honey, sugar, and milk—these are the "flower-bowed" (Kusumadhanvan) elixir; it pleases a hundred women and bestows long life and strength.
One should prepare this by saturating [the ingredients] with a decoction of gold and other substances, then combining them with clarified butter and the rest.
Furthermore, there are the Aśvagandhā-ghṛta and the great Amṛtaprāśa-ghṛta.
Candrodaya, Siddhasūta, Makaradhvaja,
Svalpacandrodaya, Kāmadroṣaka, Kāminīdarpaghna, Pūrṇacandra, and Śālmalīkalpārāyaṇa.
Oil made from sandalwood and other ingredients that kindles the fire of passion,
the auspicious *śrīmadanānandamodaka* for when the banner falls,
and medicinal elixirs (*rasāyana*) described as aphrodisiacs and virilizers.
It should be administered especially for the pacification of the defect of impotence.
Now begins the chapter on fever and diarrhea (jvarātisāra), section 31;
the symptoms of fever and diarrhea.

In a fever born of pitta, there occurs diarrhea arising from pitta; likewise, if fever should arise in one suffering from diarrhea, physicians declare it "fever-dysentery" (jvarātisāra) due to the simultaneous involvement of the dosha and the dushya. Furthermore, the etiology of fever and diarrhea has been described separately for each.
From the combination of those two, there arises the disease known as fever-typhoid (jvarātīsāra);
the treatment for fever and diarrhea is that which has been stated separately for each.
When those two are combined, they do not mutually enhance their respective effects;
for generally, that which is purgative (bhedī) alleviates fever, while that which is astringent (stambhana) cures diarrhea.
Therefore, because they are mutually contradictory, they do not reinforce one another.
Furthermore,
a medicine that is carminative, fever-destroying,
and astringent may be prescribed separately for diarrhea; however, such a medicine is mutually contradictory when administered during the simultaneous occurrence of fever and diarrhea.
Thereafter, one should treat those two with specific prescribed therapies;
for those suffering from fever and diarrhea, one should first administer fasting and digestive treatments, since these two generally do not occur without an association with undigested matter (āma).
The sequential regimen beginning with *peyā* (gruel) is beneficial for one who has undergone fasting (*laṅghita*) due to fever and diarrhea;
such a person suffering from fever and diarrhea should drink either sour or boiled *peyā*.
Furthermore:

Therefore, one should treat those two with specific prescribed therapies; indeed, there is no other medicine here than fasting (laṅghana) for one who is strong and whose accumulation of doṣas has been aggravated,
as it both digests that [dosha] and pacifies it.
Fasting is prescribed for both [types of fever]; when they are combined, it should be performed especially.
Thereafter, all [remedies] such as parched grain gruel (*lājāmaṇḍa*) prepared with *utpalashashthaka* should be administered according to the rules.
For both fever and diarrhea, a person should drink a decoction prepared with *pṛśniparṇī*, *balā*, *bilva*, *dhanikā*, *nāgara*, and *utpala*, along with sour substances; or else,
the mercury known as Gaganasundara should be administered with a beneficial after-drink (*anupāna*).
In cases of diarrhea and fever as well, Śubhā and Kanakaprabhā are beneficial.
Now begins the section on various diseases (32):
the symptoms of Vātabalāsaka fever.
A man afflicted by Vatabalāsaka suffers from chronic mild fever, dryness, swelling, and exhaustion; his limbs become stiff as he is dominated by phlegm (Kapha).
These are the symptoms of Pralepaka fever.
As if smearing the limbs with heat or heaviness,
and characterized by a mild feverish coating and coldness, this is the symptom of *pralepaka* fever, which is a type of half-body fever (*ardhāṅgajvara*).
When the essence of food has been digested and the phlegm and bile are situated within the body,
one half of the body becomes cold and the other half becomes hot;
this is the symptom of fever located in the rasa (plasma).
Heaviness, agitation of the heart, lassitude, vomiting,
and loss of appetite are the symptoms when fever resides in the rasa; furthermore, a sense of wretchedness arises in one whose fever has reached the blood.

Spitting of blood, burning sensation, delusion, vomiting, giddiness, delirium, pustules, and thirst— these are the symptoms in men when fever has reached the blood; these are the characteristics of fever that has reached the flesh.
Swelling of the calves, thirst, frequent discharge of urine and feces,
internal heat, burning sensations, restlessness, and exhaustion occur in fever located in the muscle tissue; these are the symptoms of fever that has reached the fat tissue.

Excessive perspiration, thirst, fainting, delirium, vomiting, foul odor, anorexia, debility, and intolerance— these are the symptoms of fever located in the fat; when it has reached the bones, the symptoms are as follows.
Pain in the bones, groaning, labored breathing, purging, vomiting, and the tossing about of the limbs—these are the symptoms of fever that has reached the bone;
as for the symptoms of fever that has reached the marrow: [they are as follows].
Entering darkness, hiccup, cough, coldness, vomiting, internal burning, labored breathing, and a piercing pain in the vital organs (marmans) are the symptoms of fever located in the marrow;
these are the symptoms of fever located in the semen.
In that case, when the fever has reached the seat of the semen, one may meet death;
there is stiffness of the penis and especially the discharge of semen—
these are the characteristics of natural and morbid fevers.
In the rainy season, autumn, and spring, the [doshas] beginning with Vāta are normal (prākṛta) in sequence;
any other is abnormal (vaikṛta). That which is normal is difficult to cure, as is that arising from Vāta.
In the rainy season, the vitiated Vāta, joined with Pitta and Kapha, produces fever.
One should treat pitta in autumn, and its secondary force is kapha; due to that constitution and because it is the time of elimination, there is no danger from fasting there.
Kapha is predominant in spring, and vāta and pitta follow as secondary forces.
Regarding the symptoms of internal and external fever:
excessive internal burning sensation, thirst, delirium, labored breathing, vertigo,
pain in the joints and bones, absence of perspiration, and suppression of the humors and feces [are the signs of internal fever].
One should observe these signs of internal fever: excessive internal heat and mildness of thirst and other symptoms;
whereas the signs of external fever are external heat and its being easily curable.
The symptoms of acute fever (āmajvara) are: excessive salivation, nausea, impurity of the heart, anorexia, drowsiness, lassitude, indigestion, a bad taste in the mouth, and heaviness of the limbs.
Loss of appetite, excessive urination, stiffness, and a powerful fever are the symptoms of *āmaja-jvara* (fever caused by undigested matter); one should not administer medicine in that state,
for medicine indeed causes the fever of the *āmadoṣa* to flare up even more.
The symptoms of the maturing stage of fever are:
excessive intensity of the fever, thirst, delirium, labored breathing, confusion, the discharge of waste matter, and nausea; these are the signs of the fever being in the process of maturation.
The characteristics of fever free from *āma* are:
hunger, emaciation, lightness of the limbs, mildness of the fever, the discharge of the *doṣas*, and the completion of eight days; these are the signs of a fever free from *āma*.
The wise say that fever is "recent" (taruṇa) for up to seven nights,
"intermediate" (madhya) for twelve nights, and beyond that it is "chronic" (jīrṇa). Fever is curable when it is strong [in its onset] but involves few doshas and is without complications.

That fever which remains in the bodies of men for more than twelve days, or for more than twice the duration of the three doshas, with a slow intensity, is called "chronic" (jīrṇa) by physicians; likewise, that which occurs at irregular times and with alternating cold and heat is also so described.
Furthermore, because its onset is irregular, that fever is known as *viṣama* (irregular).
The complications (*upadrava*) of fever are dyspnea, fainting, anorexia, vomiting, thirst, diarrhea, and constipation.
Hiccups, cough, pain in the limbs, and burning sensations are the ten complications of fever.
Burning, sweating, giddiness, thirst, tremors, and diarrhea are known as the premonitory symptoms of being freed from fever.
Moaning, foul odor of the body,

and a feverish appearance during the remission of fever— these are indeed the signs of a fever born of the three doṣas when the internal impulse has reached the tissues (dhātus); at the time of recovery from other types of fever, however, perspiration is observed.
The symptoms of abhinyāsa fever are as follows: in this fever, all the doshas become extremely intense and powerful,
accompanied by excessive delusion, restlessness, agitation, severe labored breathing, and profound muteness.
Burning sensation, a sticky mouth, a mild fever, and loss of strength—
this is proclaimed here by wise physicians of old as abhinyāsa.
The three aggravated doshas, following the channels of the chest and becoming knotted due to excessive increase of undigested matter (āmāśaya), reaching the intellect, the senses, and the mind,
produce the most terrible and persistent fever known as abhinyāsa.
His ears and eyes become as if asleep; he does not seek any movement, nor does his sight possess the capacity to perceive forms;
he perceives neither smell, nor touch, nor sound at all.
When one repeatedly shakes the head, has no relish for food, moans, feels as if pierced by pain, seeks to turn over in bed,
and speaks very little— if these occur, it is called *abhinyāsa*.
Most of that [treatment] is rejected; only a few here succeed.
Now he describes the disease caused by fear of water:
when phlegm alone occupies the seat of the intellect.
Then, when the intellect has ceased its activity, a person possessed by phlegm—
whether awake or asleep— perceives himself as if sinking;
he then trembles with fear of water, and this they know as "fear of water."

In that case, purificatory treatments such as cleansing and pacification that destroy phlegm (śleṣman) should be administered through dietary regulations until the patient returns to their natural state. [The author] now describes the disease known as aṇḍahrāsa.
The Vāyu, provoked by its own causes and having become disordered, reaches the channel carrying the scrotal sac and draws it upward; consequently,
the testicles indeed become invisible along with the penis.
This extremely severe disease is called *aṇḍahrāsa*.
Regarding the disease of *nābhibhraṃśa*,
it is said that there is a pulsating vascular knot (*śirāgranthi*) in the region of the navel which throbs constantly.
If it should constantly move sideways, upwards, or downwards due to the wind (vāyu),
then diseases born of wind (vātaja) will arise; if it moves upwards, vomiting occurs,
while if it moves downwards, there is diarrhea, as well as weak digestion and fever.
In the case of downward movement (tiryaggati), there is sluggishness of digestion (agnimāndya) and other diseases born of Vāta; furthermore,
there will be severe pain in the waist, as well as eruptions (piḍikā), cramps (udveṣṭana),
and disorders of the semen (śukradoṣa).

Those whose semen is characterized by wind (vāta), bile (pitta), phlegm (śleṣman), blood (śoṇita), a cadaverous odor (kuṇapagandhi), excessive knots (granthi), putrefaction (pūti), or depletion (kṣīṇa) are incapable of procreating offspring. In this regard, the color and pain of the semen caused by wind are those of wind; the color and pain caused by bile are those of bile; the color and pain caused by phlegm are those of phlegm; the color of blood with the pain of bile is caused by blood; that which has a cadaverous odor and is excessive is caused by blood; that which has become knotted is caused by phlegm and wind; that which resembles pus and is foul-smelling is caused by phlegm and bile; and the previously mentioned "depleted" semen is [caused by] the same factors.

Due to *pitta* and *vāta*, it has the odor of pus, urine, and feces, and possesses all colors and types of pain; due to *sannipāta* (the combination of all three humors), among these, those characterized by the odor of a corpse, glandular swellings, putrefaction, or diminished semen are difficult to cure, while those where the semen smells like urine or feces are incurable; any other type is curable. Thus he describes the defects of the menstrual blood (*ārtava*).

Even the *ārta* (unfertilized) seed, when afflicted by the three *doṣas*, blood as the fourth, individually, in pairs, or all together, becomes non-productive; this too is to be recognized by the color, pain, and other symptoms of the *doṣas*.
Among those, that which resembles a corpse, a knot, putrefaction, pus, emaciation, urine, or feces is incurable, while the others are curable.
[The author] now describes the disease of the sinews (*snāyu*).
The aggravated doshas in the peripheral tissues (śākhās) produce swelling like erysipelas (visarpa) and,
breaking through that ulcerated area, dry up the warm flesh; they then form a thread-like, circular, white-shining "living" (jīva) growth on the exterior.
It gradually subsides when wounded but becomes inflamed when incised;
swelling is relieved by its drainage but recurs in another location. This is known as snāyuka, and its treatment is said to be like that of visarpa.
If, through negligence, it should break anywhere in the arms or the shanks,
that severed thread causes contraction and lameness;
it has red eyes, a red luster, excessive burning, arises from all [humors], and exhibits all symptoms.
This disease is described here by the sages as having eight types: the *snāyuka* (tendon-worm) and the *tantukīṭa* (thread-worm).
That which is caused by Vāta is dark and rough, accompanied by pain; that from burning [pitta] is blue or yellow and always involves a burning sensation.
That which arises from Kapha is white and characterized by great heaviness. From the combination of two Doṣas, it possesses the symptoms of both.
Regarding the disease of *phiraṅga*:
because it occurs predominantly in the land known as *Phiraṅga*, the experts in pathology have designated this disease as *phiraṅga*.
The cause of this disease is syphilis; it certainly arises in embodied beings from contact with the body of a European man or through association with a European woman.
For this disease is indeed exogenous; here, there is a transference of the humors (doṣas). O best of physicians, one should recognize it by their symptoms.
Phiranga (syphilis) is to be known as threefold: external, internal, and another [intermediate].
I shall now describe their external and internal manifestations as well as their diagnostic signs.

Among them, the external type is the *phiraṅga* (syphilis), which resembles a vesicle (*visphoṭa*) but is slightly painful; it bursts like a carbuncle (*vradhna*) and is considered by physicians to be easily curable.
If it is internal to the joints, it resembles the *āmāghāta* fever; it certainly produces swelling and is considered by the wise to be difficult to cure. [The author] now describes its complications.
Emaciation, loss of strength, collapse of the nose, dullness of the digestive fire,
wasting of the bones, and curvature of the bones— these are the complications of syphilis (phiraṅga) that indicate whether it is curable or incurable.
A disease located externally is curable, being new and free from complications;
however, this internal disease is difficult to cure.
One that is both external and internal, chronic, occurring in a debilitated person, and accompanied by complications is incurable.
In the past, physicians declared this disease to be pervasive and incurable; however, through the treatment known as Phiraṅga,
the disease called Phiraṅga was cured by the elixir known as Karpūra.
The physicians of old have declared that this will certainly destroy [the disease];
the supreme procedure for the consumption of *rasakarpūra* is now written down.
By means of this procedure, one should eat it, and one shall not find swelling in the mouth.
Having kneaded wheat flour, one should fashion a small hollow vessel;
the physician should then place mercury measuring four *guñjās* inside it and subsequently form a pill such that it is not visible from the outside.

One should dust that pill with fine powder of cloves so that it does not come into contact with the teeth; one should swallow it with water and afterwards chew betel leaf, while avoiding vegetables, sour things, and salt.
Exhaustion, heat, travel, and especially sexual indulgence with women are the causes of seminal disorders;
pure rasa is truly nectar, while that which is impure is considered poison.
When practiced improperly, it leads to disease; when practiced properly, it is an elixir. When consumed according to the prescribed method, it destroys all maladies;
however, through its improper administration, these great diseases arise.
Coryza, nasal obstruction, loss of teeth, headache, fistula-in-ano, erysipelas, eye disease,
oral affliction, urticaria, itching, discoloration of the skin, and injury to the nose and other parts [of the body].
Indeed, there are various signs of leprosy and venereal disease on the limbs; moreover, there is swelling and hardness like a glandular tumor accompanied by pain in the scrotum,
hemiplegia, nodular rheumatism, and a severe burning sensation in the bones.
Dullness and mental disturbances—all these are the most difficult diseases to treat;
in such cases, appropriate medicinal therapy must be administered.
This is the diagnosis of Śītalā.
When afflicted by the goddess Śītalā, the eruptions (masūrikā) become cold on the outside yet cause fever, just as a chronic intermittent fever (viṣamajvara) presided over by a spirit (bhūta).
These are known to be of seven types; we shall now describe their classifications.
Preceded by fever, *bṛhatī-śītalā* manifests with large pustules;
the symptoms of *bṛhatī-śītalā* certainly subside within seven days, while after seven days it reaches its full intensity.
Then, on the third week, it withers and falls away by itself;
this is the characteristic of *kodrava*,
arising from wind and phlegm, appearing like *kodrava* grain.
Someone said of it, "It is ripe," yet it does not reach ripeness;
its limbs pierce like water-javelins (jalaśūka), especially so,
and after seven or ten days it subsides without medicine.

The *pāṇisahā* is characterized by heat, appearing as a subtle eruption accompanied by itching; it is pleasant to the touch and is known by the name *pāṇisahā*, which withers away of its own accord within seven days.
The characteristic of *sarṣapikā* is as follows:
the fourth [type] is shaped like a mustard seed and has the color of a yellow mustard seed;
it should be known by the name *sarṣapikā*, and one should avoid applying oil massage (*abhyaṅga*) in this case.
A certain mark resembling a mustard seed arises due to a slight sign of heat;
this occurs for children, and their comfort dries up of its own accord.
The symptoms of Masūrikā (smallpox) arise like those of Koṭha; on the sixth day, red and elevated circular patches appear,
preceded by fever and accompanied by pain, and the fever persists for three days.
Due to the clustering of eruptions, this [disease] is seen as having many pustules;
it should be understood that the second characteristic of *masūrikā* is when there is a single black eruption, which is designated as *carmajā*.
The means for pacifying Śītalā should be performed against the Śītalās; one should tie nimba leaves around the interior of the house along with the protective rite for Śītalā.
The entry of anything untouchable should never be permitted under any circumstances.
For boils accompanied by excessive burning, a heap of dust is beneficial as a protective measure;
likewise, sandalwood, vāsaka, musta, guḍūcī, and drākṣā [are beneficial].

A cold decoction of these [herbs] destroys fever accompanied by coldness; one should bring those fevers to subsidence through recitation, burnt offerings, oblations, gifts, rites for well-being, worship,
and the honoring of Brahmins, cows, Śambhu, and Gaurī.

A Brāhmaṇa endowed with faith should recite the hymn of the goddess Śītalā in the presence of one afflicted by Śītalā; by that, the Śītalās are pacified. [This is from another text. Now follows the description of the symptoms of fever caused by heat and wind (uṣṇavāta).
Due to physical exercise, travel, or exposure to the sun, the pitta, obstructed by vāyu, reaches the bladder;
it then causes a burning sensation in the bladder, the penis, and the anus,
and discharges urine that is yellowish, or mixed with blood, or even pure blood.
They call that *uṣṇavāta* the condition of a living being which occurs again and again with great difficulty;
its treatment consists of drinking milk cooled after boiling and eating rice with *candana* mixed with rice-water.
One should drink this excellent [mixture] with sugar when there is hot wind accompanied by blood.
Now, the etiology and symptoms of *bradhna* (scrotal enlargement): it arises from excessive unctuousness, heavy food, and the consumption of dry, putrid, or raw meat.
When the doshas produce a swelling like a knot at the joints of the groins, accompanied by fever, pain, and prostration of the limbs, one should designate that as Bradhna;
[this is its] treatment.
A paste made from *abhayā* (chebulic myrobalan) properly fried in castor oil,

combined with *kṛṣṇā* (long pepper) and rock salt, is an excellent remedy for the disease of the sun (jaundice). [Likewise, a paste of] cumin, *hapuṣā*, costus, *gomeda* (amber), and jujube fruit [is beneficial].
When ground with fermented gruel (kāñjika), that ointment is supreme for conquering *bradhna* (inguinal swellings).
As for the etiology and symptoms of chronic fever (*kālajvara*):
when the fever of a weak person whose digestive fire has been extinguished becomes latent within the depletion of the bodily tissues (*dhātu*), [it is known as chronic fever].
It causes the pain of *plīhodara* (enlargement of the spleen) accompanied by swelling; through that, it becomes known as *kālajvara*.
Having contracted this most unbearable disorder, the patient suffers from emaciation day by day, his complexion turns dark, he becomes pale, and his hair falls out due to the irregular fever.

In one who has been afflicted for a very long time by *kālajvara* (chronic fever), there may arise an extremely severe disease of diarrhea (*atisāra*). Furthermore, bleeding from the nose and inflammation of the gums (*dantaveṣṭa*) frequently occur as these two complications. [Now follows] the etiology and symptoms of *granthika-jvara*.
A swelling in the form of a gland that causes pain in the wrists, armpits, throat, or groins,
and from which a fever arises due to the aggravation of all three *doṣas*, is known as Granthika fever;
this fever is initially very intense and frequent, and later becomes mild in some places.
Pain in all the limbs, excessive coldness, trembling, fainting, delirium, vomiting, thirst,
profuse perspiration, loss of sleep, drowsiness, roughness and extreme elongation of the tongue,
flaccidity of the limbs, exhaustion, delusion, numbness of the ears and eyes, and the condition of the pulse becoming motionless— these are the signs.
This fever, characterized by incurability and known by the name Granthika, destroys the power of all the sense organs;
it undoubtedly kills one afflicted by diarrhea who has lost consciousness and is vomiting blood.
In regions where the wind, water, and soil are corrupted, those microbes— like poison and like thunderbolts—
enter the body of a rat first and kill the mice, who are the foremost heralds of death;
their bodies overwhelmed by intense poison, they go to a distant place for water to drink.
Those *mūṣikā* insects, agitated by thirst for poison, run about, faint, and carry it far; therefore, from the bodies of those *mūṣikā*s,
they enter other bodies along with the living microorganisms (*jīvāṇu*), acting as the cause of glandular fever (*granthijvara*) for the insects.
Manthara-jvara (slow fever) and Madhura-jvara (sweet/slow fever)! Its premonitory symptoms are slight cough, loss of appetite, thirst, delirium, a burning sensation in the fever,
heaviness of the limbs, exhaustion, breaking pain in the bones, and insomnia.
There is discoloration of the complexion, fever, burning sensations, vertigo, delusion, diarrhea, vomiting, thirst,
insomnia, and the mouth, palate, and tongue become parched.
When eruptions resembling mustard seeds are seen in the middle of the neck,
this sign indicates that it is called Madhuraka; this is the etiology and symptomatology of Daṇḍaka fever.
If a feverish person experiences a pain in the neck and joints that arises like the ache from being struck by a staff,
occurring throughout the nights and days, they call that fever "daṇḍaka";
it subsides for one or two days and then recurs.
Swelling that spreads throughout the entire body and an enlargement of the spleen may also arise here;
such a patient, afflicted by catarrh and cough, is generally freed from the fever on the eighth day, as it originates from an excess of wind and phlegm.
The definition of the impairment of taste (rasājñāna) is as follows:
when a person eating food does not perceive the tastes, beginning with the sweet, by means of the tongue, that is called the impairment of taste.
Some say that the impairment of the digestive bile (*pācakapitta*) is the etiology of this disease; it is a specific type of contagious, acute swelling known as *bīlī-bērī*. This is the etiology.
Through foods that increase wind and phlegm, through the consumption of both moist and dry grains, through the use of unctuous substances that are like poison due to their combination,
through diets of husked rice, and through eastern winds laden with cold spray.
Due to dwelling for a long time on moist ground and in places crowded with people,
the fire of one whose blood and flesh have been depleted becomes weak in the heart,
and disorders of the liver and spleen gradually increase.
From that, a swelling arises—a new, contagious disease.
Its symptoms will also be described briefly hereafter; first, the premonitory signs (pūrvarūpa).
Because this disease is slight, its premonitory symptoms are not perceived; only the impairment of the digestive fire and discoloration are observed there as its signs.
When swelling arises in the bones of the shanks and the heart trembles, one should recognize that as a new, contagious swelling;
the functions of the tendons and muscle-fibers do not proceed properly.
Having first appeared in the calves, the swelling spreads throughout the entire body;
there occurs diarrhea, difficulty breathing, or constipation, as well as a decrease in the quantity of urine and blood.
A wise person should recognize this disease by its various symptoms: unbearable pain throughout all the limbs and in both knees;
and observing certain signs that are similar to those of wind-disease (vātaroga).
Some physicians, due to delusion, consider this to be a wind-disease (vātaroga);
others among those learned in medicine declare, "This is a specific form of acute fever, and it is not a new disease," and so forth.
This newly manifested swelling is an infectious disease;
it kills most frequently those who eat polished rice,
whereas inhabitants of the Pañcanada region and elsewhere survive by eating wheat cakes.
People generally do not contract this contagious swelling in regions such as Vārāṇasī; however, due to the outbreak of this disease,
thousands of subjects quickly entered the jaws of death.

One whose heart, though afflicted with pain, thumps rapidly despite being emaciated, and whose veins and abdomen are filled with blood, quickly abandons his life-breaths; such is the sign of incurability.
Afflicted by this swelling, one undergoes a most grievous disorder of the head,

blindness, or extreme suffering; likewise, other terrible eye diseases spread throughout the circles of people, and through the adversity of fate, there arises a fear of death for the entire population as the region faces destruction.
Indeed, this swelling is accompanied by many pains; when it is young, it may suddenly become extremely painful due to heart disease or vomiting of blood.
This is the symptom of vāyu residing in kapha, wherein the previously accumulated mass of phlegm is followed again by a powerful wind.
When that [wind] is obstructed, it causes the drying up of the semen; furthermore, when aggravated, it produces a multitude of disorders:

cracking of the skin, edema of the hands and feet, burning sensation in the eyes, excessive dryness of the mouth, pricking pain, palpitations of the heart, weakness, extreme fatigue, vertigo, and false delusions or incoherent speech.
Hoarseness of voice, laziness, indigestion, indifference, anxiety, loss of appetite, aching of the limbs,
sleepiness, loss of strength, retention of urine and feces, entry into darkness, and inability to walk—
this wind (vāyu) accompanied by phlegm (kapha) is thus described.
Now begins the chapter on the examination of the eyes and other [senses], thirty-three:
The eye, due to wind (vāta), becomes rough, smoke-colored, or reddish; it appears as if sunken within its socket and has a fixed, unblinking gaze.
Due to the provocation of pitta, the eye may become yellowish like turmeric, red, or green, and it is always inflamed with a burning sensation;
due to an excess of phlegm (balāsa), the eye becomes oily and appears as if submerged in water.
Likewise, a white-colored eye that is devoid of luster yet possesses strength, due to the predominance of two doshas, exhibits the symptoms of those two doshas; however,
through the combination of the signs of all three doshas, it kills the patient.

An eye afflicted by the three doṣas becomes deeply sunken within; it exhibits the symptoms of all three, secretes water, and can only be opened at its outer corner. This concludes the examination of the tongue.
Due to Vāta, the tongue resembles the leaf of the Śāka plant, is rough, and cracks;
due to Pitta, it becomes red or dark-brown; due to Kapha, it is coated, moist, and pale;
when all three Doshas are predominant, it is scorched, rough to the touch, and black.
That same examination of urine, characterized by the presence of two doshas when both are in excess,
shows that the urine is pale from Vata and red or blue from Pitta.
From blood, the stool itself becomes bloody; from phlegm, it becomes white and frothy.
Regarding the examination of feces:
from wind (vāta), hardness and dryness arise in the excrement.
Yellowishness arises from bile (pitta), whiteness occurs from phlegm (śleṣman),
and indeed all the symptoms appear specifically in the case of a derangement of the three humors (sannipāta).
Due to the provocation of vāta, the stool becomes broken, frothy, rough, or smoky;
due to a disorder of vāta and śleṣman, it becomes brownish (kapiśa),
bound, very broken, yellow, or dark (śyāma).
When the discharge of feces is yellowish-white, slightly thick and slimy due to phlegm and bile,
dark, cracked, and yellowish in appearance, bound with white matter from the three humors,
and foul-smelling and cold;
Then, when the waste matter has been digested, it is described by physicians who know the humors as being tawny and formed into pills; if such feces are observed,
the patient is said to be afflicted by the depletion of waste matter and humors.

The excrement of wind (vāta) is black; that of bile (pitta) is yellow or blood-colored; and the excrement arising from phlegm (kapha) is somewhat white or undigested (āma). That which is mixed is said to be born from two humors (dvandvaja).

If digestion is impaired (*ajīrṇa*), the [semen] remains uncooked; if digestion is normal, it becomes cooked and clear. In cases of excessive digestive fire (*atyagni*), it becomes solid and dry; in cases of weak digestive fire (*mandāgni*), it remains liquid. If it is foul-smelling and mixed with *candrikā*, these characteristics of the impurity (*mala*) indicate that the condition is incurable.
Thus ends the first appendix;
the second appendix. The second appendix.
Now follows the discernment of wholesome and unwholesome diets for the diseases described in the *Śārṅgadharasaṃhitā* along with its supplements.
Regarding wholesome and unwholesome diets in fever (*jvara*): red rice (*raktaśāli*) and other such grains, as well as aged *ṣaṣṭika* rice, are recommended.
For those suffering from fever, one should provide barley gruel, boiled rice, or parched grain flour as means to alleviate the fever;
and for those fever patients who are accustomed to soups, one should administer soups made from mung beans, lentils, chickpeas, horse gram, and cowage.
The leaves of *paṭola*, *vārtāku*, *kulaka*, *kāravellaka*, *karkoṭaka*, *parpaṭaka*, *gojihvā*, young radish,
and the leaf of *guḍūcī* serve as vegetables that remove fever for those afflicted by it.
For the sake of meat, a wise person should skillfully provide deer, hares, and the like, as well as chickens, peacocks, partridges, cranes, and quails; however,
some physicians do not recommend them in cases of fever because they are heavy and hot in nature.
If, in a fever, the strength of the wind (vāyu) should become excessive,

a physician who understands the variations of dosage and knows the proper time should administer those [purgatives] as well— specifically those made with raisins, pomegranate, dates, priyāla, and parūṣaka.
Tarpaṇa (soothing therapy) should be administered to one who is worthy of it; it destroys fever.

It is indicated for one who is emaciated, has few doṣas, diminished kapha, and suffers from chronic fever, as well as for one with constipation, undischarged doṣas, dryness, and fever caused by pitta and vāta.
Afflicted by thirst and burning sensations, one becomes comfortable through milk;
in chronic fever (jīrṇajvara), when the phlegm is diminished, milk is like nectar. That very same milk, if drunk during the acute stage of fever, kills a person like poison.
One who has been freed from fever should not engage in physical exercise, sexual intercourse, bathing, or walking until they have regained their strength;
if a person who has recovered from fever bathes, it will cause the fever to return.
Therefore, even when freed from fever, one should avoid bathing as if it were poison; until strength, complexion, digestive fire, and the body have returned to their natural state,
one who has been released from fever must continue to avoid prohibited things.

2. Diet and Prohibitions in Atisara: In cases of diarrhea as well, all that is wholesome and unwholesome should be understood to be the same as in the case of indigestion; [one should avoid] bathing, immersion baths, oil massage, and the consumption of heavy, unctuous, or liquid foods.
One suffering from diarrhea should avoid physical exercise and exposure to the heat of fire.
In the disease of *grahaṇī*,
food and drink that are easily digestible and digestive-stimulating for the fire should be consumed daily.
In this matter, the wise man should consume these and avoid the opposite:
aged *śāli* rice, lentils, barley, meat broth,
as well as *madgura* fish, *śṛṅgī*, buttermilk, *bilva*, and pomegranate.

One suffering from *grahaṇī* disease should always consume such things as *śṛṅgāṭaka*, goat’s milk, eggplant, and *kaśeruka*; likewise, one should avoid daytime sleep, liquor, pungent substances, and staying awake at night.
One should diligently avoid heavy food and that which causes secretions;
likewise, in cases of indigestion and weak digestion, one should abandon everything unwholesome, difficult to digest, and all eating at night.

One suffering from indigestion and weak digestive fire should eat food that is easily digestible and light. Regarding the wholesome and unwholesome diet for hemorrhoids (arśas): whatever promotes the downward movement of flatus, is laxative, and kindles the digestive fire is beneficial.
That food and drink which is easily digested and nourishing is considered beneficial; however,
one suffering from hemorrhoids should avoid suppressing natural urges, riding on the back of a woman, sitting on a high seat, and foods that increase the respective doshas.
6. Regarding wholesome and unwholesome diet in the disease of worms (krimiroga):
Daily food that is pungent and bitter, which destroys *kapha*, eliminates worms, promotes appetite, and is an excellent stimulant for the digestive fire, is recommended.

One who desires to destroy worms should especially avoid milks, meats, ghees, curds, leafy vegetables, and sour or sweet flavors (verse 7). [The following is] the wholesome and unwholesome diet for jaundice, chlorosis, and anemia.
Old barley, wheat, and śāli rice; soups made from punarnavā, mung beans, āḍhakī, and lentils; the broth of wild game;
and patola, mature kūṣmāṇḍa, and young plantain fruit.
Among fish, the *madgura* and *śṛṅgī*; buttermilk with *dhātrī* and *abhayā*; ghee;
garlic; ripe mango; *vārttāku*, *amṛtā*, and *niśā*—these and others are declared by the wise to be beneficial in the disease of *pāṇḍu*.

Smoking, suppression of natural urges, sudation, sexual intercourse, wine, sleeping during the day, eating clay, asafoetida, black gram, and mustard seeds; excessive intake of pungent, sour, and salty foods, heavy meals, and copious amounts of water.
Leafy vegetables and legumes do not provide relief in cases of jaundice (pāṇḍu).
Regarding what is wholesome and unwholesome in the treatment of internal hemorrhage (raktapitta): aged śāli rice, wheat, barley, mung beans, and masūra lentils [are beneficial].
Chickpeas, cowpeas, old pumpkin, plantain fruit, patola, the tip of the cane, the fruit of the jackfruit and palmyra,
bilva, pomegranate, dates, emblic myrobalan, grapes, and udumbara.
The parūṣaka, coconut, wood-apple, and kaśeruka;
likewise, clarified butter from cows, buffaloes, or goats, as well as goat's milk;
and the hare, the eṇa deer, the green goat, the crane, the pigeon, and so forth.
Sugar-cane, cool water, sandalwood, moonbeams, agreeable narratives, delightful recitations,
and beautiful dwellings with full and high breasts and hips.

Embracing those intoxicated by beauty and youth without sexual union— all such things as these are beneficial for those suffering from *rakta-pitta* (blood-bile disorders), as are sharp, burning, and constipating food and drink, and water from a well.
Betel, curd, eggplant, fish, black gram, mustard, garlic, alkali, flat beans, horse gram, jaggery, liquor,
riding on elephants or horses, physical exertion, anger, and irregularity in sleep.
Physical exertion, wandering on roads, recitation, heat from fire or the sun, bloodletting, smoking, greed, and restlessness—
all such things should be avoided at all times.
Whatever etiology of *raktapitta* has been explained, that should not be indulged in by those suffering from *raktapitta* who desire life and health.
9. Wholesome and unwholesome diet in the disease of *kāsa*.
Rice, sixty-day rice, wheat, śyāmāka, barley, and kodrava;
the broth of mung beans, mudga beans, and horse gram; aged ghee; vāstūka, vāyasī, eggplant, and young radish.
Goat’s milk, goat’s ghee, lukewarm water, honey, the meat of animals from arid and marshy regions as well as carnivorous animals,
and fruits such as grapes, pomegranate, and dates are beneficial in this case.
Enemas, nasal therapy, bloodletting, physical exercise, gnashing the teeth, exposure to the sun, frequenting dusty paths,
and various kinds of foods that cause constipation, burning sensations, or dryness.
Suppressing the urges of feces, urine, eructation, and cough;
fish, tubers, and mustard; contaminated water, *tumbī*, and *podikā*; staying awake at night, sexual intercourse with village women, and [other such things] are harmful in cases of cough.
Regarding what is wholesome and unwholesome in cases of *yakṣman* (consumption):
wheat, chickpeas, mung beans, aged red rice,
goat meat, goat’s milk, goat ghee, and sugar.
Molasses, wine, musk, white sandalwood,
a palace, garlands, talk of love, the sight of young women,
the wearing of ornaments such as jewels and pearls, and a gentle breeze.
O Dhātrī! The fruits of the mango and the jackfruit, the fruit of the *vakula*,
song, laughter, moonlight, and words that grant pleasure to the ears—
all such things as these are declared to be beneficial for those suffering from consumption.

Dry food and drink, irregular eating, and that which causes a burning sensation; pungent, bitter, astringent, and sour vegetables, beans, garlic, legumes, fish, betel leaf, physical exercise, and the suppression of natural urges.
Rash actions, physical exertion, sweating, the application of collyrium,
speaking loudly, walking on roads, staying awake at night— especially sexual intercourse, as well as other activities involving pressure upon the chest.
The fourfold set of causes that has been described as the etiology—
all these must certainly be avoided in the case of *yakṣman* (consumption),
as well as whatever is wholesome or unwholesome in *raktapitta* (hemoptysis) that I have declared.
In cases of consumption as well, that which is wholesome and that which is unwholesome has been determined;
one should abandon grief, women, anger, and malice, and likewise enjoy noble objects of the senses,
as well as the twice-born, the gods, and gurus, and listen to sacred words from the twice-born.
In cases of hiccup and dyspnea,

old varieties of *śāli* rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, wheat, and barley are recommended; so too are the meat of the hare, the snake-eater (*ahibhuk*), the partridge (*tittiri*), the cock, the *dhanyamṛga*, and the parrot.
Ancient ghee, goat’s milk, honey, and likewise wine;
jīvantikā, vāstūka, garlic, and paṭola; drākṣā, truṭi, and pauṣkara; warm water, and the three pungents (kaṭutraya).

One should know that these and other such things are beneficial for hiccup and dyspnea; however, the patient suffering from dyspnea or hiccup should avoid foods and drinks that are burning or heavy, as well as physical exercise,
travel, sexual intercourse, anger, and anxiety.
In cases of anorexia,
that which is appetizing, digestive-stimulant for the fire, and a cleanser of the tongue and throat is wholesome; all else is unwholesome.

13. Regarding the wholesome and unwholesome diet in the disease of vomiting: aged *śāli* rice, parched grain (*lāja*), wheat, barley, honey, and the meat of wild animals and birds such as the hare, the common quail, and the peacock;
Citron, emblic myrobalan, grapes, pomegranate, and citron; coconut water, sugar, wine,
the enjoyment of pleasant fragrances, and anointing with sandalwood and other unguents.
Bathing the head, pleasant aromatics, and beneficial [foods] are for those suffering from vomiting.
Whatever action is harsh or causes agitation, or whatever substance is likewise [unwholesome],
all that should be avoided by a wise person desiring health during an episode of vomiting.

In cases of voice disorders (svarabheda), all food and drink that is wholesome or unwholesome, which bestows strength and nourishment, is pleasing to the heart, alleviates phlegm, and purifies the voice, is considered beneficial.
In this disease of thirst (tṛṣṇā), one should not consume substances that cause secretions, nor are cooling treatments beneficial;
one should not sleep during the day, nor should one suppress natural urges.
15. Pathogenic and non-pathogenic factors in the disease of thirst.
One afflicted by thirst should, with vigilance, consume that which is heart-pleasing, very sweet, and cool;
one should avoid everything that is harsh and causes agitation.
16. [This concludes] the wholesome and unwholesome regarding the disease of fainting (mūrchā).
Barley, red śāli rice, eggplant, and patola;
soup made from the meat of wild animals, as well as fish such as the rohita and others;
warm milk straight from the cow, buttermilk, and bathing in the pure waters of a river.
These remedies are beneficial for fainting and for the disease known as *saṃnyāsa*. [In such cases], sharp substances, sharp therapeutic procedures, and the suppression of natural urges are employed;
for this disease increases through such states as anger, grief, and the like.
17. Regarding what is wholesome and unwholesome in cases of intoxication:
in intoxication, the following are beneficial: aged *śāli* rice, mung beans, barley, sugar, milk, *paṭola*, dates, pomegranate, and coconut.
Drākṣā, āmalaka, various foods, heart-pleasing wine, and parūṣaka;
the broth derived from quail, partridge, duck, rabbit, goat, and other such animals;
cool breezes, a fountain-house, and the rays of the moon.
Sandalwood ointment, bathing, the embrace of a beloved,
betel, smoking, salt, sudation, and collyrium—
all pungent substances whatsoever— should be avoided during a disease arising from alcohol.
18. Regarding what is wholesome and unwholesome during burning sensations (dāha):

rice of the *śāli* variety, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, mung beans (*mudga*), lentils (*masūra*), chickpeas (*caṇaka*), barley (*yava*), meat-broths from arid regions (*dhanva-māṃsa-rasa*), parched grain gruel (*lāja-maṇḍa*), and parched grain flour (*lāja-śaktu*).
Ghee purified a hundred times, milk, butter derived from milk,
sugar, the bottle gourd, the plantain, the jackfruit, the sweet pomegranate,
the patola, the parpaṭa, grapes, the myrobalan fruit, and the parūṣaka.
Śimbī, tumbī, milk, a box, dates, coriander, cumin, young palmyra palm, priyāla, śṛṅgāṭaka, kaśeruka,
madhūka flowers, hrībera, and all bitter substances.
Cool poultices, cooling the ground and the house, oil massage, immersion baths, beds made of lotus and lily petals and linen, cool groves, diverse stories, songs, and the embrace of a beloved woman.
Uśīra and sandalwood ointments, cool water, refreshing breezes,
the rays of the moon, bathing, jewels, and sweet juices— these and other such things should be utilized by those desiring comfort during states of burning heat.
Incompatible foods and drinks, anger, suppression of natural urges, riding elephants or horses, travel on foot, alkaline substances, and things that increase pitta;
as well as physical exercise, exposure to the sun, buttermilk, betel leaf, honey, and asafoetida.
Sexual intercourse and pungent, bitter, and hot foods are certainly unwholesome.
19. In insanity, the wholesome and unwholesome are as follows: red śāli rice, barley, mung beans, wheat, and the meat of tortoises.
The juice of the dhanvana plant, grapes, wood-apple, coconut, vāstūka, as well as brāhmī, the large fruit of the pumpkin, patola, warm milk,
and clarified butter washed a hundred times; these are the ingredients.
Old and new, very cooling ointments, as well as wholesome foods prescribed for insanity; [avoid] wine, hot food, pungent potency, leafy vegetables, and *kaṭhillaka*.
All bitter [tastes], sexual intercourse, staying awake at night,
sleep, thirst, hunger, and the like, as well as the forced suppression of natural urges and all cruel deeds, are considered not conducive to well-being.
20. Regarding wholesome and unwholesome diet in epilepsy:
aged ghee, mung beans, wheat, red śāli rice, the meat of tortoise, the broth of animals from arid lands (dhanva), milk, the leaves of brāhmī, and vacā [are beneficial].
Patola, ripe kushmanda, vāstūka, sweet pomegranate,
śobhāñjana, coconut, as well as parūṣaka and āmalaka—
these and other such items are remembered as providing comfort when memory has declined.
Anxiety, grief, fear, anger, impure foods, liquor, fish, incompatible foods, sharp, hot, and heavy meals, overexertion, excessive sexual indulgence, and the neglect of honoring those worthy of honor.
Bimba fruit, āṣāḍha-potherb, sleep, the suppression of hunger and thirst,
immersion in water, and climbing mountains, trees, and the like—
these and other such acts must be diligently avoided when there is a lapse of memory regarding the Smṛti rules.
21. Regarding wholesome and unwholesome diet in Āmavāta:
the vāstūka vegetable, sārṣṭa vegetable, and paunarnava are beneficial;
as are paṭola, garlic, vārtāku, and kāravellaka.
Barley, koradūṣa grain, aged śāli and ṣaṣṭika rice,
as well as the meat of quails prepared with buttermilk,
and white soups made from horse gram, black gram, and chickpeas are beneficial.

One should give what is palatable, according to one's constitution, and whatever is beneficial for āmavāta; curd, fish, jaggery, milk, upodikā grown in brackish water, incompatible food, and the previous suppression of the urge to pass flatus [are causes of āmavāta].
Waking at night, bathing in cold water,
and excessive sexual intercourse are not beneficial when Vāta is associated with Āma; these constitute the wholesome and unwholesome regimen for the disease of Śūla.
Old *śāli* rice, warm milk, meat broth from wild animals,
*paṭola*, *kāravella*, grapes, ripe mango,
pomegranate, *viḍa* salt, *śāliñca* leaves, hot water, and *devapuṣpaka*.
In this condition, all wholesome things that act as laxatives are indeed beneficial;
however, a person suffering from colic should avoid physical exertion, sexual intercourse, wine, salt, pungent vegetables, suppression of natural urges, grief, and anger.

23. Regarding the wholesome and unwholesome diet for Udāvarta and Ānāha, as well as that which is easily digestible and laxative: whatever food and drink provides nourishment should be consumed in cases of Udāvarta and Ānāha; otherwise, it should be avoided.
24. Regarding what is wholesome and unwholesome for heart disease:
ancient red rice, the meat of wild animals and birds, soups of *kulattha* and *mudga* beans, *paṭola*, and the fruit of the plantain tree.
Mango, ripe pumpkin, pomegranate, chebulic myrobalan, grapes, buttermilk, and rock salt are beneficial in cases of heart disease;
whereas suppressing natural urges, sexual intercourse, physical exercise, and staying awake at night are harmful.
The water of rivers originating from the Sahya and Vindhya mountains,

as well as the milk of ewes, water that is turbid, food that is heavy, bitter, or sour, leafy vegetables, and eating before the previous meal has been digested— these are not beneficial in cases of heart disease.

25. Regarding the wholesome and unwholesome diet in cases of abdominal disease: red rice, barley, mung beans, horse gram, honey, *surā* liquor, *sīdhu* liquor, and the meat of wild animals and birds are beneficial.
Fresh garlic, buttermilk, *kulaka*, the fruit of the drumstick tree (*śigru*),

*punarnavā*, *kāravella*, betel leaf with lime, and milk— these, along with light, digestive, and bitter foods, should be administered after considering the state of the humors (*doṣas*), the digestive fire (*anala*), and the patient's strength.
"A physician should apply [these treatments] for one with abdominal enlargement," and so forth, according to the facts:
excessive drinking of milk, heavy food, oleation, the use of medicinal smoke, the meat of aquatic and marshy animals, leafy vegetables, sesame seeds, and curd.

Salt, hot foods, burning substances, and water containing impurities, as well as the water of rivers originating from Mount Mahendra; likewise, physical exercise, sexual intercourse, bathing, and walking about.
Other items of this kind should always be avoided by those suffering from abdominal enlargement (udara).
Regarding the wholesome and unwholesome diet for gulma:
dried meat, radish, fish, dried vegetables, and pulses [are generally beneficial].

One suffering from urinary obstruction (gulma) should not eat *āluka* or sweet fruits. Whatever is prescribed as wholesome for dysuria (*mūtrakṛcchra*) and stone disease (*aśmarī*) is also to be employed in cases of urinary retention (*mūtrāghāta*).

In all cases of urinary obstruction, one who knows the proper place and time should employ these [remedies]. In dysuria, the diet and drink— whether wholesome or unwholesome— should be such that it is non-irritating, diuretic, and promotes the downward movement of urine.
One should understand that what is beneficial here is the opposite of what leads to happiness.

Regarding the wholesome and unwholesome in cases of urinary calculi (aśmarī), one should follow the treatment for wounds once the foreign body has been removed, and maintain the patient on a wholesome diet.
Regarding wholesome and unwholesome diet in *prameha*: *śyāmāka*, *kōdrava*, *uddāla*, wheat, chickpeas, *āḍhakī*,
and *kulattha*— these, when old, are always beneficial for those suffering from urinary disorders as food.
Jāṅgala meat, bitter vegetables, barley-based food, physical exertion, honey, and other such items as sugar and the like that increase *kapha* do not lead to well-being in the case of *somaroga*.
31. Diet and non-diet for *somaroga*.
Barley, wheat, meat, milk from which the cream has been removed,
physical exercise, walking, sugarcane, drinking water, fruit, and a comfortable seat are beneficial for those suffering from somaroga.
Regarding obesity, physicians learned in the scriptures have prescribed what is wholesome and unwholesome:
aged *śāli* rice, mung beans, horse gram, wild millet, and *kodrava*. (32)
Purgatives and enemas should always be employed by those who are obese.

One who delights in physical exertion, mental anxiety, sexual intercourse, walking long distances, honey, and staying awake at night will certainly destroy excessive corpulence by consuming meals of barley and *śyāmāka* grain.
One who desires to abandon obesity should gradually increase the practice of sleeplessness, celibacy, physical exercise, and mental exertion;
furthermore, water mixed with honey consumed in the morning destroys obesity.
By drinking the warm scum of boiled rice, one becomes emaciated;
