bathing is a rejuvenative (rasāyana); so too are *śāli* rice, wheat, a pleasant disposition, preparations of milk and sugarcane, black gram, eating to full satisfaction, and unctuous substances.
One who desires to restore the natural state [of health] should avoid fatty foods.
Regarding the wholesome and unwholesome diet for the disease of swelling (śotha): aged *śāli* rice, mung beans, barley, peas, and *punarnavā*.
Red śigru, garlic, māṇa-root, and paṭola; meat-soup made with the flesh of cocks, peacocks, and other birds; and soups made from śṛṅgī, madgura, and tortoise meat.

The physician should recognize that neem leaves, turmeric, and bitter, digestive-stimulating substances are beneficial in cases of swelling; whereas heavy food, wine, sour items, cold water, and burning foods are harmful.

One suffering from swelling (śotha) should avoid sleeping during the day and sexual intercourse. (34) In the treatment of Vṛddhi, the diet and regimen should consist of non-obstructive food and drink, as well as treatments that are not excessively cold.
For the benefit of one suffering from goiter, one should follow this regimen and avoid its opposite.
Regarding the wholesome and unwholesome diet for diseases such as goiter: barley, mung beans, and *paṭola* gourds, along with pungent and dry foods, [are beneficial]. 35.
One should employ emesis and bloodletting in the case of goiter;
however, formulations that increase vāta and kapha are unwholesome.
(36) Wholesome and unwholesome regimens for the disease arbuda.
The drinking of old ghee, aged red rice, barley, mung beans, patola, red drumstick, and kaṭhillaka;
as well as śāliñca vegetables, the tips of vetra reeds, and substances that are dry and pungent.
All types of lamps, guggulu, and śilājatu are proclaimed as wholesome for goiter (galagaṇḍa), scrofula (gaṇḍamālā), apacī, nodules (granthi), and tumors (arbuda),
according to the specific doṣa and stage of the disease.

All products of milk and sugarcane, meat from marshy regions, flour-based foods that are sour or sweet, heavy, and obstructive to the channels (abhiṣyandi)— all these are unwholesome for an arbuda tumor; indeed,
they must be avoided by those suffering from arbuda.
37. Regarding the disease of elephantiasis (ślīpada), that which destroys *kapha*, promotes evacuation, and stimulates the digestive fire is wholesome;
that which causes obstruction (*abhiṣyanda*) is unwholesome; the wise should adopt the former and avoid the latter.

38. Regarding the disease of sinus ulcers (*vidradhi-vraṇa*), these are always beneficial: well-digested *śāli* rice, unctuous food, *jīvantī*, *punarnavā*, *paṭola*, and mung bean soup (*mudga-yūṣa*).
One should avoid sour substances, curd, leafy vegetables, meat from marshy or aquatic animals, milk, and heavy foods during a wound;
this is the regimen regarding wholesome and unwholesome items for swelling associated with a wound (vraṇa-śotha).
One should know that all those foods, drinks, and medicines which are beneficial for swelling are always conducive to healing in the case of an ulcer;
this applies to both exogenous ulcers and the suitability or unsuitability of diet.

In this case, the best of physicians should apply treatment as they would for a wound on the body. Regarding the section on fractures, the wholesome and unwholesome diet consists of meat, meat broth, milk, clarified butter, and soup made from peas.

Nutritious food and drink should be given by the wise to one who has suffered a fracture. One with a fracture should avoid salt, pungent substances, alkaline matter, sourness, sexual intercourse, exposure to the sun, physical exercise, and even dry food.

42. Regarding sinus ulcers (*nāḍī-vraṇa*), that which promotes the downward movement of *vāyu*, that which increases the strength of the digestive fire (*agni-bala*), and that which purifies the blood (*asra-śuddhi*) is wholesome; anything other than this is condemned here.
43. Regarding the wholesome and unwholesome diet for hemorrhoids (bhagaṇdara):
mustard seeds, śāli rice, mung beans, gruel (vilepī), the meat broth of wild animals (jāṅgala-rasa), patola, śigru, the tips of vetra, pattūra, and young radish.
Oil from sesame and mustard, the group of bitter substances, ghee, honey,
and other such items indeed cure fistula-in-ano;
furthermore, incompatible foods and drinks, irregular eating habits, and exposure to the sun [are causes].

A man whose ulcer has healed should avoid physical exercise, sexual intercourse, combat, riding on the back of animals, and heavy foods for one year. (44) [The wholesome and unwholesome diet in syphilis.]
One suffering from upadaṃśa (venereal disease) should consume red rice, barley, mung beans, ghee, drumstick fruit, patola, and bitter vegetables; however,
one should avoid daytime sleep, heavy foods, the suppression of natural urges, and jaggery.
One suffering from upadaṃśa (venereal disease) should avoid alcohol, intoxicants, and sour substances.

A person with pāpameha, one with vātāsra (hemorrhagic disease), a leper, or one with sinful upadaṃśa should not consort with a woman, nor should a woman afflicted by such a disease consort with a man.
45. Regarding wholesome and unwholesome diet in cases of *śūka-doṣa*:

for diseases caused by bristles, the wholesome items are clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*), *śāli* rice, barley (*yava*), *vacā*, mung bean soup (*mudga-yūṣa*), pomegranate (*dāḍima*), *paṭola*, and young radish (*bāla-mūlaka*).
Śigru, karkoṭaka, the tip of a cane, kaṭhillaka, pattūra, rock salt, oil, water from a well,
the suppression of the urge to urinate, sleeping during the day, and sexual intercourse.
Physical exertion, heavy food, and molasses are likewise not beneficial in cases of leprosy (kuṣṭha). For leprosy,
the wholesome regimen consists of aged śāli rice, mung beans, āḍhakī, and masūra lentils.
Barley, nimba leaves, paṭola, the fruit of bṛhatī,
the leaf of cakramarda, meṣaśṛṅga, hilamocikā, koṣātakī, the tip of a reed, ripe tāla, and punarnavā.
The urine of cows, donkeys, camels, horses, and buffaloes,
along with clarified butter, all bitter substances, and [avoidance of] sinful deeds, daytime sleep, and incompatible or irregular eating, are beneficial in the treatment of skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
Physical exertion, suppression of natural urges, exposure to the sun's rays, sexual intercourse, eating heavy, dry, or cold foods, as well as jaggery,
curd, milk, wine, meat, fish, black gram, and sesame seeds.
Sugarcane is sour, and radish causes constipation and produces a burning sensation;
other such items should always be avoided in cases of *kuṣṭha*. (47) [This concludes] the wholesome and unwholesome diet regarding minor diseases (*kṣudraroga*).
Those substances which facilitate the downward movement of wind (vāta), promote the passage of feces and urine,
purify the blood, alleviate the three doṣas,
and are beneficial for minor diseases— such are the ones [to be used].

All things contrary [to this] should be avoided with great effort. (48) Regarding boils (*visphoṭa*), whatever is wholesome or unwholesome, and whatever removes blood disorders (*raktadoṣa*) or destroys bile (*pitta*), [should be applied].

The physician should always apply everything here after careful discernment; in the disease of smallpox (masūrikā), one must properly manage the wholesome and unwholesome diet, as well as fevers, coughs, and other such conditions.
Afflicted by the disease of *masūrī*, one should always reside in a high, excellent, and dry house, clothed in heavy and warm garments; [one must avoid] cold,
wind, cold water, the heat of fire, and likewise the heat of the sun.
One should avoid sexual intercourse, sleeping during the day, traveling, and staying awake at night.

Fomentation with slightly warm water destroys fever localized in the hair follicles (*romāntī-jvara*). First, fasting, emesis, purgation, and bloodletting [are prescribed]; then, [medicines] as bright as the moon [should be administered].
Old *ṣaṣṭika* rice, chickpeas, mung beans, lentils, barley,
and all pecking birds such as pigeons, sparrows, gallinules, curlews, and so forth, as well as the *jīvañjīva*, parrots, and others; *kulaka*, *kāṭhilla*, and *māṣāḍhaka* [are also permitted].
Thus, wholesome diet prescribed according to the specific stage of the disease and the particular humor involved brings great joy to those suffering from Masūrikā;
however, oil, heavy food, anger, and exposure to the sun should be strictly avoided.
One suffering from *masūrikā* (smallpox) should avoid contaminated water, foul air, incompatible foods,
*niṣpāva* beans, *māluka* mushrooms, leafy vegetables, salt, uneven postures, pungent and sour tastes, and the suppression of natural urges.
In the treatment of visarpa (erysipelas),
the entire category of bitter substances, food and drink that do not cause burning acidity,
substances that purify the blood, and the application of sandalwood ointment are wholesome.

One should recognize that an action which does not cause agitation is most beneficial during the spreading stage (visarpa); the opposite should be understood as causing affliction and increasing the disease. (51) [This concludes] what is wholesome and unwholesome in cases of cold-pitta and similar conditions.
Old *śāli* rice is recommended; soups made from mung beans and horse gram (*kulattha*),
as well as *karkoṭaka*, *kāravella*, drumstick (*śigru*), *drākṣā*, and pomegranate,
along with mustard oil and hot water— all of these remove phlegm and bile.
Indeed, heavy food and drink are to be known as beneficial in diseases such as śītapitta; likewise, sweet-tasting milk alleviates disorders,
as does the flesh of aquatic and marsh-dwelling creatures, even if it is sour.

One suffering from cold-pitta (śītapitta) and similar disorders should avoid unctuous substances, wine, fresh fish, the pre-dawn and afternoon winds, drinking water [on an empty stomach], and sleeping during the day.
(52) This concludes the wholesome and unwholesome regimen for diseases such as urticaria (udarda) and skin eruptions (koṭha).
Śāli rice, mung beans, horse gram, kāravella, upodikā,
the tips of vetra, and boiled water— all these pungent, bitter, and astringent items constitute the group known as "Sakhā," which removes phlegm and bile.

For those suffering from cold-pitta (śītapitta), urticaria (udarda), and skin eruptions (koṭha), [these are contraindicated] according to one's judgment. Various disorders arising from milk and sugarcane, the meat of fish, aquatic animals, and marshy creatures, fresh wine, the suppression of the urge to vomit, the wind from the south, and sleeping during the day [are likewise harmful].

Bathing, incompatible food, exposure to the sun, as well as unctuous, sour, and sweet substances, sexual intercourse, and heavy foods and drinks are [prohibited] for those suffering from Śītapitta, Koṭha, Udarda, and poison. (53) This is the wholesome and unwholesome regimen for Amlapitta.
Old barley, wheat, mung beans, and red rice; water that has been heated and then cooled; sugar, honey, and parched grain flour;
karkoṭaka, kāravella, paṭola, and hilamocikā.
The tips of vetra, ripe kūṣmāṇḍa, the flower of rambhā, vāstuka, kapittha,
pomegranate, āmalakī, and all bitter substances should be constantly consumed by people in cases of the disease of amlapitta.
All types of new grain increase phlegm and bile;
they cause an urge to vomit, as do sesame seeds, black gram, horse gram, the consumption of oil,
undiluted curd, fermented rice water, and substances that are salty, sour, or pungent.
One suffering from *amlapitta* should avoid heavy food, curd, and wine.
(54) Regarding what is wholesome and unwholesome in *vātarakta*: barley, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, *nīvāra* millet, peas, and red *śāli* rice [are beneficial].
Wheat, chickpeas, mung beans, tuvarī, and makuṣṭhaka; likewise, the ghee and milk of goats, ewes, buffaloes, and cows; as well as upodikā, kākamācī, the tips of vetra reeds, and suniṣaṇṇaka.
Vāstūka, kāravella, old kūṣmāṇḍa, paṭola, and the group of bitter vegetables are wholesome in cases of vātaśoṇita (gout/rheumatism),
as are māṣa, kulattha, niṣpāva, kalāya, radish, and curd.

One should avoid liquor, meat, fish, fermented gruel (kāñjika), the use of alkaline substances, sleeping during the day, exposure to fire, physical exercise, sexual intercourse, as well as pungent, hot, heavy, obstructive, salty, and sour foods.
55. Regarding wholesome and unwholesome diet in diseases of wind (vāta):
rice and *ṣaṣṭika* grains stored for a year, oil and ghee, and the broth of domestic, marshy, and aquatic animals, as well as that of *māṣa* and *kulattha* beans.
Fresh sesame, wheat, eggplant, and garlic;
and the rohita, madgura, śṛṅgī, varmī, kavayī, and alliśa fish; as well as grapes, pomegranates, jambīras, and parūṣaka fruits.
Unctuous and warm foods, as well as unctuous and warm ointments—
all such things are beneficial for those afflicted by wind (vāta). Likewise, grass-grains, peas, chickpeas, and kidney-beans [are also recommended].
Potherbs, flat bean seeds, the root of the *bimbī* plant, cold water, incompatible foods, sexual indulgence, and excessive wandering—
all such things as these are not beneficial in cases of wind-related disorders (*anilāmaya*).

Bathing is specifically forbidden for those suffering from facial paralysis (ardita) and abdominal distension (ādhmāna). Regarding the wholesome and unwholesome diet in cases of thigh-stiffness (ūrustambha): one should eat old wheat, kodrava, uddāla, and śāli rice.
It is beneficial with meat from wild animals that is not prepared with ghee, and with salt-free vegetables;
the physician should serve aged śāli rice along with salt-free vegetables such as suniṣaṇṇaka, nimba, and others, which have been cooked in water, oil, or clarified butter.
One should cross a river of cool, auspicious water against the current,
and repeatedly bathe in a clear, cool lake with still waters; furthermore, one should avoid food that is heavy, cold, liquid, unctuous, incompatible, or unwholesome.
One afflicted by thigh-stiffness (ūrustambha) and chronic pain (gadā) should avoid sour and salty foods.

In cases of shivering-fever (vepathu-vāta), the wholesome diet is that which is prescribed for wind-diseases (vātavyādhi); thus, what has been declared as wholesome and what as unwholesome has been described.

In the case of trembling caused by wind (vepathu-vāta), one must know what is wholesome and what is unwholesome; in cases of immobility caused by wind (acala-vāta), epilepsy (apasmāra), fainting (mūrchā), and likewise in diseases of wind (vātāmaya), that which is wholesome is beneficial.
Whatever is wholesome and whatever is unwholesome is recognized here as such;
however, in the event of a lapse, one should understand that substance which bestows nourishment and strength is what is considered wholesome here. 59.
60. Regarding the section on the *khañjanikā* bird:

one who desires health should avoid unwholesome food; for the *khañjanikā* bird and the consumption of split pulses (*dvidala*) must be abandoned by one who indulges in their causes, since the disease does not recede.
Whatever drinks, foods, and medicines are wind-alleviating and nourishing should always be administered here by the physician after careful discernment.
(61) Thus ends the section on wholesome and unwholesome regimens for diseases of the mouth.
Food and drink that are easily digested, stimulate the digestive fire,

and alleviate the humors of wounds are considered beneficial for diseases of the mouth. Likewise, the use of a tooth-stick, bathing, sour substances, fish, meat from marshy animals, and flesh are recommended.

In all diseases of the mouth, one should avoid curd, milk, jaggery, black gram, dry food, hard meals, sleeping with the head downward, heavy foods, those that cause secretions (abhiṣyandi), and daytime sleep.
62. Regarding dental diseases, one suffering from such ailments should avoid unwholesome foods, sour fruits, cold water, dry food, brushing the teeth, as well as very hard edibles.
63. Regarding diseases of the throat: one should eat barley-based food at a single mealtime, in small quantities and with unctuousness.
64. Regarding diseases of the ear: wholesome and unwholesome diet.
Sudation, purgation, emesis, nasal medication, fumigation, and venesection;
wheat, *śāli* rice, mung beans, barley, fresh clarified butter, and the meat of the common quail, peacock, deer, partridge, and wild cock.
Patola, śigru, vārtāku, suniṣaṇṇa, and kaṭhillaka—
all these elixirs (rasāyana), along with celibacy and silence,
when employed according to the specific dosha, are beneficial for ear diseases.
One suffering from ear disease should avoid the use of a tooth-stick, bathing the head, physical exercise, foods that increase phlegm, heavy meals, scratching, and exposure to frost.
(65) Regarding what is wholesome and unwholesome in cases of nasal disease:
Oleation therapy, sudation, head massage, aged barley and *śāli* rice, soups of horse gram (*kulattha*) and mung bean (*mudga*), the meat broths of domestic and wild animals,
eggplant (*vārttāku*), *kulaka*, drumstick (*śigru*), *karkoṭa*, and young radish.
Garlic, curd, hot water, vāruṇī wine, the three pungents (kaṭutraya),
pungent, sour, and salty foods, as well as unctuous, hot, and light meals—
these should be consumed according to one's strength in cases of nasal diseases such as chronic rhinitis (pīnasa) and the like.
One suffering from nasal disease should diligently avoid bathing, anger, the urges of feces, urine, and wind, as well as grief, vomiting, and sleeping on the ground.
(66) Regarding wholesome and unwholesome practices in cases of head disease:
Rice, barley, meat broth, eggplant, and patola; grapes, pomegranate, dates, and milk;
drinking at night, bathing in a river, and the use of fragrant substances.

In all diseases of the head, whatever substances have been described as beneficial according to their respective requirements— provided they are not excessively sharp or difficult to digest— and whatever sharp therapeutic procedures exist, these are not to be employed here, as they would yield undesirable results.
67. Regarding eye diseases, the wholesome regimen consists of śāli rice, mung beans, barley, milk, paṭola, udumbara,
grapes, pomegranate, dates, āmalaka, and foods that do not cause internal burning.
One should know that those which are nourishing, easily digestible, and beneficial for eye diseases are wholesome; conversely, one should diligently avoid those that are the opposite.
(68) When the flag has fallen, [this] is the wholesome regimen.
Rice, sixty-day rice, wheat, lentils, chickpeas, and so forth; fresh butter from freshly drawn milk, clarified butter, wine, rum, the sparrow,
the quail, the partridge, and the cock.

The tender meats of the rabbit, deer, and goat, as well as the fruits of the grape, date, pomegranate, rose-apple, and mango— these wholesome items are for the pacification of the failure of the banner.
In the context of aphrodisiacs (vājīkaraṇa),
everything that is aphrodisiac (vṛṣya) is wholesome (pathya).
Whatever is sweet, unctuous, life-sustaining, nourishing, heavy, and gladdening to the mind— all that is said to be aphrodisiac, even if it is unwholesome.

It is well known among all people that one who is lustful, always desirous of sexual pleasure, and longing for women should never eat vegetables that are extremely hot, pungent, bitter, astringent, sour, alkaline, or excessively salty.
(70) Regarding the wholesome and unwholesome diet in cases of seminal diabetes (*śukrameha*).
Excessive moisture-inducing substances, extremely sharp foods, exposure to the heat of fire and the sun, addiction to women, suppression of natural urges,
staying awake at night, anger, grief, sleeping during the day, fasting, and excessive overthinking.

One should avoid excessive laziness and the company of the wicked during the increase of semen; whatever food and drink in this world is nourishing, sustaining, and increases semen should be known as wholesome, while the opposite does not lead to well-being.

71. Regarding menorrhagia, one should understand that whatever food is wholesome, wound-healing, and nourishing is for the sake of relief here; conversely, one should know its opposite to be particularly forbidden and to be avoided.
In cases of gynecological disorders (yoniroga),
one should consume food and drink that is nourishing, strengthening, digestive-stimulating, and carminative; all other types should be avoided.
73. Wholesome and unwholesome foods for a pregnant woman:
*śāli* rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, mung beans, wheat, parched grain flour, fresh butter, clarified butter, milk, *rasālā*, honey, and sugar.
The breadfruit, plantain, and emblic myrobalan; grapes that are sour and sweet and cooling; musk, sandalwood, garlands, camphor, and ointments;
moonlight, bathing, massage, a soft bed, and cool breezes.
Nourishing food, the embrace of a beloved, delightful recreation,
and agreeable food and drink are always beneficial for pregnant women; whereas sudation, emesis, alkaline substances, poor food, and irregular eating are not.
This state of indifference has been prescribed for pregnant women by the great sages.
Regarding diseases of the breasts, one should employ wholesome and unwholesome regimens, as well as drinks, food, and medicines that pacify those specific doshas.
Upon seeing that a woman's breasts have not milked, one should apply nourishing (bṛṃhaṇīya) measures.
Regarding the regimen for puerperal diseases (sūtikā-roga),
one should avoid physical exercise, sexual intercourse, anger, and exposure to cold.
After giving birth, she should properly observe her diet and lifestyle (76). Regarding diseases of childhood,
that which is wholesome and unwholesome for humans has been stated in the context of fever and other ailments.
One who knows [the nature] of those children should, according to propriety,

first determine what is wholesome and unwholesome for them; and when the fetal stage of childhood has arisen, one should apply that which was previously prescribed for weak digestion according to propriety.

One should apply, according to suitability, the wholesome and unwholesome diet prescribed for exogenous insanity and wind disorders to children afflicted by planetary possession (graha). [77] Regarding the wholesome and unwholesome diet in cases of poisoning:
Śāli rice, ṣaṣṭika rice, koradūṣa, and priyaṅgu;
mung beans, hareṇu beans, oil, and even fresh ghee; vārttāka, kulaka, dhātrī, jīvantī, and taṇḍulīyaka.

For those afflicted by poison, rock salt (saindhava) is beneficial when taken with pungent foods for the purpose of nourishment; however, even one who has been freed from poison should avoid incompatible foods, eating before the previous meal is digested, anger, hunger, fear, physical exertion, sexual intercourse, and especially sleeping during the day.
Now follows the discernment of wholesome and unwholesome regimens for the diseases mentioned in the first supplement (*pariśiṣṭa*): regarding the diseases of the spleen and liver,
whatever is considered beneficial for chronic fever (*jīrṇajvara*) is likewise beneficial here, while whatever is deemed harmful in that context is also harmful here.
In cases of liver and spleen disease as well, one should likewise understand what is beneficial and what is harmful;
however, there is a specific distinction regarding the liver: wine, fire, sunlight, exhaustion, heavy food, and irregular eating are particularly detrimental.
One suffering from liver disease (yakṛdroga) should avoid pungent food, sleeping during the day, staying awake at night,
the three types of musical performance (tauryatrika), flatulence, grief, anxiety, fear,
the impulse of anger, and the suppression of natural urges.

Regarding the disease of *urastoya* (pleural effusion), one who has suffered from this ailment should avoid sexual intercourse, travel, physical exercise, cold water, sleeping during the day, grief, and anger; these are the wholesome and unwholesome dietary and lifestyle regulations.
In cases of agitation caused by poison,
wholesome and unwholesome food and drink that is pleasing to the heart, unctuous, well-cooked, and nourishing to the body are prescribed;
in other cases of non-substantial diseases, they are declared for the sake of auspiciousness and well-being.
Śīta! Śava! Regarding what is wholesome and unwholesome in the stage of renunciation (saṃnyāsa):
barley, red rice, eggplant, and patola;
soup made from the meat of wild animals, as well as fish such as the Rohita and others.
Cow’s milk that remains warm after being boiled, buttermilk, bathing in the pure waters of a river—
these are beneficial in cases of fainting and the disease known as *saṃnyāsa*. Furthermore, sharp substances, sharp medical procedures, and the suppression of natural urges [are indicated].

The affliction increases through these factors, such as the overcoming by anger, grief, and so forth; in cases of epilepsy caused by women, that which nourishes the bodily constituents— whether drink, food, or medicine— is the wholesome regimen.
One should also employ various agents that cleanse the digestive tract (koṣṭha) in this condition; furthermore,
in cases of unmāda,
cow’s milk fresh from the udder and aged śāli rice are recommended as wholesome diet.
Barley, mung beans, and sesame seeds, as well as everything that is laxative, jesting with dear friends, and sitting together with beloved women—
these are beneficial here; the opposite leads to unhappiness.

Regarding the section on the pain of the sinews (snāyuśūla), whatever is wholesome and whatever is unwholesome has been proclaimed for vāta diseases; likewise, it has been determined by the wise that these same rules apply to the pains of the sinews.
In the disease of *tāṇḍava*, wholesome diet and drink,
nourishing food, bathing in river water, a bed free from discomfort, and whatever action is devoid of strain lead to well-being here.

All activities such as plowing and so forth were declared by the ancients to lead to inauspiciousness; now, for one afflicted by the disease of the *kloma*, here are the wholesome and unwholesome foods and drinks to be adopted or avoided.
One should diligently avoid all things that are harsh; regarding the kidneys,
the physician should cause the patient to consume wholesome and strengthening foods that are easily digestible.
In cases of *aupasargika-meha* (secondary urinary disorders), one should employ wholesome and unwholesome regimens,
medicines, drinks, and foods that promote the downward movement of the doshas, heal ulcers, and increase urine; however, one must avoid severe therapeutic procedures.
In this condition of insanity caused by passion, wholesome and unwholesome regimens have been proclaimed; furthermore, here is the medicine that cures seminal disorders (śukra-meha),
which facilitates the downward movement of Vāta, is easily digestible, and stimulates the digestive fire.
In this regard, the wise physician should administer appropriate food and avoid the opposite; for diseases of the head and eyes,
everything that is wholesome, nourishing, light, and easily digestible— whether drink or food— is beneficial.

In cases of brain edema, [a diet] consisting of milk, meat broth, and the like is wholesome; the opposite is not beneficial. Regarding the shaking of the brain, there is no specific distinction between what is wholesome and unwholesome; however, such nourishment increases the strength of the tendons.
Whatever food, drink, and so forth is easily digested, delicious, nutritious,
and beneficial for those suffering from headaches or shivering— all that is considered wholesome; one should know the opposite to be never a source of well-being.
Regarding what is wholesome and unwholesome during the depletion of the brain:
when there is a decrease or wasting of the brain, nourishing the body with light drinks and food will lead to well-being; the opposite will not bring comfort.
In the case of *aṃśughāta* poisoning, food, drink, and other substances that are unctuous (*snigdha*), strength-promoting, nourishing, laxative (*sara*), and wholesome are beneficial;
the opposite of these is not conducive to well-being.

O physicians! In cases of gynecological disorders (yoni-roga), one should consume wholesome and unwholesome foods, nourishing and strengthening agents, those that kindle the digestive fire and promote the downward movement of the humors; one should avoid everything else.
In this section on the female reproductive tract and the digestive process (*kaṇḍū*),

whatever food or drink is wholesome or unwholesome, which kindles the digestive fire, is easily digestible, and promotes the downward movement of *vāta* should be employed here; the opposite would not lead to well-being.
Regarding the section on the provocation of the *yoni*,
here the wholesome regimen consists of ghee, milk, wheat, chickpeas, and so forth; soup prepared from goat meat and the like is beneficial, whereas that of intense potency is not.
Regarding wholesome and unwholesome regimens for uterine disorders (*jarāyu-roga*):
a woman suffering from uterine disorders should not have sexual intercourse with a man,
nor should she eat substances of intense potency, nor should she engage in excessive physical exertion.
Regarding what is wholesome and unwholesome for the foundation of the *aṇḍa*:
here, the oblation is wholesome, consisting of milk, *śāli* rice, ancient barley, sesame, and the broth of goat meat; pungent substances do not lead to well-being.
Ojomeha is treated with wholesome and unwholesome diets, light food, strengthening agents, aged grains such as mung beans and barley,
as well as eggplant, patola, and kākodumbara.
Kāravella and similar vegetables are recommended; one should avoid sweet foods, heavy meat, fish, travel, exposure to the sun or fire,
and bathing, drinking, or immersion in highly contaminated or excessively cold water.
Regarding the diet for *lasikā* (serous fluid) and *meha* (urinary disorders): red *śāli* rice, green gram (*mudga*), barley, *vāstūka*, *pālakyā*,
the tips of *vetra* canes, *karkoṭī*, and likewise *kadalī* (banana).

Dwelling in the Himalayan regions or maintaining a healthy state of mind is beneficial; one should avoid heavy, obstructive food, fish, meat, as well as violent activities, travel, and physical exertion.

The wise man should diligently avoid [unwholesome things] for the sake of increasing longevity and health; likewise, he should observe the wholesome and unwholesome dietary rules regarding mercury preparations, as well as those that are wholesome for vātarakta and kuṣṭha.

"The skilled physician should prescribe [treatment] for a disease arising from the power of Śiva"— with these words, the second appendix, consisting of the discrimination between wholesome and unwholesome [regimens], is completed;
and this treatise is also finished.
